Sports.title: Premier League heroes and villains: Alexander Isak shirks responsibility but debutant looks like £80m player
Sports.content:
Premier League heroes and villains: Alexander Isak shirks responsibility but debutant looks like £80m player

Last-minute drama, comeback wins, shock defeats, an unwanted record and a red card headloss.

The Premier League is truly back.

9 Arsenal kicked off their Premier League title defence with a 3-0 win over Coventry Credit: Getty



It has been a dramatic opening weekend of top-flight football, which has seen 25 goals scored across nine matches so far.

What are the Premier League results so far this weekend?

Champions Arsenal welcomed Championship winners Coventry for the first game of the new season on Friday night, with the Gunners easing to a 3-0 victory.

While there was no surprise scoreline in north London, there certainly was in Yorkshire when newly-promoted Hull hosted Manchester United in Saturday's lunchtime kick-off.

The Red Devils were mauled by the Tigers - losing 2-0 at the MKM Stadium - their first defeat against Hull since 1974.



And it was a winning start to the campaign for Ipswich Town in their first Premier League outing since being relegated in the 2024/25 term.

They snatched a last-gasp win over Sunderland at Portman Road, while Everton beat Crystal Palace and Leeds overcome Nottingham Forest on the road.



Brentford then bullied Tottenham at the Gtech Community Stadium - winning 3-0 in what is their first home victory over Spurs in 78 years.

Moving onto Sunday, and Manchester City looked to be heading for their first opening day defeat since 2021 - and a second successive loss under Enzo Maresca following their Community Shield humbling.



Bournemouth led 1-0 heading into the 84th minute at the Etihad, only for Marc Guehi to equalise, before Josko Gvardiol spared the Citizens' blushes with a stoppage time strike that was awarded by VAR.

Aston Villa's dreadful summer then went from bad to worse after they were thrashed 4-0 by Brighton on the south coast - their joint-heaviest opening Premier League defeat in history.

9 Brighton sit top of the table after easily dispatching Villa at the Amex Stadium Credit: Getty

With all four goals shipped in by the 31st minute, it is the earliest any side has led 4-0 in an opening game since 2006, with new Villans signing Joao Gomes picking up a straight red card for a kick out on Georginio Rutter before the break to become the first player to be sent off on their Premier League debut since QPR's Samba Diakite in February 2012.



And completing Sunday's fixtures was a four-goal thriller between Newcastle and Liverpool, which saw Dominik Szoboszlai rescue a point for the Reds with a dramatic penalty in the ninth minute of stoppage time.

Fulham vs Chelsea rounds off the opening weekend at Craven Cottage on Monday night - live on talkSPORT - in a game which pits both of Real Madrid's managers from last season against each other.

With plenty to discuss from the weekend's football, talkSPORT's Sam Matterface, Alex Crook and Troy Deeney dissect the drama in our brand new Premier League All Access show.

Picking out five heroes and three villains from the fixtures so far, here is what they had to say...



Who are talkSPORT's Premier League Heroes?

Mamadou Sangare

The Brentford summer signing had a debut to remember - chipping in with a first half assist against a Spurs midfield that included £100million recruit Sandro Tonali and £85m arrival Mateus Fernandes (for the second half).

9 Sangare helped Brentford beat Tottenham at home for the first time since 1948 Credit: Getty

Lauding the 24-year-old Mali international, Matterface said: "I think Mamadou Sangare, the Brentford midfielder, was the standout Premier League debutant of the weekend.

"He looks like a proper midfield player, £80m-plus Brentford have signed [this window], he's probably the best one for £39m."



Agreeing with Matterface, Crook then added: "I thought he had a terrific debut, he left Tonali in the shade.

"It looks like another really smart piece of recruitment from Matthew Benham [club owner] and Brentford."

Konstantinos Tzolakis

The Hull goalkeeper enjoyed another debut to remember, keeping a clean sheet against United - expertly denying Bryan Mbeumo in the second half with the score at 2-0.

Lauding the Greek shot-stopper, Matterface remarked: "I'm going to go for Tzolakis, I thought he was a hero as well, the goalkeeper for Hull.



9 Tzolakis will be looking to keep more clean sheets in his quest to help Hull avoid relegation this season Credit: Getty

"He didn't have to make too many saves, but he commanded his penalty in such an area, he gave the rest of his defence confidence."

Jack Hinshelwood

The Brighton midfielder helped himself to a first half double, with the 21-year-old already halving his total tally from last season to help his side go top on goal difference.

Waxing lyrical over the Seagulls academy graduate, Deeney stated: "I'll go Hinshelwood, I thought he was really good, he's a really good player.



"And he also carries that burden of being a local lad as well and all of that, so yeah I'll go Hinshelwood."

9 Hinshelwood helped himself to a quickfire brace against a hapless Villa Credit: Getty

Jack Clarke/Gary O'Neil

The Ipswich winger curled home a late beauty against Sunderland, the club who sold him to the Tractor Boys in 2024.

Despite being part of Ipswich's last Premier League side, Clarke's strike against the Black Cats was his first in England's top-flight.



Matterface said of the 25-year-old: "Jack Clarke, the Ipswich player who was a former Sunderland winger, who scored off the bench - an injury time winner.

"It must have been great day for him."

Crook added: "It was a great day for [boss] Gary O'Neil as well, a lot of doubters about him, but obviously getting off to a winning start."

9 Clarke's winner saw Ipswich win their first opening Premier League day game since 1993 Credit: Getty

Sergej Jakirovic

The Hull boss guided the Tigers to an unlikely promotion last campaign, and despite his side being tipped to go straight back down, they outfought and outclassed a United team that will be competing in the Champions League.



Crook said: "I'm going to put up - it's a bit of a Hull love-in - but Sergej Jakirovic, I thought tactically spot-on.

"I think he is a really astute manager, he's agreed a new three-year contract, that should be announced this week.

"He is going to be Hull's trump card, he's going to keep them up.

"He's a great guy, he came into the chairman's lounge afterwards, I had both of my two lads with me, he shook both of their hands, a gentleman."

9 Jakirovic guided Hull to their first opening day top-flight victory in ten years Credit: Getty



Who are talkSPORT's Premier League Villains?

Alexander Isak

Booed with every touch and jeered with every misplaced pass and shot by the Newcastle faithful at St James' Park, it wasn't a happy return for the Liverpool striker.

Winning just five of his nine duels and missing two big chances, Isak passed up the opportunity to take the late penalty.

Nominating Isak, Matterface said: "Alexander Isak, the main villain at St James' Park, we were there, they [fans] were on his case from the very beginning.

"He was back for the first time since forcing his way out [last summer], big things expected this season, and you're [Crook] still a bit cross that he didn't take the penalty."



To which Crook remarked: "Yeah, I just think from a story point of view, whether he scored or missed, it would have been great for us.

"But Szoboszlai is probably the designated penalty taker, and he stuck it away with aplomb."

9 Isak didn't have his shooting boots on as he returned to his former stomping ground Credit: AFP

Luke Shaw

The United left-back had a torrid time in Yorkshire, while he was caught sleeping for Hull's second, which saw Nobel Mendy head home Regan Slater's free-kick.



United fan Crook said: "I'll chuck in Luke Shaw as a villain, honestly, he was so poor in that game."

To which Matterface then quipped: "You've been so cross [since United defeat], I'm going to have to take him out to a big market, that's going to cheer you up!"

9 Shaw was just one of a number of United players that failed to impress at the MKM Stadium Credit: Getty

Stuart Attwell

The Premier League referee officiated Newcastle and Liverpool's thrilling draw, but controversially awarded the visitors a spot-kick for Lewis Hall's foul on Victor Munoz.



Commenting on the decision, Matterface said: "I know that it's a penalty, OK, they've given the penalty, whatever.

"But I actually think it's a little bit too soft to be given as a penalty on the pitch.

"And if it isn't given, there's no way that VAR gives it, I understand also that VAR isn't going to overturn it, because it's not a clear error."

Having his say, Crook stated: "No, but it wasn't just that, I think there were four bookings in the first half, there wasn't really a tackle in the game.



"So I think he set the tone, and actually probably, he should have shown a second yellow card to Yoane Wissa for a pretty cynical challenge in the centre circle, so it was a poor day for one of the most experienced officials."

Sports.title: Aston Villa have second bid to sign England international as potential Ezri Konsa replacement rejected
Sports.content:
Aston Villa have second bid to sign England international as potential Ezri Konsa replacement rejected

Aston Villa have had an improved offer for Taylor Harwood-Bellis rejected by Southampton, talkSPORT understands.

Villa are looking to sign a new centre-back before the end of the summer transfer window on September 1 with Ezri Konsa completing a £50million move to Arsenal earlier in the week.

2 Villa's first offer is some £10million below Southampton's valuation of the player Credit: Getty

Tosin Adarabioyo and Fikayo Tomori are among a list of centre-back targets for Villa.

Another option is Harwood-Bellis, although Villa's offers have been rebuffed with Saints valuing him at £30million.

The first offer is understood to be a package worth £20m, and the second is an improved one but still not to the satisfaction of the Championship club.

talkSPORT understands that Villa are confident they will get a deal done, however.

Harwood-Bellis is a graduate of the Manchester City academy before making a permanent move to Southampton in 2024.

He initially joined on loan for the 2023/24 season, with his move then made permanent for a £20m fee after promotion to the top flight.

Harwood-Bellis, who is engaged to and is set to have a child with Roy Keane's daughter Leah, has made 134 appearances in defence for the Saints and been captain on numerous occasions.

The 24-year-old is also an England international as he earned his sole cap and scored against the Republic of Ireland in November 2024.

Who have Villa sold this summer?

Villa have experienced a summer of big change, despite winning the Europa League at the end of last season.

Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Lucas Digne are among the key departures for Unai Emery's side.

2 Villa need a new defender with Konsa sealing a move to Arsenal Credit: Getty

Ollie Watkins is pushing for a move to Al Hilal having missed Villa's 4-0 defeat at Brighton on Sunday, with Unai Emery hinting the striker refused to play.

Meanwhile, Emi Martinez could still leave amid a failed transfer to Juventus.

Should the pair exit Villa Park along with Konsa, then only five of the starting XI that beat SC Freiburg in the Europa League will be left.

They would be Matty Cash, Pau Torres, Victor Lindelof, John McGinn and Emi Buendia.

However, Villa have been active in terms of incomings, with Swiss star Johan Manzambi joining in a £51.2m move from Freiburg.

Joao Gomes, who endured a Villa debut from hell on Sunday, then joined from West Midlands rivals Wolves for £35m.

On Wednesday, Villa completed the signings of Matteo Ruggeri and Zion Zuzuki.

The former has arrived from Atletico Madrid, whilst the latter signed from Parma.

Sports.title: Footballer to have cheekbone reconstruction surgery after sickening collision with opponent
Sports.content:
Footballer to have cheekbone reconstruction surgery after sickening collision with opponent

A non-league footballer will undergo cheek reconstruction surgery after a horror collision with an opponent.

Joe Tennent, who plays for Dartford FC in the Isthmian Premier League, was slammed into by a Welling United striker.



2 Tennent was crunched to the ground by the brutal challenge that caused his injury

Tennent was looking to play the ball out from defence before Nahum Melvin-Lambert chased him down and smashed into him.

Melvin-Lambert charged into the Dartford star and seemed to connect with his right arm on Tennent's head.

The sickening moment left Tennent in a heap on the ground and he eventually had to be substituted after the incident.



Meanwhile, Melvin-Lambert was only booked for the foul.

Dartford went on to lose the game 4-0 to Welling on Saturday.

Update on Tennent issued

Dartford then gave an update on Tennent on Sunday afternoon.

The non-league side revealed that he was going to have to undergo surgery for his serious facial injuries.

The club wrote: "Joe sustained displaced facial fractures and will undergo cheekbone reconstruction surgery on Wednesday.



"We wish Joe and his family our very best and a speedy recovery.

"The club will explore official channels following the incident."

2 Tennent was left completely flattened by the horrendous collision

Immediate concern

Dartford boss Ben Greenhalgh was concerned about Tennent post-match and believed his injury played a big part in his side's loss.



Greenhalgh said: “I think a really big, key part of today was losing Joe Tennent.... it was a derby game so we knew there were going to be moments.

"I can’t blame the ref for the game. That has changed it but our second-half performance was really poor.

“We lost Joe and I’m not saying we capitulated, but we went a bit off-script.

“I am disappointed to lose Joe in that manner. I don’t know how it works from here onwards.



“It didn’t seem like a concussion from what we’re told, but it’s a possible broken jaw that doesn’t sound good at all.”

Sports.title: Julian Alvarez ordered down tunnel by Atletico Madrid as fans wildly boo Arsenal-linked star
Sports.content:
Julian Alvarez was left humiliated as he faced backlash from the Atletico Madrid fans amid his persistent transfer rumours.

Alvarez openly admitted in June that he wanted to leave Atletico and join La Liga rivals Barcelona to 'fulfill his dream'.

2 Alvarez faced some huge backlash at Atletico's game on Sunday Credit: Getty

Barca had an £86million bid rejected before those comments, while Arsenal are also interested in signing the Argentinian.

talkSPORT understands that the Gunners are still actively exploring a move for Alvarez before the transfer window closes.

And they may have received a boost in their bid to sign him after he was hounded by Atletico's supporters on Sunday.

Alvarez angered his own club's fan base by admitting his wish to leave and join Barca, with an exit now seemingly looking inevitable.

What happened to Alvarez?

Diego Simeone named Alvarez as a substitute for Atletico's first home game of the new La Liga season against Villarreal.

As his name appeared on the big screens at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano, wild boos and loud whistles rang out.

Footage showed him sitting and looking solemn on the bench as he faced some huge backlash from the stands.

It got worse for Alvarez too, as Simeone then decided to bring him on, with him being met with even more boos and whistles.

Atletico went on to draw 2-2 with Villarreal on the day, but post-match, things managed to hit a new low for Alvarez.

As his teammates stayed as a group to clap their fans after the full-time whistle, he walked straight down the tunnel alone, leading to further backlash and a scarf being thrown down at him.

2 Simeone says the decision for Alvarez to go down the tunnel was made above him Credit: Getty

Why did Alvarez walk away from the fans?

Alvarez faced a massive negative reaction as supporters assumed that he had chosen to walk down the tunnel alone.

But manager Simeone explained that he was actually told to leave his teammates and not stand in front of the fans.

"The club staff told me that the club decided Julian should not go over with his teammates to greet the fans, and that it was not Julián’s decision," Simeone said post-match.

"The club made the decision to keep him away and have him head to the dressing room."

On the fans' reaction to Alvarez throughout the afternoon, he added: "No, I’m not in a position to give advice to the fans. I think I need to focus on my work, which is to give my best on the sporting side for the good of Atlético de Madrid."

Meanwhile, Alvarez's teammate and Simeone's son, Giuliano Simeone, stood by his fellow Argentina international.

He said: "Julian is a top player, and we stand by him. We have to support him, and as long as he’s part of our team, we’ll fight alongside him until the very end.”

Sports.title: Brighton fan dies after being taken unwell at Aston Villa match
Sports.content:
Brighton fan dies after being taken unwell at Aston Villa match

Brighton have announced that a fan has sadly died after being taken unwell at their match against Aston Villa on Sunday.

The 72-year-old supporter was leaving the Amex Stadium to board a bus following the Premier League game when he fell ill.

2 Brighton announced the very sad news on Sunday evening after the match Credit: Getty

In a statement, Brighton wrote: "Following today’s game against Aston Villa, sadly a 72-year-old male Brighton and Hove Albion supporter passed away after the match.

"The gentleman took unwell as he was leaving the stadium to board a supporters’ club bus in the coach park.

"Despite the best efforts of emergency services and club staff, the medical team were unable to save him.

"South East Coast Ambulance Service paramedics, St John’s Ambulance, Sussex Police, MB Medical Solutions, the club’s crowd doctor and our stewards worked together to ensure the individual was given the best possible care, including prolonged CPR on the scene."

Brighton's chief executive and deputy chairman Paul Barber said: "What should have been an ordinary and happy journey home ended in heartbreaking circumstances, and we are all shocked and saddened by the loss of one of our supporters.

"We extend our sincere condolences to the gentleman’s family and friends."

Many fans sent their condolences to the supporter too, after the club announced the sad news on social media.

One supporter posted: "Horrible news. Best wishes to his family."

Another replied: "So sorry to learn this. My condolences. RIP."

"That 4-0 is for him RIP," a third Brighton fan said.

2 The Brighton fan sadly passed after the Seagulls beat Villa 4-0 Credit: Getty

Devastating news

Brighton will have been devastated to learn the news post-match after what was such an impressive win.

The Seagulls beat Aston Villa 4-0 at the Amex Stadium on Sunday afternoon in completely dominant fashion.

All four goals came in the first 31 minutes, with Jack Hinshelwood scoring two, Maxim De Cuyper netting one and Victor Lindelof deflecting home an unfortunate own goal.

Fabian Hurzeler's side are now sitting top of the Premier League table after the thrashing, sitting above Arsenal.

But the joy has turned to sadness following the match, with the terrible news of their fan's passing.

talkSPORT sends our condolences to the gentleman and his family and friends.

Sports.title: Premier League explain why Liverpool penalty decision stood as Matthias Jaissle bemoans ‘soft’ call
Sports.content:
The Premier League have explained why Liverpool were awarded their last-gasp penalty to claim a point against Newcastle.

Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the spot in the ninth minute of stoppage-time as VAR stood by the referee's on-field decision.



2 Hall brought Munoz down in the box in stoppage time to give Liverpool a penalty Credit: Getty

With the match entering the final seconds, Liverpool launched a desperate ball towards the box, looking for a chance.

It was cleared at first, but fell to new signing Victor Munoz, who drove into the box and attempted to go past Newcastle's Lewis Hall.

As he did so, Hall stepped to his left, bringing his knee and thigh across the Spanish winger and bringing him down.



Referee Stuart Atwell quickly pointed to the spot, awarding a penalty for Andoni Iraola's side in the dying moments.

VAR took a look at the incident and agreed that it was a spot-kick, much to the distaste of fans inside St. James' Park.



Szoboszlai would go on to emphatically find the top corner from the penalty, saving Liverpool as they took home a point.

Premier League explain Liverpool penalty

The awarding of the penalty was met with plenty of boos and groans from Newcastle supporters, with manager Matthias Jaissle going on to label it 'soft' when speaking post-match.



It certainly split opinion, but the Premier League have revealed their reasoning behind their decision on social media.

Posting on their Match Centre account, they explained: "The referee’s call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR.

"REF: 'He doesn’t play the ball. He makes clear contact.' VAR: 'It’s knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty'."

2 The referee pointed to the spot after Hall made contact with Munoz Credit: Getty



Did the referee make the right decision?

Despite the explanation, former Newcastle and Crystal Palace manager Alan Pardew disagreed with the penalty decision.

He said on talkSPORT's The Final Word: "They launch it into the box, it comes to him...it's light in my opinion.

"I think the referee should have let it go and not given it."

And Newcastle boss Jaissle was of a similar mind, telling Sky Sports post-match: "It's a really soft one. If you give that, then there will be so many penalties in the future.

"I am not a fan of that, but I cannot say any more."

Meanwhile, in the Liverpool camp, Ryan Gravenberch has said that he believes it was a 'clear foul' on Munoz by Hall.



That was echoed by Micah Richards and Daniel Sturridge on Sky Sports too, with the pair believing that it was 'harsh' but that the contact was there, making it a 'thoroughly deserved penalty'.

Sports.title: Journey to Wembley: After a fortnight of fretting over floodlights on the fritz, Nelson's FA Cup journey ends at Witton Albion - where home fans toasted victory with pina coladas!
Sports.content:
It’s the annual pina colada festival in the Witton area of Cheshire – the song about the drink, which topped the US charts in the late 1970s, was written by someone local to the place and they’ve spotted the commercial opportunity – so there are people walking around dressed as pineapples and wearing big yellow glasses on Saturday lunchtime. But life has not exactly been a cocktail party for Nelson, an East Lancashire ninth tier club, just lately.

They breeze through one of the challenges which faces them after arriving to face opponents one step above them in the pyramid. Their new yellow away kits for the season haven’t arrived and last season’s issue, which they’re still using, don’t have a No 18 jersey – needed today because you’re allowed seven subs in the FA Cup. Someone finds a white marker pen and inks the number on to a plain yellow away shirt. Wearing numbers on your back is mandatory in the tournament.

This is a minor obstacle compared with the floodlight problems which has been testing Nelson minds since we left them celebrating extra preliminary round victory at their ‘Little Wembley’ ground two weeks ago. That was the first part of our journey to Wembley told in 13 instalments, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

They’d signed off on a £30,000 contract, helped by FA grants, to replace the system of lights which had started to fail during evening games, only to find that the new ones still didn’t work.

The approved contractors didn’t seem to have mentioned that the cables and wiring supplying the lights also needed ripping out, and yet were sending the club legal letters demanding payment, as Nelson’s directors sought advice from the FA about the black hole they risked disappearing into.

Inside the home dressing room at the Bedspace Trust Community Stadium

Nelson captain Bill Priestley receives some treatment ahead of kick-off

A home steward - proudly sporting Witton Albion's colours - tucks into a pie at half-time

When we caught up with Nelson at their league away game at Charnock Richard in Lancashire, last Tuesday night, the floodlights were the prime topic of conversation as the players arrived in the car park. There had even been talk of a temporary ground move, which did not exactly delight the North West Counties League. Nelson’s proactive club sponsor Monks Contractors had offered supplying temporary structures.

In the end, they just went to work again. Volunteers helped dig two 100m trenches to lay the new cabling to the new lights and on Wednesday, they flicked the switch once more. ‘Let there be light?’ The look on Nelson director Rob Doherty’s face as the visiting contingent are welcomed into Witton’s snug little boardroom suggests so. ‘As of three days ago, they were working,’ he relates. The FA provided emergency funding.

Both these teams badly want to win this FA Cup Preliminary Round game. In his extremely modestly proportioned office Witton manager Benny Harrison, whose day job is a teacher at a special educational school, reflects at 2pm on the profound effects Marine experienced after playing Tottenham in the Third Round in 2021. The windfall helped win them two promotions in three years.

But as the rival teams’ executives gather in that boardroom, there’s a sense of mutual empathy about the existential threats which can be just around the corner for any non-league club.

‘There’s what goes on out on the pitch, and the fans and all that the lovely stuff,’ says Witton director Paul Sanderson, when Nelson relate their floodlight troubles. ‘And then there’s survivability stuff that fans don't know about. Trying to navigate things that can threaten your existence if you’re not prepared for anything.’

Nelson were on a precipice before new co-owners Stewart Fort and Chris Price arrived three years ago, invested and built up the team of volunteers who are their lifeblood. But Witton’s excellent little club museum, charting a 139-year history and signposted ‘Probably the best non-League football museum in the world’, shows that they’ve also ridden football’s rollercoaster.

The museum chronicles the club’s journey to the 1992 FA Trophy final at Wembley, where they lost to Colchester. That period, which included a brief stay in the Vauxhall Conference, saw them splashing the surplus earned after selling their old ground to Sainsburys and building a new one, on players. The rewards were painful temporary. Witton struggled when the money ran out and the new stadium required major repair sooner than anticipated.

The sun’s out, though, and the FA Cup is blowing everyone’s troubles away. ‘Welcome to the best football competition in the world by a long chalk,’ states the stadium announcer. The appropriately named Witton groundsman James Spruce is reversing his mower out onto the excellent playing surface, his partner Katy Hulse is nursing a pina colada and her friend Barbara Bazley is watching the warm-up.

Groundsman James Spruce applies the finishing touches to the playing surface

Katy Hulse (left) enjoys a pina colada with her friend Barbara Bazley

Albion statistician Phil Chadwick has helped to curate one of the best club museum's in non-League

Nelson's 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader

‘When you make s*** decisions, it goes pear-shaped, so if someone makes a s*** decision, back them up and help sort it out,’ shouts assistant coach Liam Lishman, as he puts the squad through their paces. Thursday’s training session focussed on not allowing Freddie Garbutt, Witton’s towering 22-year-old striker, the chance to control and shoot.

At Charnock Richard, Nelson won 2-0, led by their own dangerous target man Sefton Gonzalez, who scored and hurled himself through his trademark somersault. Today, goalkeeper Chris Thompson is back after a bout of sciatica. There’s optimism in the air.

Against the backdrop of the chemical plants in salt-mining territory, Nelson discover what they’re up against in Garbutt and Witton’s attacking pace. Nelson wing-back Darren Holden, outstanding in the previous round and at Charnock in midweek, is operating in his own half far more, protecting Nelson territory, yet removing one of the Lancashire team's attacking dimensions.

Jamie Edwards, Nelson’s force field, draws a sharp save and Gonzales has just headed a great opportunity into the ground when Witton’s Garbutt leaps to meet a corner and send his team ahead.

He’s one of only two players Witton have signed up to a contract, protecting his match fee if he’s injured and protecting the club if someone else tries to sign him, Witton chairman Graham Wood relates, back in the boardroom at half-time.

The winners today will collect £1,444 in prize money and that would be just as precious to Witton, a fan-owned club with 400 registered shareholders, none of them hugely wealthy, who are currently trying to make a community football facility.

Nelson players warm up at the side of the pitch before kick-off

Witton Albion play in the Northern Premier League Division One West, one divsion higher than Nelson

Visiting goalkeeper Chris Thompson keeps a Witton Albion player at bay

Freddy Garbutt's first-half goal settled the game and sent Witton through to the next round of the FA Cup

Home boss Ben Harrison addresses his players at full-time

‘That will bring us an income to put back into the club,’ says Wood, who has helped bring a commercial sponsorship deal with a locally based homelessness charity.

Nelson dominate a second half in which Holden is pushed forward more, encouraged by his wife Abi, who is live tweeting the match for the club’s website with another volunteer, Amy Holden, and taking photographs for next week’s match programme and the website.

In the main stand, 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes, which will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader, reflect the growing frustration. The ‘18’ inked onto sub James Hooper’s jersey is impressive. But it’s raining in Nelson hearts when the whistle blows and they tumble out of the competition.

Manager Arron Ripley stands in the sun-dappled centre circle ten minutes later and reflects on the way his ambitious side are evolving. ‘Last year we’d have kept launching it in a situation like that but we’re looking after the ball. We look like we’re enjoying it. We just weren’t clinical enough.’

Nelson can return fortified to their league campaign, confident, in so many ways, that the lights will stay on.

Sports.title: England cricketer Brydon Carse handcuffed after nightclub incident - with former captain Ben Stokes spotted watching on
Sports.content:
England cricketer Brydon Carse handcuffed after nightclub incident - with former captain Ben Stokes spotted watching on

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

English cricket is dealing with yet more embarrassing headlines after footage emerged of fast bowler Brydon Carse handcuffed by police outside a Derby nightclub late on Saturday.

Carse, who was part of England’s squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan and their leading wicket-taker during the Ashes defeat in Australia, was released without charge, having been out celebrating with Durham team-mates following their win over Derbyshire in the county championship.

A short video posted on social media showed Carse, 31, surrounded by four policemen outside the club, with fellow Durham stars Ben Stokes and Matthew Potts in the background. One of the policemen is heard to say: ‘Just get him over there.’

It is unclear why Carse was placed in handcuffs, and he is understood to have returned to the team hotel soon after.

The England and Wales Cricket Board said: ‘We are aware of an incident which is reported to have taken place in Derby [on Saturday] night, and are currently investigating. We will provide a further update when possible.’

No decision has yet been made over whether Carse will be removed from England’s 16-man squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord’s, starting on Thursday, while the ECB and the independent Cricket Regulator investigate the incident.

Brydon Carse was spotted in handcuffs surrounded by police outside a nightclub in Derby

The news comes not long after England’s new Test captain, Joe Root, abolished the team curfew that had been in place since the Ashes defeat in January, insisting his players should be trusted to behave like ‘grown adults’.

That followed a string of drink-related incidents over the past year that have sparked fresh debate about cricket’s relationship with alcohol.

In October, white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer on the eve of a one-day international in Wellington, New Zealand – an incident the ECB hushed up until the story broke on the last day of the fifth Test against Australia at Sydney in January.

In the meantime, England’s Ashes squad spent four high-profile days between the second and third Tests in the Sunshine Coast resort of Noosa. Opening batsman Ben Duckett was filmed by a member of the public slurring his words during a late-night exchange, while observers likened the trip to a ‘stag-do’.

In June, Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson missed the second Test against New Zealand after they broke the team curfew at a west London nightclub celebrating England’s first-Test win at Lord’s. They both claimed they didn’t know the curfew still operated after the end of a home Test, and Stokes retired from international cricket soon after.

Carse, who has won 14 Test caps, has been in trouble with the authorities before, having been suspended for three months in 2024 for historic betting offences, which involved placing 303 bets on matches between 2017 and 2019.

Sports.title: 'No chance!': Peter Schmeichel is shot down live on TV by Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle on Man United's hopes of signing Lewis Hall
Sports.content:
Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle hilariously dismissed Man United's hopes of signing Lewis Hall live on TV.

Speaking in the aftermath of his side's 2-2 draw with Liverpool at St James' Park on Sunday, Jaissle was conducting a pitchside interview with Viaplay.

As the conversation turned to the transfer market, Jaissle was pressed on whether he hoped Newcastle would do any further business during what has been a turbulent summer for the club.

Key players Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon have already departed, and there has also been speculation over the futures of other stars including Joe Willock, Tino Livramento and Hall.

And when questioned on his aspirations to sign more players, Jaissle responded: 'I think it will be a stressful period for the sporting director, because we have some needs.

'But if we bring players in maybe there will also be some players who go out.'

Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle shot down Man United's hopes of signing Lewis Hall

Hall has been linked to United this summer, but Jaissle insisted the left-back is going nowhere

Former Man United keeper Peter Schmeichel, who played 398 times for the club, then cheekily said: 'We are looking at your left back.'

That comment was in reference to Hall, with United having made enquiries for the defender this summer.

But to that, Jaissle said: 'No chance, no chance,' as he chuckled.

Daily Mail Sport reported earlier this month that Hall has been on United's radar as it is clear they need to strengthen that position, with Luke Shaw, now 31, in the final year of his contract while youngster Harry Amass has been told he may be best leaving for first team football.

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current deal, and would require a substantial fee, with the defender now seen as one of Newcastle's biggest assets after joining from Chelsea in 2023.

United, meanwhile, feel they are light in the position. Shaw started all 38 Premier League matches last season, though there is no obvious back-up, with Patrick Dorgu viewed as a winger by Michael Carrick.

Jaissle's comments came after an impressive opening day performance from Newcastle as they drew 2-2 with Liverpool.

They had looked set for all three points after goals from Anthony Elanga and Joe Willock had them 2-1 ahead, but Dominik Szoboszlai equalised with a penalty in the 99th minute.

'In the end, I am a bit disappointed,' the German said after the game. 'But there is also some brightness, definitely, because the guys were doing an amazing job for over 90 minutes.

'We are a young squad and they really left their heart on the pitch and this is something we can build on.

'I'm proud. We are proud to see a unit on the pitch. The guys were trying to do it the intense way that we wanted to play. Front-footed, vertical in our approach.

'This, after such a short amount of time, I'm really happy. I felt the goosebumps straight away. You get energy from the stands and you just want to deliver it on the pitch. This synergy will be something special.'

Sports.title: 'Come on, that's ridiculous!': Man United boss Michael Carrick snaps at ex-player interviewer as pressure hits on first question about his team's 'passion' after collapsing at promoted Hull City
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick snapped at a reporter's 'ridiculous' opening question after Manchester United's shock defeat by Hull City on Saturday.

The United manager was affronted when asked if his players had lost against the newly promoted club due to a lack of 'passion'.

United's Premier League season got off to a nightmare start as goals from Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy – both stemming from set-pieces – put them to the sword in Yorkshire.

Carrick was interviewed afterwards by Viaplay broadcaster Jan Age Fjortoft, the Norwegian who played for Swindon, Middlesbrough, Sheffield United, and Barnsley in the 1990s.

'Would you accept that there was a lack of passion in the first half?' asked Fjortoft.

'Oh come on, that's ridiculous,' Carrick hit back.

Michael Carrick said it was 'ridiculous' to suggest his Manchester United team lacked passion in their 2-0 defeat by Hull City

He was vexed by the question posed by Viaplay reporter and former play Jan Age Fjortoft

“Come on, that’s ridiculous.”



Michael Carrick wasn’t happy when asked if there was a lack of passion from #mufc in their first half vs Hull.



via @ViaplayFotball pic.twitter.com/zyca5r5iSr — utdreport (@utdreport) August 23, 2026

'That's not how you would assess it?' asked Fjortoft.

Carrick replied: 'Come on, you played football, you understand, that's a ridiculous thing to say. Just because you got beat doesn't mean you don't care about it.'

Fjortoft said: 'I'm not saying that you didn't care about it. If you look at it, they came with passion, that's what I mean. I understand that you care about it, but would you accept that they took you on that front, so to say?'

'No, no. Their two goals came from set plays. Other than that, we had opportunities,' Carrick said. 'That was where the game was. I don't think it was passion or anything to do with that. I think it was just their moment that made the difference in the game.'

Fjortoft said: 'Is it these duels? Is that what you mean? That these two duels were the goals? Because they had chances. There were consequences there from the game that you could see that they would get at you.'

'It’s a game of football, it’s a Premier League game,' Carrick replied.

'It’s their first game at home, and we’ve seen it many times before. You know, I said it before the game because it was always going to be a tough game.

'And set-plays, yeah, that’s it. We’ve been decent over a period of time at dealing with them, and today we didn’t.

Any title talk for Manchester United was quickly dulled by their lacklustre performance

Semi Ajayi gave the hosts the lead after a kerfuffle in the box in the 17th minute

Nobel Mendy made matters worse for United when he added Hull's second after 38 minutes

Marcus Rashford came off the bench wearing the number nine shirt but was unable to change the match

'We can look into that, we can dissect it. We certainly won’t get carried away with the positives or the negatives. We never do. So I think we can stay calm and understand what we need to get better at.'

It was a humbling experience for Carrick, who lost just two of his 17 matches in interim charge of United.

They started with a new-look midfield in the form of Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, but neither was overly convincing and the former even got nutmegged at one point.

Carrick did a fantastic job to lead United into the Champions League and the hope is that they will imitate that. Carlos Baleba is soon arriving from Brighton for £70million to further bolster their midfield.

Reporting on the match at the MKM Stadium, Daily Mail Sport's Manchester United reporter Chris Wheeler called any talk of a title challenge a 'joke'.

Wheeler wrote: 'Even in his worst nightmares, Carrick couldn't have foreseen this: an opening-day humiliation at the hands of a team that sneaked into the Premier League via the Championship play-offs in May, and have been prepped for their return to the top-flight with a summer spend of just £70million on 12 players – the same as it is costing United to sign Carlos Baleba from Brighton.'

He added: 'After a summer of guarded optimism over the signing of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, the new midfield failed to launch.

'Both players were replaced midway through the second half on their Premier League debuts with United two goals down, having been eclipsed by Matt Crooks and Slater, a mere £50,000 signing from Sheffield United in 2022.

'Instead, it was the business that United haven't done that becomes the main talking point. The new striker that hasn't arrived. The missing defensive cover for Luke Shaw. Baleba, the third midfield signing, coming in too late to start the season.

Considering Carrick only lost two of his 17 games after taking over in January, this was a serious setback. He talked in the week about touting United as title contenders being 'a jump'. On this evidence, it's a joke.'

Sports.title: Mutiny-hit Match of the Day review: BBC try to go with same old, same old amid Alan Shearer backing out - and no sign of the 'modernisation'
Sports.content:
Mutiny-hit Match of the Day review: BBC try to go with same old, same old amid Alan Shearer backing out - and no sign of the 'modernisation'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Before the action, we had that lovely old intro, old clips, old voices, old logos, old Kenneth Wolstenholme telling us from August 1964: 'Welcome to Match of the Day.'

Ah, familiarity, our old friend. Despite an addiction to trying to fix what is not broken, the BBC begin each and every MOTD by celebrating how long this staple of Saturday nights has been on our screens, since a time when Wolstenholme was being beamed to us in black and white.

It was at least with relief that the Beeb stuck with this theme of familiarity for their first broadcast of the 2026-27 season, if accompanied by some apprehension over whether that feeling would last.

They had advertised their new line-up this last week, after all, telling us to expect to see Thomas Frank, Toby Alderweireld, Robbie Keane and Ashley Young on our screens while simultaneously plugging their four new YouTube shows in a bid to tap into the young'uns.

Got to modernise. Go after the audience that apparently doesn't think terrestrially.

But this particular MOTD was more a case of same old, same old, and not only because it started with that vintage montage and theme tune which, if they tried to bin next in favour of some modern track, I'd be tempted to launch a petition of my own.

The BBC stuck with a sense of familiarity for the first Match of the Day of the season

I would launch a petition if they ever changed the show's opening, writes Kieran Gill

The Beeb did not want to suddenly beam fresh faces into our living rooms. They saved the new blood, and scrutiny, for another time. Instead we saw those we know and trust.

Mark Chapman was in the hot seat. We know Chappers. We like Chappers. He, along with Kelly Cates and Gabby Logan, were chosen well as Gary Lineker's successors.

After a week in which we learned there is discontent behind the scenes at MOTD at the direction of this crown jewel's travel, Chapman's tongue-in-cheek opener was: 'Happy new season. Match of the Day returns. We're all smiles here. Just look at Alan Shearer and Wayne Rooney.'

More familiarity. We like them, too. They add to the broadcast. We could watch the highlights online if we wanted, hours before MOTD. We tune in because it adds analysis in between the action, including the stylish statistical graphics they show, and that is what we want.

When we will next see Shearer in one of these seats, who knows. We are told he has scaled back his contractual commitments, and as well as giving him back his weekends by only doing one show a month if that, he supposedly has beef with those above him.

In his place, Frank should be a good addition. He has authority. Despite what happened with Tottenham Hotspur, he is a fine, modern, intelligent coach, and impressed during the 2026 World Cup, which the BBC predominantly covered from Salford as we know.

Also entering via the revolving door, Alderweireld and Keane can expect their takes on Spurs will end up being separate stories online, especially if they are controversial.

Rooney branding Manchester United's defending as 'schoolboy' on Saturday will have had the odd news editor tempted to ask for copy to be bashed up, I'm sure.

Alan Shearer and Wayne Rooney are good pundits, but we will see a heavily revolving cast

Yet it will be intriguing to see how they all click together and if there is chemistry, the type that Shearer, Richards and Lineker forged over time spent working together. Apparently that concern surrounding camaraderie forms part of the mutiny occurring within MOTD.

Millions still trust their Saturday nights in the hands of the BBC. Myself included, having watched this show since my parents let me stay up late enough to do so.

Those of us who love the company of MOTD never want it to go the same way as Football Focus, its sister show which ended in May after 52 years on air.

Changing it too much would be a risk. At least the Beeb saw enough sense to show us what we wanted to see on this occasion as we settled in for Hull's big win on their return to the Premier League and the other highlights thereafter. On to what next week brings.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick must make his mark as capitulation in dismal defeat by Hull raises fresh concerns over this Man United squad's ability to build on his achievements, writes CHRIS WHEELER
Sports.content:
When Michael Carrick celebrated his return to Old Trafford in January with back-to-back wins against Manchester City and Arsenal, the message from the head coach was calm and consistent. 'Nobody is getting carried away,' was Carrick's mantra at the time.

So he was never likely to have a public meltdown at the MKM Stadium on Saturday after Manchester United suffered a shocking defeat at Hull City, losing to a newly-promoted team on the opening weekend for the first time in the club's history.

As bad as the result and United's performance were, Carrick's approach remained the same as it was seven months ago. Calm down, it's just one game.

He is right, of course, but Carrick has also been around United long enough to know that you are only ever one game from a crisis.

Lose to Ipswich in United's first home game of the season on Sunday, and Carrick's softly softly approach will be drowned out by the alarm bells ringing around Old Trafford.

The 45-year-old's placid exterior has always masked his real emotions, first as a player and now as a coach. At United, his calm demeanour and measured approach have been a welcome antidote to the emotional incontinence and public self-flagellation of his emotional predecessor Ruben Amorim.

Michael Carrick exuded calmness despite seeing Manchester United lose 2-0 at Hull City

The 45-year-old hides his emotions a lot better than his United predecessor Ruben Amorim

Nobody who knows Carrick would doubt the competitive edge and hunger to win that was seared into the heart of all Sir Alex Ferguson's teams - and which he must imbue into the squad that surrendered so tamely on Humberside.

The players certainly got the message after Carrick suffered his first defeat in charge at Newcastle in March, but the manner of their capitulation to Hull has raised fresh concerns over the ability of this group to build on what he achieved in the second half of last season after replacing Amorim.

Managers react differently to defeat. Erik ten Hag took his players on a 13.8km run the day after United lost their first away game of the season 4-0 at Brentford in 2022 to make up for the overall distance they had lagged behind their opponents - a result just as shocking as this defeat at Hull. Amorim damaged a TV during a dressing-room rant after his team lost at home to Brighton in January last year.

The challenge for Carrick this week is to strike the right balance. He is the last man to press the panic button - certainly after one game - but he also has to make it abundantly clear to the players and supporters that Manchester United losing to Hull City is not acceptable.

At the MKM Stadium, he was asked if the cool-headed approach that has served him so well thus far might actually be viewed negatively by fans expecting a few choice words from their head coach.

'I know there's a lot goes on outside of our football club, yeah,' Carrick said with a smile. 'I understand. I understand the responsibility I've got, but it doesn't make me do things differently just because of that.

'I'm talking to you quite calmly, but I'm not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day, you know? So there's a big difference. I played here for a long time. You don't get to play here for a long time without just going day by day, the results, the ups and downs, but you just carry on as normal. It's 100 per cent not that, trust me.

'It just doesn't mean that we all have to shout and scream and create some chaos just because of it. Inside we're hurting. The boys know, and we need to get better. But the calmness doesn't mean that there's no emotion in it, for sure.

'It's not a nice feeling at all. It doesn't mean it's going to change the direction of how we're going as a team or as a football club. It's one game and results can happen in football, we all understand that. It's not nice when they do, but it does happen. We can be better, and we will be better.'

Reflecting post-match, Carrick insisted that his side know they have to be better after losing

Youri Tielemans was worryingly ineffective in midfield for Manchester United on his debut

United couldn't be much worse, in fairness, but at least Carrick will have a stronger squad available against Ipswich.

Carlos Baleba won't be available once his £70million move from Brighton goes through due to an ankle injury, but Kobbie Mainoo will have benefitted from another appearance off the bench at Hull, and Mason Mount could be fit again after impressing in pre-season until he was injured in the friendly against Paris Saint-Germain.

The two midfielders United have already bought for a total of £85m so far this summer, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, were worryingly ineffective at Hull.

The minor nature of the injury Amad Diallo suffered in training late last week suggests he could return on the right flank, potentially releasing Bryan Mbeumo to play through the middle again after Matheus Cunha struggled there on Saturday. Benjamin Sesko is another option after making his first appearance of the summer off the bench due to a shin problem.

Lisandro Martinez and Diogo Dalot could also return to the line-up after another week of training following their late return from the World Cup, in place of Ayden Heaven - who struggled against Hull's combative striker Oli McBurnie - and Noussair Mazraoui.

Carrick has no shortage of options. He just has to get the balance right on and off the pitch.

Sports.title: Alexander Isak's Newcastle return was full of vitriol and vicious noise - the £125m man looked paralysed by pressure in performance that will not have endeared him to ambivalent Liverpool fans, writes CRAIG HOPE
Sports.content:
Four, four-letter words. Love. Hate. King. Isak.

Just when we thought the most emotionally-charged collective of the afternoon would be the minute's applause for Kevin Keegan, Alexander Isak stepped from the line of red jerseys to take kick-off.

How foolish of the visitors. How naive to play so willingly into the hands - and mouths - of their hosts. As if they needed any extra encouragement. They had already hissed their hatred when Isak left the team bus. This time, he could not hide behind his AirPods.

From Keegan to Isak, The Messiah to The Pariah, this was a different noise entirely. Hostile does not come close. This was vicious. This was vitriol. The Toon Army had waited a year to take aim at their former striker and, when the moment came, they did not miss. It set the tone for what followed.

The home crowd had to wait only four minutes more for Isak's first touch to go wrong. Sixty seconds later and, for Newcastle at least, everything felt so right. The breakaway goal was the sort that used to involve Isak - fast, direct and ruthless.

How fitting, then, that it was a Swede who scored. Anthony Elanga was bought last summer to play with his compatriot, before he defected to Merseyside. Unlike Keegan, Isak is not loved by both sets of supporters. In fact, you wonder if Liverpool's are even that keen. His performance here would have done nothing to endear him. It said everything that those in black and white loved it, as Keegan might say.

Alexander Isak endured a difficult afternoon on his first return to Newcastle since leaving

His long-awaited return to St James' Park saw him greeted by a vitriolic and vicious reception

Indeed, there were two moments to rival Newcastle's goals for noise, and they both, to little surprise, involved Isak. First, after a challenge by Lewis Hall to leave the Premier League's most expensive player clutching his ankle, new Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle, standing only yards away, threw his arms in the air. Not in protest at Isak staying down, but in invitation of a little more Geordie scorn for this fallen foe. They duly obliged. Isak did not like it and was quickly on his feet to let the German know. Not that he cared.

Jaissle, you suspect, will care for little beyond that which affects him and his team. For 95 minutes, he got the better of fellow managerial debutant Andoni Iraola on the pitch, and when it came to animation and aggression, the touchline too. His cajoling, his snarl and disregard for the boundaries of his technical area will quickly win him friends on Tyneside. Mocking their enemy with not hurt, either. That brings us to the second explosion of noise.

At 2-1 in the 69th minute, Isak was presented with his first big chance. It would prove to be his last. Those in the low rows of the Leazes End were ready to bury their heads in their hands - Isak had a clear sight at goal from 14 yards - only to use those same palms as a form of protection. Isak's shot flew hopelessly into the stands.

As the clock then ticked beyond the last of five added minutes, it felt like Isak's miss would be Liverpool's last inglorious act in front of goal. When they then won a penalty, you wondered whether he would take it. You wondered, too, whether his own fans would have wanted him to - the odds on redemption felt considerably longer than those on ridicule. Dominik Szoboszlai was a wiser choice and, with his blast, the points were shared.

Maybe that is what Keegan would have wanted, albeit without the reminder of a stoppage-time goal from Liverpool. The sight of him slouched behind the Anfield advertising hoarding in 1996, following Stan Collymore's 92nd-minute winner in the 4-3 classic, will forever capture the ecstasy and agony of Keegan and his great Entertainers side, who were all present here.

Newcastle fared better in terms of result this time, but the hurt was just the same. They had deserved to win. They had done what teams are told to avoid - they had played the occasion. They played it with, at times, some beauty. But more so, a brutal intensity that suggests they will not be feeling sorry for themselves on the back of a turbulent summer.

The challenge, of course, is to replicate that when the likes of Bournemouth and Hull City come to St James' Park in the coming weeks. There will be no occasion to play then, no former hero to vilify or emotional current to ride. The emphasis will be on breaking teams down as opposed to running them over.

Still, Newcastle's supporters would have left this opener more enthused than Liverpool's. The Reds were unconvincing and Isak was not alone in appearing paralysed by pressure. The man who now wears his old No 9, Yoane Wissa, was the game's best player, save for the miss that would have made it 3-1 four minutes from time.

Newcastle fans paid homage to Kevin Keegan before the match following his recent death

Before the match, Newcastle supporters unfurled a Keegan quote about dreaming big

Before the game, a Keegan quote was unfurled across the Gallowgate End. 'I want people to dream about their football club. They should. We should all be dreamers at heart. Some people are the opposite and say, "we can't do that". But when you ask them why they can't give a reason. Well, I say, "why not?".'

Until the very last kick, at least, this was the dream the Geordies had imagined - and the nightmare they had wished upon Isak. Then came the equaliser. Four, four-letter words had framed the afternoon. Four goals settled it.

And, for Newcastle, there was one more. Pain.

Sports.title: Why Andoni Iraola should be concerned after Newcastle draw: The key problem Liverpool must solve, the player they desperately need in the transfer window and a worrying lack of depth in attack
Sports.content:
Nearly a year to the day that Rio Ngumoha scored a 100th-minute winner at St James's Park, Liverpool fans were again toasting a last-second goal as they descended the many steps down from the away end up in the skies.

Last August, they were singing and dancing as they left the stadium. They were doing the same here but with a nagging worry in the backs of their minds.

When the pulses and emotions lowered as they trudged back down the A1(M), everyone connected to Liverpool would know that, despite the drama and joy that came from the last-gasp equaliser, there are a lot more issues than this time last year.

Back then, remember, the Reds were the reigning champions and had started the defence on fire. Many observers, like they do now with Arsenal, expected this team to win the league at a canter. Now, there are hints of optimism but that is overridden by uncertainty.

Twelve months on and a change of manager later, this opening performance prompted more questions than answers. The issues that ultimately led to Arne Slot losing his job were still evident and, despite the late celebrations, fans might be worried for the season ahead.

The chief problem for new boss Andoni Iraola was the midfield – or lack thereof. Both goals were accomplished counter-attacks from Newcastle but both were highly preventable as Liverpool were cut through at ease.

Dominik Szoboszlai salvaged a point for Liverpool at Newcastle with a last-gasp penalty

Ryan Gravenberch, Florian Wirtz and late hero Dominik Szoboszlai are all incredibly talented footballers. But do they work as a midfield three? They are all more naturally inclined to be attack-minded and the back door is left ajar to let teams punish them.

This summer has been all about replacing Mohamed Salah, who scored on his Trabzonspor league debut on Sunday, but why has there been no attempts to sign a midfielder?

It is not like this is a new problem. Alexis Mac Allister and Gravenberch were both poor for the entirety of last season and Liverpool have needed a deep-lying player since Fabinho left in the summer of 2023.

'The team needs a defensive midfielder, we have been talking about this at Liverpool for three years,' said Daniel Sturridge on Sky Sports. 'Gravenberch changed that philosophy but if you analyse the midfield, they are all naturally more attacking players.

'You look at Mamadou Sangare at Brentford, the stats jump off the page, he was only £39million which is not a load of money.'

Both of Newcastle's goals came from Gravenberch having possession on the edge of the home penalty area. Before they knew it, Liverpool were chasing back, there was no midfield enforcer to stop the counter-attack, the defence was stretched and they conceded.

Think of some of the great Premier League teams, they have always had someone happy to sit in and break up the play: Claude Makelele, Ngolo Kante, Rodri, Fernandinho, some of the greats at Manchester United.

Gravenberch was adept in 2024-25, when Liverpool won the title, but has not reached that same level since. Mac Allister likewise. Szoboszlai is a mercurial footballer but better further forward, as is Wirtz who was anonymous again here at the start of a defining season for him.

Ryan Gravenberch was at fault for both of Newcastle's goal and Liverpool should focus on signing a No6

Dominik Szoboszlai is far too attacking of a midfielder to fill the need deeper in the middle

Liverpool remain hopeful of signing Paris Saint-Germain's Bradley Barcola this week and are weighing up whether to make a third bid for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh. Those will be crucial additions, given the wide options are limited at present.

But signing a deep-lying midfielder is just as important. They could have the best front three in the world yet they will win no trophies if they are so vulnerable and exposed to the counter-attack like they were here.

Lionel Messi, Xavi and Andres Iniesta took the headlines in Pep Guardiola's Barcelona super-team, but No 6 Sergio Busquets was the most important cog in that machine.

Iraola thought Liverpool were the better team here but might be delighted with the point given, for most of the match, they looked likely to leave with nothing.

At Bournemouth, he played with an energetic and dynamic double-pivot of Tyler Adams and Lewis Cook. So far, the Basque boss seems unsure about the make-up of his top-heavy midfield. How to get the best of Wirtz and Szoboszlai but also keep the team solid?

It is now over to those upstairs to ensure the impressive Iraola has the tools to thrive this season, as the bench looked weak.

A winger or two would be great but a new holding midfielder should join the wide forwards at the top of that shopping list.

Isak's day to forget

We cannot repeat the words used by Newcastle fans but you can have a good guess at the sentiments expressed towards Alexander Isak, once of this parish.

Most words were four letters long and let us just say that they were not kind.

Isak, all £125m of him, saw his every touch jeered and booed by the hostile, raucous crowd at St James'.

This was a day to forget for the Swede, who has looked sharp in pre-season but failed to translate that form to when it really matters.

He had a couple of chances but fluffed his lines, much to the delight of the home fans. If Liverpool are to succeed this season, they need a lot more from Isak and Wirtz.

A returning Alexander Isak was booed with every touch and struggled against his former side

Lack of depth in attack is a real worry

Lewis Koumas has been impressive in pre-season, is a talented player who can play across the front three and the manager has taken a shine to the Welshman in training.

But the sight of him coming on as a substitute to try to salvage a point might worry some Liverpool fans.

Koumas, son of former Premier League midfielder Jason, spent the second half of last season at Hull City – and was an unused substitute in the play-off final despite scoring some important goals on the way to promotion for the Tigers.

He has deserved his top-flight debut but fans are right to ask why Iraola was left to rely on a player who has spent the last few years in the second tier, with loans also at Birmingham and Stoke.

The other wingers had mixed afternoons. Victor Munoz looked bright off the bench, asking constant questions and winning the foul that led to the decisive penalty.

Cody Gakpo took his goal incredibly well with a fine hit from distance and was Liverpool's most effective attacker – yet he has question-marks over his future given Tottenham have shown interest in signing him this summer.

Ngumoha is an exciting talent and has all the tools to be a future world-beater but failed to make a serious impression here, with just 21 touches. The 17-year-old is better on the left flank and was largely ineffective on the right flank.

All this came as, 2,000 miles south-east, Salah was scoring on his Turkish Superlig debut for Trabzonspor. With little over a week left of the window to go, the Egyptian King has still not been replaced.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
