World.title: EKO 2026: NSC inspects facilities ahead of maiden National Intermediate Games
World.content:
The National Sports Commission (NSC), alongside members of the Main Organising Committee (MOC) and the Local Organising Committee (LOC), has undertaken another round of inspections of facilities in Lagos.

The move is in preparation for the maiden National Intermediate Games.

The games, scheduled for 1-15 October, would be hosted at Teslim Balogun Stadium in Lagos.

Director of Information at the NSC, Kehinde Ajayi, in a statement on Sunday, noted that the inspection tour began at the Teslim Balogun Stadium.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The delegation assessed the readiness and suitability of the facilities earmarked for the games.

“The tour was led by the Head of Grassroots Development, Niyi Beyioku, with the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Grassroots Development, Adeboye Adeyinka, representing the Director General of the commission.

“Members of the LOC showcased key facilities, including the stadium turf, indoor sports hall and other sporting infrastructure, as the inspection team evaluated their preparedness for the competition,” she said.

According to her, the delegation subsequently inspected other major venues and facilities, including the National Stadium complex in Surulere, the National Institute for Sports (NIS) Rowe Park Sports Centre and the Yaba College of Technology.

Other venues visited include the University of Lagos sports facilities and hostels, the Elegbata Sports Centre, the Cricket Oval at Tafawa Balewa Square, and the Mobolaji Johnson Arena, which is being considered for the opening and closing ceremonies.

“Following the facility inspection, the MOC and LOC held a technical meeting to deliberate on key operational and technical matters and strengthen preparations for the successful delivery of the games.

“Twenty-eight sports have been pencilled down for the maiden National Intermediate Games. Athletes are expected to arrive from Oct. 1, while the opening ceremony is scheduled for Oct 5.

“The National Intermediate Games is a multi-sports competition organised under the authority of the NSC, to provide a platform for the development and identification of young sporting talents across Nigeria,” she said.

Ajayi further disclosed that the games were specifically designed for athletes in the Under-19 category, comprising athletes born between Jan. 1, 2008 and Sept. 30.

According to her, the competition will bring together athletes from all 36 states of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), as well as diaspora athletes, who will compete as one contingent in Lagos for two weeks

“Notable members of the inspection delegation included Yusuf Alli, Olalekan Alabi, and Kola Daniel, Special Assistant, Media, to the DG, NSC, alongside other officials of the NSC, the MOC and the LOC.

“The inspection underscores the commitment of the organisers in ensuring that all facilities, technical arrangements and operational structures are in place for a safe, competitive and successful maiden edition of the National Intermediate Games,” she said. (NAN)

World.title: Manipulating the price of consumer welfare, By Uddin Ifeanyi
World.content:
After a fashion, an economy is like a latex balloon. Squeeze air out of a part of it, and it shows up in a new bulge elsewhere. Without blowing up the balloon, the air it contains remains unchanged irrespective of any shape one attempts to force on it. When a government raises taxes for example, the resulting enhancement to the national treasury simply reflects a lessening in consumers’ disposable incomes and/or in the funds available for businesses to invest — technically, both are drags on the economy. However, were the economy to grow on the back of the government’s deployment of these new funds this dynamic changes radically.

Government spending could also improve an economy’s outcomes. But this takes place only when governments spend to remove constraints to business growth and Investment (by reducing red tape, improving and extending infrastructure, easing logistics bottlenecks, etc.), or on health and education that increase both labour productivity and young school leavers’ employability, or through conditional transfers that drive up effective demand at lower income levels.

A report, last week, by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) adds colour to this dilemma. After a three-month cross-border investigation in “response to widespread public complaints over the high cost of cement”, the commission established a preliminary basis for investigating possible price manipulation in the industry.

Does the FCCPC’s description of the state of the local cement industry underline the tension between consumer welfare and the profit initiative? While this conclusion is the easiest to reach, it is not necessarily the only one. Neither is it an entirely accurate description. First, the contradiction between both concepts is a false one. In any economy, the nature of the market is the most important variable for determining how well resources are allocated and used. In a competitive market, businesses make profits by producing things or services that people want, and at prices they are willing to pay. The presence of competing products or services, motivates firms to improve quality, reduce costs, and innovate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Where market imperfections exist — because of the existence of monopolies, oligopolies, information asymmetry, natural monopolies, network effects, externalities, or high barriers to market entry — and the regulatory space is insufficiently developed, firms make profits without adequately serving customers. Otherwise, a functioning regulatory space intervenes to protect consumers and preserve the conditions for competition, and not to make businesses unprofitable.

Aside from the burdens posed by a weak-to-non-existent domestic regulatory framework, an additional vulnerability in the Nigerian example lies in the structure, and intent of our industrial policy. For a variety of reasons, including poor macroeconomic conditions that have ceaselessly driven up domestic prices and eroded consumer spending, doing business in Nigeria is a mug’s game. Beginning in the early 1970s, successive federal governments have interpreted the task of enhancing domestic manufacturing capacity as one of circling the wagons around local industry — even when some of the lead entities in these industries bore marques such as Volkswagen and Peugeot.

As a result, for just as long, national industrial policy has ignored the latex balloon plasticity of the economy. Import and tax waivers along with tariff and non-tariff barriers have been erected to protect domestic industry even when all these achieved was simply move scarce resources from the treasury to the profit and loss accounts of the cosseted businesses. The higher profits that these protected segments of the economy also enjoyed from not having to compete with imports or other local firms encouraged the price gouging that again just moved money from people’s pockets to businesses’ books of accounts. Any which way, the national ledger suffered, especially because, thus protected, our domestic businesses have had no incentive for leaving their babyish stages.

As incentives to further rapid development of the economy, there is an ironclad case for including strong expiry clauses in the design of tariff and non-tariff protection for local “virgin” businesses. The choice of the “why” of the sunsets on these protections matters as much if not more so than the decision about their duration. This is why in the design of our industrial policies, the quid pro quo for protection must be that such businesses are able to stand their own against foreign competition after clearly defined time periods. In designing the sweeteners that industrial policy is built on, clear agreements on the period over which this should happen and after which all protections fall off is of the essence.

Even then, it is a far better application of scarce domestic resources for government to fix structural impediments to doing business in the country — by dismantling barriers to entry across all markets, making information generation and exchange less opaque, removing incentives to market power, fixing the logistic chokepoints that impede the movement of people, goods, and capital across the economy, etc. — than to endlessly erect barriers purporting to protect domestic businesses, but which end up allowing captains of industry to fleece consumers. Along this path, government could do one better, by also addressing the volatility that afflicts domestic prices from fiscal incontinence, and amateurish management of monetary policy.

Uddin Ifeanyi, a journalist manqué and retired civil servant, can be reached @IfeanyiUddin.

World.title: Amnesty demands rescue of worshippers abducted in Niger mosque attack
World.content:
Amnesty International has called on Nigerian authorities to ensure the safe rescue of worshippers abducted at a mosque during the Muslim Friday prayers in Kpenya, Dekara District, Borgu Local Government Area of Niger State.

The rights organisation said in a statement published on its verified social media handle that an unspecified number of worshippers were abducted during the attack on 21 August, while residents claimed that more than 80 people may have been taken.

Amnesty urged the Nigerian authorities to act urgently to secure the victims’ release and address the growing wave of abductions targeting rural communities across northern Nigeria.

The organisation said the incident was particularly concerning because the victims were abducted while observing Friday prayers, adding that survivors of previous mass abductions had reported torture, starvation, sexual violence, amputation and being forced to witness or participate in atrocities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Niger State Government confirmed the attack in a statement by the Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Obed Nana, saying suspected terrorists stormed Kpenya Mosque while worshippers were observing Juma’at prayers.

According to the government, the attack occurred at Gidan-Zana and Kpenya communities. Some residents fled into nearby areas, while the attackers abducted an unspecified number of worshippers.

The government said efforts were ongoing to establish the precise number of people abducted.

Governor Mohammed Bago directed security agencies to intensify efforts to locate and safely rescue the victims.

“A joint security operation has been deployed to assess the situation, track the attackers, and facilitate the rescue of the abducted worshippers,” Mr Nana said.

He said the government would not disclose operational details that could compromise the rescue effort, while urging residents to avoid spreading unverified figures and provide credible information to security agencies.

Amnesty also called on President Bola Tinubu’s administration to urgently address the rising incidence of mass abductions in northern Nigeria.

The organisation said at least 1,100 people were abducted between January and April 2026, while acknowledging that estimates vary and may significantly understate the scale of the problem.

Worsening insecurity

The Kpenya attack occurred barely a week after gunmen killed at least 32 people during Friday prayers at a mosque in Ungushi community, Kebbe Local Government Area of Sokoto State. The Imam of the mosque, Malam Aliyu, was also killed.

The incident adds to a series of attacks PREMIUM TIMES has reported in Borgu, particularly around the Kainji Lake National Park and the Niger-Kebbi border corridor.

In January, PREMIUM TIMES reported that at least 35 people were killed and several others, mostly women and children, abducted when gunmen attacked Kasuwan Daji in Borgu.

Following the attack, Governor Bago ordered residents of communities around the Kainji Lake area to evacuate, warning that military operations could be conducted against terrorists operating in the surrounding forests.

In February, PREMIUM TIMES reported that attacks on Feyi, Tungan Makeri and Nkpaso communities over three consecutive days left about 26 people dead and several houses burnt.

ALSO READ: Niger State orders security forces to rescue abducted worshippers in Borgu

In June, suspected Boko Haram terrorists attacked Pissa, killing an unspecified number of residents, abducting others and setting houses ablaze. The attackers also threatened neighbouring communities, including Kabe and Sukumba.

PREMIUM TIMES also reported in April that a medical doctor, Anthony Enahoro, was abducted by terrorists operating around Kainji National Park in Wawa District, Borgu.

In June, armed bandits were also reported to have entered Zugurma, a community near Kainji Lake National Park, where they held a gathering and delivered a sermon. Residents and security analysts linked the fighters to jihadist groups operating in the Kainji forest, although their identities could not be independently verified.

The repeated attacks have heightened concerns over the vulnerability of rural communities, travellers and worshippers in the Borgu-Kainji corridor.

Amnesty International said the Nigerian government must ensure that civilians are protected and that victims and their families receive effective assistance and remedies.

The organisation also urged authorities to strengthen measures to prevent further attacks and ensure that those responsible for the abductions are held accountable.

World.title: Gunmen kill two security operatives, seize rifles in Plateau
World.content:
Two security operatives were reportedly killed on Sunday after some gunmen attacked Tanjol and Tarai communities in Jol District of Riyom Local Government Area of Plateau State.

The incident occurred at about 2:30 p.m., with the attackers reportedly seizing the firearms of the slain personnel, according to a report by PUNCH newspaper, which quoted residents of the affected communities.

Residents told the newspaper that security personnel responded to the attack but encountered resistance from the gunmen, leading to a gun battle that lasted several minutes.

“Information available indicated that at least two security operatives were killed during the encounter, while their firearms were reportedly taken away by the attackers,” a resident, John Dalyop, was quoted as saying.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Another resident, Chollom Jerry, said that several people were injured during the attack while a civilian was also reported missing.

He said the incident had heightened fear among residents of Jol and surrounding communities, with residents worried about the safety of their lives and property.

“Residents were worried about the safety of their lives and property, urging security agencies to intensify efforts to protect vulnerable communities in the area,” Mr Jerry said.

Efforts by PREMIUM TIMES to obtain official reactions from security agencies, including the Plateau State Police Command, were reportedly unsuccessful. Sources at the command headquarters in Jos, however, said additional security personnel had been deployed to the affected communities.

Repeated attacks

The latest incident adds to a series of attacks involving civilians and security personnel in Riyom and other parts of Plateau State in recent weeks.

On 4 August, PREMIUM TIMES reported that gunmen ambushed a joint security patrol along the Ganawuri-Sabon Gida Road in Riyom Local Government Area, killing a police inspector and a Nigerian Air Force corporal.

The attackers reportedly took the service rifles of the slain personnel, after which security forces launched cordon-and-search operations in surrounding communities.

Following the attack, troops of Operation Enduring Peace reportedly arrested 19 suspects in Tongoron community, Riyom, for profiling and investigation as the military intensified efforts to identify those responsible for the ambush and recover the stolen weapons.

ALSO READ: Gunmen kill former Plateau councillor in Riyom

The latest attack also occurred in the same local government where PREMIUM TIMES recently reported the killing of former councillor Daniel Chong, popularly known as “Hon. Star,” during a late-night attack on Torok community.

Mr Chong, a former councillor representing Rim Ward, was reportedly killed at about 11:45 p.m. during the attack, while another resident sustained gunshot injuries.

The renewed attacks have heightened concerns over security in Riyom, which has recorded repeated incidents involving armed groups and attacks on security personnel.

The seizure of service rifles in the latest incident also raises concerns over the proliferation of firearms and the possibility of weapons taken from slain security personnel being used in subsequent attacks.

Security agencies are yet to publicly provide details on the identities of the slain operatives or the circumstances surrounding the attack as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: 2027: Kwankwaso knocks APC campaign council, says election choice between oppressors, oppressed
World.content:
Former Governor of Kano State and vice presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Rabiu Kwankwaso, has criticised the newly constituted All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council for the 2027 general election.

In a statement posted on X on Sunday, Mr Kwankwaso said the election is an impending battle between the “oppressed Nigerian masses” and political figures who have sustained policies responsible for widespread economic hardship.

Mr Kwankwaso argued that the composition of the campaign council, which includes key figures associated with the current administration, gives citizens a clear preview of the choices ahead in 2027.

“The council brings together many of the same political actors who have supported, defended or participated in the present administration.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Their coming together raises a fundamental question: what exactly are they asking Nigerians to vote for in 2027, a new beginning, or the continuation of the same system that has brought severe hardship to our people?” Mr Kwankwaso questioned.

The former governor said families are struggling with food inflation and basic costs of living, young Nigerians face diminishing job opportunities, and businesses, farmers, and public services—such as healthcare and education—remain under severe strain due to ongoing insecurity.

“This ruling campaign structure presents another scenario between the oppressors and the oppressed,” Mr Kwankwaso asserted. “We must use it come the 2027 election to reject continued oppression and demand accountable, people-centred governance. If Osun people can do it, so can all other parts of the country.”

Appeal to Abdul’aziz Yari

In a direct message to former Zamfara State Governor, Abdul’aziz Yari, who was appointed Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Mr Kwankwaso urged Mr Yari to reconsider taking up the assignment.

Mr Kwankwaso stated that Mr Yari, as a prominent northern leader and former governor, is fully aware of the socioeconomic and security collapse in the North-west and across the federation.

“I particularly appeal to my brother, Senator Abdul’aziz Yari, who has accepted to serve as Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, to reflect deeply and reconsider accepting this responsibility,” he said.

“As a former governor of Zamfara State and a prominent leader from the North-west, I believe Senator Yari has a clear understanding of the devastating consequences of insecurity, poverty, unemployment, displacement and the destruction of livelihoods in the region and the country at large.

“I therefore will be surprised if in his good conscience, [he] will lead a campaign whose principal objective is to secure the continuation of a government under which many of the people he once governed… remain trapped in these challenges”, Mr Kwankwaso said.

Concerns over neutrality of institutional heads

Mr Kwankwaso also raised concerns over the inclusion of key public finance officials in the partisan campaign council, pointing out the appointment of Zacch Adedeji, Executive Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service, and Tanimu Kurfi, Director-General of the Budget Office of the Federation, into the campaign’s financial and fundraising organs.

Highlighting the need for institutional integrity, Mr Kwankwaso questioned how public officials managing national treasury infrastructure could simultaneously serve active political roles without compromising public trust.

“The leadership of critical public institutions demands neutrality, integrity and public confidence,” Mr Kwankwaso maintained. “It is therefore legitimate to ask whether the responsibilities of senior officials entrusted with managing public revenue and national finances can appropriately coexist with senior partisan campaign roles.

“The government and the APC should explain how such arrangements are consistent with institutional neutrality and public trust”, he stated.

Mr Kwankwaso expressed confidence in the electorate, declaring, “Ultimately, no campaign council is more powerful than the Nigerian people.”

Reaction

Responding directly to Mr Kwankwaso’s statement on X, former presidential media aide Bashir Ahmad, countered Kwankwaso’s assertion that the upcoming contest would be between “the oppressors and the oppressed.”

​Mr Ahmad stated that Mr Kwankwaso’s criticism of the APC Presidential Campaign Council “does little to advance serious national debate.”

“I respectfully disagree with this characterisation of the APC Presidential Campaign Council. It is fair to scrutinise government and demand better governance, but reducing the 2027 contest to a simplistic battle between oppressors and the oppressed does little to advance serious national debate.

“The APC’s campaign council should be judged by the policies, programmes and vision it presents to Nigerians, not merely by the political identities of the individuals serving in it and the 2027 election should be a contest of ideas, records, competence and competing visions for Nigeria’s future.

“On Senator Abdul’aziz Yari, we all believe he is experienced enough to make his own judgement about whether to accept a national responsibility. His experience as a former governor and senior political leader should be seen as an asset to the political process, not automatically interpreted as complicity in every challenge confronting the country.

“Nigerians are not passive victims waiting for political actors to tell them what their choices are. They are intelligent citizens capable of examining the records of governments, comparing alternatives and deciding for themselves what direction they want the country to take.

“The 2027 election should therefore be about performance, ideas and the future of Nigeria, not inflammatory labels of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed.’” Let Nigerians decide”, Mr Ahmad stated.

World.title: EDITORIAL: Osun election, the rise of civic action, and 2027
World.content:
Governor Ademola Adeleke of Osun State was re-elected for a second term in the 15 August governorship contest. It was an off-cycle election like no other before it, in the build-up, with its eerie elements of tension, violence and resultant deaths.

Also, while there was a general public scepticism about the integrity of the electoral processes, informed by events in the recent past, a number of stakeholders have pointed out that the administration of the election appeared fairly better on the technological front than INEC’s disastrous outing in the 2023 general elections.

Nevertheless, all the indicated negatives of the polls, conflated in a manner that made the poll prefigure what is likely to occur during the 2027 elections.

The election had initially put some political pressure on President Bola Tinubu due to the action of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) in freezing the bank accounts of the Osun State government, due to its declared concerns around the suspicious movement of public funds. Yet, to forestall speculations of federal interference, the President had to order the swift de-freezing of these accounts.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Although the contest involved 15 political parties, it was largely a two-horse race between Governor Ademola, who contested under a new political platform – the Accord Party – following his defection from the PeoplesDemocratic Party (PDP), on whose platform he got into office in 2022, and Bola Oyebamiji of the All Progressives Congress (APC).

In the result declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Mr Adeleke polled a total of 511,069 votes, winning in 19 Local Government Areas out of 30 in the state. However, Mr Oyebamiji secured 444,815 votes, and won in 11 council areas. The African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate, Najeem Salaam, received only 17,180 votes.

The number of accredited voters were 1,010,684, out of which 1,005,800 voted. Valid votes stood at 985,079, while 20,721 votes were voided. With 2,399,233 total registered voters in the state, the polling of less than 50 per cent people, signal voter apathy as continuing to plague elections in the country, even if the ratio in Osun was higher than the national average.

The uncertainties that foreshadowed the poll were so high that 12 local government areas were identified as high-risk by the police, with 17 persons killed in the build-up to and during the elections. This malevolent landscape compelled the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, to deploy 15,000 police personnel, a new Commissioner of Police and a Deputy Inspector-General to supervise the poll in the state.

A week to the election, the governor had accused the state’s Commissioner of Police, Ibrahim Gotan, of partisanship, with the operation of a parallel police structure, targeted at opponents of the APC, making Mr Adeleke openly call on the president to redeploy him. The IGP wasted no time in enforcing this.

The APC didn’t hide its desire to add Osun State to its present national hegemony of 31 states. Its chieftain, Farouq Aliyu, matter-of-factly, said so shortly after the election, “We did everything humanly possible to win the election.” The storming of Osogbo – the state capital – by 17 APC governors on the eve of the poll, made this desire a lot clearer. It was patently an act of intimidation and show of force.

But the dreaded cataclysm on Election Day never occurred. Instead, the uploading of results on INEC’s digital platform, the IReV, in real time, enhanced the transparency and timely declaration of the results. It was a clear indication that the proper deployment of technology certainly plays a critical role in the conduct of credible polls.

Besides, Mr Adeleke’s “man of the people” image and grassroot appeal, counted quite for much. He is hyperactive socially; ever present in social gatherings and dancing with the people. He was savvy to have cleared the backlog of salaries and ₦47 billion in pension obligations that he inherited from the Rauf Aregbesola and Gboyega Oyetola APC administrations in the state. This endeared him to the civil servants, a crucial voting bloc, who equally sought to avoid a return to Egypt.

However, there are two sides to every coin. Vote-trading, which has become an incubus in our elections, was common. Many people were allegedly suborned with between ₦10,000 and ₦20,000 each for the purchase oftheir votes.

The European Union Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria Election Observation Hub says it recorded a total of 103 of such cases. There were 31 cases of voter obstructions, 85 cases of misconduct by electoral officials, and 38 cases of campaigning at polling units, among the 323 electoral offences and irregularities it

tracked.

With a political culture that doesn’t appear to recognise such acts as an aberration, this and other impunities might spiral out of control in the 2027 general elections. Electioneering towards the next national polls flagged off officially last Wednesday. As a result, the red flags evident in Osun should not be trivialised.

Yet, all said, INEC deserves some commendation for its performance in this recent recorded election. But to imagine that this past recorded improvement would easily become its operational template going forward, might simply be naïve.

An off-cycle poll in one state cannot be equated with a general election across several elective offices and for the president in 36 states of the country. Police personnel will be thinly spread then, and so would INEC’s staff be. 30 Electoral Commissioners were in the 30 local councils of Osun State. Again, the terrains would be remarkable different from each other.

With Adeleke and the Osun people’s demonstration that resilience and vigilance count in our elections, this lesson should not be lost on the electorate as we move into 2027. Nigerians should see elections as a veritable tool with which to hold public office holders to account.

Impressively, the watchdog role display of some electoral observers was no less critical. By 10 p.m., Atedo Peterside, in a post that went viral, admonished INEC, “Many of us have been monitoring your Osun Governorship Election result uploads on your IREV. Why have your uploads stopped at 87.48% for some hours now? If you could show us 3,292 Polling Units Results with little or no alterations, why are you unable to show us the results from the remaining 472 Polling Units? It is now past 10 p.m.”

It was a laudable civic response that checked possible mischief, which Yiaga Africa, an NGO, and others also brought to bear on the election. Critically, it serves as a warning to INEC, ahead of next elections, to improve on its public communications during the collation of results. When a genuine delay arises, it should not waste time in communicating what has gone wrong. A sudden and unexplained abeyance naturally breeds suspicion of manipulation, more so with INEC’s silence still on the “technical glitch” that marred the 2023 presidential election.

Equally laudable were the civic technology tools that were deployed by a number of organisations to record and analyse the results as they were being posted on the IReV platform, making the possibility of manipulation of results close to impossible, as long as original results were being uploaded from the Polling Units.

This reinforced the popular aphorism that eternal vigilance remains the prize of liberty. And signals that many citizens and groups – such iReportINEC and Dataphyte, etc. – staking for credible elections in the country are now commendably marshalling their innovations and competencies in enduring acts of civic action.

Yet, moving forward, PREMIUM TIMES believes that the 2027 elections stand imperilled if security agencies allow the Osun politicians who openly incited the electorate to “kill Accord Party members,” or campaigned that “don’t vote for any other candidate except the APC candidate,” are allowed to get away with their incendiary outbursts.

The scandalous statement by Nyesom Wike, the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, that if the president had desired to win Osun State “at all cost,” “he would have been there, and we would have won it, and there’s nothing the governor can do,” is nothing short of the sort of impunity that stands condemned.

It is a clear alert, and a poster of the vile and wiles of a few that undermine the integrity of elections. We hold dearly the orthodox principle of one person, one vote in an election. This principle must not be allowed to degenerate into a farce if Nigerian democracy is to survive.
