Inspired by President Ronald Reagan — Freedom & Hope:

“Freedom is not simply the right to choose our leaders; it is the opportunity to build a Liberia where every citizen can choose hope over fear, opportunity over despair, and progress over stagnation.”

Inspired by Machiavelli — Leadership & Responsibility:

“A new dawn does not come merely because the night has ended; it comes when leaders possess the courage, wisdom, and discipline to turn freedom into progress and power into service.”

Inspired by Socrates — Wisdom & Citizenship: “A nation awakens when its people begin to question not only who governs them, but whether those who govern are worthy of the trust placed in them. Liberia’s new dawn must therefore begin with wisdom, truth, and responsible citizenship.”

Inspired by Other Philosophical Traditions — Unity & Progress: “The greatness of a few individuals will not determine the destiny of Liberia, but the courage of a united people who understand that freedom without responsible leadership is incomplete, and leadership without service is empty.”

Austin S Fallah: “A new dawn for Liberia begins when freedom becomes more than a promise, when courageous leadership transforms liberty into opportunity, justice into action, and hope into lasting national progress.”

Austin S Fallah: “Liberia’s path to a brighter future rests on two enduring pillars: the freedom of its people and the leadership to protect, strengthen, and transform that freedom into peace, prosperity, and progress for all.”

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

In the landscape of political discourse, few statements resonate as deeply as those made by former President Ronald Reagan: “Freedom and progress go hand in hand.”

This assertion encapsulates the critical intertwining of liberty, empowerment, and development, especially in contexts where nations are emerging from periods of hardship and instability.

Liberia, a nation long haunted by the specters of civil war, corruption, and economic malaise, stands on the precipice of a new chapter.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, a coalition government is poised to usher in transformative change that could redefine progress for the Liberian people.

As they seek to free Liberia from the shackles of drug cartels and foster growth through infrastructure and economic development, it is imperative to acknowledge that the country’s future is ripe with potential.

I argue that the current leadership has the opportunity in the second half of the 21st century to redefine progress in Liberia through a commitment to freedom, infrastructure, and economic empowerment, ultimately aligning the nation with the ideals expressed by Reagan.

The Historical Context of Liberia:

To appreciate the significance of Liberia’s current political climate, one must first examine its historical context.

Liberia, an area that existed in the early 19th century and was settled by settlers, has always held a unique position in African history.

However, the country’s trajectory has been marred by civil conflicts that erupted during the Yuletide (Presidential Press-Secretary Hon. Patrick Kumeh introduced me to this word in 1986, during my interactions with President Samuel K Doe) of 1989 and culminated in another catastrophic war in the 1990s and early 2000s.

These conflicts not only decimated the population but also destroyed the institutions necessary for stable governance and economic viability.

Consequently, Liberia has been left grappling with high unemployment rates, widespread poverty, and inadequate infrastructure.

The aftermath of civil conflict often leads to a culture of dependency, where the populace relies on external aid rather than cultivating local resources and governance.

The pervasive influence of drug cartels and the illegal economy further complicate the development path.

However, the dawning leadership of Fe-nya-nah- Keh-keh Boakai and Fe-Nya-Nah Pow-morh Vice President Koung offers a potential turning point in this narrative.

Their coalition government symbolizes a break from the past, fostering an environment where citizens are seen as agents of change rather than mere subjects of political maneuvering.

Freedom as a Catalyst for Progress:

The concept of freedom is foundational to any society’s evolution.

In Liberia, it is not enough merely to declare independence from corrupt systems; rather, it is essential to empower citizens to take part in shaping their destiny.

President Boakai and Vice President Koung understand that true progress is predicated on instilling a sense of ownership in the citizenry.

Freedom in this context means creating opportunities for individuals to participate actively in the economy, enabling them to contribute to their nation’s and community’s social and financial fabric.

Liberians cannot remain hostages to outdated ideologies that endorse oppression and dependence on foreign entities.

The coalition government’s agenda aims to dismantle the economic structures that thrive on corruption and illegal activities (such as drug trafficking and cartels), instead promoting lawful trade and investment as foundational pillars of progress.

When citizens feel free to engage in legitimate business without fear of exploitation or violence, they can cultivate innovation and contribute to the economy, laying the groundwork for sustainable development.

Infrastructure Development: Paving the Way for Progress

One of the most pressing issues facing Liberia is its severely inadequate infrastructure.

Poor road conditions hinder access to markets, restrict transportation of goods, and stifle economic activity. Ma-sa-noh Ben-dor Keh-Keh Boakai and Ma-sa-noh pow-morh fe-nya-nah pow-morh Koung’s administration has recognized that infrastructure development is not merely an ancillary concern; it is central to the nation’s sovereignty and prosperity.

With plans to asphalt interior roads, the coalition government signals its commitment to enhancing connectivity across the country.

Asphalted roads will significantly impact agricultural development, a cornerstone of the Liberian economy.

By facilitating transportation, farmers can access larger markets, ensuring their produce reaches consumers efficiently.

This will not only enhance food security but also boost the rural economy, lifting many out of poverty. Furthermore, improved infrastructure attracts foreign investment, which is integral to sustainable growth.

When international businesses see a commitment to modern infrastructure, they are more likely to invest in long-term projects that create jobs and build skills within the local workforce.

Economic Empowerment as a Cornerstone of Development:

Beyond infrastructure, the coalition government emphasizes economic empowerment as a fundamental aspect of national progress.

This initiative requires a multifaceted approach, including education, vocational training, and supportive policies that encourage entrepreneurship.

By equipping citizens with the skills necessary to thrive in a competitive marketplace, Liberia can foster a culture of self-sufficiency and innovation.

Education plays a pivotal role in this strategy.

Historically, access to quality education has been limited in Liberia, particularly for marginalized populations.

By prioritizing educational reforms, the coalition government can ensure that the next generation is not only literate but also capable of critical thinking and innovation.

Investment in vocational training programs will equip young adults with tangible skills for local and international markets, allowing them to pursue various income-generating avenues from agriculture to technology.

Moreover, supportive economic policies, such as microfinance initiatives and tax incentives for small businesses, can stimulate local entrepreneurship.

When citizens are empowered to establish their own enterprises, they contribute to a more diverse and resilient economy.

This economic dynamism helps to reduce dependence on any single industry, shielding the nation from the vulnerabilities associated with socio-political turmoil.

The Role of Governance and Leadership Integrity:

As Liberia embarks on this journey toward revitalization, the importance of governance and integrity must not be overlooked.

The coalition government led by Wa-na-ba-nah (Big person) Boakai and Wa-wa-ba-nah pow-mor (Small person) Koung has a unique opportunity to set a precedent for transparent leadership by actively engaging citizens in the political process.

By promoting accountability and ethical governance, they can build public trust, a critical component of successful policy implementation.

Fighting corruption is paramount in this endeavor.

The Liberian people have long suffered from the consequences of corrupt leadership, which has undermined development efforts and perpetuated socio-economic disparity.

Transparency in government processes, along with the establishment of independent bodies to oversee public officials’ activities, can help eliminate corruption and restore faith in public institutions.

In addition, fostering dialogue between the government and the citizenry is essential for inclusive governance.

By actively seeking public input on policy decisions and allowing citizens to voice their concerns, the coalition government can ensure that development initiatives align with the needs of the populace.

This approach not only strengthens the democratic process but also cultivates a sense of belonging and commitment among Liberians.

A Bright Future for Liberia:

Liberia’s current political landscape represents a watershed moment in the nation’s journey toward prosperity and stability.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, the coalition government stands poised to redefine what progress means for the Liberian people.

Freedom and progress are not abstract ideals; they are actionable principles that can breathe life into a nation long beset by challenges.

By embracing freedom as a catalyst for empowerment, prioritizing infrastructure development, and committing to economic empowerment, Liberia can rise above the shadows of its past.

The coalition government has the opportunity to build a future where citizens are no longer mere spectators in their own country but active participants in shaping a prosperous and peaceful Liberia.

As Reagan eloquently put it, “freedom and progress go hand in hand,” and it is through this synergy that Liberia can reclaim its rightful place in the annals of human history, writing a new chapter of hope and resilience for generations to come.

World.title: The Empowering Journey of Liberian Women through Education: A Pathway to Freedom and Integrity
World.content:
“The Empowering Journey of Liberian Women through Education: A Pathway to Freedom and Integrity begins when every Liberian girl understands that education is not merely a certificate; it is the knowledge, confidence, and independence needed to shape her own future and contribute meaningfully to Liberia’s development.”

“Liberian women and girls must never be used as punching bags in the fight against drug trafficking and cartels. Women must also learn not to be used as political pundits by so-called politicians seeking to score public political points. Let the accused face due process, and let us reject unnecessary political noise.”

“Liberian women must be vigilant about the company they keep. Do not allow money, political influence, or social pressure to draw you into drug trafficking, criminal networks, or destructive political activities. Protect your dignity, your future, and the integrity of Liberia.”

“In the 21st-century AI age, no Liberian woman should be left behind. Education must become her bridge to technology, innovation, leadership, and economic opportunity because an educated woman not only transforms her own life, she strengthens her family, community, and nation.”

“Liberian women deserve dignity, justice, and protection—not to be turned into political tools. Women must learn to recognize when so-called politicians are using them as political pundits to score public points. Let every accused person face due process, while we put an end to political manipulation

“A woman’s strength is reflected in the choices she makes and the people she allows to influence her. Let Liberian women reject criminal exploitation, drug trafficking, and political manipulation, and instead embrace education, integrity, peace, and responsible leadership for the advancement of Liberia.”

“Let every Liberian girl and woman embrace The Empowering Journey of Liberian Women through Education: A Pathway to Freedom and Integrity; for in an age driven by artificial intelligence, those who learn, adapt, and lead with knowledge and integrity will help determine Liberia’s place in the world.”

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

In global development and human rights, education is one of the most powerful tools for liberation, empowerment, and societal transformation.

For Liberian girls and women, this truth resonates deeply as education not only equips them with knowledge but also galvanizes their ability to discern between detrimental choices and constructive life paths.

In this disquisition, I argue that educating Liberian women is critical to their personal development and serves as a salute to the nation’s future female leaders.

Through the testimony of Ms. Abigail Musu Kpakar, an embodiment of ambition and intelligence, we will explore the transformative power of education and its role in fostering critical thinking, discerning judgment, and a refined moral compass.

From an early age, Ms.Abigail Musu Kpakar’s father instilled in her the fundamental truth of education: “Musu, please go to school and be educated, so that you will learn how to read and write not only for your betterment but that of the future female leaders, and so that one day you will not see your boyfriend’s or husband’s girlfriend letter and give it to him and say, here is your receipt.”

This advice encapsulates the essence of education as a pathway to self-awareness and discernment.

Education equips women with the ability to differentiate between intoxicating substances like cocaine and innocuous everyday products such as cooking soda or baby powder, brown sand, or brown sugar.

In a society marred by the consequences of drug abuse and fraudulent practices, an educated woman is likely to make informed choices that benefit her life and her community.

It is a salutary pursuit, an endeavor that holds “inestimable” value. Only through education can young women rise above the pangs of ignorance and resist the siren calls of corrupt influences that often seduce the vulnerable.

The transformative impact of education can be compared to a serendipitous discovery; it unveils hidden potential and talent.

For many Liberian women, the quest for knowledge has helped them uncover skills and capabilities that lay dormant because of socio-cultural constraints.

This journey is not without its challenges; they often face a noisome environment filled with societal expectations that dismiss the importance of female education.

However, those who persevere emerge as unstoppable forces for change, even in the face of opprobrium directed towards women seeking education.

In a society that has, for too long, relegated women to mendicant roles, the audacity to seek education is revolutionary.

Education allows women to assert themselves, to engage in intellectual discourse, and to create futures beyond the limited horizons previously imposed upon them.

By educating female leaders, we foster an environment where young girls can flap their wings and soar unencumbered by the limitations of traditional roles.

As Machiavelli famously asserted, “Politics have no relation to morals.” Yet education imbues women with a nuanced understanding of morality, the ability to question the status quo, and to stand firmly against injustices crafted by a system blind to ethical considerations.

This moral clarity becomes their shield, protecting them from acquiescing to corrupt practices that might otherwise lead to societal degeneration.

In contrast, those who succumb to the phlegmatic complacency that fuels corruption are outdone by educated women, who emerge as instigators of reform and advocate for justice and equality.

Furthermore, education cultivates critical thinking skills, enabling women to dissect complex issues and reach enlightened conclusions.

Armed with knowledge, educated women seize opportunities in various spheres- journalism, politics, business, leadership, and medicine- often using their positions to advocate for other women and girls.

Women of valor, not cocaine invested, drug traffickers, drug cartels, political manipulators, or corrupt individuals, can become mentors, guiding the next generation toward achievements that were once deemed unattainable.

The communities benefit immensely, as the daughters of educated women often outperform their predecessors, breaking cycles of ignorance and lifting those around them.

The road to education for Liberian women is paved with myriad obstacles.

The societal narrative that positions women as inferior not only discourages them from seeking knowledge but also reinforces systemic issues that hinder progress.

By adhering to the expectations of being obsequious and compliant, many women find themselves trapped in cycles of poverty and dependency, perpetuating the stigma that they are unworthy of education.

However, education serves as the antidote to this oppression; it punctures the enigmatic facade of societal norms and reveals an empowering truth.

In addition to breaking barriers, education also instills self-worth and confidence amongst women.

The ability to read and write transforms mundane tasks into thriving opportunities for growth and realization.

Such empowerment envelops them in a state of mental audacity; they begin to envision lives filled with promise rather than resignation.

Through education, they shed the soporific tendencies of complacency and embrace their roles as leaders and change-makers.

Promoting the education of Liberian women should not be an audacious act limited to local communities, but an international mission aimed at global systemic change. Governments, NGOs, and positive civil society must collectively foster environments for female education, tackling the barriers and societal stigmas that hinder such aspirations.

Initiatives must be formulated to provide financial backing, mentorship programs, and educational resources designed for women at all stages of life.

The education of Liberian women emerges as a powerful catalyst for transformation, allowing them to navigate their futures with maturity and insight.

The words of Ms.Abigail Musu Kpakar ring true: “Go to school and be educated” stands not just as advice but as a rallying cry for a generation on the verge of initiating monumental changes.

Education opens the mind’s eye to the dynamic interplay between knowledge and morality.

This relationship ultimately reinforces the notion that women who wield pen and paper will create a legacy far richer than those who succumb to intemperance and ignorance.

As a society, we must nurture and support the educational pursuits of Liberian women, allowing them to create communities led by informed, fearless, and morally conscious individuals.

Indeed, empowering women through education is an undeniably invaluable endeavor that promises not only their personal success but also the flourishing of future generations.

The road ahead may be fraught with challenges, yet the collective spirit of educated women will illuminate the path toward a future forged in resilience, integrity, and unyielding ambition.

Ultimately, as we invest in the minds and hearts of Liberian women, we redefine life trajectories and reshape our society’s narrative into one that celebrates strength, knowledge, and equality.

World.title: The Legal and Ethical Implications of Responsibility in National Security Operations
World.content:
A few days ago, I had the opportunity to have a tête-à-tête with my friend and traditional intellectual and academic militant nephew, Binyah C. Kesselly (Kezzo), who made a comment that struck me on several national issues, particularly national security regarding our beloved motherland, Liberia, which prompted this article.

“National security is a sacred responsibility, but it is not a license to operate beyond the law. Those entrusted with protecting the Republic must protect not only its borders and institutions but also its Constitution, its citizens, their rights, and their dignity.”

President Boakai’s June 3, 2026, launch of Liberia’s National Security Strategy 2026–2036 provides particularly relevant language for discussing the legal and ethical responsibilities of security institutions.

“Security is foundational—it is both a prerequisite and a catalyst for development.”

“National security is not the sole responsibility of the traditional security sector; rather, it is a shared responsibility that encompasses good governance, justice, economic security, and social cohesion.”

“We will continue to invest in intelligence coordination, border security, and community-based policing approaches that foster trust between citizens and security agencies.”

“Our true security rests upon how well we fulfill our democratic promise.”

Samuel Kofi Woods II — National Security Advisor:

At the 2026 launch of the National Security Strategy, National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods II emphasized the people-centered character of national security. “Security must serve the people, and the people must be an active part of delivering security.”

Major General Daniel D. Ziankahn (Retired) — Military Advisor to the President: “This strategy will address both hard and soft security issues and will serve the purpose of safeguarding our nation’s sovereignty, stability, and development objectives.”

Major General Prince Charles Johnson III (Retired): The Liberian National Security Agency identifies Major General Prince Charles Johnson III as its director. It describes the NSA’s primary mission as collecting, analyzing, evaluating, and disseminating intelligence to help the president and senior policymakers make national-security decisions.

“Every Liberian is obligated to protect the national security of the country.”

National Chronicles Newspaper and Philipbert S. Browne v. Government of Liberia — Supreme Court of Liberia, 2015: The Court stated: “We see no tangible reason for the continued closure of the offices of the National Chronicles Newspaper.”

The Court concluded: “To continue to have the offices of the National Chronicles Newspaper closed without a court order long after the state of emergency is a violation of the petitioners’ rights not contemplated by law.”

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

In the intricate landscape of national security, the interplay between instructions given and actions taken can blur moral lines and complicate accountability.

At the heart of this discussion is a troubling question: can a government successfully prosecute a messenger directed to execute national-security orders while simultaneously absolving the individual who issued them, especially when those commands may carry a deceptive or criminal undertone?

The scenario raises legal, ethical, and practical challenges that warrant thorough exploration.

To unpack this conundrum, one must first contextualize the legal principles surrounding agency, liability, and national security.

In jurisprudence, the concept of agency establishes that an agent (in this case, the messenger) acts on behalf of a principal (the individual who provided the instructions).

When a clear crime is orchestrated under the guise of legitimate national security operations, the question of who bears responsibility becomes paramount.

Courts generally adhere to the principle that an agent who acts within the scope of their authority should not bear liability for actions taken in good faith, even if those directives may ultimately be deemed unlawful.

Yet, if the principal harbors malfeasance, a court may struggle to align equitable treatment of the messenger with holding the principal accountable.

The legal ramifications of such a case could prove analogous to the doctrine of vicarious liability, wherein an employer (or, in this case, a government as the agent’s principal) may be held responsible for the actions of its employees if those actions were taken in the course of employment.

However, national security operations are often shrouded in secrecy, complicating liability.

How could a court ethically navigate the testimony of a messenger acting under orders, especially if these orders implicitly involve dangerous legal interpretations?

To delve deeper, consider a hypothetical scenario in which a government agent, John, is instructed to transfer funds for a classified initiative labeled “Project Vanguard.”

Unbeknownst to John, the project’s true purpose is not to bolster national security but to line the pockets of a corrupt official.

If John carries out the transfer without awareness of the underlying fraud, can he truly be held liable for participating in a scheme he believed served his country’s interests?

Legally, he may indeed have a robust defense grounded in the doctrine of acting under lawful authority.

The burden of proof lies with the government to demonstrate not only that the messenger acted negligently but also that he had knowledge or ought to have known about the wrongdoing.

Yet, if the government pursues this case while refraining from addressing the actions of the principal directing the funds, it raises serious questions of credibility and fairness.

The optics of prosecuting only the messenger, while leaving the orchestrator free from examination, may lead the public to perceive the government’s actions as a “witch hunt.”

Such a perception could undermine public trust in the judicial system and call into question the integrity of the national security apparatus, which relies on public cooperation and secrecy.

This dilemma resonates with historical examples where messengers faced scrutiny.

Consider journalists or informants who inadvertently relay false information after being manipulated by authoritative sources.

While prosecuting an individual for disseminating misinformation may seem just, the judiciary’s moral fortitude may be compromised if the source remains unexamined.

The implications stretch beyond the courtroom; they highlight the potential for abuse in operations cloaked in national security that demand an accountability mechanism for principals directing such actions.

Drawing parallels with corporate law, consider the Enron scandal, where lower-level employees who executed orders in perceived compliance with management faced severe consequences for actions taken under managerial directives.

The disparity in accountability between those higher up in the hierarchy and those merely executing directions is a recurring theme in discussions of justice and ethics.

It underscores an innate contradiction: how can society champion ethical conduct when, often, only the lower-tier individuals face repercussions for systemic failures underpinned by higher-level misconduct?

In contexts fraught with national security implications, the challenge takes on another dimension.

The army of legal protections afforded to whistleblowers illuminates the treacherous territory surrounding accountability.

Often, individuals who expose wrongdoing must navigate a labyrinth of legal protections, which raises the question: if a messenger can present evidence of wrongdoing at the highest level, should they be granted protections that extend beyond mere employee status?

The balance of power is precarious; one misstep and trust in those safeguarding national interests could fracture, chilling legitimate voices that might otherwise shine light on clandestine activities.

The core issue then remains: how may justice not only be preserved but enhanced in multi-layered national security operations?

The judiciary, being the arbiter of morality and ethics, must function with agility to discern between lawful directives and those that mask criminality.

A judicial framework robust enough to hold principals accountable while adequately protecting messengers is critical.

It requires comprehensive oversight from legislative bodies, clear guidelines for prosecuting individuals involved in national security, and an unwavering commitment to ethical legal practices.

An effective solution could emerge in the formation of independent oversight committees.

These bodies could investigate allegations of misconduct and serve to bridge the accountability gap by assessing the legality of actions taken by both messengers and principals.

Such an initiative would not only serve as a legal mechanism but also signal transparency and a commitment to ethical governance.

As governments navigate the complex ethics and laws surrounding national security operations, prosecuting messengers while shielding principals risks diminishing public confidence and casting doubt on the intentions of those at the helm.

Striking a balance that holds everyone accountable, especially those who may exploit the veil of national security, is not only a judicial necessity but also a societal imperative.

Through proactive legal frameworks and a vigorous commitment to ethical governance, it is possible to address this intricate scenario, which remains central to the discourse on ensuring justice and integrity in governance.

The pursuit of justice should ensure that while messengers are protected for following lawful orders, principals issuing dubious commands are held equally accountable, thus fortifying the very foundations on which societal trust rests.

World.title: The Dangers of Misleading Rhetoric: Analyzing Political Discourse and Youth Empowerment in Liberia
World.content:
“Never allow a politician or political activist to think for you. Listen carefully, examine the evidence, ask difficult questions, and then reach your own conclusion. A generation that allows empty rhetoric to dictate its choices risks surrendering its future to people who have done little to build it.”

“The strength of Liberia’s young people will not be measured by how loudly they repeat political rhetoric, but by how intelligently they evaluate it. Whether an allegation concerns crime, corruption, or drug trafficking, demand evidence and respect the rule of law. Let the courts speak before you allow politicians to speak for your conscience.”

“Liberian Youth, do not let Political Rhetoric think for you.”

“Young Liberians must learn to reach their own conclusions through facts, evidence, and reason. Do not surrender the direction of your life to empty political rhetoric from individuals who have added little or no value to your progress. Your future belongs to those who educate themselves, think independently, and act responsibly.”

“Your mind is your power. Your voice is your future. Do not surrender either to political manipulation.”

“In this second half of the 21st century, Liberia’s youth must graduate from the politics of slogans to the politics of evidence. When individuals are arrested in connection with alleged drug trafficking or drug cartels, let the courts determine the facts. Justice requires due process—not political noise, premature judgment, or manipulation of public opinion.”

“The Future of Liberia Belongs to an Informed Youth.”

“Young Liberians, do not become prisoners of political propaganda. Your life, education, character, and future are too valuable to be dictated by individuals who offer rhetoric without results. Think independently, respect due process, follow the evidence, and have the courage to reach conclusions based on truth rather than political convenience.”

By: Austin S Fallah – A True Son of the Planet Earth Soil: [email protected]

In contemporary Liberia, a nation battered by a tumultuous past and striving for a better future, an alarming trend exists: politically uneducated and self-proclaimed leaders misuse platforms to spread misinformation and toxic rhetoric.

This phenomenon does not merely affect political discourse; it poses a significant risk to the intellectual and moral fabric of Liberia’s youth.

It is essential to dissect this situation and confront the reality that the culture of misleading rhetoric must cease, for the sake of young minds and the nation’s future trajectory.

Indeed, the conversations that dominate social media platforms today often serve to misinform rather than enlighten, spreading a toxic narrative that could derail progress and stability in Liberia.

The Role of Discourse in Leadership:

The nature of political discourse shapes public perception and the course of national development.

Unfortunately, in Liberia, much of the rhetoric espoused by influential figures lacks substance.

Rather than offering actionable insights and constructive criticism, such figures often resort to what can only be described as “political tautology”: statements that sound profound but lack meaning and substance.

This pattern of communication is corrosive; it undermines the very foundation of political engagement and civic responsibility, especially among the youth, the future leaders of Liberia.

Liberia’s youth are at a critical juncture. They stand on the precipice of possibility, equipped to catalyze change and innovation.

However, when they are bombarded with vacuous rhetoric that glorifies self-interest over national interest, they are ensnared in a web of cynicism and disillusionment.

This narrative invites young people to adopt a dangerous mindset, one in which engagement with their country’s problems is either seen as futile or, worse, as a betrayal of their identity.

The Poison of Misinformation on Social Media:

Social media platforms, in particular, have emerged as battlegrounds for ideological conflict.

While these platforms can facilitate important dialogue about national issues, they can also poison young minds.

The misuse of these platforms by individuals who claim political leadership has led to an atmosphere of suspicion and animosity, where hateful and divisive narratives predominate.

This dynamic not only stifles meaningful discourse but also actively dismantles the ideals of unity and progress that Liberia so desperately needs.

The danger lies in the heavy reliance on sensationalism that hallmarks much of the political dialogue on social media.

Young people often find themselves consuming information that is heavily biased, or worse, entirely fabricated.

Studies indicate that misinformation spreads more rapidly than factual content, implicating social media in cultivating a culture of distrust.

When influential leaders engage in this practice, they effectively co-opt the youth into a cycle of negativity that discourages critical thinking, innovation, and productive discourse.

Thus, young people’s potential to become problem-solvers and national builders diminishes, giving way to a generation more focused on blame than on solutions.

Moving Beyond Tautologies: The Path to Empowerment:

To pull Liberia out of its persistent state of underdevelopment, a paradigm shift in rhetoric is paramount.

The youth must be nourished by ideas that encourage creativity, innovation, and critical thinking.

As such, leaders, both emerging and established, must replace empty promises and oversimplified narratives with grounded discussions that promote growth and national pride.

Liberians are yearning for a dialogue that emphasizes actionable solutions rather than empty platitudes.

Intellectual engagement is essential to creating an informed citizenry capable of tackling complex social, economic, and political issues.

The youth must be encouraged to engage with contemporary challenges in a way that fosters entrepreneurial spirit and technological literacy.

Rather than falling prey to the allure of sensationalist headlines, they should be driven to seek out knowledge, engage in constructive debate, and work toward solutions that uplift the community.

Highlighting the Imperative of Development:

Development must be the centerpiece of Liberia’s future narrative.

A nation cannot thrive on empty rhetoric or the transient popularity of social media influencers; it requires a collective movement toward substantive progress.

This entails not only economic growth but also social well-being, encompassing education, health, and civic engagement.

The challenge lies in transforming abstract concepts of development into tangible realities that resonate with the daily lives of Liberians.

Real development is woven into the fabric of society through initiatives that empower the youth, those who will inherit this nation.

Educational institutions must be revitalized to embrace 21st-century skills that dovetail with technological advancements. Programs should promote critical thinking, entrepreneurship, and innovation, as these are essential in preparing young people to compete in a globalized economy.

Eliminating the “good-for-nothing” rhetoric that so deeply pervades the discourse is crucial.

What needs to replace it is a commitment to integrity, leadership, and communal advancement.

A collective endeavor is necessary to foster an environment where young people can see their potential mirrored in the efforts of political leaders and role models.

They must understand that the pathway to the presidency, and indeed to any form of leadership, lies in lifting those around them, building a community that embraces shared aspirations rather than divisive rhetoric.

Toward a Cohesive Liberian Identity:

In essence, Liberia faces the imperative of personal and communal reinvention, urged on by the recognition that youthful minds are the bedrock of future leadership.

The challenge of misleading rhetoric from self-proclaimed, politically unqualified figures must be met with a resolute stand against toxicity in discourse.

As a society, we must champion messages that inspire, empower, and lift the intellectual and moral aspirations of young Liberians.

Only then can the nation move beyond the remnants of its troubled past to adopt a forward-thinking approach that seeks not just to fill positions of power, but also to cultivate meaningful contributions from all corners of society.

The days of empty, unverifiable logic and hollow promises made in pursuit of political power are numbered.

The youth are increasingly aware, and they will not stand for an intellectual environment that fosters ignorance over enlightenment.

The road ahead demands a concerted effort to engage young people with sincerity, provide authentic narratives, and encourage their participation in an evolving Liberia that promises greater opportunity for all.

Development is not merely key to progress; it represents an essential commitment to building a cohesive and vibrant Liberian identity that honors both the past and the future.

Only through development can Liberia hope to heal, grow, and rise to its fullest potential.

World.title: Liberia: Grand Bassa Mourns Former Superintendent Baikpeh
World.content:
Buchanan – The port city of Buchanan, Grand Bassa County and other parts of the county are in the moment of deep sorrow as they morn the passing of their immediate for Superintendent, Janjay Baikpeh.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The cause of death has not been established, but the former Grand Bassa County chief administrator died at a hospital in Accra, Ghana, where he had gone to seek medical attention.

Initial Health Report

In earlier years, reports circulated that Supt. Baikpeh was hit with an “unknown illness” and had been transferred for treatment. At that time, a family source clarified he was “gradually recovering” and did not suffer a stroke.

CDC Eulogizes Baikpeh

The former ruling Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) released a statement of eulogy moments following the confirmation of his death.

The party, in a statetement signed by National Chairman Atty. Janga Augustus Kowo, the party said it received the news “With profound grief and a deep sense of revolutionary loss.”

The CDC described Baikpeh as “Our compatriot, comrade, and leader” whose passing represents a major loss to the party and Grand Bassa County.

The CDC recalled Baikpeh’s years of service to the party, noting he was a tested servant of the people, a disciplined revolutionary, and a steadfast son of the Mighty Congress.

“His passing has robbed the CDC of an erudite comrade, a courageous political soldier, and a leader whose loyalty to the cause remained firm through the most difficult seasons,” the statement added.

In honor of the late chairman, the CDC directedthe immediate hanging of a symbolic black cloth at the CDC Temporary National Headquarters as a visible expression of mourning and revolutionary solidarity.

The party extended condolences to the bereaved family and Grand Bassa County.

“The Political Leader, National Executive Committee, and entire membership of the CDC stand in grief and solidarity with the Baikpeh family, our comrades in Grand Bassa County, and the people of Grand Bassa County during this painful hour,” added the CDC statement.

Janjay’s Life With The CDC

During his time with the CDC, the late Baikpeh served as Vice Chairman for Operations of the Revolutionary National Youth League (RNYL), and was the CDC’s senatorial candidate for Grand Bassa County in the 2023 elections.

Until his death, the former Grand Bassa County Superintendent served as Chairman of the CDC Grand Bassa County Chapter.

World.title: Mundubile petition window closes as courts shut for business
World.content:
The window for losing presidential candidate Brian Mundubile to petition the results of the August 13 general election closes today amid the closure of court premises in Lusaka and several other parts of the country, with police deployed at some of the affected judicial facilities.

The developments have placed particular attention on the Constitutional Court because today marks the final day on which Mundubile can challenge the election of President Hakainde Hichilema. There had been no confirmation by Sunday evening that Mundubile had lodged his petition.

Under Article 105 of the Constitution, a challenge to a presidential election result must be lodged within seven days of the declaration. President Hichilema was declared winner on August 16 with 2,965,326 votes against Mundubile’s 1,856,217, making today the final day available for a petition to be filed.

The Supreme Court premises in Lusaka have been closed today for what has been described as “security reasons”, while reports indicate that the High Court and Constitutional Court premises have also been affected. Police tape has been placed around parts of the court premises, restricting access.

Some Local Courts have equally been closed, with scheduled cases adjourned to later dates. Information circulating around the Judiciary indicates that the affected courts will remain closed until further notice.

The closure has immediately raised questions over how litigants with time-sensitive matters are expected to access the courts, particularly Mundubile, whose constitutional window for challenging the presidential election expires today.

The situation is not confined to Lusaka. High Court premises in Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone have also been reported closed or inaccessible, with police officers deployed at the facilities.

In Chipata, the High Court premises were sealed off by armed police officers, with no one being allowed access. Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer Robertson Mweemba referred questions concerning the closure to the Zambia Police Service spokesperson.

In Livingstone, the High Court premises were also closed, with a heavy police presence guarding the area. Similar scenes were reported at the Ndola High Court, where police officers were deployed around the premises.

The simultaneous restrictions at judicial premises have attracted political attention because they have occurred on the final day available for Mundubile to commence his presidential election challenge.

Former politician Muhabi Lungu said he personally visited the High Court premises in Lusaka and found the gates closed and police tape around the facility.

“The High Court premises are closed. Gates closed and are yellow police like tape, the one we see in the movies that screams ‘Crime Scene, do not pass beyond this point’,” Lungu wrote.

Lungu said he had passed the High Court at about 07:45 hours and later returned to the premises, expressing shock at what he witnessed and the information he subsequently received.

Phoenix FM Zambia also reported that the High Court, Constitutional Court and Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security premises were visibly closed with tight security, pointing out that the development had occurred on August 24, the final day for Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance presidential candidate Mundubile to file his challenge against the August 13 presidential election results.

The closures come at a difficult moment for Mundubile, who contested the election under the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) banner backed by the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance.

Mundubile is reported to have sought protection at United Nations agency premises in Lusaka following security operations after the election. As of Sunday evening, he had not lodged the anticipated presidential petition, according to sources close to the matter.

His position has also become more complicated following developments within his political camp. NRPUP Secretary General Nonde Mubanga announced on Sunday that the party was withdrawing from the Tonse Alliance, saying the party needed to reposition itself around its own long-term objectives.

NRPUP president Ezra Tembo, the party’s legally registered leader and newly elected Member of Parliament for Dag Hammarskjöld, has separately conceded the presidential election outcome and called on Zambians to give President Hichilema and the UPND space to govern.

Resolute Party president Martin Phiri and Tonse Alliance Secretary General Chris Zumani Zimba have also distanced themselves from pursuing a legal challenge. Zimba has warned against continuing with confrontational post-election politics and has instead advocated political dialogue and reconciliation between the competing political camps.

Civil society lawyer Linda Kasonde, who had been exploring a separate citizen-led petition, also said last week that she did not have sufficient evidence to proceed with such a challenge.

Against that background, the closure of court premises today has introduced another dimension to the approaching deadline.

Opposition-linked statements circulating online have accused Chief Justice Mumba Malila, as head of the Judiciary, and Judiciary administrators of deliberately closing the superior courts to prevent Mundubile from filing his petition. Other statements have accused President Hakainde Hichilema of directing the closure.

The Judiciary has cited security reasons for the closure. However, the timing has led to demands for a fuller explanation of what security circumstances necessitated closing the courts on the final day for filing a presidential election petition and what arrangements, if any, have been made for urgent and constitutionally time-bound filings.

Social media commentator Andrew Kazembe raised concerns about the implications for judicial independence, arguing that if courts were closed in circumstances that prevented a lawful election petition from being lodged, serious constitutional questions would arise regardless of which political party or candidate was affected. He called for transparency over who authorised the closures and the reasons behind the decision.

Mwamba Payne Kapema similarly linked the court closures to allegations of election rigging, writing that the developments reinforced her concerns over the handling of the election.

The dispute follows the declaration of President Hichilema as winner of the August 13 presidential election. Final consolidated results from all 226 constituencies gave Hichilema 2,965,326 votes, or 60.49 percent, against Mundubile’s 1,856,217 votes, or 37.87 percent.

Mundubile and sections of the opposition have disputed the fairness of the electoral process and raised allegations concerning vote counting, verification and result management.

Opposition representatives have also alleged that the Electoral Commission of Zambia halted vote counting at a stage when Mundubile was leading, and have linked that interruption to their broader complaints about the final results.

The appropriate forum for determining such allegations would ordinarily be the courts, where claims can be supported by evidence, challenged by respondents and determined under the Constitution.

That is what makes today’s closure particularly consequential. Beyond the political arguments surrounding the election itself, the immediate question is whether Mundubile has practical access to the Constitutional Court registry before the seven-day period expires.

The Wake Up Campaign for a Better Zambia has separately urged Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu not to rush into seeking asylum and instead allow the police to clear them of any allegations through established legal processes.

Government has yet to issue a detailed statement addressing the court closures and their relationship, if any, to today’s petition deadline.

The Judiciary and Zambia Police Service are now expected to clarify the security circumstances behind the closures, which judicial facilities are affected, how long the restrictions will remain in place and, most importantly, whether arrangements have been made to receive urgent filings despite the physical closure of the premises.

For Mundubile, however, the constitutional clock continues to run.

With the petition window expiring today and court premises in Lusaka, Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone closed or under restricted access, attention now turns to whether Mundubile will manage to lodge his presidential election petition before the deadline and whether the Judiciary will explain how access to the Constitutional Court is being maintained on the final day available for the challenge.

World.title: Women volleyball team leaves for Nairobi
World.content:
The Zambia Women’s National Volleyball Team this afternoon left the country for Nairobi, Kenya for the 2026 African Volleyball Confederation, African Women’s Volleyball Nations Championship.

The continental championship will run from , August 23rd to September 5th, 2026, in Nairobi, with Zambia aiming to make a strong impression at the competition.

Zambia Volleyball Association (ZAVA) has stated that the 14-member squad is headed by setters Sally Bwalya and Annie Kalaba, while the middle blockers are Mwelwa Ngosa, Isabel Mudenda, Jane Kamwa and Limpo Mombotwa.

The outside attackers are Alice Nankamba, Naomi Kahalu, Betina Zulu and Beene Matongo.The association said the team also includes opposites Lubasi Nakena and Beatrice Besa, as well as liberos Tendai Zulu and Belia Ngoyi.

And Coach Arnold Simulezi, who will be assisted by Lloyd Mweemba and Monde Akalaluka, has assured that the girls are ready for the championship after seven days of training.

Meanwhile, ZAVA described Zambia’s participation in the continental championship as an important milestone in the continued development and promotion of volleyball in the country.

The association has also recognised the support of the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, the National Sports Council of Zambia, sponsors, partners, stakeholders and the media in promoting national sport.

World.title: Pule Urges Opposition to Respect Election Outcome
World.content:
Christian Democratic Party President Professor DANIEL PULE has called on all opposition leaders to respect the outcome of the 2026 General Election and move on.

Professor PULE says petitioning the election results could delay national reconciliation, unity, peace and development.

He has further cautioned that, given the current political atmosphere, a petition could risk the lives of innocent citizens and trigger unnecessary disturbances.

Professor PULE says the Christian Democratic Party, having participated in the elections, is confident that Zambians have spoken through the ballot and chosen to retain President HAKAINDE HICHILEMA for a second term.

He has congratulated the President-elect on the victory in the just-concluded General and Presidential Elections.

In a statement released to ZNBC News, Professor PULE said the time has come for Zambians to put the past behind them, unite and focus on rebuilding the country.

He said Zambia needs healing more than ever and has urged political leaders to put national interests above personal interests.

Professor PULE has emphasized that campaigns are now over and all Zambians should focus on building the country, stressing that Zambia is bigger than any individual or political party.

He has reaffirmed the Christian Democratic Party’s commitment to a peaceful, united and prosperous Zambia.

World.title: UPND Urges Commonwealth, EU to Apply Consistent Standards
World.content:
The United Party for National Development -UPND- has called on the Commonwealth and European Union to apply consistent standards when addressing alleged security threats and political violence in Zambia.

UPND Media Director MARK SIMUUWE says international organisations should be careful not to issue statements that may appear to support or ignore terrorism, insurgency or violence.

Mr. SIMUUWE says the same measures applied to such threats in other parts of the world should equally apply to Zambia.

In a statement to the media, Mr. SIMUUWE said the Commonwealth and EU should be concerned by reports of the alleged militarisation of an opposition political party and activities that may threaten national security.

He added that political affiliation should not shield anyone from scrutiny where there are credible allegations of organised violence or unlawful possession of military weapons.

Mr. SIMUUWE said the UPND supports fair investigations and respect for people’s rights, but the law must apply equally to everyone regardless of political affiliation.

He said political parties should not have armed or military groups, and any claims of terrorism, violence or illegal possession of weapons should be properly investigated by the law.

Mr. SIMUUWE has called on the Commonwealth, European Union and other international partners to support Zambia’s democratic institutions while respecting the country’s independence.

World.title: NRPUP Pulls Out of Tonse Alliance
World.content:
The National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity -NRPUP- has, with immediate effect, pulled out of the TONSE Alliance.

NRPUP Secretary General NONDE MUBANGA announced the development at a press briefing this evening.

Mr. MUBANGA said this follows the NRPUP’s careful consideration in collaboration with stakeholders.

He also said the party has objectively made the decision to pull out of the TONSE Alliance owing to the prevailing circumstances in the nation.

Mr. MUBANGA said the party will, in due course, chart the way forward on its political affiliation.

World.title: Buyzed Campaign Founder salutes re-election of President Hichilema
World.content:
BuyZed Campaign Founder, Evans Ngoma, has noted that the re-election of President Hakainde Hichilema as Zambia’s President for the second term, entails his responsibility to further unite the country and deliver development as demonstrated in his previous term.

Speaking during a press briefing in Lundazi District in Eastern Province, Mr Ngoma who also congratulated President Hichilema, called for calm, responsible political conduct and, thorough, professional and impartial investigations into allegations of political violence, and any attempts to undermine Zambia’s democratic process and national security.

Mr Ngoma stated that while serious allegations must not be swept under the carpet, investigations must be guided by evidence, due process and the constitutional principle that every suspect is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

“Let the evidence speak and let the law take its course,” Mr Ngoma said.

He also urged all political leaders and their supporters to desist from using misinformation, disinformation and inflammatory rhetoric that could heighten political tensions and create hostility among Zambians.

And Mr Ngoma charged that being in opposition should never become a licence to deliberately mislead citizens, spread fear, promote hatred or create conditions capable of disturbing national peace.

He further commended National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) President Ezra Tembo for demonstrating statesmanship by accepting the election outcome announced by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ), congratulating President Hakainde Hichilema and the United Party for National Development (UPND) on their victory.

He says such political maturity is important for Zambia, particularly following a highly competitive election.

Mr Ngoma welcomed Mr Tembo’s call for Zambia to move beyond electioneering and concentrate on economic and social development.

He said once elections are concluded, elected leaders must return to work and serve the people who gave them the mandate.

“Elections must have a beginning and an end. Members of parliament must return to their constituencies and represent the people. Mayors and council chairpersons must lead development in their respective councils, while councillors must serve their wards,” he added.

Mr Ngoma said Zambia needs a strong but responsible opposition that provides constructive checks and balances while supporting policies and programmes that advance the national interest.

He cited the Constituency Development Fund CDF) as an example of a development programme that should be supported when it benefits citizens, regardless of political affiliation.

He says Zambia’s peace is bigger than any political party or individual political ambition.

He therefore urged Zambians across the political divide to remember that political fortunes can change, with one party in government today and another tomorrow, but that the people remain neighbours, relatives, workmates and citizens of the same Republic.

Mr Ngoma further implored political leaders and citizens to put Zambia first, respect constitutional institutions, allow investigations to proceed without interference, and resolve political differences through lawful and democratic means.

World.title: Late Mbala mayor-elect put to rest
World.content:
Mbala Mayor-elect Steward Simutenda, who died on Wednesday, August 19, 2026, has been put to rest.

Scores of Mbala residents turned up at Mbala Central Seventh Day Adventist Church, to pay their last respects to the late Mr Simutenda.

Speaking during the church service, Seventh Day Adventist Church Pastor, Bryson Katele encouraged the family and believers to find solace in God.

Pastor Katele urged mourners to remain firm in their faith, saying death is not the end for those who believe in God.

And speaking at Mutambalike Cemetery, where the late Mr Simutenda was laid to rest, United Party for National Development (UPND) Saise Lawmaker Remmy Sikazwe described the mayor’s death as shocking.

Mr Sikazwe commended Mbala residents for demonstrating unity during the funeral.

“This gathering has demonstrated the unity that exists among the people of Mbala, and we should continue with this spirit of togetherness even beyond the funeral,” said Mr Sikazwe.

Meanwhile, Mbala Central Member of Parliament Raphael Chilufya urged the bereaved family to remain united during the difficult period.

Mr Chilufya pledged to work with the family and the people of Mbala in honour of the late mayor, stressing the importance of supporting one another.

And Mbala District Commissioner, Jestus Sikazwe, in a speech read on his behalf by Mbala District Livestock Coordinator, Jones Kabaso said the late mayor-elect was a dedicated individual who demonstrated commitment in serving the community.

The District Commissioner said Mr Simutenda’s dedication to public service and community development will be remembered by the people he served.

“He was passionate about working for the people even during his time as Councillor for Kazimolwa Ward, as well as through his personal business activities,” he said.

Mr Simutenda died on Wednesday, August 19, 2026 at Mbala General Hospital after an illness

World.title: Govt. praised for security measures
World.content:
Former Special Assistant to the President for Policy, Project Implementation, and Monitoring under the late President, Levy Mwanawasa, Jack Kalala, has commended the government for taking steps to safeguard the country.

Mr Kalala has emphasised that such measures should remain within the law, be necessary, proportionate, in addition to the rule of law being fully observed.

He made the remarks in a statement issued to the media, in response to the Commonwealth’s comment and position regarding recent events in the country.

Mr Kalala highlighted that priority must be to preserve peace, protect lives and property, and ensure that Zambia remains stable and secure.

“Zambians should understand that the measures taken to protect national security and maintain peace and stability are ultimately aimed at safeguarding their lives, property, and livelihoods,” Mr Kalala stated.

And, underlining the evidence reportedly recovered from a named house in Kabulonga, particularly weapons and indications of preparations, Mr Kalala wondered why given such evidence, the Commonwealth expected the government not to act rather than allow potentially dangerous plans to proceed.

He further pointed out that when there is an imminent threat to national security, the government has a duty to take lawful measures to prevent greater loss of life and destruction.

Mr Kalala also expressed deep regret over the loss of life during the process, emphasising that such loss should never be taken lightly.

Meanwhile, Mr Kalala stated that the international community must also recognize that Zambia has laws and institutions in place.

“Under such circumstances, it would have been irresponsible for the government to ignore credible threats and wait until the situation escalated into something far worse,” he added.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 24, 2026
World.content:
30 Killed as Rubbish Mound Collapses in Guinea

At least 30 people have been killed and 22 injured after a mound of rubbish collapsed onto homes at a major waste site in Conakry, Guinea, following heavy rain. Six of the injured are in serious condition. Fears remain that the death toll could rise. Rescue teams, including the military, have been searching through the debris with excavators for survivors. Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah visited the site to oversee the response. The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses . A similar landslide at the waste site killed 10 people in 2017.

DR Congo and M23 Rebels Agree on Peace Roadmap



The Democratic Republic of Congo government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group have agreed on a roadmap for peace talks after five days of negotiations in Switzerland. The deal includes a mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations and sets timelines for negotiations under a 2025 US-brokered peace framework. However, disagreements remain over sanctions, detainees and political reforms. The latest negotiations were attended by M23, the government of DR Congo, Qatar, the US, the Republic of Togo, the African Union Commission and host Switzerland. Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo despite previous ceasefire commitments, with the conflict having killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

Mogadishu Home Demolitions Spark Clashes

The demolition of homes in Mogadishu's Tookiyo neighbourhood has sparked clashes between government forces and residents resisting the operation, with nearly 10 people reportedly injured. Authorities began demolishing homes as part of efforts to reclaim land considered government property. Residents have said that they have lived in the area for decades and are demanding clarity over land ownership and a proper legal process. Concerns are growing over further violence and displacement. The Somali government has yet to issue an official statement on the reported injuries.

Nigeria Police Rescue 75 Kidnap Victims

Nigerian police have rescued 75 people, including men, women and children, after they were kidnapped from commercial buses in Kaduna State. The victims, identified as Fulani travellers, were abducted by gunmen on August 19. They were held inside a cave in a mountainous forest near Birnin Gwari. Police, acting on intelligence from the local transport workers' union, raided the area and forced the kidnappers to flee, rescuing all 75 victims unharmed. Authorities urged residents to remain vigilant and share information with police while warning against vigilante action. They further warned members of the public against taking the law into their own hands, cautioning that vigilante actions or reprisals could escalate violence and result in the loss of innocent lives.

Close 

Mystery Elephant Deaths Alarm Kenya Conservationists

Since June, at least 20 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem have died after developing symptoms of extreme weakness and paralysis, leaving conservationists and Maasai communities searching for answers. The Kenya Wildlife Service has said that toxicology tests found high levels of cyanide in some carcasses, raising suspicions of pesticide poisoning. However, local wildlife experts dispute the theory. They said that scavengers feeding on the carcasses have not shown signs of poisoning. Authorities have said that there is currently no evidence of an infectious disease. Investigations continue to determine what is killing the elephants.

World.title: South Africa: Cape Town Taxi Violence Sparks Talks - South African News Briefs - August 24, 2026
World.content:
Cape Town Taxi Violence Sparks Talks

The Western Cape Department of Mobility is engaging taxi industry stakeholders following a recent flare-up of taxi-related violence in Cape Town, reports EWN. Four men were killed and two wounded in two separate shootings. An informal trader was also shot dead at Dunoon Taxi Rank. The latest violence comes weeks after authorities mediated a deadly dispute between four taxi associations over routes in the southern suburbs. The department has said that it is working with stakeholders on measures to restore stability. The South African National Taxi Council (SANTACO) is attempting to facilitate peace talks between rival associations.

Three More Arrested Over Boxer Zolani Tete Murder



Eastern Cape police have arrested three more suspects in connection with the murder of former two-division boxing world champion Zolani Tete, reports SABC News. This brings the total number in custody to four. Tete, 38, was shot dead outside his home in Mdantsane. A 27-year-old woman travelling with him was wounded and remains in hospital. One of the suspects, a 22-year-old man, has been charged with murder and attempted murder and is due to appear in the Mdantsane Magistrate's Court. Police say further arrests are expected.

Steve Biko Death Inquest Set to Resume

The reopened inquest into the death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko is set to resume at the Gqeberha High Court, nearly five decades after he died in police custody, reports EWN. Biko was arrested in August 1977 and died weeks later from severe injuries sustained in custody. A 1977 inquest accepted the police account that he had been injured in a scuffle, and no one was prosecuted. The new inquest will examine whether any acts or omissions surrounding Biko's death amounted to criminal offences, potentially providing long-awaited answers to his family and the country.
