World.title: Africa: The Deadly Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak Can Be Stopped
World.content:
Dr Mohamed Janabi (WHO Regional Director for Africa -left), Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus (WHO Director-General - center), and Dr Jean Kaseya (Director-General of Africa CDC -right) at a press briefing in Kinshasa during a joint high-level mission to Uganda and DRC on 4 and 5 August 2026.

guest column

Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we first go to listen.

In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas. Their message is direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They are right.

Ebola spreads through communities, and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it. They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help identify and trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through access to treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response always moves faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.



Communities are not just part of the response. They are at its heart." - Tedros

One hundred days ago, the Government of the DRC declared the country's 17th Ebola outbreak following confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus. WHO subsequently declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, followed by Africa CDC's declaration of a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security.

Priorities are clear: reach every affected area, protect frontline workers and turn commitments into action.

The scale of the emergency is immense. As of 21 August 2026, the DRC has reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths across 56 health zones. This is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded, and it is moving faster than any previous one. It is being fuelled by insecurity caused by decades of armed conflict that have undermined law, order and social services and displaced more than a million people.

At the centre of the response are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.

They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure and hard-to-reach areas. Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty.

Their service must be met with action: safety, protective equipment, training, sufficient medical supplies, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill. The safety of frontline workers is central to stopping transmission.

The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, Africa CDC and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.

Uganda has interrupted locally acquired transmission of the virus. Several health zones in northern Ituri province and South Kivu have also interrupted transmission. These experiences prove that the outbreak can be stopped more quickly when rapid detection, decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities break the chains of transmission. But the continued emergency in Ituri and five other provinces demands urgently scaled up action.

To turn the corner, surveillance teams are being expanded and equipped to detect cases early and rapidly identify contacts. Safe clinical care and infection prevention measures are being increased wherever people seek treatment. More risk communication and community engagement teams are being deployed to reach out to communities to empower them to participate in the response and address barriers to care. More safe and dignified burial teams are working to prevent transmission associated with deaths. Special efforts are being made to reach vulnerable populations and communities in insecure and hard-to-reach areas.

But despite all these efforts, more is needed. We need to scale our response by two to three times current capacities, across all the response pillars.

Front-line workers' safety is essential to stopping Ebola.

Health facilities require urgent protection from infection. As of 20 August 2026, 158 health workers have been infected and 45 have died. Every facility in an affected or high-risk area needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water, sanitation and functioning infection-prevention systems.

National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Local organisations need direct support to work consistently with communities. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.

Delayed financing costs lives. Fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both. On the ground we at WHO and Africa CDC have established tight integration among health and relief organizations working with the government. Donors therefore need to support and enhance that integration, rather than support siloed and disconnected efforts.

Cross-border also coordination must remain strong. People move within and between countries to trade, work, study, seek care and support their families. Borders must serve as bridges for coordinated public health action. This does not require closing borders or imposing blanket travel and trade restrictions. Such measures can disrupt response operations and livelihoods without stopping transmission.

Close 

The priority is coordinated surveillance, rapid information-sharing and prepared health services along movement routes. Find every case. Follow every contact. Break every chain of transmission, protect every health and frontline worker, save lives and ensure that no community is left behind. Bring testing, and treatment closer to every affected community. Bolster cross-border coordination. Scale up international support. Turn every pledge into action.

African leadership and international support are necessary.

WHO and Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, neighbouring countries, communities and partners to deliver on these priorities. Our responsibility is to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.

Uganda and areas in DRC have shown how the course of the outbreak can be turned, through rapid detection, decisive action and close cooperation with communities. But these measures must be delivered at scale. Success depends on sustained national leadership, continental solidarity and international support. We must rise to this challenge, together.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization. Mohamed Yakub Janabi is Regional Director of the World Health Organization African Region. Jean Kaseya is Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

World.title: Congo-Brazzaville: Congo's Wealth Is Not Yet Power
World.content:
guest column

Across Africa, the decisive economic contest lies between raw material and finished product. For cotton, it is the distance from fibre to fabric. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, it is the distance from mineral and hydropower wealth to electricity, industrial capacity and productive work. The sectors differ, but the development question is the same: who captures the value created between extraction and the final product?

The Democratic Republic of Congo contains a startling share of the raw materials on which the modern economy depends. It is the world’s leading producer of cobalt. It has vast copper deposits, one of the planet’s great river systems and a population of roughly 100 million people, most of them young. On a map of the energy transition, the country appears indispensable.

On a map of lived prosperity, it looks very different. Only about 21 per cent of Congolese people have access to electricity, according to the World Bank. Poverty remains deep, insecurity persistent and the state distant or predatory for many citizens. The country’s most important economic question is therefore not how much wealth lies beneath its soil or runs through its rivers. It is whether that wealth can be converted into power, production and broadly shared opportunity.

That distinction separates endowment from development. Congo has never lacked resources. It has lacked the durable institutions and infrastructure that allow resources to become public value.

An extractive inheritance

The origins of that failure reach back to the formation of the state itself. Under King Leopold II, the Congo Free State became synonymous with forced labour and brutal extraction. Coercive labour practices persisted after Belgium assumed direct colonial rule in 1908, and a genuinely free labour market emerged only slowly before independence in 1960, according to academic research cited in the original manuscript.

The colonial economy was designed to remove value and administer territory, not to cultivate a broad Congolese political, managerial and technical class. At independence, the country inherited immense land and mineral wealth but little indigenous administrative capacity. A World Bank historical assessment cited in the manuscript describes both the shortage of trained Congolese personnel and Belgium’s effort to retain influence through technical advisers placed alongside key officials.

The crisis that followed independence, the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, Mobutu Sese Seko’s long authoritarian rule and the Congo wars deepened those institutional weaknesses. Mobutu did not invent the extractive state, but his personalised system entrenched it: institutions weakened, patronage expanded and public resources served political survival. Later conflicts and regional interventions fragmented authority further and allowed armed groups to flourish.

This history matters not because it condemns Congo to failure, but because it explains why geology alone has proved such a poor development strategy. Resources create possibilities. States, markets and public institutions determine who captures them.

From quarry to factory

The scale of the opportunity is nonetheless exceptional. The US Geological Survey estimated that in 2024 the DRC accounted for about 75 per cent of global cobalt production and roughly 55 per cent of global reserves. It was also the leading producer of tantalum and among the leading producers of copper, diamonds, tin and other strategic minerals.

These materials sit inside the energy, electronics, telecommunications, defence and manufacturing supply chains that are reshaping global commerce. Yet the familiar model remains one in which the highest-value activity occurs elsewhere. Minerals are extracted in Congo; more sophisticated processing and manufacturing take place abroad.

The policy choice is often described as one between exporting minerals and exporting products. But moving from one to the other requires more than declaring an industrial ambition. Copper processing, battery materials, electrical equipment, construction inputs, machinery and chemicals all require dependable electricity, transport, skills, capital, enforceable contracts and access to markets.

The real transition, then, is not simply from “quarry” to “factory”. It is from an extractive system to a productive one. The measure of success is not how many tonnes leave the ground, but how much capability, employment and domestic value are created before they leave the country.

The river and the grid

Congo’s most consequential industrial asset may be the one that flows through it. The Congo River and its tributaries give the country extraordinary hydropower potential. The Inga site alone has an estimated capacity of about 42,000 megawatts, which the World Bank describes as one of the world’s largest hydropower opportunities.

That number is dazzling. The national power deficit is sobering. With electricity reaching only about one in five people, the first claim on Congo’s hydropower future must be domestic: households, schools, clinics, farms and businesses that cannot develop without reliable power. The country’s National Energy Compact aims to raise access to 62 per cent by 2030, potentially reaching about 82 million people, according to the World Bank.

Power is also the bridge between Congo’s mineral base and its industrial ambitions. A processing plant cannot run on geological promise. Mines, smelters, factories and cities need generation connected to functioning transmission and distribution networks. The Inga opportunity therefore cannot be judged only by installed capacity. It must be judged by whether electricity reaches Congolese users reliably and affordably.

Regional trade could extend the value of that system. The DRC participates in the Southern African Power Pool, and electricity from Inga has historically been supplied to countries including South Africa and Zimbabwe. The World Bank has identified stronger transmission links between Inga, Zambia and the wider southern African market as strategically important.

The proposed Inga 3 project illustrates both the promise and the uncertainty. World Bank analysis cited in the manuscript places its possible generation between 2 and 11 gigawatts, depending on the final design. Congo’s position could eventually allow power to move across southern, central and eastern African pools. But “could” is the operative word. Regional electricity trade depends on finance, transmission lines, credible contracts, regulatory alignment and political confidence—not capacity estimates alone.

World Bank/ Ai Generated Congo at the centre. Country and river geometry: Natural Earth.

Europe’s interest, Congo’s choice

The strongest European connection is not a speculative cable from the Congo River to European homes. It is the prospect of a different industrial relationship. Europe seeks secure supplies of critical minerals and lower-carbon industrial inputs. Congo needs energy, jobs and greater value addition.

If renewable power can be combined with copper, cobalt and other minerals, Congo could produce more of the intermediate goods required by the energy transition. That would allow trading partners to buy higher-value Congolese output rather than raw material alone.

But the arrangement will be developmental only if industrial capacity takes root inside Congo. Supply security for foreign buyers is not the same as prosperity for Congolese citizens. The terms of contracts, the distribution of rents, local skills, environmental safeguards and the strength of domestic suppliers will decide whether a new mineral boom merely modernises extraction or changes the structure of the economy.

A young country needs work

The urgency is demographic. A World Bank assessment cited in the manuscript estimates that almost 65 per cent of the population is under 25. About 22 million people were aged 15 to 24 in 2025; that figure is projected to reach roughly 26 million by 2030. About a third of young people are neither in education, employment nor training, while roughly 40 per cent struggle to find work.

A young population is neither automatically a dividend nor inevitably a danger. It becomes an economic advantage when education, electricity, investment and functioning markets allow people to be productive. Without those conditions, demographic scale can intensify exclusion and instability.

This is why Congo’s industrial debate must be about jobs as much as exports. Capital-intensive mining can generate revenue without employing people on the scale the country requires. Processing, construction, energy, logistics, agriculture, services and regional manufacturing offer a broader employment base—but only if skills policy and industrial policy are designed together.

Peace as economic infrastructure

No such strategy can succeed while conflict continues in the east. Violence is first a human catastrophe. It is also a destruction of economic possibility: roads go unbuilt, schools are disrupted, responsible investment becomes harder and informal or illicit systems gain ground.

The IMF has identified governance weaknesses, mineral dependence, youth exclusion, conflict and the regional dimensions of insecurity among the DRC’s drivers of fragility. The implication is that peace cannot be treated as a security file isolated from economic policy.

The DRC and its neighbours have a material interest in replacing the economics of conflict with the economics of connection. Electricity links, roads, railways, ports, digital networks, agricultural value chains and lawful cross-border trade can raise the opportunity cost of destabilisation. Integration is no guarantee of peace. But an economy organised around shared production and exchange offers a stronger foundation than one organised around contested extraction.

Finance, and the test of delivery

Development institutions have begun to finance parts of this agenda. As of September 2023, the African Development Bank’s active DRC portfolio consisted of 27 operations worth about $1.45bn across transport, information and communications technology, energy, water and sanitation, and agriculture. Its 2023–2028 country strategy focuses on industrialisation, employment, infrastructure, agricultural value chains, human capital and the business environment.

The energy commitments cited in the manuscript include $22.4mn in parallel AfDB financing alongside $73.1mn of World Bank support approved in 2014 for Inga-related technical assistance. In December 2024, the AfDB was appointed mandated lead arranger for the $340mn Moyi Power Metro-Grids project, intended to bring cleaner, more reliable electricity to more than one million people in three cities.

These commitments show that Congo’s needs are recognised. They do not, by themselves, prove transformation. Portfolios, strategies and mandates are inputs. The meaningful outputs are functioning grids, reliable transport, competitive firms, transparent institutions and work that pays.

The missing chain

Congo’s agenda is often presented as a list: better mining contracts, more roads and rail, stronger security, technical education, regional power links, a better business climate. Each item is necessary. The more difficult insight is that they are interdependent.

Electricity without transmission cannot power a factory. A railway without predictable freight may not be financeable. Mineral processing without skills and reliable energy will not compete. Investment without accountable institutions can reproduce the very extractive bargain Congo needs to escape. Peace without legal economic opportunities may remain fragile.

The country therefore needs more than projects. It needs a sequence: secure productive regions; improve public institutions and contract transparency; expand electricity access and transmission; connect mines, farms and cities to markets; build technical capabilities; and use mineral and energy policy to support industries that can compete.

None of this is quick. Nor is it guaranteed. The same resources that make Congo strategically valuable also intensify struggles over rents and influence. Large infrastructure can create debt, displacement and governance risks if projects are badly designed. Regional interconnection creates opportunity, but it also requires patient diplomacy and institutions able to enforce agreements.

Yet the alternative is not stasis. Global demand for strategic minerals is placing Congo closer to the centre of the world economy. The country can remain indispensable as a source of raw materials while its citizens remain excluded from the value those materials create. Or it can use this moment to negotiate a more productive bargain.

The real test will not be whether the Democratic Republic of Congo finally “wakes”. Countries are not giants in fairy tales. They are political economies, built through choices and constrained by institutions.

Congo already has the assets. What it has not yet secured is the chain that joins them: peace to investment, power to production, minerals to industry, and national wealth to household prosperity. Building that chain would not merely alter Congo’s fortunes. It could change the economic geography of Africa.

World.title: Uganda: I'm Alive and Well Because of Jesus - Janet Museveni
World.content:
Kampala, Uganda — First Lady Mama Janet Museveni made a major public appearance on Sunday after more than five months away from the public spotlight due to health challenges, telling worshippers that 2026 will forever remain the year God "delivered" her life from the jaws of death.

Mama Janet was speaking during the consecration of her daughter, Patience Kokundeka Museveni Rwabwogo, as Bishop of Covenant Nations Church at Maya-Luzira in Kampala.

Although she made a brief public appearance several days ago during a reception for visiting American evangelist Bishop Dr LaDonna C. Osborn, Sunday's ceremony marked her first appearance before a huge gathering since her prolonged absence.

Mama Janet delivered a prayer lasting more than 14 minutes, which she used to publicly reflect on her health ordeal, Uganda's history and the growth of the church, while thanking Ugandans and Christians who prayed for her during her illness.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

She said she was grateful that people for whom she had prayed over the years, including widows, orphans and vulnerable Ugandans, also remembered her in her hour of need.

The First Lady also linked her recovery to her Christian faith, describing Jesus as "the healer, the great physician" and quoting Isaiah 53:5 on healing.

Her prayer also became a reflection on the history of Uganda, with Janet crediting God for guiding the country through years of civil war, HIV/AIDS, insurgencies, poverty and the challenges of rebuilding after conflict.

She praised President Yoweri Museveni for leading the country through what she described as a 40-year journey of rebuilding and recovery.

"It was your presence that defeated the innumerable challenges we have faced these past 40 years," she said, citing the war in northern Uganda by the Lord's Resistance Army and other conflicts.

Mama Janet said she was particularly thankful that Uganda had transformed from a war-ravaged country into a nation supporting regional peace and hosting refugees from neighbouring countries.

On the consecration of her daughter, she said it is a moment of great honour and joy for the family.

"Today, we celebrate the consecration of our daughter, Patience, to the office of a bishop," she said. "We are overwhelmed with joy and thanksgiving at the great honour you have bestowed over us in choosing one of our children to serve you in this capacity."

She said Patience answered the call to ministry 20 years ago and prayed that she and her husband, Odrek Rwabwogo, would receive "a fresh anointing of the Holy Spirit" to continue their work.

She also prayed for Covenant Nations Church to expand beyond Uganda while remaining grounded in prayer, love, and the preaching of what she called the undiluted word of God.

At the conclusion of the prayer, President Museveni ionately recognized his wife before stepping onto the podium to deliver what he described as his "brief speech." Museveni began by thanking God for his wife's recovery and also acknowledged the medical personnel and their children who supported her during her illness.

The President then commended Patience on becoming a bishop, saying the development represented a significant milestone for his family.

Museveni traced his family's encounter with Christianity, saying his ancestors had lived in the region for millions of years before the arrival of Islam and Christianity. He said Islam arrived in Uganda in the 1840s, followed by the Anglican Church in 1877 and Catholic missionaries in 1879.

According to Museveni, his great-grandparents and grandparents did not join the church nor the colonial administration, with his own family only embracing Christianity in 1947.

Museveni also praised his daughter's biblical knowledge, revealing that he had spent 12 years studying the Bible but found himself learning new things from Patience's writings.

He said he was particularly surprised by her explanation of the descendants of Lot and Esau, which led him to conclude that his daughter had studied the Bible more deeply than he had.

Close 

"So I said, this young person has really read the Bible much more than myself, I surrendered," he said.

Museveni said Patience would bring "a lot of energy" to the church and thanked Bishop Osborn and Nigerian preacher Pastor Enoch Adeboye for travelling to Uganda for the consecration.

He also used the occasion to call on religious leaders to focus on the substance of Christianity.

The ceremony was attended by Vice President Jessica Alupo, ministers, Members of Parliament and religious and cultural leaders.

Among those present were Pastor Robert Kayanja, Prince Wasajja Kiwanuka representing the Buganda Kingdom, and representatives of the Anglican, Catholic and Muslim communities.

The consecration also attracted religious leaders and dignitaries from Uganda and abroad, as Covenant Nations Church marked 20 years since Patience began pastoring the church.

As a gesture of support to his daughter, Museveni announced that he and Mama Janet would give Patience 50 cows.

World.title: Guinea: Garbage Collapse at Landfill Kills Dozens
World.content:
Heavy seasonal rains caused a mound of garbage to collapse, burying dozens of people and nearby homes before the break of dawn.

At least 30 people have died after a landfill collapsed in Guinea's capital, Conakry, officials said on Sunday.

Heavy rains overnight caused a large mound of rubbish to collapse at the Dar Es Salam landfill, burying nearby homes before dawn.

At least six other people were seriously injured.

Guinea's minister for territorial administration, Djenabou Toure, visited the site, where workers used excavators to search for more bodies.

Landfill was slated for closure

The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses.

Balde Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the Military Engineering Battalion, said the Dar Es Salam site had been slated for closure on Sunday.

Heavy seasonal rains have been known to trigger collapses at landfills in some countries, with Uganda and Ethiopia suffering similar tragedies in recent years.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Somalia: Mogadishu's 'Forced' Eviction Turns Into War
World.content:
The skyline beyond the northern suburbs of Mogadishu in Somalia, seen through a bullet hole in the window of a hotel.

The demolition of homes in Tookiyo neighbourhood, in Mogadishu's Yaqshiid district, has triggered tensions and clashes between government forces and local residents who opposed the operation. The demolitions began around midnight and were still continuing, with local reports saying nearly 10 people had been injured in the confrontation.

The operation has raised concerns among residents over the fate of families living in the area and renewed a wider dispute over land ownership and evictions in parts of Mogadishu. Residents say they have lived in Tookiyo for decades and are demanding clarity over the legal basis for the demolitions.

Government forces were accompanied by workers carrying tools used to dismantle the corrugated iron roofing of homes, according to residents and local reports. Several houses occupied by civilians were reportedly targeted during the operation.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Tensions escalated when some residents attempted to prevent the demolitions. The confrontation reportedly led to violence between the security forces and residents, with reports of gunfire in the area.

Local sources said nearly 10 people were injured in the clashes, including civilians. Reports of fatalities have also circulated, but the number of deaths has not been independently verified.

Residents said they were particularly concerned about families who could be left without shelter if the demolitions continue. Some said they had lived in the neighbourhood for many years and had no immediate alternative accommodation.

One resident said the community wanted authorities to clarify who legally owns the land before homes are demolished, arguing that families should not be removed without a clear legal process and adequate consideration for those affected.

The Somali government has not yet issued an official statement specifically addressing the operation in Tookiyo or the reported injuries. Local reports have, however, linked the demolitions to wider efforts by authorities to reclaim land considered government property.

The developments come amid continuing disputes over land ownership and evictions in Mogadishu, where residents in several areas have raised concerns about demolitions and displacement.

The situation in Tookiyo remains tense, with residents worried that further demolitions could lead to additional confrontations and displacement.

The immediate challenge for authorities is how to resolve the dispute over the land while preventing further violence and protecting civilians who live in the affected area.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia Says It Is Aware of Military Operations Off Puntland Coast
World.content:
Mogadishu, Somalia — Somalia's federal government is aware of military operations and shelling off the coast of Puntland, the state minister for defence said Saturday, amid growing concern over attacks linked to a resurgence of piracy.

State Minister for Defence Omar Ali Abdi told reporters in Mogadishu that if military operations were being carried out against pirate groups off Somalia's coast, the federal government was the legal authority responsible for authorising such actions.

"The federal government is aware of the incidents, and a comprehensive report will be submitted," Abdi said, without identifying the forces involved in the reported operations.

He said the government was preparing a detailed report on the incidents and would take measures to address the escalating situation.



His comments came hours after Puntland authorities demanded explanations over shelling they said was carried out by unidentified international warships off the region's coast on Aug. 18 and 20.

Puntland said the attacks had targeted fishermen and damaged civilian property, raising concerns over the safety of residents in coastal areas.

The Puntland Ministry of Security and Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration said it was particularly concerned about the potential impact of military operations in the Garmaal area, near coastal locations where vessels seized by pirates are reportedly being held.

The ministry warned that such operations could harm civilians who have no involvement in piracy and undermine cooperation between Puntland security agencies and international partners involved in efforts to combat maritime crime.

The latest developments come as Somali piracy has made a comeback after years of relative decline, with several commercial vessels seized in recent months in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.

Puntland authorities have previously said they were investigating information suggesting that forces outside the regional administration could be involved in the renewed piracy, but they have not publicly identified any group or country or provided evidence to support the claim.

The incidents have also raised questions over the role of foreign military forces operating against pirate groups in waters off Somalia.

The reported shelling follows the burial on Thursday of four suspected Somali pirates in Garmaal, in Puntland's Nugaal region, after what local sources described as a Turkish strike.

The men were reportedly killed when a small boat carrying individuals allegedly linked to the hijacking of a commercial vessel was targeted.

Close 

Relatives of the deceased blamed Turkey for the strike, but Turkish authorities have not publicly confirmed or commented on the reported operation.

Somalia's federal government has been seeking to strengthen coordination with international partners as it confronts the renewed piracy threat, while also asserting its authority over military operations conducted in Somali waters.

The government has not publicly disclosed details of the reported foreign operations or said which forces were responsible for the shelling.

The latest dispute comes at a sensitive time for Somalia, where authorities are trying to suppress piracy while avoiding civilian casualties and maintaining cooperation with international maritime security partners.

The Defence Ministry's promise of a comprehensive report could provide further details on the circumstances surrounding the operations and clarify the respective roles of the federal and regional authorities in responding to the renewed piracy threat.

World.title: I have eight kids. Here's why the 'back-to-school' mom memes break my heart
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Summer is the best season. My kids have no school commitments and our time is spent getting together with friends, doing weekend trips, camping, going to the lake, and enjoying the time we have with each other. My oldest is already in college so I know the feeling of time slipping through my fingers as my kids get older and create lives of their own. Time with my husband and eight children is my most precious gift and while back-to-school season is exciting, it’s certainly bittersweet.

The joy of watching my kids grow into the next stage of life is balanced out by the feeling that most of August is the Sunday before school starts.

Raising kids is hard, and it’s okay to feel a little relief when structure returns. But I think we should be thoughtful about the message our children receive in the way we celebrate.

JO FROST CALLS OUT MODERN PARENTING MISTAKES SHE SAYS ARE ROBBING CHILDREN OF BASIC LIFE SKILLS

Scrolling through social media this time of year brings meme after meme of parents, usually moms, who are thrilled the school year is starting because it’s time to ship their kids off to someone else five days a week. The photos of moms in robes on their doorstep holding a glass of wine are everywhere.

Kids notice when we seem overly eager to send them away. They remember whether we treated their presence as a burden or a gift. They hear how their parents are elated about sending them elsewhere for hours every day. Kids are much more perceptive than we give them credit for. Even if all of the back-to-school jubilation is in jest, deep down they know they are of some undue burden to their parents.

NEW STUDY REVEALS THE SINGLE MOST CRITICAL FACTOR IN WHETHER CHILDREN KEEP THEIR FAITH INTO ADULTHOOD

Conflicting emotions are common and parents shouldn’t beat themselves up over them. A study of 2,000 parents over the summer revealed 57% were happy about their kids returning to school but also felt guilty about it. Yet a different study showed 67% of parents who thought summer break was too long.

I get that parents need a break, especially from the endless snack requests and demands of kids over the summer. No parent should be shamed for taking care of themselves in order to be a better parent for their kids. Yet that’s not what back-to-school season has become. It’s become a time when parents can thrillingly announce to the world that they are so happy to dump their kids at school and make them someone else’s problem.

WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE

In a culture that has so devalued the family and children, this isn’t a surprise but it is disheartening. I used to think these kinds of posts were funny until I really thought about it. We only have so much time with our kids until they move out, go to school, and have lives of their own. I’m proud to watch my kids begin a new school year. I’m excited for what they’ll learn and who they’ll become. But I’m also sad to see summer end because I love having them home. I love the memories, the slow mornings, the time together, and the little moments that pass far too quickly.

Parenting is hard and no one could ever be prepared for it, no matter how many books they read or other parents they talk to. We have so much responsibility on our plates that it can easily be overwhelming. Humans will make decisions based on their priorities — that’s what it all comes down to. Faith, marriage, kids, work, and hobbies all vie for the top spot and we have to make hard decisions every day but if those priorities are in order, it will be much easier to choose the right thing.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

I’m not suggesting every parent homeschool or drop everything to spend 24 hours a day catering to their kids. I’m saying that our children are incredible gifts and we should not be so anxious to shove them out the door and on the school bus for eight hours a day for nine or ten months of the year. Get involved in your kid’s school. Coach their rec team. Invite their friends for a movie night or ice cream or pizza making party at your house. Go on a hike with your kids and their friends. Be present. Put your phone down. Ask questions. Say ‘yes’ more.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

We only have one life. Our kids are only young once and they see everything. I make plenty of mistakes as a mom but valuing the time I have with them is one mistake I try the hardest to avoid.

So yes, celebrate back-to-school season. Just make sure your kids know they are loved, wanted, and deeply missed when they’re away.

World.title: 9/11 is becoming history. My generation must make sure America never forgets
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

I was 9 years old, in my second week of middle school, 25 miles from lower Manhattan when the world changed.

I remember being gathered on the carpeted floor of our homeroom when the principal’s aide delivered a note to our teacher. She read it to us with a perplexed look on her face, unaware that the plane she described as having been involved in a tragic accident had passed just a few miles from our school along the Hudson River only minutes earlier.

We’d soon learn this was no accident.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

We were too young to understand the magnitude of what was happening, but old enough to know something was terribly wrong. For millennials, September 11, 2001 was the moment that divided our lives into "before" and "after."

There is an innocence in the photographs and memories from before 9/11 that is hard to explain. The people and the streets look the same, but everything feels different because we know what they did not yet know was about to happen.

MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA

And in the weeks and months after that tragic day, everything changed. We remember the anthrax scares, the new airport security measures, and the fear that another attack could happen at any moment.

But we should remember something else, too: the extraordinary sense of unity that followed. For a kid growing up just outside New York City, the shared sense of patriotism and American flags seemingly everywhere is impossible to forget. In those days, before social media became a force for division and politics consumed so much of our national conversation, Americans seemed determined to stand together.

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

I still vividly remember watching President George W. Bush’s first pitch before Game 3 of the World Series at Yankee Stadium a little over a month after the attacks. In a city still grieving, our leader in a bulletproof vest humming a strike right down the middle felt like a small but powerful sign that America was still standing, too.

But 25 years later, September 11 is becoming history rather than memory. For a younger generation, it is increasingly just a chapter in a textbook—or worse, fodder for internet conspiracy theories, memes and jokes.

TUNNEL TO TOWERS ANNOUNCES 'STEEL ACROSS AMERICA' TOUR TO MARK 25 YEARS SINCE 9/11 ATTACKS

We cannot let that happen.

As the last generation to have firsthand memories of September 11, it is incumbent on us to remind younger Americans of the extraordinary things ordinary Americans did when confronted with the unimaginable that fateful day.

If you’ve visited any of the three September 11 memorial sites — the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York, the Pentagon Memorial or the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pa. — you understand why remembrance matters.

Nearly 3,000 people died that day. They were parents, children, spouses, friends, firefighters, police officers, office workers and travelers.

Innocent people who had simply shown up for a normal day at work were suddenly forced to make horrific decisions that no person should ever have to make.

And for countless others, the consequences of that day never ended. First responders and others exposed to the toxic air at Ground Zero have spent the decades since battling cancers, respiratory illnesses and other health problems tied to September 11.

There is no shortage of stories from that day. Some are harrowing stories of survival. Others are stories of heroism and extraordinary courage.

There was Betty Ong, the American Airlines flight attendant who helped authorities understand that Flight 11 had been hijacked. There were the passengers of Flight 93, who fought back against their hijackers and prevented the plane from reaching Washington.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

There were Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark, strangers who miraculously helped one another escape the impact zone of South Tower after it was struck. And there was Rick Rescorla, the Morgan Stanley security chief who evacuated thousands from the South Tower before returning inside to help others and never making it out himself.

We were the children who watched the towers fall and the teenagers who grew up in the shadow of the two wars that followed. We are now the parents, teachers, and citizens responsible for explaining to the next generation why September 11 mattered.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

We need to tell them about the first responders who ran toward danger while everyone else ran away, the passengers who refused to surrender, and the strangers who helped strangers.

And we need to tell them why we must never let it happen again.

World.title: Four ways to make sure your will protects your family and avoids added grief
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

There is no worse feeling in life than when a loved one passes away. And when that individual has not communicated his or her wishes or shared key information, that can add an additional burden of time, money and stress to loved ones’ grief.

As August is National Make a Will Month, here are four suggestions to help you make sure you have your will made and updated in a manner that will help your loved ones sort through your estate and continue your legacy in the best manner possible.

Make your will today!

CEO’S FIRE DEATH SPARKS MYSTERY, WILL FIGHT OVER TECH TITAN'S FORTUNE

When it comes to estate planning, having a will is important. Having one that is done properly is more important. There are online services that can help you, but I recommend meeting with a local estate planning attorney.

Not only will a professional make sure that your wishes are accounted for properly, but they will understand state-specific requirements and regulations.

Moreover, many estate planning attorneys can help with more than just the legal aspects of estate planning; they can also help or find you someone to help with tax planning and any related entities, such as trusts, to make sure your assets are passed down in the most tax-efficient manner.

Explore making gifts and other plans now

RICKY GERVAIS JOKES UK INHERITANCE TAX MAY FINALLY PUSH HIM TO MARRY LONGTIME PARTNER AFTER 40 YEARS

As you meet with an estate planning professional or your accountant, you can explore making gifts to loved ones today. This may bring you more satisfaction, so that you can see your loved ones benefit from what you plan to leave them instead of waiting until you are gone.

In 2026, you can gift $19,000 individually ($38,000 for married couples) per person, tax free for the year. Again, consult a professional for assistance to make sure you are crossing all your "t’s" and dotting your "is" regarding any gifting.

Also, if you have family members who can handle the discussion, dividing up possessions, whether passed now or later, as a family can help minimize fighting among family members down the road.

Moreover, many in the younger generations aren’t interested in the same physical mementos as those who are older. If you have a china set or a collection of statues that hasn’t been used in years, and nobody in the family wants them, you can explore making plans for disposal now – whether that means selling or donating the items. This can generate extra cash, tax deductions or even find a home with someone who you know will enjoy them.

As a bonus, it will create less "cleanup" down the road for loved ones.

Make your will findable

MAN ACCUSED OF STEALING MORE THAN $735K AS POWER OF ATTORNEY TO PURCHASE PROPERTY, ONLYFANS AND LIFE COACHING

One of the biggest issues I have seen with those who have wills is that their loved ones can’t find it (or don’t know which is the most recent copy). Preparing your wishes and information but not making them accessible to your loved ones defeats the purpose.

Put your will, along with other key information (like a listing of your financial accounts and advisors or a key to your safe deposit box) and any personal wishes in a legacy and wishes planning kit. You can use one like the kit I created after my father’s passing, Future File, or you can make your own if you prefer.

As you meet with an estate planning professional or your accountant, you can explore making gifts to loved ones today. This may bring you more satisfaction, so that you can see your loved ones benefit from what you plan to leave them instead of waiting until you are gone.

Whichever route you go, make sure your family members either have access to your kit and its contents now or know how to access it and can do so in case of an emergency or if you pass.

Review your will regularly

OLIVER TREE MADE EERIE COMMENTS ABOUT HIS WILL WEEKS BEFORE FATAL HELICOPTER CRASH IN RIO DE JANEIRO

A friend of mine’s mother was gravely ill and told my friend about her will. When my friend had an estate planning attorney review it, it turned out that it did not reflect what her mother’s current wishes were; rather, it contained some changes other family members had suggested many years ago that her mother had forgotten about.

If this hadn’t been reviewed, her mother would not have left her assets to her grandchildren, but rather to distant cousins.

That underscores why it is important to review your will regularly and make any updates if circumstances change over the years.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Additionally, if you have financial accounts, retirement plans or policies, such as insurance policies, that have beneficiaries, make sure that those are up to date, accurate and match your wishes. Beneficiary designations supersede wills, and so beneficiaries will receive the payments, even if they differ from your will. Check this on a regular basis as you review and update your will.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Saving your loved ones dozens of hours of time, giving them peace of mind and reducing uncertainty and even infighting during a very difficult time are the best things that you can leave behind as part of your legacy. That only happens with the proper planning today.

World.title: Trump's Bedminster turf could make or break his last two years in the White House
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

WASHINGTON, N.J. — Washington, D.C. is undoubtedly the center of gravity in American politics, but another Washington over 100 miles away could help decide the fate of Congress for the latter half of President Donald Trump's term.

It's a small town in New Jersey where Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., urged GOP supporters to help get Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J., re-elected to the House in November. Kean is seeking a third term representing the Garden State's 7th Congressional District, which is notably home to Trump's Bedminster golf course where he spends a significant amount of time.

"We consider this a top three race, not just a top ten. That's how important it is to us. It has a target on its back," Johnson told the room at Hawke Point Golf Club, Fox News Digital heard. "They're investing tons of money to try to take [Kean] down, but they are not going to be successful."

The district happens to be one of the most critical battlegrounds in the country this year. Trump narrowly won the area by two points in 2024, though it flipped for Democrat Gov. Mikie Sherrill by the same margin in 2025.

HOW ONE NYC SUBURB COULD DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE HOUSE

Democrats are now betting they have a real opportunity to score another victory in November by sending former Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett to the House. And with such a small number of House seats still considered politically neutral, it could prove decisive for which party controls the House next year.

DEMS PICK CHALLENGER FOR GOP CONGRESSMAN WHO VANISHED FROM PUBLIC VIEW AMID HEALTH MYSTERY

If Republicans win, that means enacting Trump's agenda for another two years. Johnson told Fox News Digital the GOP has "aggressive" plans to tackle government waste and excessive spending. But if Democrats win the district — and potentially the House — Trump's goals could grind to a halt.

Kean, for his part, told Fox News Digital that he's confident he can win again.

"I've been a really effective legislator who's brought things back to the district, who's listened to my constituents on their needs and their concerns, in contrast to my opponent, who has really been a very abject partisan," Kean said on the sidelines of his event.

"She's actually stopped going to church because there are Republicans [there]. So when you think about that contrast — a person can't even go to religious services with people of the other party — she'll never work across the aisle. She'll be always in the far-left corner of whoever is in her caucus and whoever is in her leadership. And that's not what this district needs."

ANTI-SOCIALISM PUSH CAN FLIP BATTLEGROUNDS, REPUBLICAN LEADER BETS AS PARTY FIGHTS TO HOLD HOUSE

Bennett spokesperson Carly Jones hit back at Kean's accusation, "Rebecca is an active member of her local church and talks openly on the campaign trail about her faith, which inspired her to serve her country in uniform and run for office. She is proudly building a coalition of Democrats, Independents and Republicans to flip this seat in November."

Kean noted he's seen legislative success under both the Biden and Trump administrations, and his bipartisan efforts were on display — by what was not on display. The congressman's name appeared throughout the event, but without mention of "GOP" or "Republican." A sign outside the door only said "Tom Kean for Congress."

Conventional wisdom dictates that the party in power faces significant losses in Congress during the midterms. Critics of whoever is president generally turn out in droves to vote for the other side, in this case, Democrats.

Kean noted that he's had legislation signed into law by former President Joe Biden, but also insisted he backed Trump "fully."

SOCIALIST VICTORIES SHOW DEMS' DESCENT DOWN 'DEADLY PATH OF COMMUNISM,' JOHNSON WARNS

"He's done great things for this country and will continue to do great things for this country. He has been a very effective leader," Kean said of the current president.

And Johnson deployed a pinch-hitter to help gin up enthusiasm on Friday: All-Star professional baseball player Mark Teixeira, who posed for photos with excited attendees. Teixeira is running his own campaign for Congress and is likely to win a safe red seat in Texas.

Republican leaders are also seizing on the far-left insurgency that's toppled establishment Democrats in recent months as evidence that they should not get control of the House.

"It's very effective because people see what's happening. This isn't campaign rhetoric. They give us new illustrations every day," Johnson told Fox News Digital in an interview. "It's a challenge to the very foundational principles of America, and that is increasingly what the Democrat Party represents...The Marxist-communist element is taking over that party, sadly, and it's really alarming for our country."

Kean was notably absent from the campaign trail and the halls of Congress from March through June this year, with few knowing the circumstances until the congressman publicly admitted he was being treated for depression. Upon his return, he introduced legislation aimed at making it easier for people to pay for mental healthcare.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Bennett did not criticize the reason for his absence but has previously accused him of continuing to trade stocks during that time. She similarly told Fox News Digital in a written statement that Kean made millions from the stock market.

"I spent 15 years serving our country in the military, and I felt called to serve once again because I can’t sit on the sidelines while Washington corruption, rising costs, and devastating healthcare cuts crush New Jersey families. Congressman Tom Kean Jr. has failed to show up for our community while trading more than $3 million worth of stocks during his time in office," she told Fox News Digital.

World.title: Linda McMahon vows crackdown on teachers sexually harassing students: 'Must end'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Secretary of Education Linda McMahon on Sunday said the federal government is committed to "cracking down" on sexual misconduct involving teachers, staff and other adults in positions of authority in schools across the country.

In an interview, McMahon denounced what she described as school districts reassigning, rather than firing, teachers accused of misconduct involving students.

"And it’s not part of their record or anything, so we have really been cracking down on that as well," she said during an appearance on CNN's "State of the Union."

McMahon, citing a 2004 Education Department literature review, said about one in 10 eighth- through 11th-grade students reported sexual misconduct by an educator. The review used a broad definition that included physical, verbal and visual conduct; the department cautioned that sexual misconduct should not be equated with the narrower legal definition of sexual abuse.

TRUMP EDUCATION DEPARTMENT PROBES SCHOOL AFTER TEACHER ALLEGEDLY REQUIRED SAME-SEX STUDENTS TO KISS

California officials at the state’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing did not revoke the licenses of at least 67 educators after school districts determined they committed sexual misconduct against students from 2019 through 2025, according to ProPublica and KQED.

At least 14 of those educators were later hired by other school districts and at least 12 of those were still working in education as of May, according to the reports.

Separately, the Department of Education in May opened a Title IX investigation into the Los Angeles Unified School District.

"Our schools must protect America’s children. Parents should never have to wonder whether their kids’ school employs and protects sexual predators," McMahon said in a previous statement. "Schools that receive federal funding have a duty to protect students, report sexual misconduct honestly, and follow the law."

The department said it was investigating an agreement with the United Teachers of Los Angeles that it said appeared to require teachers credibly accused of certain misconduct to be reassigned, rather than terminated or immediately removed from student-facing roles, while officials investigated allegations they engaged in conduct including having a sexual or romantic relationship with a student, creating child pornography or failing to report suspected child abuse.

LAUSD and UTLA disputed the department’s characterization, saying reassignment means an employee is sent home and kept away from students while an investigation proceeds, not transferred to another classroom or school. They said termination remains possible when allegations are substantiated.

COLORADO TEACHER FIRED AFTER STUDENTS ALLEGEDLY PRESSURED TO KISS CLASSMATES IN SKITS

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

McMahon said in the letter that schools that fail to comply with federal requirements under Title IX and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act risk enforcement action, including the potential termination of applicable federal assistance, pledging a nationwide effort to "crack down" on sexual misconduct by adults in positions of authority.

"Make no mistake, the Department will fully enforce federal law and employ every resource at its disposal to protect children from sexual predators," she wrote at the time. "Those schools that allow sexual misconduct to occur risk the termination of applicable federal assistance provided by the federal government."

"This epidemic of nationwide sexual abuse in our schools must end," McMahon added.

World.title: Enes Kanter Freedom opens up on confrontation with Natasha Cloud that led to ejection, WNBA pursuit
World.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom said Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud made a vulgar remark toward him and repeatedly cursed before security removed him from Sunday night’s game against the Indiana Fever.

Freedom, who was sitting near the baseline at Wintrust Arena, said the confrontation began after he celebrated a 3-pointer by Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

"Sophie Cunningham shot a three, and I put my hands up to celebrate," Freedom said. "Literally, a couple possessions later, Natasha came back and started screaming and yelling and said, ‘She’s not gonna sleep with you.’

ENES KANTER FREEDOM MET WITH HOSTILE WNBA FANS EN ROUTE TO FEVER-SKY MATCHUP

"And I was like, ‘I am not trying to sleep with her. I’m just here to protect women and support her.’ And then, obviously, after that she started yapping, and she started to walk towards me, and literally I just got up, and then I was like, ‘I’m just here to protect women, and that’s all.’"

Video of the incident showed Cloud walking toward Freedom, yelling and pointing at him late in the third quarter. Freedom stood, extended his arms and took a step onto the court as security and Sky players moved between them.

Freedom said Cloud then began using profanity in front of young fans.

"She started to yell. She started to use some very heavy language. She started to actually cuss, and I was very shocked that there were a lot of kids and that there were a lot of teenagers at that game," Freedom said.

"I just cannot believe that she was just cussing and using those F-bombs in front of all these kids. I’m sure she’s loved in Chicago and many kids are idolizing her and stuff, but that’s not how a WNBA athlete should react."

The confrontation came with 1:22 remaining in the third quarter, after Cloud scored inside and celebrated with teammate Aicha Coulibaly. Cloud then turned and approached Freedom, who was wearing a black shirt that read, "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

He said he believes the shirt contributed to Cloud’s reaction.

"I was cheering for my friend Sophie because when she shot that three, I put my hands in the air," Freedom said. "A couple possessions later, she came back and said, ‘She’s not gonna sleep with you.’ And I was shocked. I was like, ‘Listen, I’m not trying to sleep with her. I think she’s awesome. She’s a good friend.’ But I think it has a lot to do with my shirt.

FORMER NBA STAR ENES KANTER FREEDOM WRITES LETTER TO WNBA OFFICIALLY DECLARING FOR 2027 DRAFT

"I was obviously wearing a shirt explaining what a woman is, and I think that had a lot to do with what she thinks about women. I think it triggered her a lot."

OutKick reached out to Cloud's rep for further comment. She wasn't made available during the team's postgame press conference.

Cloud sent a message to the trans community after the game, in a post on Threads.

"To every trans kid/person, You are apart of MY community & tribe. You belong. You’re loved. You’re seen. You’re perfect as you are. & you will always be protected by me," Cloud wrote.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh defended Cloud after the game, telling reporters, "We all embrace her as someone who protects our team and protects people who need to be protected."

However, Freedom insists the words exchanged with Cloud had nothing to do with the issue of transgender people or his plans to compete in the WNBA.

"Definitely not," Freedom said of the interaction being related at all to those issues.

Still, even without directly invoking the debate overshadowing the WNBA right now, Freedom was ordered out of the arena.

He said security approached him and ordered him to leave without providing an explanation.

"I was like, ‘Can you please tell me why I need to leave?’ They said, ‘Look, you just need to leave,’" Freedom said. "They pretty much pushed me to leave the gym."

Footage showed arena staff touching Freedom and sharing intense words with him as he was being escorted out. Freedom said he asked an arena employee not to touch him as he was escorted away from the court.

"I told her, ‘First of all, please don’t touch me because I didn’t do anything wrong. I can get myself out of the game,’" he said. "And the second, I was like, ‘Do you guys realize that you guys are only kicking me out of this game because I support women and I try to protect women?’"

Freedom said security again declined to give him a reason for his removal.

"They were like, ‘Listen, we can’t give you any reason right now. Just leave, please,’" he said. "I played 11 years of basketball in the NBA, and I know how tough the security’s job can get. So I didn’t want to make their job even tougher."

OutKick reached out to the Sky and Wintrust Arena for comment.

The Sky had advanced notice that Freedom would be coming to the game, according to him. He said his manager had notified Sky general manager Jeff Pagliocca before the game that he planned to attend.

"My manager texted the GM of the Chicago Sky," Freedom said. "We texted him and said, ‘Hey, just so you know, we are coming to the game. We’re not here to cause any kind of drama. We’re not here to cause anything bad. We are just here to watch the game and leave in peace.’ My manager texted the GM, and he said, ‘Enjoy the game.’ That’s it."

The Fever defeated the Sky 113-90. Clark scored 37 points, while Kelsey Mitchell added 30.

Earlier in the night, Freedom attended a rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game. Cunningham has faced protests and counterprotests since saying she opposes transgender girls and women competing in female sports divisions.

Freedom announced earlier this month that he intends to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft. He has said he is using the league’s rules to challenge the WNBA to clarify its eligibility standards.

The WNBA’s collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but it does not publicly define the term or establish specific eligibility requirements for transgender athletes. No transgender woman is known to have played in the league.

After Freedom and former NBA player Royce White announced their intentions to enter the draft, the WNBA said its anti-hate task force had discussed transgender athletes and online attacks against players.

"There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA, and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others," the league said in its Aug. 12 statement.

Freedom rejected the characterization of his campaign as anti-transgender or anti-LGBTQ.

"I want to make that very clear because, unfortunately, many media organizations and many journalists are making me look like I am anti-trans or anti-LGBTQ," he said. "That is wrong. I respect anyone’s personal decision, and I do respect any kind of group out there."

Freedom said the confrontation with Cloud has now made him more determined to pursue a place in the league, especially so he can play her.

"If anything, I’m more pumped up," he said. "I cannot wait to go against Natasha now. I think it will be fun for me if I get drafted by any other team. I don’t think Chicago will select me. We know that now. But any other team, I just cannot wait to go against her."

Freedom said he has not heard from the WNBA since announcing his plans. He offered to speak directly with WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert.

"If the commissioner of the WNBA wants to sit down and have a conversation with me, I am open to do that as well," Freedom said. "I respect everybody, and I would like to listen to everybody and see what their perspective is."

Sunday marked Freedom's first time attending a WNBA game in person, although he regularly watched the league during his NBA career.

"I’m obviously a huge fan of basketball, a huge fan of women’s basketball, and I was there to watch the game," Freedom said. "I watched on TV so many times, obviously, but I think this was my first WNBA game ever."

He added that he had never spoken with Cloud before the confrontation. Despite their exchange, he praised the veteran guard’s ability and influence on the court.

"I think she’s an excellent player," Freedom said. "I don’t really know what she does off the court, so I can’t really speak about it. But I think on the court, she makes herself better and she makes everyone else better around her, and I think that’s a very special player."

After leaving the arena, Freedom said he encountered a young girl and her mother while preparing to eat dinner. He said their interaction became the most emotional part of his night.

"One of those little girls came with her mother, and then her mother said, ‘Thank you for what you’re doing for my little daughter,’" Freedom said. "I think that was the most emotional part of the whole night."

Freedom said the interaction reinforced his belief that the dispute should not be viewed through a strictly partisan lens.

"This is not a right or left issue," he said. "People need to understand this is not a political issue. This is just common sense. People are trying to make me look like I’m taking a political stance. People are wrong."

Golden State Valkyries player Gabby Williams is the reason Freedom is now pursuing the WNBA, according to him, after a resurfaced clip of Williams saying she would welcome a trans player in the WNBA went viral earlier this month. Freedom confirmed that clip of Williams is what inspired him to declare for the WNBA Draft.

"If they don’t come up with a rule, then I am ready and prepared to play in May and just get ready for the draft in April," Freedom said. "These are the rules. People are mad at me. I’m confused why people are mad at me. These are the rules that literally they put, so I’m just literally following their rules."

And the 6-foot-10 former center intends to play well beyond just one season if the league allows it.

"I’m 34 now, and I can go out there and dunk everything," Freedom said. "I watched the game tonight. I feel like every time I touch the ball, I can dunk everything, so the physical advantage obviously is there. I think I can play till 40, 45. I don’t even think there is a limit, as long as I want."

When asked whether he would feel guilty competing against women or entering a WNBA locker room, Freedom said he would not.

"Why would I?" he said. "These are the rules that they set, and I’m just following their rules. All these players, all these coaches and the league itself advocated and encouraged this whole thing. You see all these players come out and say, ‘I will welcome a trans athlete on my team or against my team.’ And the same thing with coaches. You see all these T-shirts that they’re wearing. So, because of that, I would not feel any guilt."

Freedom identified the Fever as his preferred destination and said he would like to play alongside Clark.

"I think we need to bring back the modern-day Kobe and Shaq, so I think I’m going with the Indiana Fever, for sure," he said. "Me and Caitlin will be the modern-day Kobe and Shaq."

White announced his own intention to enter the WNBA draft shortly after Freedom. Freedom said the two former NBA players have never spoken and are not coordinating their efforts.

"He is his own man. I’m doing my own thing," Freedom said. "What Royce is doing is going to affect him, and what I’m doing is going to affect me. So we are two separate people. We’re doing our own thing, and I’m not affiliated with anyone."

However, Freedom said other former professional players have privately expressed interest in following him. He claimed he was communicating with two former NBA players, three European players and three NBA G League players.

"You’ll be shocked, actually, other than one other player that already came out, how many other players I’m actually talking to right now," Freedom said. "There are two former NBA players, three European players and three G League players that I’m currently talking to about this whole thing."

Freedom said the G League players pointed to the potential financial incentive created by the WNBA’s new salary structure.

"The G League players said, ‘Listen, we are only making $45,000 a year. All we have to do is identify as a woman, and we will be making $1.4 million a year,’" Freedom said. "That’s almost a $1.3 million difference. So the WNBA has no idea what they’re about to face."

But it hasn't been all support since Freedom in recent weeks, as he revealed he's received death threats and abusive messages since announcing his draft plans.

"I do get a lot of death threats and cuss words every day," he said. "I really want people to understand I’m not doing this for any kind of political reasons. This is not a right or left issue. I’m only here to defend women."

Freedom said he has not discussed his campaign with Cunningham or any other current WNBA player or coach. He said no one from the league has contacted him since his announcement, but he remains willing to engage directly with its leadership.

"I’m here to sit down and listen," Freedom said. "If the commissioner or whoever wants to sit down and have a conversation with me about this whole thing, then I would love to sit down and hear her side."

A man suspected of killing five people in a rural area outside Portland, Oregon, was found dead inside a vehicle in Enumclaw, Washington, on Sunday in an apparent suicide, according to authorities.

The sheriff's office previously said it responded early Saturday to reports of a vehicle fire at a property in Forest Grove, where the remains of five people and "several domestic animals" were discovered.

World.title: Sean Grayson, ex-deputy convicted of fatally shooting Sonya Massey, dies, attorney says
World.content:
Sean Grayson, the former Illinois sheriff’s deputy convicted of fatally shooting Sonya Massey in her home in 2024 after she called 911 to report a prowler, has died, his attorney said Sunday.

Daniel Fultz, the attorney who represented Grayson during his murder trial, said he died around noon. He was six months into his 20-year sentence for second-degree murder.

Grayson, 32, was diagnosed with Stage 3 colon cancer in 2023, and it had progressed to Stage 4 and spread to his liver, lungs and rectum, another defense attorney, Mark Wykoff, said at his sentencing in January. In July, he was denied medical release by the Illinois Prisoner Review Board.

It was not immediately clear whether cancer is what caused Grayson’s death.

Grayson shot Massey, 36, after he responded to her 911 call shortly before 1 a.m. July 6, 2024. The shooting, which was captured on body camera video, set off protests and calls for justice.

Grayson was convicted last year.

During the 911 response, Massey picked up a pot of boiling water from her stove, prompting Grayson to back away, according to court testimony.

Grayson testified that he believed Massey was going to throw the boiling water on him after she said, “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.” When Grayson looked confused, Massey repeated the sentence.

He testified that he took the remark as a threat.

Grayson pointed his gun at Massey and threatened to shoot her, according to body camera video. She apologized and dropped to the floor, but he fired three times, striking her.

Grayson declined to offer medical care, Sangamon County State’s Attorney John Milhiser said in court. Massey was pronounced dead at St. John’s Hospital in Springfield.

First Assistant State’s Attorney Mary Beth Rodgers said in court: “‘I’m sorry.’ That is the last thing Sonya Massey said before the defendant murdered her, just like he said he would.”

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker signed the Sonya Massey Act, a law requiring stricter background checks for law enforcement hires, and it went into effect at the beginning of the year.

Sangamon County officials agreed in early 2025 to pay a $10 million settlement to Massey’s family.

World.title: Father of sailor aboard USS Lincoln detained by immigration authorities, family says
World.content:
The immigrant father of a sailor on board the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln was detained Saturday by immigration officials, family members said.

Luis Manuel Aviles, originally from Nicaragua, was detained shortly after 11 a.m. ET in Key West, Florida, where he lives, stepdaughter Katty Delgado told NBC News on Saturday evening.

She said that Aviles has been in the U.S. for roughly 20 years and that she has no knowledge of an arrest history or criminal allegations against him.

“He’s doing everything the right way,” she said.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Sunday that the Border Patrol arrested Aviles during a traffic stop in Key West. The agency said Aviles entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

“We are simply enforcing the laws passed by Congress. This Administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce,” a DHS spokesperson said.

Delgado said she learned the news from family members, including Aviles’ wife and his son Joshua Aviles, who posted a note about the detention on Facebook. Her stepfather, Delgado said, was arrested near a Publix supermarket as he was headed to a mechanic.

Luis Manuel Aviles and his son Joshua Aviles. Katty Delgado

Joshua Aviles said on Facebook that he’s on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which is on its way back to the U.S. after its prolonged stretch at sea, including its deployment to the Middle East to engage in the war with Iran.

“I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything,” he wrote Saturday.

He said that his father is hard-working, giving and humble and that he has a work permit, a Social Security card and a driver’s license.

“This is heartbreaking for me,” Joshua Aviles said. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal.”

Asked to confirm whether Luis Manuel Aviles had a Social Security number, a work permit or pending immigration cases, as his family indicated, DHS told Telemundo, NBCUniversal’s Spanish-language network, that “work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.”

The Lincoln left its home port of San Diego on Nov. 25, and, with more than eight months since it visited a port in December, it broke the Navy record for time without a port call. Relatives of sailors on board the carrier have described reports of deteriorating conditions and morale. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said claims about the situation on board have been “completely misrepresented.”

The Navy said Saturday that the Lincoln has officially left the Middle East en route to the West Coast, a journey that could take a month or more.

Joshua Aviles, who told NBC News he has limited internet access, wrote on Facebook that he’s doing everything he can to get his father released from detention.

“I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I’m coming home, Dad,” he wrote.

President Donald Trump has stood by his administration’s immigration crackdown, including ICE’s expanded enforcement and arrests, which in recent months have included the arrests of children and spouses of service members, a San Diego Padres minor-league catching coordinator and a grandmother from India who’s a schoolteacher with a green card.

Immigration authorities have detained more than 50 parents and spouses of service members during Trump’s second term, according to a recent Associated Press investigation. There has been backlash to the detentions, which come despite programs for military members that can sometimes offer immediate family protection from deportation.

The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website says those “discretionary options” are offered on a “case-by-case basis.”

It was not immediately clear whether Luis Manuel Aviles was in the program.

The DHS spokesperson said in a statement Sunday that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws.”

“Military service by an immediate relative does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement,” the spokesperson said.

Delgado lamented that her stepbrother has spent nine months out at sea, without seeing his family, “and this is what his father gets.”
