World.title: Thousands in northwest Indiana still without power nearly two weeks after storm
World.content:
Thousands in northwest Indiana still without power nearly two weeks after storm

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

More than 20,000 people are still without power in northwest Indiana after severe storms rolled through the area nearly two weeks ago.

A bout of severe weather, including wind gusts up to 100 mph, heavily affected the region on Aug. 11.

Homes in Gary, Portage, Lake Station and Munster still lacked electricity as of Sunday morning, according to NIPSCO , the local power company. In Gary, Mayor Eddie Melton said at least 17,000 citizens remained without power Saturday. NIPSCO officials have estimated electricity will be restored to Gary by the end of day on Tuesday, Aug. 25.

Sponsor Message

Frustration among residents is high, as many seek aid at shelters and receive food from distribution centers. The city's schools remain closed.

Indiana Gov. Mike Braun has activated the National Guard to assist with restoration efforts, while President Trump has approved an emergency declaration for the state. This allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency to assist with recovery efforts from the storm.

Gov. Braun on Saturday also demanded NIPSCO hurry to restore power. "Bring in more crews. Put every available resource into the field. Get creative. Get the job done. Hoosiers have waited long enough," Braun wrote on social media .

The start of the prolonged outage coincided with an announcement by the local power company's parent, NiSource Inc., that it would be paying out around $140 million in dividends to its shareholders.

Melody Birmingham, executive vice president of NIPSCO's parent company NiSource and president of NiSource's utilities division, said during a press conference last week that the storm's damage represented one of "the most extensive and complex" situations their recovery crews had ever encountered.

"When I say complex, these aren't simple repairs. These are systems that are being rebuilt," Birmingham said. "These are lines that ordinarily take us—and systems that ordinarily take weeks or months, that we are trying to accomplish in days and or weeks."

Sponsor Message

The company's slow response has also been criticized by civil rights leaders and advocacy groups who have raised questions about systemic inequity. Gary's population is nearly 80% Black.

Civil rights leader Bernice King, daughter of Rev. Martin Luther King, Jr., said last week that the power outage in Gary is "part of a pattern" and that residents there "deserve more than survival."

"Black communities have too often been expected to endure conditions that would be treated as intolerable somewhere else," King wrote on social media. "We are expected to survive the neglect, absorb the loss, help ourselves, and wait for urgency to arrive."

World.title: Nonprofits are helping musicians pay for insurance in Austin, Texas, and beyond
World.content:
Nonprofits are helping musicians pay for insurance in Austin, Texas, and beyond

toggle caption Ysa Mendoza/KUT News

Musician Zack Morgan jokes that when he lost his corporate job in 2015, it was like being pushed off a cliff. For years, he said, he'd been playing both sides of the Austin coin: tech worker by day, funk keyboardist by night.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

"Maybe this is my sign to try the full-time music thing," Morgan recalled thinking. "Step one in that was: Get health insurance again."

Austin, Texas bills itself as "the Live Music Capital of the World," but it can be unaffordable for the artists who provide the city with its cultural cachet — and help drive its tourism revenue.

Morgan has supported himself by patching together gigs with a number of bands. To help pay for health insurance, he turned to a local nonprofit, the Health Alliance for Austin Musicians, or HAAM.

Sponsor Message

"That's part of being able to make this whole thing work," Morgan said.

HAAM subsidizes the monthly insurance premiums of local musicians who purchase plans through the Affordable Care Act marketplace.

To fund the roughly $4 million program, it works with Central Health, a public agency that provides healthcare resources for low-income residents of Austin and surrounding Travis County.

Many of the performing artists pay $0 toward monthly premiums.

After more than a decade, including through the coronavirus pandemic, the assistance program has become an established and reliable financial support for Austin's musician community.

toggle caption Ysa Mendoza/KUT News

This year, after Congress failed to extend pandemic-era subsidies, premiums skyrocketed for many ACA plans. A recent report found that 5 million people nationwide had dropped the coverage.

HAAM helped blunt the impact for its members. It has emerged as a potential model for other cities hoping to make healthcare more affordable for key populations and industries.

A growing idea

Texas had the highest uninsured rate among states, with 19% of people age 64 and under uninsured as of 2024.

Even before the launch of the ACA marketplace in 2014, HAAM had spent a decade connecting musicians with free and low-cost care at clinics and hospitals in and around Austin.

But roughly 85% of HAAM members remained uninsured, leaving them exposed when traveling to gigs in other cities and states.

Sponsor Message

"When the Affordable Care Act came out and we knew it was here to stay, it really made sense for us to start getting our musicians fully insured," said Rachel Blair, HAAM's chief strategy officer.

Similar nonprofits in other U.S. cities with strong live music cultures, such as Seattle, New Orleans and Nashville, help musicians get medical care.

With the advent of the ACA, some of these organizations began helping musicians navigate the sometimes complex enrollment process for the online marketplaces, though they stopped short of pitching in on premiums.

But the team at HAAM recognized that without direct support to help pay premiums, many of their members would still struggle to retain coverage.

"When you think about the average HAAM member making about $30,000 a year, there's no way that they would be able to spend a third of their income on healthcare," Blair said.

toggle caption Shunya Carroll/KUT News



The organization's membership has grown by 77% to more than 3,300 people since HAAM began offering premium assistance, and more than 90% of members are now insured.

To help subsidize costs for members, HAAM partnered with Central Health, which is Travis County's public hospital district — a type of health agency in Texas charged with using tax dollars to fund safety-net healthcare for poor residents.

Central Health also operates the nonprofit Sendero Health Plans, which offers marketplace insurance to Travis County residents.

To qualify, HAAM members must enroll in one of Sendero's silver-level, or benchmark, plans. If their income is between one and two times the federal poverty level, Central Health pays the balance of their monthly premium after federal tax credits have been applied.

For members who fall above that income range, HAAM offers a more limited subsidy, covering 50% of their premium balances.

In 2017, HAAM helped set up a similar program in Denton, a college town north of Dallas that has served as a testing ground for successful musicians, from Meat Loaf to Norah Jones.

Sponsor Message

The Denton Music and Arts Collaborative works differently: It connects members with an independent insurance agent who helps them find the best health plan for their needs. The nonprofit then offers members a monthly subsidy of $100.

The subsidies are a way of keeping Denton's culture of jazz and "weird art rock" alive, said the collaborative's president, Jennifer Kapinos.

"More and more people were maybe graduating college and leaving and going to find better opportunities in other places," Kapinos said.

"People who had lived here a long time suddenly were finding it harder and harder to afford to be here."

toggle caption Shunya Carroll/KUT News

In Austin, other sectors have been watching HAAM's work. In 2025, Good Work Austin, a nonprofit that advocates for restaurant workers, launched a small pilot program with Central Health to help local food workers enroll in Sendero plans and cover their premiums.

Kit Abney Spelce, vice president of operations for Central Health, said partnering with an advocacy group focused on a particular workforce is key because simply announcing "free insurance for you" doesn't mean people will sign up.

"We are very much dependent on our partner entity to go out and connect with the community, to have that relationship and that trust," she said.

Navigating federal headwinds

Though insurance premium payments often increase year over year, the 2026 plan year was particularly expensive, increasing by 58% on average.

Citing medical and pharmacy costs, Sendero raised rates by an average of 16% for its enrollees.

At the same time, Congress allowed the pandemic-era enhanced premium tax credits to expire, reducing the federal subsidies that many marketplace customers relied on.

"Our premiums for our members went up 60% from one year to the next," Blair said.

HAAM stepped up its fundraising into 2026, but it wasn't enough to cover everyone who requested assistance.

They had to turn away hundreds of qualified people. Still, they were able to buffer existing members, said Spelce with Central Health.

Sponsor Message

"We're going to make sure their monthly premium is paid every month," she said.

A viable, if limited, assistance model

Beyond the eligible musicians they turned away in 2026, another population remains out of HAAM's coverage reach for premium assistance: Austin's poorest residents.

Under the ACA, the marketplace plans that HAAM helps subsidize are for low- and middle-income earners, but the people with the very lowest incomes — below 100% of the federal poverty level, set at about $15,000 in Texas — are supposed to be covered by expanded Medicaid.

But Texas is one of 10 states that chose not to expand Medicaid after the ACA became law, so many of the poorest Texans remain uncovered.

With no federal subsidies available for that group, HAAM and Central Health have tried to develop separate solutions for this subpopulation.

Central Health has its Medical Access Program, an alternative to health insurance that gives low-income, uninsured people access to a network of local care providers.

HAAM has also established relationships with primary care providers to serve its uninsured musician members — but Blair acknowledges that it's not an equivalent benefit to what Medicaid expansion would offer.

"It's not a very sustainable solution, especially when there's a really good alternative," Blair said.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KUT and KFF Health News.

World.title: Documents reveal Ambassador Bridge owner's private meeting with Ottawa ahead of Gordie Howe opening
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The American owner of the Ambassador Bridge, Matthew Moroun, sought a meeting with senior Canadian government officials about the new Gordie Howe International Bridge three and a half months before the rival crossing opened — but what was discussed at that meeting remains largely a secret.

CBC News learned of the April 7 meeting through federal briefing notes obtained under the Access to Information Act. The 17-page release package is available for public view at the bottom of this story.

According to the documents, Moroun, who's based in Michigan, was accompanied by Kevin Kalczynski, a senior lawyer with the family's companies, and Brennan Lee, a senior financial executive and Moroun's son-in-law.

On the Canadian side were Housing Infrastructure and Communities Canada deputy minister Paul Halucha, assistant deputy minister Marco Presutti and Jesse Tracey, a senior federal government lawyer.

'You are here to listen'

The records show Moroun requested the meeting with Canadian officials, but portions of the agenda, as well as the government's account and analysis of the meeting, were redacted.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, adding publicly owned competition to the privately owned Ambassador Bridge. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

CBC News contacted the Ambassador Bridge seeking Moroun's account of the meeting and what he wanted from Canadian officials, but did not receive a response before publication.

The stakes were enormous. Moroun had a lot on the line financially — the new bridge was expected to take almost half the Ambassador Bridge's traffic, according to U.S. government estimates.

By itself, the Ambassador Bridge is a vital link between both countries, and in 2021 it handled more than $140 billion in merchandise trade — about $390 million a day and 26 per cent of Canada's exports by road, according to Transport Canada.

The Canadian government had its own interests going into the meeting. Officials were trying to get the $6.4 billion Gordie Howe bridge open under intense political pressure from the White House to stop.

Briefing materials prepared for Halucha describe his role in the meeting with Moroun this way:

"Note you are here to listen and look forward to hearing Mr. Moroun's perspective and better understand his views on corridor operations as the new bridge prepares to come into service, as well as views he may have on resolution of outstanding issues."

Much of the material detailing those issues and portions of the government's subsequent account of the meeting are redacted.

Behind closed doors

Laurie Trautman, director of the Border Policy Research Institute at Western Washington University in Bellingham, Wash., said the involvement of a private owner adds a dimension that would not ordinarily be present in the management of an international border crossing.

The Ambassador Bridge is seen on July 28, the day after the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which ended nearly a century of private monopoly over commercial bridge traffic between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"It's not necessarily about better accessibility or more efficiency of trade flows. It's about profits," she said.

The arrangement itself may also be unique: Trautman said she knows of no comparable example of a fully privately owned international crossing operating alongside a publicly owned competitor.

She said the unusual relationship, with the inclusion of a private business, adds another layer to diplomacy, raising questions about transparency at a time when relations between Canada and the United States are strained.

"Those government-to-government channels are only as strong as the government-to-government relations," she said. "I think Canada and the U.S. are becoming a little bit more transactional in their diplomacy."

WATCH | A look at the Gordie Howe bridge deal: What's inside the new Gordie Howe bridge deal? | Duration 1:38 The Canadian government has released the text of a new pact with the U.S. to open the long-awaited Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Michigan and Ontario. CBC Windsor's Emma Loop breaks down what's inside the controversial agreement.

Housing Infrastructure and Communities Canada wrote in an email that discussions with private bridge owners are not unusual.

"Discussions with international bridge owners who facilitate trade and commerce to Canada are continuous and occur through various channels," the department said.

The department would not discuss the outstanding litigation, but said it continues to work with stakeholders to "strengthen a vital trade corridor that generates billions of dollars in economic activity on both sides of the border."

From monopoly to competition

A federal briefing note written after the meeting dated April 24 and included in the package obtained by CBC News said, "Mr. Moroun acknowledged that GHIB will proceed to opening," referring to the Gordie Howe bridge. The note said that acknowledgement came a day after the April 7 meeting with senior Canadian officials.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge is seen from the air on July 27, its opening day. The event brought a second major bridge crossing to the Windsor-Detroit corridor. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Whatever was discussed behind closed doors, the competitive landscape changed soon afterward.

The same briefing note said 11 days after the meeting "the Ambassador Bridge announced reductions to toll rates for some of its users, positioning them slightly below those planned for the GHIB."

John Sutcliffe, a political science professor at the University of Windsor, has studied the Moroun family's decades-long efforts to protect the Ambassador Bridge from a competing crossing.

"You have a classic case of moving from a monopoly situation to one where there's competition, and therefore prices come down in those situations usually," he said.

New rival, new strategy

Sutcliffe said for the smaller, older and less accessible Ambassador Bridge, the new, publicly owned competition presents a significant challenge.

Trucks funnel through the Ambassador Bridge's customs facilities on July 28. The new six-lane Gordie Howe bridge offers modern border infrastructure and a direct highway-to-highway connection. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"Having a new competitor that is much larger, has state-the-art infrastructure and the capacity to handle traffic and deal with it more quickly is a huge problem," he said.

Sutcliffe said the tactics may have changed as the Gordie Howe bridge moved from proposal to reality, but the objective has remained the same: protect the family business.

Since 2014, that campaign has included strategic land purchases whenever a route for a rival bridge was identified and political lobbying on both sides of the border, Sutcliffe said. The briefing notes also identify 22 separate legal challenges launched by the Marouns over the past two decades.

Strange political bedfellows

"Trying to secure political support is sort of a long-standing part of the Ambassador Bridge's operation," Sutcliffe said.

U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, left, and Moroun, right, are seen in the composite image. The Trump administration's 'America First' agenda makes for an unusual alignment with a family whose business depends on cross-border trade. (Alex Brandon and Carlos Osorio/The Associated Press)

Sutcliffe said the Trump administration may also represent a unusually receptive audience. He said he sees similarities between Trump's preference for private enterprise and the Moroun family's long-standing opposition to a publicly owned competitor.

"Moroun's position sort of fits with Trump's view of the world and so you have that political dynamic, the view that it's about what's in it for us and what's in it for the United States," Sutcliffe said.

Sutcliffe said the Morouns found themselves aligned with Trump's "America First" approach, even though disrupting cross-border trade could ultimately hurt the Ambassador Bridge itself.

World.title: Trump says Canada 'wants the benefits' of being a U.S. state 'without being one' as trade dispute deepens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In his first response to the failed Canada-U.S. trade deal, President Donald Trump blamed Canada and accused it of wanting 'the benefits of being a State, without being one.' But some Republicans think hitting Canada with new tariffs is a mistake.

U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada "wants the benefits" of being a U.S. state "without being one."

Trump's comments, in a brief post on his Truth Social platform early Sunday, are his first since trade talks between the two countries broke down and come after a slate of new U.S. tariffs came into effect.

Trump also accused Canada of imposing "massive amounts of Tariffs" on American farmers for years. "No more!!!" he wrote in the post.

There was no immediate reaction from the Canadian government to the remarks from Trump, who has repeatedly said since entering his second term in office in 2025 that he wants Canada to become the 51st U.S. state.

Fifty per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods were ushered in early Saturday after extended negotiations aimed at reaching a trade deal fell apart.

WATCH | U.S. tariffs designed to 'hurt and divide,' Carney says: Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’ | Duration 0:38 Prime Minister Mark Carney called U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs a 'miscalculation' because Canadians are united and 'masters of our destiny.'

Carney says U.S. made 'unacceptable' demands

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters that Canadian negotiators walked away from the talks after the Trump administration made "unacceptable" demands, including restrictions on Canada's ability to make trade deals with other countries.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," said Carney, adding that the U.S. "asked too much and offered too little."

Carney also announced that his government would impose reciprocal, "dollar for dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods, starting Sept. 8.

Under the Trump administration's new policy, tariffs of 50 per cent will apply to hundreds of products worth more than $28 billion — from plywood and cement to wine and hockey sticks.

Cross Country Checkup wants your reaction to Canada's trade dispute with the U.S. Leave your comment here and our team may get in touch or read your comment on air

The trade deal was also expected to lower existing U.S. tariffs on the Canadian aluminum, steel and automobile sectors, sources told CBC.

On Sunday morning, Conservative MP Shuvaloy Majumdar urged the federal government to release "the full details of the proposed deal."

Majumdar, the party's shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations, said Conservatives aren't asking for "negotiating secrets," but are seeking information that Ottawa and Washington already knows.

"This information will allow Canadians to debate and discuss the way forward as a country," Majumdar wrote in a letter addressed to Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and shared on X.

Premiers back decision not to back the pact

Provincial and territorial premiers have largely backed Carney's decision to walk away from the negotiations.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, for instance, said Saturday that he was "glad" the prime minister didn't sign the pact "because it was a bad deal."

"We need to fight these tariffs, tariff to tariff, dollar to dollar," Ford told reporters.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Saturday there were no plans for new talks with Canada.

"Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains," Greer said in an interview with Fox News.

He said the Trump administration had offered to cut tariffs on steel, automobiles and lumber.

"They've always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn't want that," Greer said, referring to Canada.

WATCH | B.C. premier weighs in on the Canada-U.S. trade situation: B.C. premier says U.S. alcohol won't return to provincial shelves amid tariffs | Duration 0:59 B.C. Premier David Eby says that U.S. booze won't be seen on provincial liquor store shelves until the softwood lumber sector is treated fairly. Eby says even Russian forest products have better access to the U.S. economy than Canadian forest products

'Canadians do not want to be bullied'

Jamie Gillies, co-ordinator of the communications and public policy program at St. Thomas University in New Brunswick, said there was an expectation that Canada "would match" U.S. tariffs "dollar for dollar."

"Polling has shown that Canadians do not want to be bullied by the U.S. administration," Gillies told CBC News.

Despite the escalating dispute, he said, there is "some wiggle room" to get back to the negotiating table because Canada's retaliatory tariffs aren't expected to come into effect until Sept. 8.

Gillies also said the Trump administration is looking for a trade win as the cost of living in the U.S. is rising and could become a major issue for Republicans ahead of midterm elections in November.

"There might be some pressure on Greer to salvage parts of what they were trying to negotiate; maybe [there is] something that Canada and the U.S. can agree to, where we can climb down from just this set of tariffs."

World.title: London is famous for its great trees. More than 70% are at risk due to climate change, research finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the middle of a heat wave and severe drought this summer, Divya Hariramani was pruning a plum tree in south London when she noticed something wrong with one of the tree's branches.

The branch was beginning to split completely from the tree. The workers at Mitcham Community Orchard told her it was because the fruit tree was stressed.

"Because of the heat essentially. Like, when the trees can't provide enough water to its parts and like some parts will just drop," said Hariramani, who documents fruit trees and the people who tend to them across the city on a social media account called Fruity Walks .

While London’s stone architecture may be more famous to some tourists, the 2,000-year-old city is also renowned for its mature urban forest, which has been called the largest in the world.

Divya Hariramani documents fruit trees and the people who tend to them across London on her social media account Fruity Walks. (Submitted by Divya Hariramani)

This year has proven difficult for the normally lush canopy, though, as five successive heat waves and a serious lack of rain have strained plants and wildlife.

And it’s projected to get much worse for the city’s eight million trees.

By the end of the century, according to a recent report from Royal Botanic Gardens Kew forecasting the vulnerability of London’s urban forest, some 73 per cent of the city’s trees could be at risk of dying due to climate change.

Driest July on record

The Kew Gardens tree collections and arboriculture team worked with the Greater London Authority to assess a sample of over a million public trees and found that 62 per cent of them already have "low suitability" to the climate conditions that can be expected by 2090 without action to reduce emissions. On top of that, nearly 11 per cent are “vulnerable."

It’s not just a future problem. In 2022, 400 of Kew's 11,000 trees died amid extreme heat and drought conditions. The gardens have left the skeleton of one red oak standing, and painted it red as a symbol of what climate change is already doing to London's trees.

Kevin Martin, head of tree collections at Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, views a willow beech tree suffering from drought dieback in 2024. Martin led a recent report from Kew Gardens estimating how much of London's urban tree canopy is at risk due to climate change. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Kew highlighted the findings and unveiled the red tree ahead of Climate Action Week in June, when Britain and Europe were already in the throes of a second heat wave. By August, there had been two more and a major drought was declared in much of England and Wales. Virtually no rain fell in July, resulting in the driest July on record in Britain.

Farmers lost crops, warned of food shortages and had to dip into winter feed reserves for cattle. Wildfires in parts of the country prompted an emergency cellphone alert in August. In the city, park grass turned yellow and brittle; tree branches and leaves looked droopier than usual. In some places, trees lost their leaves altogether, giving an autumnal look to the ground in the middle of summer.

The week in June when Kew publicized its report, Hariramani, in an ironic twist of fate, had to cancel a group walk she had organized in light of Climate Action Week due to the heat.

"Literally one of the most important walks in a way, for such an important situation and we couldn't even do it," said Hariramani, whose day job is in sustainable design.

More like Barcelona?

With a London that’s getting warmer than its current trees can handle, botanists are exploring whether they should start planting different trees.

"From most projections, we're expecting the climate in London in 2050 to look more like Barcelona's is now," Joe Richomme, a botanical horticulturist at Kew Gardens, told CBC on a recent visit to Kew’s Carbon Garden, where 35 trees and 6,500 plants have been selected to show how different species respond to changing conditions.

The Carbon Garden in London's Kew Gardens is meant to raise awareness about climate change through its wide range of plants showing how biodiversity can remain resilient amid warming temperatures. (Lyza Sale/CBC)

Richomme explained that Kew has been exploring what types of tree species could fare better in hotter, drier weather, while also being able to withstand England’s notorious wetter winters.

For example, English oak, which are native to Britain, have struggled in the heat, but have also adapted to grow in warmer places, such as the southern United States.

'They’re irreplaceable’

Paul Wood has written four books and two maps about London's trees, which he attributes to growing up playing in the forests of southern England — and also, his name.

"It's called nominative determinism," Wood said over the phone in mid-August with a chuckle, referring to the idea that people gravitate toward work that suits their name.

Paul Wood is the author of a blog and several books about London's trees. (Submitted by Paul Wood)

He too has made a career of writing about the British capital's storied tree canopy, and the cooling and relaxing benefits it brings to residents and visitors.

But these days he worries about what could happen to London's leafy streets and pockets of ancient woodland in the future as he sees the city struggling in record extreme heat and drought.

"Places like Highgate Woods and Sydenham Hill Woods, Oxleas Woods, Hampstead Heath, where there is native woodland which is really struggling in the current climate," Wood said.

Trees as old as 1,000 years live in some of those places, meaning they’ve stood through the Norman conquest, the Magna Carta and Shakespeare. They saw Victorian railways being built and felt the first rumblings of the London Underground.

"That would be really devastating to lose," Wood said, noting it's not just the trees' history that's valuable but the biodiversity they support as well.

"They're irreplaceable."

World.title: F-bombs at the Opera? Empire of Wild does things differently
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Indigenous-led creative process, a nearly $4-million budget, and big hopes Empire of Wild will thrill opera audiences the same way the novel thrilled readers. CBC News spoke with some of the creative team as they workshopped the music in Toronto.

In Cherie Dimaline’s Empire of Wild, three generations of women struggle to free their loved one from the grips of the werewolf-like Rogarou in an effort to bring home a missing husband and protect their land from corporate interests.

The story is so gritty, sexy and dramatic, it was named Indigo’s top book of 2019, beating out big titles like The Testaments by Margaret Atwood and Daisy Jones & The Six by Taylor Jenkins Reid.

Now, about $4 million is being invested for an Indigenous-led creative team to turn the book into an opera, and stage the world premiere next spring in Toronto.

It's a gamble that could draw in a younger audience and opera neophytes — and challenge purists who prefer the "core" repertoire.

Author Cherie Dimaline and composer Ian Cusson are both from the Métis community on the shores of Georgian Bay, Ont., where Empire of Wild takes place. (Submitted by Cherie Dimaline, John Arano)

Empire of Wild takes place in the Georgian Bay Métis community of Penetanguishene, Ont., where Dimaline grew up. Composer Ian Cusson is also from there, and when he read the book, he recognized the Rogarou from the stories his mother used to tell.

“Even though it's a work of fiction, I was reading people that I knew and ways of speaking that I'd heard growing up,” he told CBC News earlier this month in Toronto when the cast and orchestra were workshopping the new music.

“The sort of radical offer that we're making is to say [the opera] is a space where stories like this one can exist,” Cusson said.

“They don't just have to be stories from 200 years ago or from Europe.… They can be stories that resonate with people today.”

Modern voices

Cusson said he and Dimaline, who wrote the libretto, wanted to create modern characters modern audiences could see themselves in.

"There's queer characters and ... a family who are roofers and blue collar and they're going about their lives and having to deal with like the most extreme scenarios."

They also talk the way modern people talk. That includes swear words and dick jokes. “Oh there are f-bombs,” said Cusson, acknowledging that's perhaps not what people expect to hear when listening to the huge voices singing arias.

He also likened this production to a "film on steroids" and said he loved working with the more macabre, horror-like elements of the story too.

“I feel like it really resonates with what especially younger people are hoping for in a night of entertainment,” he said.

Innu soprano Elisabeth St-Gelais will play the role of Joan, whose husband disappears one night after a disagreement about whether to sell her land. (Taylor Long/Canadian Opera Company)

Innu soprano Elisabeth St-Gelais, 30, plays the protagonist, Joan. She has read Empire of Wild twice – and agrees there is a lot in this story young audiences can connect with.

“[Joan] has a couple of … maybe bad habits that she relies on when she's in crisis…. And I mean, everybody has that. So I think it's very interesting to show something like that,” she said, referring to her character’s hard-drinking nights as she grapples with the disappearance of her husband.

Challenging the status quo

At its heart, Empire of Wild is a story about power, resistance and resilience.

Joan’s husband goes missing one night, after a fight about whether or not to sell her land. When she finds him 11 months later, he’s working as a preacher, seems not to remember her, and is being carefully managed by a man who seems all too concerned with industrial projects in the region.

There are darker forces at play and only old magic, passed down from generation to generation, can reunite Joan with her love. Both Cusson and St-Gelais said that is a key element of this story: intergenerational support along strong matrilineal lines.

The tale was inspired by the Métis story of the Rogarou, but the characters are embodied by a wide range of talents including Kwagiulth and Stó:lō mezzo-soprano Marion Newman and Anishinaabe baritone Evan Korbut.

Johannes Debus conducts the orchestra as the cast and Indigenous-led creative team workshop the music for Empire of Wild in Toronto on Aug. 14. (Taylor Long/Canadian Opera Company)

“The Indigenous artists that get to bring to life these roles … while they may be different from their own specific lived experiences, they tell a truth that has a commonality and is unique among many Indigenous people,” said Cusson. “The story of resilience, the story of survivance and survival.”

"Survivance," a combination of survival and resistance, is used by Indigenous scholars to describe how Indigenous peoples have not only survived settler colonialism, but also continued their cultural customs — enhancing them and generating new ones along the way.

A different kind of creation story

St-Gelais said it has been a phenomenal experience working on an opera led by Indigenous creators.

“Indigenous people are going through a moment, an era of … blooming in every, every side of society, in science and art, in business,” she told CBC.

Canadian countertenor Sean Haid speaks with Empire of Wild composer Ian Cusson at opera workshop in Toronto. (Taylor Long/Canadian Opera Company)

Cree costume designer Jeff Chief is part of the creative team, as is Algonquin director Yvette Nolan, who Cusson likes to quote when he describes how an Indigenous approach to creating art is different:

“Instead of having this triangular shape, where there's usually a person at the top, how do we bend the triangle and expand its edges to make the circle?”

It’s about an equality of voices, where everyone involved – down to the person who empties garbage cans – is invited into the circle of creation where their contribution is seen as valuable.

Cusson said he wants to see this method of creation repeated in other operas and other opera companies.

“It should be done everywhere. It's the best way to make art.”

World.title: Fast-moving wildfire threatens Reno, Nevada, forcing thousands to evacuate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A fast-moving wildfire that jumped over fire trucks and made it difficult for crews to reach hot spots destroyed homes in northwest Reno, Nevada, on Sunday. Shifting winds challenged firefighters trying to bring it under control, and authorities urged some 90,000 people to evacuate.

At least six people — three first responders and three civilians — were injured, officials said. Officials said the fire was "human-caused" but did not provide details on how they reached that conclusion, or whether it was intentionally set or accidental.

The Hawk Fire began Saturday and quickly grew to more than 60 square kilometres as it spread across the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt–Toiyabe National Forest, where rugged foothills are ringed by homes and businesses near the California state line.

'Please get out'

Some 42,000 residents have been ordered evacuated as the "GO NOW" zone expanded, reaching the edge of the University of Nevada. An additional 45,000 people were in the adjacent evacuation warning zone. Authorities implored all of them to leave and be prepared to stay away for several days, because shifting and strengthening winds were expected to make the fire even more unpredictable.

"Please get out if you can right now," Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said.

Some 42,000 residents have been ordered evacuated and an additional 45,000 people were in the adjacent evacuation warning zone. Authorities have implored all of them to leave. (Natalie Wainwright/Reuters)

Cari Kieffer said a video posted on social media showed her house entirely burned down, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.

"I woke up this morning and just started crying — all my kids, they lost everything," Kieffer said Sunday. "We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone."

Kieffer had been watching her son's football game Saturday when she learned that their home on the outskirts of Reno was in the evacuation zone. An app the family used to track the fire's progress had been lagging significantly behind its actual location, she said, so they thought firefighters had kept the blaze from their neighbourhood.

Instead, Kieffer, her husband and their four children ages 3 to 16 raced to save their dogs and whatever possessions they could retrieve. Ash rained down, and the wind blew like an oven blast from a wall of flames advancing down the hillside toward their neighborhood, she said.

"I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," Kieffer said. "I was like, we gotta go like now."

Eyes watering and throat burning, Kieffer grabbed a handful of clothes, a Bible, her wedding photos and her mother's ashes. In the frenzy, as firefighters yelled at her family to leave immediately, she said she forgot her family's birth certificates and was unable to salvage her childhood photos.

National Guard mobilized

The family drove to a friend's home but had to evacuate again. They learned later Saturday evening that their own home was gone.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the Nevada National Guard to support aerial firefighting with two helicopter crews as well as 60 troops to help police safeguard evacuated neighborhoods. Also responding were 800 fire personnel.

Nearly 10,000 customers were without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from 60,000 on Saturday. Portions of U.S. Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed due to the fire. Reno, with more than 280,000 residents, is the largest city in Nevada outside of metro Las Vegas.

Washoe County emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said they couldn't bring their pets — small animals and large animals were to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.

On Saturday alone, 15 new fires popped up across Nevada. Changing winds sent the flames in different directions. (Trevor Bexon/Getty Images)

Fire quickly turned destructive

The fire was so small Saturday morning that it wasn't even a concern, said Tyler Duvall, who went camping over the weekend. By the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone.

"The wind really blew it up," Duvall said.

On Saturday alone, 15 new fires popped up across Nevada. Months of dry weather and a record lack of snow this past winter across the American West have created prime fire conditions. Earlier this month, wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area, while three wildfires north of Reno forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes.

The University of Nevada, where many of the 20,000 undergraduates moved into their housing this weekend, was just outside the evacuation zone Sunday.

Two hospitals evacuated patients and the sheriff said his office was keeping a close watch on whether to evacuate the county jail.

The fire moved exceptionally fast Saturday night, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hot spots while residents were trying to get out, the sheriff said.

"It was extremely confusing," Balaam said, describing how changing winds sent the flames in different directions.

World.title: Partial lunar eclipse to grace Canadian skies this week
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the night of Aug. 27-28, a partial lunar eclipse will be visible across the country.

The eclipse comes roughly two weeks after the total solar eclipse that was seen across Iceland, Spain and a small portion of Portugal.

While this will be a partial eclipse, it will be a deep one, with 93 per cent coverage at its maximum.

Lunar eclipses occur when the moon moves through Earth’s shadow, called its umbra. Before it enters the umbra, however, it passes through Earth’s outer, dimmer shadow, called the penumbra. However, because it is much dimmer, it’s difficult to see with the naked eye when this occurs.

This illustration shows the movement of the moon through Earth's shadow for the Aug. 27-28 partial eclipse. (Sky &Telescope)

Most of Canada will see the entire duration of the eclipse, while Western Canada will see the partial eclipse already taking place as the moon rises.

The great news is that, unlike with a solar eclipse, you don’t need any protective eyewear to watch the event.

Also unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse takes place over hours, not minutes.

All (or most) of the lunar eclipse on August 27-28 will be viewable across North and South America. (Leah Tiscione/Sky & Telescope)

When to see it

The eclipse will begin as the moon enters Earth’s penumbra at roughly 10 p.m. ET, but that’s not when you want to go out to start observing.

Instead, the visible part of the eclipse begins at 10:33 p.m. ET on Aug. 27 and ends at 1:52 a.m. on Aug. 28. The deepest part of the eclipse will occur at 12:13 a.m. with almost all of the moon appearing darkened.

This is just one of many astronomical events taking place this month.

"It's kind of a fun one because … August had so many great things going on for it and still does," said Elaina Hyde, director of the Allan I. Carswell Observatory York University’s department of physics and astronomy in Toronto.

"We had, of course, the very, very partial solar eclipse back on August 12th. We had the Perseids, which were either fabulous or slightly less fabulous, depending on how cloudy your skies were. And, of course, the Jupiter-Mercury conjunction ."

Will it be a "blood moon"?

"It's a partial eclipse, so it's not going to turn 100 per cent red, but depending on where you are in Canada, it will still be pretty red," Hyde said.

The great thing about lunar eclipses is that there's no need for any equipment — just your eyes.

"This is a naked eye object, but if you have binoculars or a small telescope or just a [cellphone] camera with a really good night mode, you should be able to get pretty good pictures," Hyde said.

World.title: Soccer fans boo U.S. anthem as Canadians react to breakdown in trade negotiations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Soccer fans booed the U.S. national anthem on the weekend as Canadians reacted to news that trade talks between the two countries had broken down again.

The Canadian Press reported jeers echoing through Vancouver's B.C. Place ahead of a Major League Soccer game between the Whitecaps and FC Dallas on Saturday, following booing at Stade Saputo, where CF Montréal hosted the L.A. Galaxy earlier in the day.

This came hours after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended talks with the United States and recalled his negotiators, saying the U.S. made unreasonable demands at the last minute after previously agreeing to a tentative framework.

The U.S. followed through on its threat to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods, and Canada promised to match the U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar by Sept. 8, a move that was largely backed by premiers across the country.

Many Canadians who spoke with CBC News over the weekend seemed to echo the sentiments from those inside the stadiums.

'We've got to stand up'

Niiamaa Laryea in Vancouver said the tariff news is "horrible" but that it's important for Canada to stand up to the U.S. "We're in a tough situation, but I think Carney is doing the right thing," he told CBC Vancouver. "We've got to stand up eventually. We can't let the U.S. bully us into submission."

In Ottawa, Lesley Combden said the economic pain will get worse before it gets better, and she would like to see Canada continue to diversify its trade away from the U.S.

Niiamaa Laryea in Vancouver, left, and Lesley Combden in Ottawa were among the Canadians reacting to news that trade talks between Canada and the U.S. had broken down again. (CBC)

"I think that Carney made the right decision in walking away," she told CBC Ottawa. "Why would we want to deal with the U.S. when they won't take away tariffs, they want us to make concessions?"

The sweeping tariffs will cover about $28 billion worth of Canadian exports, or about five per cent of products sent to the U.S.

Ontario, B.C. and Quebec are expected to feel the biggest impacts, with some of the most affected industries including agriculture, textile, electronics, furniture and plastics manufacturing.

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates some 87,000 jobs could be lost across the country as a result of the new duties.

WATCH | Layoffs in Canada on the horizon: Canada could lose tens of thousands of jobs due to Trump’s 50% tariffs | Duration 2:32 After Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down, U.S. President Donald Trump hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on various items. Analysis from economist Trevor Tombe indicates that if the tariffs last, Canada would shed tens of thousands of jobs.

Retaliatory tariffs questioned

Some callers to CBC's Cross Country Checkup on Sunday were more critical of Carney.

While few criticized the prime minister for ending negotiations, some questioned the wisdom of retaliatory tariffs.

Peter Arndt in Pickering, Ont., said Carney "100 per cent" had to walk away based on what he's heard about the U.S. demands, but he said retaliatory tariffs are not the right way to go off the bat because they'll also hurt Canadians.

"Tariffs are just a bad plan all around," Arndt said.

Economists have also told CBC News that retaliatory tariffs will further hurt Canadians financially.

Kathy Woudzia in Vancouver said it's hard to know what to make of the prime minister's decision without having more details about what exactly was on the table in the negotiations.

"I really think that before Sept. 8, it would be nice to have some transparency about the deal that was rejected," she said.

"Without really knowing what was offered and why it was rejected, we can't meaningfully compare that option with the economic consequences of the current 50 per cent tariff environment."

WATCH | Most Canadians support Canada's tough approach to talks, poll suggests: Canadians broadly behind Carney's U.S. trade stance: polls | Duration 1:57 New polling shows some 76 per cent of Canadians support Prime Minister Mark Carney's decision to break off U.S. trade talks and to fight fire with fire on the tariff front. Other recent polling shows most Canadians no longer trust the United States.

Officials have not released many specifics about what was on the table, but Carney said the U.S. made unacceptable demands at the last minute on culture, autos and sovereignty — and ultimately "asked too much and offered too little."

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said the Americans had proposed negotiating matters around the province's French-language legislation, such as the requirement that French be included on consumer devices like electronics or household appliances and user manuals.

Trump, writing on his Truth Social platform early Sunday in his first public comment since the talks broke down, did not mention the negotiations specifically but said Canada "wants the benefits" of being a U.S. state "without being one" and accused Canada of imposing "massive amounts of Tariffs" on American farmers for years.

Canadians feeling 'betrayed': pollster

Matt Ambida in Markham, Ont., said he thinks the Canadian government is doing a "great" job in its negotiations and needs to take a more serious approach to trade with other countries. "At the end of the day, we have to hold firm on our stance," he said. "We're not dealing with the same America that we were dealing with before, and that means that we have to make tougher calls."

An Angus Reid Institute poll conducted online Saturday and Sunday found that 76 per cent of Canadians support the Carney government's decision to walk away from negotiations.

Angus Reid president Shachi Kurl said the findings are a "snapshot in time" but fall in line with a long-expressed resolve from Canadians to see officials take a hard line with Washington.

"It's unusual for a majority of Canadians, especially coast to coast to coast, in every province and territory, to agree on something," Kurl told CBC News.

The poll found Canadians are still bracing for the impacts of the new tariffs, with 89 per cent expressing concern about the costs of goods and services and 38 per cent saying they have some level of anxiety about losing their job.

The randomized sample of 1,468 Canadians polled was weighted to represent adults nationwide according to region, gender, age, household income and education, Angus Reid says. A sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points, 19 times out of 20, according to the non-profit foundation.

David Coletto, founder and CEO of Abacus Data, said his polling firm has found most Canadians feel "deeply betrayed" by the U.S. and are willing to endure short-term economic pain for a better deal in the future.

"I get a sense from my polling that the majority of Canadians have decided that deeper integration with the United States, continuing to be reliant on them, is not going to do Canada well in the long term," Coletto told CBC News Network on Sunday.

World.title: Conservative MP calls for 'full details' of failed Canada-U.S. trade deal to be released
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservatives are urging Prime Minister Mark Carney to release details of the failed Canada-U.S. trade deal so Canadians can 'debate and discuss the way forward.'

The Conservative Party is urging Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to release "the full details" of the proposed Canada-U.S. trade deal that was on the table before negotiations collapsed late on Friday.

Conservative MP Shuvaloy Majumdar, the party's shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations, said in a letter to Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc on Sunday that the Conservatives aren't asking for "negotiating secrets."

But the party is seeking information that Ottawa and Washington already know, Majumdar said. "This information will allow Canadians to debate and discuss the way forward as a country."

Fifty per cent U.S. tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect early on Saturday after extended trade negotiations between the two countries fell apart.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Saturday that Canadian negotiators decided to walk away from the talks after the United States had made what he said were unacceptable demands.

That included " efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals ," Carney said.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or to undermine our key industries," he said, adding that his government would impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods, starting Sept. 8.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the talks failed after "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada."

The U.S. "offer would have led to supply chain co-ordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals co-operation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labour and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement negotiations," he said in a statement early Saturday.

Greer also told the New York Times in an interview on Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration offered, in part, to cut 10 per cent tariffs on softwood lumber and lower steel tariffs from 50 to 25 per cent.

WATCH | Canada could lose tens of thousands of jobs: Canada could lose tens of thousands of jobs due to Trump's 50% tariffs | Duration 5:40 After Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down, U.S. President Donald Trump hits Canada with 50 per cent tariffs. CBC’s David Common says this could result in the loss of thousands of Canadian jobs.

Exact details not yet released

But neither government has released the exact details of the deal that was being negotiated.

Despite that, Carney's decision to walk away from the talks appears to have garnered widespread support in Canada, including from provincial leaders like Ontario Premier Doug Ford and B.C. Premier David Eby.

Many also have backed Carney's plans to impose reciprocal tariffs on the U.S. next month.

There is "anxiety" among Canadians for what the escalating trade dispute means for the economy and their daily lives, said David Coletto, founder and CEO of the Abacus Data polling firm.

But there is also a sense that "we're not going to let Donald Trump bully us," Coletto told CBC News in an interview Sunday. "And I think most Canadians still feel good about what the prime minister said yesterday and now are going to wait to see what comes next."

After Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed, Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre said Canada 'cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country' or 'a bad deal.' (Christopher Drost/The Canadian Press)

Opposition party leaders have also said Canada should remain united in the face of Trump's tariffs.

" Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade," Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a social media post Saturday morning.

Poilievre said he would seek a call with Carney "to discuss what we can do to fight for our workers, businesses and economy."

Asked by reporters on Saturday if he would brief opposition leaders on the trade situation, Carney said that would likely happen Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning.

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.
