World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: Fonatur Nayarit Resort Is Mexico’s First in Twenty Years
World.content:
Mexico · TOURISM

Key Facts — What happened Fonatur has started work on its first new resort in twenty years, in Nayarit.

— How big The first phase covers 542 hectares and costs 7,134.7 million pesos (US$422 million).

— The real story The agency is returning to its classic role of building destinations from scratch.

— The catch No completion date or hotel count has been announced; only the first phase is underway.

— On the map Centro Turístico Sustentable Compostela sits in Compostela, Nayarit, on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

— What comes next Later phases remain undefined, with the focus now on Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas.

The new Pacific coast project marks a return to Fonatur’s classic role as a state developer. Meanwhile, the agency’s focus shifts toward the Tren Maya.

Empty coastline in Nayarit on Mexico’s Pacific shore, the kind of shore Fonatur has spent fifty years turning into resort towns.

The Fonatur Nayarit resort is Mexico’s first new state tourism development in twenty years. The federal agency, Fonatur, has begun work on the Centro Turístico Sustentable Compostela in the Pacific state of Nayarit.

A New Beginning for Fonatur

However, Mexico’s state tourism developer is building a new destination for the first time in two decades. According to El Economista, the project is the Centro Turístico Sustentable (CTS) Compostela, in the municipality of Compostela, Nayarit.

Work has already started this year. The first phase covers 542.32 hectares, about 1,340 acres, and requires an investment of 7,134.7 million pesos (US$422 million).

The project marks a return to Fonatur’s traditional role. After two decades, the agency is again building a destination from scratch.

The project is located in Nayarit, a Pacific coast state north of Puerto Vallarta. However, this marks a significant shift for the agency, which has focused on other duties.

What Is Fonatur?

Fonatur is the Fondo Nacional de Fomento al Turismo, or National Tourism Promotion Fund. Moreover, it is a federal agency that assembles land and lays down roads, water, and power.

The agency sits under the tourism ministry. In fact, according to the Diario Oficial de la Federación, Fonatur is a parastatal body assigned to the Secretariat of Tourism.

Fonatur develops land for tourism, then sells or leases it to developers. This model has produced major resort cities across Mexico.

Fonatur’s model involves assembling land and providing infrastructure, then attracting private investment. As a result, it has created major destinations like Cancún and Los Cabos.

The New Project’s Components

The site brings together two sustainable tourism projects. El Economista reported that CTS Compostela will integrate Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas.

These are part of the first phase, which has already begun. The investment figure is 7,134.7 million pesos, which at the Banxico FIX rate of 16.90 pesos per dollar is about US$422 million.

The first phase covers 542.32 hectares, or about 1,340 acres. This area includes two sustainable tourism projects, Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas.

Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas are the two sub-projects within the first phase. Meanwhile, the investment of 7,134.7 million pesos (US$422 million) will fund this initial development.

Fonatur’s Past Creations

Fonatur has a long history of building resort cities from scratch. Its own list names five Centros Integralmente Planeados, meaning resort cities planned from scratch: Cancún, Ixtapa, Huatulco, Los Cabos and Loreto.

In short, these are large, planned destinations with airports, hotel zones and road grids. Cancún is the most famous example.

These planned centres are designed from scratch on empty coastline. Each includes its own airport, hotel zone, and residential areas.

These five centres are known as Centros Integralmente Planeados, or CIPs. In addition, they represent the agency’s most ambitious projects, each with its own airport and infrastructure.

Smaller Projects in the Mix

In addition, Fonatur lists three Proyectos Turísticos Integrales, or Integral Tourism Projects. These are Marina Cozumel, Litibú and Playa Espíritu, and they are smaller than the CIPs.

The new Nayarit project is a different category, a sustainable tourism centre. Still, it follows the same model of state-led development.

These smaller projects are part of Fonatur’s portfolio. They are less extensive than the five major centres.

These Proyectos Turísticos Integrales are smaller than the CIPs but still significant. However, the new CTS Compostela is a different category, focusing on sustainability.

What Is the Mexico Diesel Subsidy?

The Mexico diesel subsidy is a fiscal stimulus, not a direct payment. It waives part of the IEPS, the special tax on production and services, charged on every litre of fuel.

The finance ministry, known as SHCP, decides each week how much of the per-litre tax to forgo. Because the tax is part of the pump price, waiving it holds retail costs down.

The weekly quota is published in the official gazette ahead of each Saturday-to-Friday period. However, the waiver is decided by the finance ministry, not by fuel retailers.

The waiver is not a payment to drivers or retailers. Instead, the state simply collects less tax on each litre sold.

Key Facts — What happened Argentine households are borrowing to pay for food and medicine, not luxuries.

— How big 91.7% of households are in debt, with 20.9 million people owing money to banks or digital wallets.

— The real story Falling purchasing power is forcing families to finance basic needs, turning credit into a survival tool.

— The catch The 15.5% arrears rate includes digital wallets, which official bank statistics often miss.

— Who it hits Families in Buenos Aires province, where 60% borrowed for essentials like rent and utility bills.

— What comes next President Milei rejects state intervention, leaving borrowers to negotiate privately with lenders.

Argentines are turning to credit just for groceries and medicine as prices outpace wages. This shift is reshaping how the country borrows.

Inside a supermarket in Buenos Aires. Food and medicine are what most Argentine families now put on credit.

Argentine household debt is not about buying luxuries; it is about putting food on the table. According to the country’s main small-business federation, families are borrowing because their wages no longer stretch to cover basic needs.

The Real Reason Behind Argentine Household Debt

Argentine household debt is rising, but not because people are splurging. In fact, Salvador Femenía of CAME says borrowing is driven by a fall in purchasing power.

In an interview with Diario El Esquiú, Femenía explained that households are forced to finance basic products such as food and medicine. He stressed that loans do not go on entertainment goods but barely cover spending on food, drink, and the chemist.

CAME is the Argentine Confederation of Medium-Sized Enterprises, the country’s main small-business federation. However, its spokesman’s remarks were made in a press interview, not in a published report.

Femenía’s remarks were made in a press interview, not in a published CAME report. However, they echo a broader concern about falling purchasing power, known as poder adquisitivo.

What Households Actually Spend On

The numbers back up this picture. Financial daily El Cronista reported that 64% of households that take on financing do so to buy food and medicine.

Another survey found that 63.8% of households used their credit or loan to cover spending on food and health, above all medicines. In short, borrowing is a survival tool, not a lifestyle choice.

In addition, the provincial ombudsman’s office in Buenos Aires province found the same pattern. Its report stated that 60% of households had to borrow for food or essential costs.

The ombudsman’s office, an independent public body, confirmed the same trend. In addition, it listed rent and utility bills as key triggers for borrowing.

A Widespread Problem Across the Country

The issue is not confined to one region. As a result, a report found 60% of households in Buenos Aires province had to borrow for food or essential costs.

The same report listed the main triggers: food, rent, medicines, and utility bills. Meanwhile, a third-edition study from March 2026 found that 91.7% of Argentine households are in debt.

In addition, there was a sharp rise in those carrying more than three debts. Meanwhile, the study from March 2026 found 91.7% of households in debt, with many carrying multiple debts.

As a result, the quality of borrowing has deteriorated, making the situation more fragile. The provincial ombudsman’s report, titled “Hablemos de deudas,” highlighted inequalities and gender issues.

Meanwhile, the national study showed a sharp rise in households with multiple debts.

The Scale of Arrears

The Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA), a Buenos Aires think tank, tracks household debt through its CENDEU database. It puts real household arrears, counting digital wallets as well as banks, at 15.5%, affecting 5.91 million people.

A separate measure counts 20.9 million debtors across banks and digital wallets, of whom 5.8 million are behind on payments. These figures are higher than bank-only measures because digital wallets, known as billeteras virtuales, are mobile payment apps that also lend.

CEPA’s CENDEU database counts digital wallets, which official bank statistics often miss. Therefore, the arrears rate of 15.5% is higher than a bank-only measure.

The 15.5% arrears rate, or morosidad, includes digital wallets. However, the 5.91 million and 5.8 million figures are separate measures and must not be merged.

Government Response: A Private Matter

President Javier Milei has taken a different view. Still, in early August, he rejected the idea that the state should take on the difficulties of people who took out credit.

Moreover, his government’s approach is that falling inflation and interest rates should let banks and debtors find solutions through private refinancing. Therefore, no official relief or refinancing scheme has been announced.

Perfil reported that Milei defined the situation as a problem between private parties. In addition, his approach relies on falling inflation and interest rates to encourage private refinancing.

Milei’s government has resisted intervening in private credit disputes. As a result, no official relief or refinancing scheme has been announced.

Why This Matters for the Economy

The reliance on credit for basics signals a deeper economic strain. When families borrow to eat, they have less room to spend on other goods, which can slow retail sales and consumption.

CAME, which represents small and medium businesses, regularly publishes readings on retail sales and consumption. Its spokesman’s remarks highlight how household debt is a symptom of a broader purchasing power problem.

When families borrow for basics, they have less to spend on other goods, slowing retail sales. However, CAME’s spokesman argues that this borrowing is not discretionary but forced by falling purchasing power.

The Role of Digital Wallets

Digital wallets have become a major source of credit, but official bank statistics miss much of this lending. That is why the CEPA reading is higher than a bank-only measure.

In fact, the inclusion of digital wallets in the data reveals a larger pool of debtors and arrears. Therefore, it paints a more complete picture.

Digital wallets, known as billeteras virtuales, are mobile payment apps that also lend. Including them in the data reveals a larger pool of debtors and arrears, offering a more complete picture.

A Regional Pattern

The pattern is consistent across the country. In Buenos Aires province, the ombudsman’s report highlighted that borrowing for essentials is widespread, not just in urban centers.

Meanwhile, the national study from March 2026 showed a deterioration in the quality of borrowing, with more households carrying multiple debts. This suggests that Argentine household debt is becoming both more common and more fragile.

The ombudsman’s report from Buenos Aires province listed food, rent, medicines, and utility bills as main triggers. Meanwhile, the national study from March 2026 showed a sharp rise in households with more than three debts.

Looking Ahead

As long as purchasing power remains under pressure, households will likely continue to rely on credit for basics. The government’s hands-off approach means the burden falls on private negotiations between lenders and borrowers.

In short, the data make clear that Argentine household debt is a daily reality for millions, not a distant statistic. The question is whether falling inflation will ease the strain, but that remains to be seen.

As long as purchasing power remains under pressure, households will likely continue to rely on credit for basics. However, the government has declined to intervene, leaving the burden on private negotiations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Argentine household debt?

Argentine household debt refers to the money that families owe to banks, digital wallets, and other lenders. According to recent studies, a large share of this borrowing is used to buy food and medicine, not luxuries.

How much debt do Argentine households have?

The exact total is not known, but CEPA data shows that 20.9 million people are debtors, with 5.91 million in arrears. Another measure counts 5.8 million behind on payments, and 91.7% of households are in debt overall.

Why are Argentine families borrowing?

The main reason is a fall in purchasing power, or poder adquisitivo. This forces families to finance basic products like food and medicine.

What is the government doing about household debt?

President Javier Milei has said the state should not take on the difficulties of borrowers, calling it a private matter. The government expects falling inflation and interest rates to allow private refinancing, without a specific state policy.

Argentina signs the Río Negro highway transfer on Monday 24 August 2026. The province takes over two national routes and a passenger railway.

Cabinet chief Diego Santilli and economy minister Luis Caputo will sign the agreement with governor Alberto Weretilneck at 1pm. The signing will take place at the presidential palace, Casa Rosada.

What the Río Negro Highway Transfer Includes

The Río Negro highway transfer covers National Route 22 and National Route 151, together about 560 kilometres of key corridors. Route 22 connects Río Colorado to Cipolletti, while Route 151 links Cipolletti to the La Pampa border.

In addition, the agreement includes the Tren del Valle, a passenger service running between Plottier and Cipolletti. The province will take over operation after a six-month transition period, according to Ámbito Financiero.

The signing is set for Monday 24 August 2026 at 1pm at the presidential palace. Cabinet chief Diego Santilli and economy minister Luis Caputo will formalize the agreement with governor Alberto Weretilneck.

Ownership Stays National

This is not a transfer of ownership, as regional outlet ANRoca explained. The roads remain national.

However, the power to decide what is done with them passes to the provincial government in Viedma. Therefore, the province can carry out works and sign contracts without permission from Buenos Aires.

It assumes full responsibility for the national roads, including technical design and dealing with companies. As a result, the roads remain national, but the province gains decision-making power.

This arrangement was described by ANRoca in April. The roads will remain national routes, owned by the federal government.

However, the province gains the power to decide what is done with them, as ANRoca explained.

Twenty-Year Term Confirmed

The cession runs for 20 years, the same term agreed with other provinces, reported Ámbito Financiero. Río Negro had initially asked for 30 years, but the signing reflects the shorter period.

Meanwhile, the railway piece has its own timeline. A six-month transition period was set before the province assumes operation of the Tren del Valle, according to the same report.

However, the term is 20 years, not the 30 years originally requested. This matches the period agreed with other provinces, though none are named.

Province Takes on Maintenance and Works

The federal government framed the deal as transferring operation and maintenance of the national roads, without losing their national status. Mejor Informado reported that a decree would define this arrangement.

As a result, Río Negro will handle daily upkeep and future projects. Investments, according to the April description, would be financed through peaje, or tolls, rather than federal transfers.

Separate Loan for Repaving

It is not compensation from the federal government. The loan would fund initial road works, but no budget figures or start dates were confirmed.

The US$60 million loan is under discussion and not part of the agreement. It would fund initial repaving, but no start dates were confirmed.

Wider Policy Context

The 20-year term matches what other provinces have agreed, according to Ámbito Financiero. However, the report does not say how many provinces have signed or name them.

Still, this deal fits a broader pattern of the federal government shifting road responsibilities to provinces. Río Negro is one province that has offered to take charge of its national routes.

In addition, this deal reflects a broader trend of transferring road responsibilities to provinces. Río Negro is one province that has offered to take charge of its routes.

What Happens Next

After the signing, the province will begin the six-month transition for the railway and prepare to take over road operations. In short, the Río Negro highway transfer shifts decision-making to Viedma while keeping the roads federal.

The railway will follow a similar path, with the province taking control of the Tren del Valle. After the signing, the province will begin the six-month transition for the railway.

Meanwhile, it will prepare to take over road operations, though specific powers of Vialidad Nacional remain unspecified.

What is the Río Negro highway transfer?

It is an agreement signed on 24 August 2026. It transfers the running and upkeep of National Routes 22 and 151 to Río Negro province.

How long does the transfer last?

The term is 20 years, according to Ámbito Financiero, the same period agreed with other provinces. Río Negro had initially asked for 30 years.

World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Mexico · Markets & Economy

Mexican Stocks Post Their Best Day Since June

Key Facts — The session. The S&P/BMV IPC closed Friday at 65,729.18, up 2.14%, its biggest one-day gain since 11 June. The FTSE BIVA rose 2.17%.

— The peso. The Banxico FIX in force today is 16.9018 pesos to the dollar. The analyst consensus is that it weakens to 17.68 by year end, not that it strengthens.

— The diesel. Fuel duty relief on diesel reached 82.59% for 22–28 August, worth 6.08 pesos a litre. That is the highest of 2026, above April’s 81.20%.

— The underspend. The government spent 499,000 million pesos, about US$29.5 billion, less than programmed in the first half. Pemex accounted for 45,297 million of it.

— The energy cut. Ramo 21, the energy budget branch, lost 61.7% of its approved first-half budget as transfers to Pemex were cut by 164,000 million pesos.

— The bond. FONDO, one of the four public agricultural trusts run by the central bank, raised 4,500 million pesos, about US$266 million, in three tranches on the Mexican exchange.

A strong Friday on the exchange, the year’s largest diesel tax break, and half a trillion pesos the government did not spend.

Paseo de la Reforma at dusk. (Photo: Ricardo Esquivel, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

A good Friday, after a bad week

The S&P/BMV IPC closed on Friday at 65,729.18, up 2.14%. That is its largest single-day gain since 11 June, a gap of just over ten weeks, and it came three days after the index touched its 2026 low of 63,933.69. The FTSE BIVA, the rival exchange’s benchmark, rose 2.17% in step.

Grupo México led, up 4.17%, with GCC up 5.05%, Pinfra 3.16% and Cemex 2.40%. Walmex fell 1.55%, and the consumer names generally lagged — which fits the retail data. Sales were down 0.2% month on month in June, against expectations of a small rise.

One correction worth making plainly, because the number is circulating. There is no analyst forecast of 16.50 pesos to the dollar. The Citi survey published on 20 August, covering 37 institutions, has a year-end consensus of 17.68, with the most optimistic house at 17.00 and the most pessimistic at 19.03. The currency is near 16.90 now, so the consensus view is mild weakening, not strengthening.

The state is paying most of the diesel tax for you

The finance ministry publishes a fuel duty waiver every Friday in the official gazette. For the week of 22 to 28 August it set the diesel stimulus at 82.59%, worth 6.0813 pesos a litre and leaving drivers paying 1.2821 pesos of the duty.

That is the highest diesel relief of 2026. The previous peak was 81.20% in early April, and the year’s low was 14.63% in late June. Petrol relief is far smaller: 22.44% on regular, and 4.03% on premium.

The reason is upstream. Brent rose more than 6% in the week to 21 August and WTI more than 5%, on Iran sanctions and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Because the Mexican fuel excise is a fixed peso amount per litre rather than a percentage, it does not fall automatically when crude climbs — so the government waives it instead, and takes the hit on tax collection.

The bigger fiscal story is what was not spent

The finance ministry’s second-quarter report, presented on 30 July, records net spending of 4.856 trillion pesos in the first half — 499,000 million pesos below what was programmed. Finance Secretary Edgar Amador Zamora said the pace of spending “will have to normalise”.

Energy took the deepest cut of any branch. Ramo 21, the budget line through which federal transfers to Pemex flow, lost 61.7% of its approved first-half budget, as the government withdrew 164,000 million pesos in subsidies to the oil company. Pemex’s own underspend was 45,297 million pesos, a 16.1% real contraction against its calendared budget, concentrated in physical investment, pensions and plant maintenance.

This is not an accounting curiosity. Pemex’s second-quarter profit fell 69.7% year on year, and fuel theft cost it 9,180 million pesos in operating losses between April and June, the worst since 2018. Deferred maintenance at a company in that condition is a liability being carried forward, not a saving.

Money for the countryside

On Friday FONDO placed 4,500 million pesos of long-term certificates on the Mexican exchange, about US$266 million. It came in three tranches: 1,337.5 million at a floating rate over 18 months, 2,234.25 million fixed at 9.11% over five and a half years, and a 928.25 million social bond at 8.84% over four and a half.

FONDO is one of four public trusts run by the Bank of Mexico under the FIRA umbrella. They are a second-tier development bank: they do not lend to farmers, they fund and guarantee the commercial banks that do, and they raise the money in the bond market. The paper carries top national-scale ratings from all three agencies that rated it. This was FONDO’s first long-term issue, though its sister trust FEFA placed 8,000 million pesos in July.

One story we are not running

A claim circulating on Monday held that the state tourism fund Fonatur will build its first new resort development in twenty years, in Nayarit, for 1,734 million pesos. We could not verify any element of it, and we are not publishing it.

Fonatur has announced no such project, in Nayarit or elsewhere; its August news was a sale of existing lots in Huatulco, Ixtapa, Loreto and Los Cabos. The agency’s own published strategy explicitly abandons the resort-building model. There is a large new development in Nayarit — Costa Nayarit, in Compostela, presented in April — but it is private, led by Grupo Prodi and partners, and worth more than 20 billion pesos, twelve times the figure quoted.

Why this matters if you are invested here

Two numbers frame Mexico this week. The policy rate is 6.50% and most analysts expect it to stay there through next year, which is what has been holding the peso up alongside remittances and nearshoring flows. Growth consensus for 2026 is 1.2%.

Against that, the state is forgoing fuel tax revenue at the highest rate of the year while running 499,000 million pesos behind its own spending plan, and the company at the centre of both is losing money faster than it is being recapitalised. Friday’s rally was real. The fiscal arithmetic behind it has not changed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Mexican peso expected to strengthen to 16.50?

No. The most recent Citi survey of 37 analysts, published on 20 August, puts the year-end 2026 consensus at 17.68 pesos to the dollar. The most bullish house in the survey is Barclays at 17.00. With the currency near 16.90 today, the consensus expects it to weaken from here, not strengthen.

What is the IEPS diesel stimulus and who pays for it?

IEPS is Mexico’s federal fuel excise, charged as a fixed number of pesos per litre rather than as a percentage of the price. When crude rises, the tax does not rise with it, so the government’s lever is to waive part of the duty each week. An 82.59% stimulus means the state forgoes 82.59% of the charge. It shows up as weaker tax collection rather than as spending.

Why did the energy ministry underspend so heavily?

Because federal transfers to Pemex flow through it. The finance ministry attributes the shortfall to “lower resources allocated to the financial strengthening of Pemex”. Ramo 21 lost 61.7% of its approved first-half budget while the state oil company’s own underspend concentrated in physical investment, pensions and maintenance.

What is FIRA, and what did it sell?

FIRA is a group of four public trusts administered by the Bank of Mexico that function as a second-tier agricultural development bank. They do not lend to farmers directly; they fund and guarantee the banks that do. FONDO, the oldest of the four, placed 4,500 million pesos in its first long-term issue, including a social bond at 8.84%.

Colombia mining output is rebounding, driven by coal and gold, even as crude oil production slows. In the second quarter of 2026, coal activity expanded 16.2 percent and metallic minerals rose 15.4 percent, according to Portafolio.

Coal and Gold Drive the Rebound

Overall, Colombia mining output is on the upswing, according to Portafolio. The news outlet said coal and metallic minerals ‘saved the day’ for the mining and energy sector.

Coal activity expanded 16.2 percent in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. Metallic minerals, which include gold, rose 15.4 percent over the same stretch.

However, no volume figures for coal or gold were published for that quarter. The percentages are the only official data available.

Meanwhile, the 15.4 percent rise in metallic minerals includes gold, but no separate gold percentage was published. As a result, only the broader category figure is available for analysis.

Colombia Mining Output Outpaces Economy

In fact, DANE reported mining and quarrying value added grew 4.2 percent in Q2 2026 versus Q2 2025. This branch covers coal, metal ores, quarry materials, and also crude oil and natural gas extraction.

Meanwhile, Colombia’s whole economy grew 3.5 percent in the same period. As a result, mining and quarrying grew faster than the overall economy.

Meanwhile, the statistics agency DANE compiles these figures as part of its national accounts. This branch includes crude oil and natural gas extraction, which can mask declines.

In addition, the 4.2 percent growth in mining and quarrying outpaces the 3.5 percent expansion of the entire economy. However, this branch includes oil and gas, which can mask declines.

Year-to-Date and Quarterly Trends

DANE also provided two other figures for mining and quarrying. For the year to date, the sector grew 1.6 percent compared with the first half of 2025.

In addition, quarter-on-quarter, the sector expanded 0.4 percent. These numbers show a steady, if modest, recovery.

In addition, DANE revised its first-quarter data due to updates from the mining regulator. These revisions affect coal, metallic minerals, and natural gas figures.

Meanwhile, the year-to-date growth of 1.6 percent is lower than the annual rate, indicating a slowdown. In addition, DANE revised first-quarter data due to updates from the mining regulator.

Coming Out of the Red

El Espectador described the turn as mining and quarrying finally coming out of the red. The activity grew 4.2 percent, it said.

Therefore, this marks a positive shift for a sector that had been struggling. Still, the recovery is uneven across different minerals.

Still, the recovery is uneven across different minerals. While coal and gold surged, crude oil and gas output declined.

However, the recovery is uneven because crude oil and gas output declined. Still, the aggregate growth shows a positive turn for the sector.

Crude Oil Output Slips

In contrast, crude oil production fell. Meanwhile, Campetrol said fiscalised oil output averaged 722.2 thousand barrels per day in Q2 2026.

That figure is down 1.9 percent from the same quarter of 2025. Fiscalised production is the volume officially measured and certified at the wellhead for royalty and tax purposes.

Meanwhile, Campetrol is a private industry association, not a government body. No official quarterly figure from the hydrocarbons agency was found.

Meanwhile, the Campetrol figure is an industry association estimate, not an official government number. Since no official figure was found, this remains the only available data.

Natural Gas Contraction

Natural gas also saw a decline, though over a different period. By contrast, commercialised natural gas output fell 14.0 percent in H1 2026 versus H1 2025.

The daily average dropped from 811.2 to 699.0 million cubic feet. This is a first-half figure, not a second-quarter one.

This decline is based on press coverage, not an official bulletin. Still, it highlights a broader trend in the sector.

However, this decline covers the first half of 2026, not just the second quarter. In addition, the data comes from press coverage rather than an official bulletin.

Free Trade Zone Exports Dip

In a separate statistic, DANE reported that goods exports from Colombia’s free trade zones fell 0.9 percent in June 2026. However, the value dropped from US$237.6 million to US$235.3 million, free on board.

A free trade zone is an area treated as outside the customs territory, offering tariff benefits. No cause for the decline was published.

Meanwhile, this figure covers all goods from free zones, with no commodity breakdown. Therefore, it should not be linked to mining or energy exports.

Meanwhile, this statistic covers all goods from free zones, with no commodity breakdown. Therefore, it cannot be linked to mining or energy exports.

River Levels Fall on Magdalena and Cauca

The state weather institute IDEAM reported falling water levels on the Cauca and Magdalena rivers. Levels and flows are below historic values for this time of year.

IDEAM expects flows to drop by 20 to 60 percent during August across wide stretches of the middle and lower Magdalena basin. This could intensify in September.

Meanwhile, IDEAM is the national institute for hydrology, meteorology, and environmental studies. The river flow, or caudal, is measured in volume per second.

In addition, the river flow, or caudal, is the volume of water passing a point per second. However, no specific impact on navigation or water supply was quantified.

Possible Impacts on Navigation and Water Supply

IDEAM warned of possible effects on navigation, water supply, and associated ecosystems if conditions persist. The outlook runs to moderate, severe, and extreme drought between September 2026 and January 2027.

This is a separate concern from mining output, but it highlights broader environmental risks. In addition, the drought outlook extends to severe conditions through January 2027.

However, no specific effects on shipping or companies were quantified. Meanwhile, IDEAM’s outlook runs to severe drought through January 2027.

However, no effects on shipping or companies were published.

Frequently Asked Questions

What drove Colombia mining output in Q2 2026?

Coal and metallic minerals, including gold, drove the rebound. Coal expanded 16.2 percent and metallic minerals rose 15.4 percent, according to Portafolio.

How fast did mining and quarrying grow?

Mining and quarrying value added grew 4.2 percent in Q2 2026 versus Q2 2025, per DANE. The whole economy grew 3.5 percent in the same period.

Did crude oil production rise?

No, crude oil output fell. Campetrol reported a 1.9 percent decline to 722.2 thousand barrels per day in Q2 2026.

Are river levels affecting mining?

IDEAM reported falling river levels on the Magdalena and Cauca, but no link to mining output has been published. The institute warns of possible impacts on navigation and water supply.

World.title: Rincón de la Vieja Erupts Twice Ahead of Free National Parks Day
World.content:
The Rincón de la Vieja volcano erupted twice today and the Observatorio Vulcanológico y Sismológico de Costa Rica (Ovsicori-UNA) reported no ashfall and no lahars from either event. The larger of the two came at 7:38 a.m. and lasted under a minute. Ovsicori classified it as moderate. A smaller eruption had already occurred at 12:30 a.m.

Neither eruption was visible on the observatory’s webcams. Cloud cover sat over the summit all morning, so nobody got a look at the column. That happens often during the rainy season, and it is one reason the seismic and infrasound networks matter more than the cameras this time of year.

The volcano stays at caution, which is level 3 on Ovsicori’s four-step scale. Ovsicori moved it up from level 2 in early August after counting 48 eruptions in roughly a month, including 23 in a single week. Volcanologist Cyrill Müller said at the time that a volcano at level 3 can produce eruptions, lahars and ashfall — a plain description of the range, not a forecast that any of those will happen on a given day.

Several dozen phreatic eruptions have hit the mountain this year. Some of them sent primary and secondary lahars down the slopes in July and August. Phreatic is worth understanding, because it explains why this volcano behaves the way it does. Groundwater seeps down until it meets hot rock, flashes to steam, and blows out through the crater carrying mud, rock fragments and gas.

There is no fresh magma rising to the surface. That is why these eruptions are usually short, usually small, and almost never announced in advance — the trigger is water, and water moves fast.Lahars are the part that reaches beyond the crater. They are slurries of volcanic debris and water that run down river channels, and they are far more likely when heavy rain falls on loose material the volcano has already deposited. Ovsicori has repeatedly flagged the rainy season as the higher-risk window for exactly this reason.

That matters right now as the Instituto Meteorológico Nacional forecast gusts reaching 80 km/h (50 mph) in northern Guanacaste today, with afternoon downpours and thunderstorms across the region. Rivers draining the massif, including the Pénjamo and the Azul, have discolored after past eruptions as material washed downslope.

If you are near those drainages during heavy rain, move away from the channel and onto higher ground. Do not wait to see the water rise. Lahars travel faster than people expect and arrive without warning. The summit trail has been closed for years and remains closed, and SINAC will keep it shut until eruptive activity drops enough for access to be considered safe.

That route climbs about 8 kilometers (5 miles) one way with roughly 1,000 meters (3,300 feet) of gain, and it ends at the active crater — the single worst place to be standing when a phreatic eruption fires with no warning. The rest of the park operates on its own schedule.

Rincón de la Vieja National Park covers 14,300 hectares (35,300 acres) and splits into two visitor sectors, Las Pailas and Santa María. Las Pailas takes most of the traffic and centers on a 3-kilometer (1.9-mile) loop past mud pots, fumaroles and steam vents, well below the summit. Entry tickets must be booked through SINAC’s online reservation system before you arrive.

Tomorrow is National Parks Day, and entry to Costa Rica’s national parks is free. That comes from Decree 16847-MAG-MEP, signed in 1986, which waives admission for every visitor on 24 August regardless of nationality. SINAC has confirmed the waiver applies countrywide this year, with the national celebration centered in Puntarenas. Free does not mean the volcano rules change, and there are two things worth sorting out before you drive to Guanacaste.

The first is the calendar as Rincón de la Vieja normally closes on Mondays — the park runs Tuesday through Sunday, and the Monday shutdown exists so crews can maintain the Las Pailas trails. This year 24 August lands on a Monday. SINAC has not published whether it is waiving that closure for the free-entry day, so do not assume the gates open just because admission is waived. Call the Las Pailas sector or check sinac.go.cr before you commit to the drive from Liberia or the coast.

The second is the summit trail, and this one is not ambiguous. Free entry does not reopen it and that trail is closed on volcanic grounds and stays closed until Ovsicori’s activity level supports reopening it, which is a separate decision from anything to do with ticket prices. You still need a reservation even when the ticket costs nothing. Parks inside SINAC’s online system, and Rincón de la Vieja is one of them, release free tickets through the same platform and cap them the same way.

The cap is about how many people the trails can carry safely, not about revenue. Free days draw crowds, and slots go. Nothing Ovsicori reported today changes the park’s status on its own as the volcano sat at level 3 before those two eruptions and it sits at level 3 after them. What changes access is a closure decision, and those arrive on their own schedule — rain on a mountain that has been shedding loose material for two months is the likelier trigger.

Check the park’s status the day you go rather than the week before since sector and trail access shifts with volcanic activity and with weather, and a closure decided on Saturday will not appear in a tour operator’s brochure. The volcano rises to 1,916 meters (6,286 feet) roughly 25 kilometers (16 miles) northeast of Liberia. Ovsicori monitors it continuously through seismic, gas and deformation instruments, and publishes updates as events occur.

Costa Rica lives with six active volcanoes, and Rincón de la Vieja has been among the busiest of them for the better part of a decade. Level 3 is not an emergency but it is a standing instruction to pay attention to where you are and what the sky is doing.

World.title: Why Costa Rica’s Solar Potential Remains Almost Entirely Untapped
World.content:
Costa Rica has some of the best solar radiation conditions anywhere in the world and already runs on nearly 100 percent renewable electricity. Yet solar power contributes less than one percent of the national grid, a gap that has little to do with sunshine and everything to do with law.

The Costa Rican Electricity Institute, known as ICE, has held a legal monopoly over the commercialization of electricity since 1949, and it remains in force today. Private generators face a hard ceiling, limited to 30 percent of total generation capacity, with foreign investment inside that private share separately capped at 65 percent.

Any generation project larger than five megawatts must connect through ICE’s own transmission network and receive ICE’s authorization, since ICE owns every transmission line in the country and is the only entity permitted to trade electricity in the regional market. Private companies are, in effect, limited to generation only, and are mandated to sell their output exclusively to ICE, competing for contracts through ICE’s own tendering process, which sets both the quantity and terms of what it will buy.

Homeowners fare somewhat better, though the constraints remain real. Costa Ricans who install rooftop solar can sell excess power back to the grid under net metering rules, but those rules include a limit that has puzzled energy analysts for years: generate more than 49 percent of what gets fed back into the grid and the utility will not credit the surplus.

One legal analysis of the regulation found no technical grid justification for that specific number, describing it instead as an arbitrary ceiling meant to prevent generation from growing too large. A separate rule caps all private distributed generation on any given circuit at just 15 percent of that circuit’s peak demand, meaning even a popular neighborhood full of enthusiastic solar adopters eventually hits a wall regardless of how much rooftop capacity homeowners want to add.

This is not a new complaint. Costa Rica has cycled through more than a decade of solar policy whiplash: a promising pilot program in 2010 that ran through roughly 300 participants, new fee disputes in 2015 that required renewable energy advocates to fight for workable regulations, a stronger legal framework passed in 2021 that pushed installed distributed capacity past 3,500 active systems and nearly 100 megawatts, and then a fresh round of controversial tariffs in 2023 that slowed the market again just as it was gaining real momentum.

Each round of reform runs into the same structural fact: ICE is simultaneously the dominant generator, the transmission monopoly, and the government body responsible for planning the country’s entire energy expansion, which means the same institution that stands to lose market share from private solar growth is also the one deciding how much room to leave for it.

That structural conflict is precisely why international investors are watching a bill currently before Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly that would restructure the electricity market itself. The proposal would create a new National Electricity Market and hand coordination to a newly created body operating under the environment ministry and the national utility regulator, a shift toward the kind of separation between generation, transmission, and retail supply that international economic reviewers have recommended for years, arguing it would spur the innovation, customer responsiveness, and lower prices seen in countries that have taken similar steps.

If enacted in anything resembling its current form, the bill would open the door to direct power purchase agreements between private generators and large consumers, the exact mechanism that has driven utility scale solar booms elsewhere in Latin America, from Chile to Colombia to increasingly Mexico.

But the reform is now in serious jeopardy. The National Liberation Party, whose own lawmakers helped shape the current bill text during the prior legislative session, reversed course this year and pulled its support, arguing the proposal would weaken ICE, break the long standing solidarity principle underpinning Costa Rica’s electricity model, and benefit large consumers at the expense of households and small businesses.

The party says it will introduce its own competing energy security bill instead, aimed at preventing rationing and speeding up renewable generation without the deeper market restructuring the original bill proposed. The dispute has taken on added urgency after Panama recently suspended electricity sales to Costa Rica amid a trade disagreement, even though ICE maintains the country currently has enough supply to meet demand without those contracts.

The reversal lands against a broader backdrop of renewed investor optimism about Costa Rica generally. A new legislature took office this year with early momentum behind a pro-growth agenda, and some emerging markets analysts see a real possibility of Costa Rica reaching investment grade credit status if political fragmentation eases and reform momentum holds, a shift that would mark a meaningful re-rating of the country’s borrowing costs on international markets.

Electricity market liberalization sits near the top of that reform agenda specifically because foreign capital is watching to see whether Costa Rica will finally dismantle the barriers, the generation caps, the foreign ownership limits, the mandatory sale through ICE, that have kept its considerable renewable energy potential, especially solar, so far below what the country’s natural resources would otherwise allow.

None of this is entirely new territory for Costa Rica. The last serious attempt to open ICE’s monopoly, a 2000 package known as the Combo ICE, triggered some of the largest social protests in the country’s modern history and was ultimately withdrawn amid fears of privatization and foreign intrusion into a deeply popular public institution.

That history helps explain why the current reversal carries so much political weight, and why investors continue to treat electricity market reform in Costa Rica as a genuine open question rather than a foregone conclusion, even as the economic case for opening the market, and finally letting Costa Rica’s solar potential compete on equal footing, grows harder to ignore.

World.title: Costa Rica Asked to Explain Fishing Boats Seen in Puntarenas Estuary
World.content:
The appearance of two fishing boats in the Puntarenas estuary has led a Costa Rican ocean conservation advocate to ask authorities for more information about the vessels, their owners and why they entered the area. Jorge Serendero Hülssner, director of Fundación For the Oceans and a member of the Marine Commission of the Presidential Council on the Ocean, raised the concern in a recent opinion column.

Serendero described the two boats as being of Chinese origin and identified one as TUNG HAI 168. However, he did not accuse either vessel of illegal fishing or any other crime. Instead, he asked authorities to clarify who owns and operates the boats, where they came from, what permission they had to enter the estuary and whether they had previously fished or transferred catches elsewhere in the region.

Public vessel-tracking information reviewed after the alert adds an important complication. Global Fishing Watch and commercial tracking services list TUNG HAI 168 as operating under the Costa Rican flag, not the Chinese flag. The vessel is approximately 24 meters (79 feet) long.

Those databases do not publicly identify its owner or explain why it carries a Chinese name. A boat’s name, appearance or country of construction does not prove its current nationality or ownership. The second vessel mentioned by Serendero was not identified in the column.

The available information therefore does not establish that TUNG HAI 168 is a foreign vessel. It also does not answer whether the boat had the necessary fishing, port or navigation permits. The location has added to the calls for an official explanation. The Puntarenas estuary is part of a protected wetland created in 2001 and expanded in 2005 and 2006.

The area includes mangroves, mudflats and important breeding grounds for fish and other wildlife. Puntarenas is also the legal headquarters of the Costa Rican Fisheries and Aquaculture Institute (INCOPESCA), which regulates the country’s fishing industry.

Serendero used the sighting to raise a wider concern about Costa Rica’s ability to monitor fishing activity across its waters. Large fishing operations can remain at sea for months with help from fuel, supply and refrigerated cargo vessels. Some transfer their catch to other ships without returning to port, a practice known as transshipment.

Transshipment is not automatically illegal, however, international fisheries organizations warn that weak oversight can make it harder to determine where fish were caught and whether fishing rules were followed. The concern also extends beyond Costa Rica. Isla del Coco forms part of the Eastern Tropical Pacific Marine Corridor, known as CMAR. Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia and Ecuador created the regional initiative to coordinate protection of connected marine areas that include Cocos, Coiba, Malpelo, Gorgona and the Galápagos Islands.

Sharks, tuna, turtles, rays and whales regularly move between these areas, meaning fishing or environmental damage in one part of the region can affect marine life elsewhere. Costa Rica has improved some of its monitoring tools and shares tracking information for Costa Rican fishing vessels with Global Fishing Watch, while radar systems help authorities monitor waters around Isla del Coco. Those systems, however, do not by themselves establish who owns the two boats seen in Puntarenas or what authorization they had.

No public response addressing the specific vessels could be located from INCOPESCA or the National Coast Guard as of today. The central question remains straightforward: whether Costa Rican authorities can identify the boats, their operators and the reason they were inside the Puntarenas estuary.

World.title: Young mother pleads for help from Special Envoy, Women’s Department over alleged coercive and financial abuse by children’s father who made her lose her job, took away her car and washing machine
World.content:
Young mother pleads for help from Special Envoy, Women’s Department over alleged coercive and financial abuse by children’s father who made her lose her job, took away her car and washing machine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A young mother who claims she is trapped in a cycle of coercive and financial abuse at the hands of her children’s father, a prominent attorney and businessman whose father is a sitting Minister of Government, is pleading for help from the Office of the Special Envoy, the Women’s Department and the National Women’s Commission.

The young mother, identified as Selia Stephen on Facebook, said she has faced months of alleged financial, emotional and psychological pressure since leaving the relationship and quitting her employment with the father of her children.

Stephen claims that after she found another job, he stopped arranging for the children to be picked up from school and stopped paying the babysitter, which she says caused her to lose the job. She further alleges that he took away the vehicle she used to transport the children, stopped paying for their daughter’s tutoring and even removed the washing machine after she refused to return to work for him.

“At every turn this man has found ways to create chaos to force me back into the abusive situation with him I ran from,” Stephen wrote.

She also alleges that he sometimes refuses at the last minute to take the children during scheduled visitation weekends, has withheld child support since December and is attempting to block her decision to enroll the children in public school because it is more affordable and easier for her to manage transportation.

Screenshots shared alongside the matter, purportedly showing messages from a contact saved as “Kids Dad,” contain a string of insults and remarks about money and the children. In one message, the sender calls Stephen a “dead beat mother” and says, “if you move her I will simply spend the savings on my woman n book a trip from that money u dying for.” The sender also repeatedly calls her a “dummy” and “ghetto,” and later writes that another person “might get the 1000 to prepare your child.”

Stephen further claims she has a restraining order against the children’s father for alleged harassment and for showing up at her home after she told him she did not want him to know where she lived. Despite that, she says he has questioned her sanity in court and succeeded in having the court order her to attend counselling with him.

Now saying she is at her “wits end,” Stephen is asking where women in similar situations can turn after what she describes as repeated failures by the courts and police.

“I am not asking for sympathy, I am at my wits end and seeking some kind of help to get out of this coercive and mental abuse,” she wrote, directly appealing to the Women’s Department, Special Envoy and Women’s Commission.

Stephen said she believes the alleged conduct is intended to “break me financially, emotionally and mentally.”

The allegations and the authenticity and authorship of the message screenshots have not been independently established. A response from the father of her children was not included in the material reviewed for this story.

World.title: PUP says this is the year, but can Aaron Mai actually beat Earl Trapp?
World.content:
PUP says this is the year, but can Aaron Mai actually beat Earl Trapp?

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Four terms. Four wins. Earl Trapp has held San Ignacio and Santa Elena through every challenger the PUP has thrown at him, and now he is going for a fifth.

The PUP says 2027 is different.

Last month, at the party’s National Party Council meeting in Dangriga, Prime Minister John Briceño boasted that the Twin Towns are coming home.

“We are going to win San Ignacio and Santa Elena for the People’s United Party,” he told the room.

The party has since assembled what it calls its strongest municipal slate yet. Leading it is Aaron Mai, a two term councilor and the only PUP voice currently sitting on the town council. Behind him: Edel Espat, Matthew Preston, Joe Awe, Nadime Hegar, Eliu Yacab and Nazim Lisbey.
