Does the missing Santa Elena candidate matter to you?

World.title: New system will track unsafe medicines, vaccines and fake medical products in Belize
World.content:
New system will track unsafe medicines, vaccines and fake medical products in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Ministry of Health and Wellness has moved forward with the operationalisation of a National Post-Market Surveillance System for medicines and vaccines.

The work took place during a three day workshop last week supported by the Pan American Health Organization, bringing together officials from government agencies, health facility representatives, academia, private sector specialists and patient organisations.

The aim is to strengthen Belize’s capacity to detect, assess, investigate, communicate and respond to safety and quality concerns related to medicines and vaccines.

Belize recently became a full member of the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring and has advanced the use of pharmacovigilance tools including VigiFlow and VigiMobile, along with national reporting forms and pathways.

With PAHO support, the country is building an integrated approach that combines monitoring of medicine and vaccine safety with the detection and management of product quality issues, suspected substandard and falsified medical products, and unregistered products.

Participants examined the proposed terms of reference for the system, including its mandate, scope, functions and coordination mechanisms.

Officials stressed that an effective system depends on clearly defined responsibilities, good quality reports, timely feedback and coordination across institutions.

World.title: Two detained after armed robbery at Independence Village shop
World.content:
Two detained after armed robbery at Independence Village shop

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Two men were detained within hours of an armed robbery at a shop on Big Creek Road in Independence Village on Saturday afternoon.

Police received information of a robbery in progress around 2:30pm. On arrival, officers found a wallet on the floor of the shop containing a social security card and other items.

The shop attendant told police that two men barged into the shop. One pulled out a 9mm pistol and demanded cash while the other took the cash register pan containing an undisclosed amount of money.

Both men then left the shop in an SUV heading toward Belize City.

Coordinated information was sent to G13 personnel, who stopped and detained both suspects at the junction of George Town Village in the Stann Creek District. An undisclosed amount of money was recovered.

Police are continuing investigations. No charges have been laid as yet.

World.title: ‘Long overdue’
World.content:
Minister of National Security and Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang and Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange are all smiles as they receive the keys to the third Government-run shelter for women facing domestic abuse. (Photo: JIS)

LOCAL gender advocates have welcomed news that work has been completed on a third shelter for victims of domestic abuse.

Minister with responsibility for gender affairs Olivia Grange made the announcement last Friday as she toured the facility at an undisclosed location.

“We made a commitment that we would establish three centres, safe spaces for women, and we have achieved that,” said Grange as she pointed out that prior to the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration there were no State-run shelters for women wishing to leave violent relationships.

In the last few years the Government completed, and is operating, two shelters for women. Grange said the addition of the third shelter will enable the ministry to offer up to 70 safe spaces for women and their children.

Grange said the completion of this third shelter, which is scheduled to begin providing a safe space for women after September 1, enables the Government to provide much-needed services to vulnerable females across the entire island.

“The completion of this space advances the gender agenda, because what we have been able to do now is to provide the spaces across the island, and we are now better equipped that when we get the call we are able to activate the kind of network that is necessary to move [women in abusive situations] into safe spaces,” said Grange.

On Sunday, gender and development practitioner Judith Wedderburn told the Jamaica Observer that the new shelter was long overdue.

“It is certainly very welcome because, not only from my experience but from the reports of women who do suffer, they have been beaten by a male partner and have experienced gender-based violence. The data does show us that it’s not getting better. More and more reports are coming out that it is happening,” said Wedderburn

According to Wedderburn, she became aware of plans to construct the new shelter through discussions with officials of the Bureau of Gender Affairs, however she was uncertain of the completion time.

“I am acknowledging that I have been in meetings in the last couple months where it was reported by somebody from the bureau that a third shelter was going to be built in a different part of the island, outside of Kingston. My understanding was it was going to serve the western part of the island,” said Wedderburn.

Pointing to a recent article published by the Jamaica Gleaner headlined, ‘The cop who finally listened’, Wedderburn said the presence of another shelter in the country serves as a call to action.

“Two women who recounted years of fear after ending abusive relationships are grateful to a corporal for standing with them. What it said was the woman who had been so badly abused was paying tribute to the only policeman who took her report seriously, the only policeman that supported her. And if you reflect on not just this article but other reports, on many occasions, unfortunately, a woman will not gather up the strength to go to a police station to report the incident,” Wedderburn argued.

Welcoming the initiative Joy Crawford, co-founder and executive director of female support group Eve for Life, told the Observer that the move strengthens the national response to gender-based violence (GBV) and expands access to safety for women and children leaving abusive situations.

“We recommend convening a robust, national GBV shelter working group comprising Government, NGOs, community-based organisations and other stakeholders to improve coordination, effectiveness, and accountability across the shelter system. This should include deliberate efforts to strengthen and expand non-government shelter models, recognising that Government cannot do this alone,” said Crawford.

She told the Observer that the country needs more diverse, accessible safe spaces across the island for survivors with different needs, including women with children, women with complex needs, adolescents, and other vulnerable groups.

“NGOs and community organisations play vital roles in victim identification, referral, psychosocial support, and sustained engagement. Formal referral pathways and partnerships can help survivors access appropriate services and safe accommodation earlier,” added Crawford.

For advocacy officer at Jamaica Coalition for a Healthy Society Philippa Davies, the provision of a third shelter by the Government is a commendable initiative but it is unfortunate that the problem of GBV exists.

“It is always better that society encourages, teaches, and supports healthy, safe relationships between men and women. As such, the family is the fundamental foundational institution of any society. The very real need for such places is evidence of family pathology, which is often passed on through generations,” said Davies.

She argued that the Government needs to establish a Ministry of the Family to address the critical role of the family and the need to prioritise its welfare.

“This would include strongly encouraging women and men to exercise discernment when choosing romantic and life partners, and to seek wise advice before and when challenges arise. It is scientifically established that the brain hormones released during sex bonds partners to the point of overshadowing danger signals such as the potential for or the occurrence of abuse,” added Davies who argued that the Government should also consider providing support for men who may be victims of abuse.

In announcing the completion of the new facility Grange said the Government-run shelters not only provide safety but also provide a therapeutic environment for women to rebuild their lives.

“We not only ensure that we protect them, but we help them to gain skills where they don’t have skills, we provide counselling, we have adequate space that we can facilitate a family — mother and children,” said Grange.

She revealed that during the last few years, one shelter hosted a mother and five of her children, while another mother gave birth while residing at another shelter.

Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang, acting in his capacity as chairman of the Citizens Business Group — a Government team that is mandated to manage social interventions across the country — said the establishment of Government-run shelters for women has been a big part of a programme to seek to impact, in a positive way, a number of vulnerable communities in Jamaica and, in particular in this case, women who have suffered abuse.

Chang noted that in the past few years the ministry has established domestic violence intervention centres at selected police stations as part of the strategy to eliminate domestic violence.

World.title: People and culture give Ja tourism edge, says Tortuga Resorts CEO
World.content:
Member of Parliament for St James East Central, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett (front row, third right), members of his East Central Education Fund team, and chief executive officer of Tortuga Resorts Leonardo Schlesinger (front row, right), stand with recipients of the constituency’s 2026 tertiary awards at the Montego Bay Convention Centre last Thursday. Horace Hines

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Leo Schlesinger, chief executive officer of Tortuga Resorts which recently acquired Hyatt Hotels’ interest in Playa Hotels & Resorts brand, says Jamaica’s greatest competitive tourism advantage is its culture and people — which no other destination can reproduce.

“Many countries have beautiful beaches. Anyone can copy a beach [but] nobody can copy Jamaican culture — that is Jamaica’s true competitive advantage,” Schlesinger told the St James East Central Scholarship and Welfare Fund’s annual tertiary awards at Montego Bay Convention Centre last Thursday.

According to Schlesinger, the warmth, energy, music, food, humour and authenticity associated with Jamaica give the island a distinctive appeal in the global tourism marketplace.

“Guests may forget the room they stayed in [but] they never forget how Jamaicans make them feel,” declared Schlesinger.

He said the value of that cultural advantage extends well beyond tourism branding as culture has become an important economic asset for Jamaica.

“When tourism is 30 per cent of the economy, culture is, in a very real sense, one-third of the Jamaican economy.

“Culture is not just heritage; it is a tool for the future. We often talk about culture as something to preserve. In Jamaica’s case, we should also think of culture as something we use to create the future,” added Schlesinger.

Tortuga Resorts has expanded its footprint in Jamaica through the acquisition of the former Playa properties — including Secrets, Breathless, Hyatt Ziva, Hyatt Zilara and Dreams resorts — and Schlesinger said the company plans to maintain its focus on the Jamaican market.

“We are deeply invested in Jamaica, and we intend to keep investing in the country,” said Schlesinger.

He argued that tourism’s economic impact reaches far beyond hotels, with visitors generating opportunities for airport workers, taxi operators, hotel employees, farmers, fishermen, construction workers, retailers, musicians, and other service providers.

The Tortuga Resorts CEO warned, however, that Jamaica’s ability to sustain its competitive advantage would ultimately depend on the quality of its human capital.

“The countries that succeed will not necessarily be the ones with the most resources. They will be the ones with the best educated, most adaptable, and most innovative people,” he said.

Schlesinger said while Jamaica faces significant challenges — including climate change, hurricanes, labour constraints, immigration, and infrastructure gaps — its people remain its most valuable resource.

“If you invest in a person in their education, skill, confidence, and creativity, the person grows,” he said. “Knowledge grows when it’s shared. Skills grow when they’re practised. Ideas grow when people collaborate,”

He called on universities to move beyond simply preparing students for employment and underscored that tertiary institutions have an equally important responsibility to develop critical thinkers and responsible citizens who will question, analyse, distinguish fact from opinion, listen to ideas they disagree with, and think independently.

“A healthy democracy does not just need educated professionals, it needs educated citizens,” he added.

For his part, Member of Parliament for St James East Central, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett said he wants his contribution to education and human capital development to be his enduring legacy.

Bartlett revealed that 60 tertiary students from the constituency received scholarships from his education programme, valued at just under $10 million this year.

He said the scholarship programme — which began 47 years ago at the start of his political life in St Andrew Eastern and has continued for the past 30 years in St James East Central — reflects his long-standing commitment to education as a vehicle for social mobility and national development.

“If I should be asked, ‘What is it that you would really like to be remembered by 100 years from now?’ — and somebody wants to remember this fat-faced fellow from Westmoreland — I would want to be remembered as the person who made a difference in the lives of the people in this country,” Bartlett said.

“And I would like to be remembered as the one who recognised that education was the surest way for social mobility and human advancement,” added Bartlett.

World.title: Right injection for Percy Junor Hospital
World.content:
Director of Right Now For Jamaica Dr Trudy Hall (left) pointing to some of the medical supplies the group donated to the Percy Junor Hospital on Friday, while president of the organisation Dr Maurice Miles (right) and Director Rosalee Gordon look on. Kasey Williams

SPALDING, CLARENDON — A donation of critical equipment valued at $60 million and plans to digitise the medical records of patients have provided a well-needed shot in the arm for the Type C Percy Junor Hospital located on the border of Manchester and Clarendon which also serves people in parts of south St Ann and south Trelawny.

The donation was made to the hospital last Friday by Diaspora group Right Now For Jamaica, which has adopted the facility.

President of Right Now For Jamaica Dr Maurice Miles said the organisation was formed in the aftermath of Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, which hit Jamaica last October, to raise funds to assist facilities in the country.

“A group of us decided that we wanted to do something… We wanted to be very specific and detailed. I called Ambassador [Audrey] Marks [Member of Parliament for Manchester North Eastern] and asked how we can help and she said that we need help in Jamaica, specifically, at the hospital. It turns out we are heavy on health and education. In November we took our first trip and assessed the hospital,” said Mills.

“We decided to not just give gloves and gauze but rather to see what the hospital needs to give better care to function,” Miles added.

In welcoming the donation Marks said the gift of four containers filled with equipment including ventilators, automatic external defibrillators, hospital beds, IV poles, and recliners is the second handing over of well-needed supplies to the hospital by Right Now For Jamaica.

“When we invest in Percy Junor Hospital we are strengthening a critical part of the health-care network [that is] serving hundreds of thousands Jamaicans across central Jamaica. The first handover in January brought 15 computers, tablets, medical supplies, furniture and other essential items. At that time we identified some of the larger clinical equipment that you wanted to secure, including ventilators,” said Marks.

She announced that the group has also committed $30 million towards an outpatient clinic on the hospital grounds by converting the containers now storing the donated equipment.

“The proposed facility is designed to include eight fully equipped examination rooms, a triage capacity, procedural and surgical care, office space and patient recovery bays supporting primary care, paediatric services, surgical procedures and specialist consultations,” said Marks who pointed out that an off-the-national grid power supply and independent water infrastructure are included in the proposed project.

“The computers and tablets that are already provided through the partnership can support electronic medical records and an even more modern approach to patient care,” Marks added.

That position was endorsed by senior medical officer at the facility Dr Carlos Wilson who told the Jamaica Observer that efforts are well underway to have patients’ records digitised.

“We are going to work as fast as we can. We have to work within what we are able to produce locally and then we have to coordinate that with the Ministry of Health and Wellness, so it is difficult to give a definitive timeline. But certainly, what I am hoping is that we will have something up and running here at Percy Junor that we can start using in three months,” said Wilson as he pointed to the significance of efficiency of the hospital through digitisation.

“The importance of medical records being electronic [allows] it to be easy to retrieve and it gives critical information that you need to make very urgent decisions, so it will improve the health care of the patients we serve,” added Wilson, who noted that the hospital sees upwards of 30,000 patients yearly in its Accident and Emergency Department.

World.title: How Dis Mek: RIVER RAFTS
World.content:
Visitors to the island boarding a raft at the start of the Rafting on the Martha Brae tour. (Photos: Gavin Jones)

RIVER rafting is one of Jamaica’s popular vacation activities for locals and visitors alike but have you ever considered the mechanics behind the making of the rafts?

Claude Johnson, raft captain #102 at Rafting on the Martha Brae, explained to the Jamaica Observer’s How Dis Mek the process behind the making of rafts during an interview on the banks of the Martha Brae river in the hills of Trelawny, where dozens of his coworkers’ rafts were docked.

Bamboo, Johnson explained, is ideal for raft creation because each joint on a stalk is essentially an air-filled sealed vacuum, allowing the stalks to float extremely well.

“The reason why we choose bamboo is because it’s air-packed, so as the joints don’t burst, everything is okay. The bamboo can take [withstand] up to a thousand [pounds] on it. You see the more length you have, the more weight you can take on top of it. You can build it 28 feet, 29 feet — those lengths are the good lengths,” said Johnson.

He explained that even if some of the bamboo joints pop open, due to age or sun damage, as long as the others remain sealed the integrity of the raft is maintained.

The use of rafts in Trelawny is well documented. Initially, rafts were used to ferry goods from rural Trelawny to the parish capital of Falmouth. Recreational rafting began in the 1970s under the Jamaica Tourist Board and has been operated by River Raft Limited since 1985.

Raft captains must be fully trained and certified before they can operate, with lessons in controlling the raft and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) certification compulsory.

Once licensed, the captains are responsible for the creation of their own rafts. To create the raft, captains need what they refer to as a “dozen stalks of bamboo”.

“If you don’t have any and you can’t go into the field to cut it, you have some people cut it and sell it for $10,000 for a dozen, [but] when we say dozen we mean 14 bamboo to make a raft,” Johnson explained.

Then to move forward, captains need a partner, because raft building is a two-person job.

Working alongside Richardo Geinues, Captain #114, Johnson demonstrated that the stalks must first be cut to the same length, placed exactly next to each other, and bound tightly to create a flat surface.

Captains use ratcheting straps to tightly bind the stalks and prevent any chance of movement. Before the binding, the stalks are pierced at one end, at the same spot, to allow for a stick to be threaded through them and bound with metal wire and pliers.

The tension from the metal wire keeps the stalks together, forming the flat bed of the raft. Then another stalk is cut into five pieces and threaded in a similar manner on top of the raft.

World.title: Fire Brigade gets critical gear
World.content:
Granville Gayle (left), CEO of National Safety Limited, presents donated equipment to Jamaica Fire Brigade officials (from second left) Deputy Commissioner Sean Martin, Acting Deputy Commissioner Julian Davis-Buckle, and Commissioner Stewart Beckford.

NATIONAL Safety Limited, Jamaica’s leading provider of industrial safety and emergency response solutions, has facilitated the donation of critical fire fighting and rescue equipment from global emergency services leaders Rosenbauer and Holmatro to the Jamaica Fire Brigade.

The equipment was handed over recently by Granville Gayle, chief executive officer of National Safety, to head of fire brigade Commissioner Stewart Beckford.

The donation is in support of the Jamaica Fire Brigade’s continuing recovery and operational enhancement efforts following the impact of Hurricane Melissa last October.

Through National Safety’s long-standing relationships with international manufacturers Rosenbauer and Holmatro, the organisations responded positively to the brigade’s needs by providing essential equipment designed to enhance the safety and effectiveness of front-line firefighters and rescue personnel.

Rosenbauer’s contribution includes 100 HEROS NFPA firefighting helmets together with a range of accessories, spare parts, helmet-mounted lighting systems, and related components — providing valuable protective equipment for firefighters operating in hazardous environments.

Holmatro’s donation consists of specialised lifting bag systems and supporting equipment used in rescue and recovery operations.

These tools are designed to assist emergency responders in lifting, stabilising, and moving heavy objects during rescue incidents, helping to improve operational efficiency and enhance victim recovery efforts.

Speaking at the handover ceremony Gayle emphasised the importance of collaboration between industry partners and emergency services.

“National Safety is honoured to serve as the bridge between our valued international partners and the Jamaica Fire Brigade. We recognise the vital role the brigade plays in protecting lives and property across Jamaica, and we are proud to support initiatives that help equip our firefighters with the tools they need to carry out their duties safely and effectively,” said Gayle.

He argued that the initiative underscores National Safety’s ongoing commitment to advancing occupational safety, emergency preparedness, and resilience throughout Jamaica.

“By working closely with internationally recognised manufacturers and local stakeholders the company continues to support organisations which play a critical role in protecting communities and saving lives,” added Gayle.

Fire chief Beckford expressed appreciation for the gesture and acknowledged the significance of the donation.

“We are deeply grateful to National Safety, Rosenbauer, and Holmatro for this generous contribution. These resources will strengthen our firefighting and rescue capabilities and support the dedicated men and women who serve on the front lines every day,” said Beckford.

World.title: Jamaica dethroned as Haiti claim CFU U-14 boys title
World.content:
Haitian players celebrate after beating defending champions Jamaica 4-0 to take the CFU-U14 Tier 1 Challenge Series on Sunday (Photo: CFU Instagram)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica were dethroned as kings of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) Under-14 Boys Tier 1 Challenge Series on Sunday after they were outplayed and beaten 4-0 by Haiti in the final played at Cap Cana, Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic.

Wensley Dumorne scored twice early in the second half to take the game away from Jamaica, who trailed 1-0 at half-time and were losing for the first time in two trips to the competition.

It was the first time Jamaica had conceded a goal in the tournament after winning their previous four games by an 8-0 aggregate, including a 1-0 win over Bermuda in Friday’s semi-final.

Haiti went into the final as favourites after dismantling hosts Dominican Republic 6-1 in their semi-final.

After dominating early, Haiti were rewarded when Jodeley Sheeck Delmas opened the scoring in the 28th minute.

Dumorne doubled the lead in the 39th minute and then completed his brace in the 47th minute before Ronelson Pele Janvier added a fourth in the 59th minute.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Dr Gabrielle Henry set for first official public appearance since Miss Universe fall
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Dr Gabrielle Henry .

KINGSTON, JAMAICA — Dr Gabrielle Henry, Miss Universe Jamaica 2024, is set to make her first public appearance since her participation in the Miss Universe competition in 2025, where she was badly injured after an on-stage fall.

Miss Universe Jamaica made the announcement late Saturday, indicating that Henry will participate in the Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 Grand Coronation on Sunday, August 23, at the AC Hotel Kingston.

Henry spent much of her reign recovering from injuries she received while participating in the worldwide competition on November 19, 2025, in Thailand, including a fracture and intracranial haemorrhage.

She will return to the spotlight to crown her successor as Miss Universe Jamaica 2026.

Miss Universe Jamaica said the highly anticipated return is expected to be one of the defining moments of the Grand Coronation, bringing Henry back before a Jamaican audience as the organisation celebrates a new chapter in the country’s pageant journey.

Henry’s return comes as 33 contestants conclude their Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 journey, having competed for the opportunity to become Jamaica’s next representative at Miss Universe.

The competition stressed that for Henry, Sunday’s appearance represents a return to the public stage and a meaningful continuation of her Miss Universe Jamaica journey, this time with the responsibility of crowning the woman who will follow in her footsteps.

The Grand Coronation is expected to bring together personalities from Jamaica’s pageant, fashion and beauty industries, members of the media, industry leaders, special guests and supporters of the pageant community for an evening celebrating the women who have taken part in this year’s competition.

World.title: Stray animal highway horror
World.content:
The mangled Mitsubishi Pajero involved in the August 15 crash on the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000.

TOLL GATE, Clarendon — A night of T20 cricket enjoyment at Sabina Park in Kingston just over a week ago almost ended in death for three people when the sport utility vehicle in which they were travelling back to Mandeville crashed into a cow that had wandered onto the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000 in pitch darkness.

Hopeton McCatty, the driver and owner of the Mitsubishi Pajero; his friend Wensworth Skeffery, a former Opposition senator; and Skeffery’s 24-year-old daughter were not injured, but the cow died in the August 15 collision that revived fears of the danger posed to life by stray animals on the high-speed road.

“We took my friend’s daughter to cricket for the first time and she enjoyed it; a very good game of cricket, a fantastic crowd. We left Sabina Park and went downtown then joined the toll road at Portmore,” McCatty told the Jamaica Observer.

“We were talking about the experience of interacting with people and how to be humble. We were cruising along. We came through the tolls at Portmore, Vineyards, and May Pen. We were approaching the last one at Toll Gate driving at about 103 kilometres per hour… I had on the high beam, because the road was dark. We were in the left lane and while talking Skeffery said ‘Cow!’ ” McCatty related.

“I spotted this animal coming onto the road, so I braked and swerved to the right and we really thought we had missed it, but the cow kept coming and we hit the cow. The two airbags [deployed] and I swerved back to the left to avoid the median in the road. I wasn’t even able to see what was in front of me and I stopped,” added McCatty.

On Saturday, TransJamaican Highway (TJH) Limited Chief Executive Officer Ivan Anderson told the Sunday Observer that he had received a report on the incident and raised concern about residents living along that section of the highway repeatedly cutting through the fencing to get to their homes after disembarking buses travelling along the highway.

“The fence in this location has been cut and repaired several times since the start of the year. Since the initial cutting we doubled the fencing in this location by adding hog wire to the barbed wire; it is being cut by persons coming off buses on the highway and going into the community,” Anderson said in a WhatsApp response.

He said TJH is now in the process of identifying the owner of the cow as the animal was tagged.

On September 13 last year a woman had to be rushed to hospital after cattle strayed onto the highway shortly after midnight, causing extensive damage to two vehicles, a Toyota Axio and a Toyota Tacoma, and injuring occupants.

At that time the highway was toll-free. But when TJH commenced charging on December 27, 2025 it assured motorists of a First-World roadway supported by 24-hour patrols and consistent maintenance.

“Our commitment is to deliver a safe, reliable, and efficient driving experience across this new section in a manner that is consistent with our offerings on all legs of the TransJam Highway’s network. In order to deliver these services sustainably, we will introduce a toll rate structure at both the Toll Gate-MainLine Toll Plaza and the Toll Gate-Ramp Toll Plaza,” TJH said in an Instagram post.

However, for McCatty, the issue of stray cattle was compounded by him not seeing any patrols near midnight, and for close to an hour after the collision.

“The scary part about it is that when the car hit the cow all the lights went, because the battery got dislodged completely. We were out there on the highway in complete darkness,” he said.

“I didn’t know if a truck was going to come and run straight into us; and there has been an incident before on the highway network where people died after having an accident and then an oncoming vehicle hit them,” he added.

He said he was relieved when a tow truck, en route to Mandeville, stopped at the accident scene and subsequently removed his vehicle.

“God is good, because a wrecker was passing and stopped and had on its hazard lights; that give us some sense of calm that people wouldn’t run up into us in the darkness,” he said.

“The car bonnet seemed to have cut the cow’s neck. It took us about an hour to get off the road. During that time other vehicles stopped, but we didn’t see anybody from the toll [company] patrolling,” added McCatty.

He said he returned to Clarendon the Sunday afternoon following the accident to report it.

“We filed a report at the Four Paths Police Station on Sunday afternoon, because Sunday morning I couldn’t miss church. I had to give God thanks. We came out with no wounds. I reported the accident to the insurance company and the vehicle is basically written off,” he explained.

Vice chairman of the National Road Safety Council Dr Lucien Jones said he previously engaged the National Road Operating and Constructing Company (NROCC) — which is responsible for overseeing the design, construction, and maintenance of Jamaica’s highways — about the danger of stray animals on the high-speed road.

“Having a stray animal on a road which provides for driving at a fairly high speed to enable people to get from point A to point B in a fairly short time and therefore aid in the whole transportation sector carrying goods and people across the country, poses a severe problem,” he said.

“We have had this issue before. We have had discussions about it with operators of the highway [and] NROCC. We have had remedial things done on the highway, because the primary problem, as I understand it, has to do with people breaking or stealing the wires [fencing] on the highway and thus allowing cows to enter into a guarded space,” added Jones.

He is calling for the municipal corporations across Jamaica to reinstitute animal pounds and remove stray animals from endangering road users.

“We have had discussions about the role of the owners and now to hear that there was a crash recently involving a cow and a vehicle, thank God nobody died. It again raises the issue of how well we are guarding the space across the country on the highways. Not only the East-West or the North-South, but the one going from May Pen up into Mandeville. It raises an important issue which was addressed recently in an Observer editorial,” Dr Jones said.

He argued that the municipal authorities have “a mandate to provide for and enable the leading of stray cattle into pounds and to prevent individuals from allowing this kind of very dangerous situation to continue”.

Jones pointed to statistics indicating that 214 people have died on the nation’s roads since the start of the year, compared to 242 for the corresponding period last year.

“I would once again appeal to those who are so empowered — the municipal authorities and NROCC — to make sure, either separately or jointly, that our highways are made free of any kind of animal straying onto the road,” he said.

Dr Jones also pointed to another worrying trend of motorists driving the wrong way on highways.

On August 13 Parton Buchanan, a 56-year-old resident of Blenheim district in Hanover, died in a crash after he reportedly drove the wrong way onto the Porus off-ramp section of the highway near Williamsfield.

“In those instances where people have gone off-ramp in the wrong direction, they did so to either escape paying the toll or they are not aware of [how to use] that particular part of the highway. [It] requires an increase in public education as to how in certain areas we use the highways and to get people to be aware of the dangers,” said Jones.

McCatty is hoping that another layer of safety will be added by illuminating sections of the highway.

“When you have no light out there it is completely dark. If we can have lights where the toll booths are, why can’t we have it along the toll road? I am not saying you should have lights three feet apart, but there should be more light on the road,” he said.

World.content:
After a summer of setting out his stall, Andy Burnham now faces the hard task: turning ambition into action.

In the last of the summer boxset, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy take a deep dive into five big challenges facing the government in the coming months.

From defining the 10-year plan to unresolved pressure at home and abroad, the duo give their take and analysis on a critical parliamentary term ahead.

With party conferences and a key budget on the horizon, can Burnham’s government deliver on the change it has promised?

World.title: The shipping industry profits from conflict and looks East
World.content:
The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects.

​​The industry also treats this as a lasting reset rather than a temporary challenge. 76​ percent​​​ expect the effects of the Hormuz crisis on global shipping to outlast six months, and opinion splits almost in half on whether this is the sector’s most serious crisis of the past 50 years, ​which covers​​​ the oil shocks, the tanker war, the global financial crisis and C​ovid​​​-19. One phrase from our interviews captures the mindset behind optimism: ​“​​​​Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​​”​​​​

We therefore asked the uncomfortable question directly. Does global shipping today want peace​​ or does it benefit from turmoil? The peace camp wins, but only just: 54​ percent​​​ to 46​ percent​​​. Even among those who say the crisis hurts their own company, a third concede that the industry gains. Such cando​​r is rare in any sector, and it tempers any expectation that shipping will lobby hard for de-escalation. Markets gaining on volatility do not vote against it.

Confidence, however, does not mean that the influence equilibrium stays the same. Asked which power will affect developments in global shipping the most in the years ahead, 76​ percent​​​ of our respondents point to the East, meaning China and India, while 17​ percent​​​ choose the West. China is rated the leading shipbuilding nation by 69​ percent​​​, the operator of the most competitive fleet by 62​ percent​​​ and a near-universal 96​ percent​​​ ​​call its role important for ​​strengthening ​​global shipping. Trust, though, has not moved East with the tonnage. Only 17​ percent​​​ rate Chinese ship management highly, while traditional maritime powers such as Greece, Norway​​ and Germany continue to be recognized as the industry’s superior managers.

The same shift appears when executives rate the world’s leaders. Xi Jinping​, the president of China,​ stands alone at the top with a net favourability (percent of positive minus percent of negative views) of ​​+44, ahead of Narendra Modi​, the prime minister of India,​ at +24, while the bottom of the ranking is crowded with political leaders at the cent​er​​​ of today’s wars and confrontations. For an industry that plans in decades, predictability seems to weigh more than political alignment, and maritime leaders reward the global actors who ensure a more predictable environment.

Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​

The study’s technology section shows where the next edge will be decided. Shipping’s digital core has advanced from its experimentation phase. Remote monitoring and voyage optimi​z​​​ation are standard equipment, used by over seven in ten companies, while a second wave, predictive maintenance and ​Internet of Things ​​​sensors, is scaling, and a third, ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ analytics and digital twins, is only emerging. Each wave reaches roughly half the companies of the one before it. Tradition survives alongside the sensors, since 70​ percent​​​ still track fleet performance with the noon report (a holdover from the age of sail). ​AI​​​ is the divide to watch​:​​​ 65​ percent​​​ of companies already use or pilot AI, yet only 7​ percent​​​ use it extensively​​ and adoption splits along tonnage lines. Among fleets above one million deadweight ​​tonnes, 79​ percent​​​ work with AI, against 50​ percent​​​ in the mid-sized tier. Scale buys data, teams and budgets, the returns compound, and command of AI and cybersecurity will help set the new shipping hierarchy. As one shipowner told us, “Better positioning produces better data, which produces better positioning.”

No such technology will replace shipping crews. The shortage of skilled personnel remains the third most serious problem in the ranking, at 37​ percent​​​, and companies respond with high safety standards, competitive pay, internet access on board and training. Two findings point to a deeper change​:​​​ 72​ percent​​​ of companies intend to employ more women at sea​​ and 74​ percent​​​ now call ESG​ (environment, social, governance)​ performance important to their overall business strategy.

World.title: Britain told EU citizens to trust its settled status system. Then it mixed up identical twins.
World.content:
The eVisa database keeps a record of a person’s full name, date of birth, nationality, and a facial photograph. But these traits are by definition often a very close match for identical twins, including Webb, whose name is similar to that of her sister.

Many such cases

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, which campaigns for the rights of EU citizens living in the U.K., said problems with the eVisa system sometimes left people unable to prove their identity when they needed it most.

“We have seen many cases where someone else’s immigration status is entangled with another person’s eVisa account. We had hoped, after repeatedly raising this issue, that the Home Office had taken more steps to prevent it happening. It just shows how, despite claims that the eVisa system is highly resilient, it can fail people at the critical moments they need it to work,” she said.

Hawkins said it was “crucial that people have a genuinely stable means by which to prove their status” and described the digital-only system as “rushed,” adding: “We regularly see people not only denied boarding, but also compensation, as carriers and the Home Office play a blame game shifting responsibility between each other.”

While a Home Office spokesperson did not dispute Webb’s account, they defended the eVisa system, arguing it had worked for many people.

“Over 10 million people have already successfully used eVisas to prove their immigration status,” the spokesperson said. “As we expand our digital system, we are committed to data accuracy and ensuring that the safeguards in place to support eVisa users are accessible to anyone reliant on the digital system. In the rare cases where errors are identified, the majority of cases are resolved within 24 hours.”

World.title: Ukraine widens its targets — and its tolerance for causing civilian casualties
World.content:
The numbers help illustrate the change. In 2025, Ukrainian attacks inside Russia killed 253 civilians, according to the United Nations, which says it was not able to independently verify the numbers. This year, in the month of July alone, Russian authorities reported that 79 civilians were killed and 601 injured, a marked increase in the casualty rate.

Zelenskyy has said that Wildberries is a legitimate target because it has been “used by the aggressor to ensure the supply of sanctioned components for the production of drones and navigation equipment.” Russian soldiers supplement their equipment by purchasing items from Wildberries.

Maryana Bezuhla, a Ukrainian lawmaker and one of the most outspoken critics of Zelenskyy and Ukraine’s military leadership, is unapologetic about the increased risk to civilians. “Russia’s logistics system is used to wage the war of aggression against Ukraine,” she told POLITICO. “Russia has been targeting Ukrainian civilians all the years of the war.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military supplies but conceded to journalists that “the situation is indeed difficult” for the company.

Dmitry Peskov attends a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow on June 3, 2026. | Pool photo by Ramil Sitdikov via AFP/Getty Images

There is no indication that Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilians — even as Russia continues to hit apartment buildings, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones. And yet, there is no indication that the rising civilian toll in Russia is causing Kyiv to reconsider its approach.

“It is a very important thing to stress from the outset, that any civilian casualties resulting from Ukrainian attacks are collateral damage,” said Jaroslava Barbieri, Ukraine expert at Britain’s Chatham House. “No Ukrainian strikes have deliberately targeted civilian districts.”

World.title: Germany’s establishment has a plan to contain the far right. Sort of.
World.content:
As premier, one of Siegmund’s earliest duties would be to take over the annually rotating chair position of the regular conferences of Germany’s 16 state premiers. The role usually comes with a visit to Berlin and a joint appearance with the chancellor before the press.

Calling this uncharted territory would be an understatement. “The AfD is questioning the fundamental decisions made by the Federal Republic of Germany since 1949,” Merz once said.

The chancellor is not alone in his concern. All other major parties, and large parts of the German media, see the AfD as a threat to the country’s liberal postwar order. Yet, if the party takes power in a state for the first time, the political establishment will no longer be able to keep it at arm’s length. While normal relations may be out of the question, at least for the foreseeable future, Germany’s federal system requires a minimum of cooperation and mutual support.

So how would the German establishment deal with a state governed by the AfD?

POLITICO put this question to officials in the federal government and several state governments. The reluctance to answer was striking, especially among Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union. Senior party figures and state ministers either refused to comment or would not be quoted by name.

The hesitation is understandable. The CDU and the CSU once owned the political space to the right of center. Today, the AfD is eating into it. State ministers from both the Social Democrats and the Greens were more prepared to discuss strategy on the record.

World.title: The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration.
World.content:
Though Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model — unbearable suffering is not a criterion for eligibility in her bill — she found it helpful to see how assisted dying has worked in practice the last time British MPs tackled this issue.

It’s an experience from which many in Labour still bear the scars — and on which new Prime Minister Andy Burnham already appears to have drawn a line in the sand.

Stepping forward

MPs passed fellow Labour backbencher Kim Leadbeater’s Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill last year by 314 votes to 291. But it failed to become law after delays in the U.K.’s House of Lords.

Now Edwards is reintroducing the bill — and is adamant that the groundbreaking social change can succeed this time around.

It means that next month, the House of Commons will once again be thrust into a divisive vote on a matter of conscience, deciding whether to legalize assisted dying in England and Wales for terminally ill adults judged as having fewer than six months left to live.

“When Kim’s bill came up, I did have conversations with my dad about how things have gone in Australia,” Edwards says. The situation reassured her compared to “more extreme examples” like Canada, where a terminal condition is not required for patients to be eligible, but instead an irreversible, “advanced state of decline” and “unbearable physical or mental suffering.”

World.title: US threatens Iran with 'economic D-Day' as markets await sanctions announcement
World.content:
The US is ramping up its economic pressure on Iran after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared the start of an "economic D-Day".

 

According to Bessent, this represents "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary." He set out the position in a post on X late on Sunday and in a Financial Times opinion article published the same day.

Bessent stated that US President Donald Trump's military campaign had "significantly dismantled Iran’s military capabilities and weakened its nuclear programme". He added that the administration is now "entering the endgame" and that the economic measures begin at dawn.

The objective, according to the US Treasury Secretary, is to "sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone".

Bessent cautioned countries that continue to buy or transport Iranian petroleum, facilitate financial flows through exchange houses and free trade zones, handle flights, maintain ship registries or enable seaborne fuel transfers, that any remaining links would accelerate their own isolation.

The comments follow remarks by US President Donald Trump last week. At the time, Trump announced in a Truth Social post "the most crushing economic operation ever taken agaisnt any country!"

Despite both declarations, specific measures have not yet been set out.

According to Bessent's outline, the package could centre on secondary sanctions against nations and entities that keep purchasing Iranian oil, process its finances, operate related banks or support shipping and other commercial channels, layered on top of the existing naval blockade.

Bessent is scheduled to hold a press conference at 7 PM CET on Monday to announce the concrete steps.

Market reaction

Oil prices are lower on Monday morning even as the rhetoric intensifies.

At the time of writing, Brent crude, the international standard, is trading at around $91.5 which is 2% lower than Friday's close while West Texas Intermediate stands at roughly $86.2, about 1.5% lower than last week's close.

The fall may stem from profit-taking after recent gains and from reports of a temporary rise in tanker movements through the Strait of Hormuz.

According to shipping information cited by Axios, around 40 tankers transited the southern channel on Friday night, moving roughly 16 million barrels of oil, higher than the 15-20 vessels recorded on preceding nights.

Overall volumes through the waterway remain well below pre-conflict levels.

On the other hand, US futures are also in the red ahead of market open while European stocks are trading flat.

World.title: Erling Haaland's new haircut goes viral and sends both fans and celebrities into a frenzy
World.content:
You know you’ve reached a rarified stratum of fame when changing your hairstyle makes headline news and sparks online frenzy... And Erling Haaland definitely falls in that exclusive category.

 

The 26-year-old viral star of this year’s World Cup has shocked fans by ditching his signature flowing locks and debuting a dramatically shorter haircut.

That’s right, the lion’s mane is no more. The glorious Norwegian locks have been sheared. The majestic blond tresses have been cut down in their prime. We’ll stop there.

Haaland took to social media on Sunday (23 August) to share his new hairstyle, ahead of the new Premier League season and Manchester City’s opening match against Bournemouth.

"New season, new trim," Haaland wrote in the caption... And it didn't take long for the post to go viral, with fans flooding the comment section with their reactions.

Much like David Beckham when he chopped his locks in 2000 and went for the buzzcut, The Striking Viking’s haircut has divided opinions.

"I’m gone for one hour, and Haaland has short hair, sure” wrote one user on X, while another wrote: “Erling Haaland cutting his hair is worse than when Keri Russell cut her hair on Felicity, this looks so awful omg.”

“THE VIKING ERA IS OVER”, bemoaned another.

Even celebrities got involved...

Oasis’ Noel Gallagher said: “You look about 17 years old. It’s good. Change is good.”

Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola commented: “No Way. You’re lucky you have hair. I would love to have it. I love it.”

Haaland previously joked that Zlatan Ibrahimovic had told him “never cut your hair, because you strength is in your hair.”

That’s Samson, but we move on...

It turned out that Ibrahimovic was not impressed that Haaland did not follow his advice.

“What did you do? You lost a bet or what? Block me and erase my number,” joked Ibrahimovic.

At least we hope he was joking. And we hope Zlatan was wrong, as the shorter cut did not help Haaland during his opening match. The star striker missed a few great chances in City's 2-1 win at Etihad Stadium. Still, at least they won...

Haaland's new cut AP Photo

What do you make of the clipped Viking's new look?

World.title: Netherlands withdraws from 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, says competition 'no longer' neutral
World.content:
The Netherlands will not participate in next year's Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster said on Monday, saying the event can "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over the Gaza war.

 

"It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division," said Taco Zimmerman, Director-General of AVROTROS, in a statement from the broadcaster.

The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation.

Earlier this month, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

"However, the recently announced changes...do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored," said the AVROTROS statement.

Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.

Dara from Bulgaria holds up the trophy after winning the Grand Final of the 70th Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna, 17 May, 2026 AP Photo

Next year's event, the world's biggest live televised music event, will take place on 15 May in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.

It will be the first time that the Balkan nation hosts the contest, coming after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year's contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler "Bangaranga."

Since its launch in 1956, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.

The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the contest, with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all.

World.title: 41-year-old French tourist dies while hiking in Crete
World.content:
A 41-year-old French tourist died on Sunday near Balos, in the Chania region of Crete, after collapsing while hiking in high temperatures and intense sunshine.

 

The woman had gone to the area in the afternoon with her partner. According to information from the Coordination Centre of the Hellenic Fire Service, passed on to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency (ANA-MPA), the couple left their car in a car park at Falasarna and continued on foot towards Balos beach, following the path of a difficult trail.

Despite warning signs in the area prohibiting access, the two tourists took a route which involves a lengthy hike and is particularly demanding because of the rugged terrain.

On their way back, when they were about a kilometre from the car park, the 41-year-old lost consciousness after suffering severe dehydration. Her partner returned to the car to get water and at the same time alerted the authorities by calling 112.

A large-scale operation was then launched to locate and rescue her, involving firefighters from the Kissamos Fire Station and a team from EMODE. The firefighters found the woman unconscious and immediately administered first aid, performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) until paramedics from the National Emergency Centre (EKAB) arrived.

The EKAB crew continued efforts to revive her and transfered the 41-year-old to hospital. However, according to the authorities, the woman died during transport.

As the Coordination Centre underlined, high temperatures and intense sunshine make hiking on long and demanding routes particularly dangerous.

The Fire Service also stressed that the strain on the body in such weather conditions is extremely high. For this reason, it urged residents and visitors to take particular caution and strictly adhere to safety notices.

World.title: Potato shortages could hit France as farmers warn of record-low yields following heatwaves
World.content:
French farmers are warning that they may not be able to deliver the amounts of potatoes set out in contracts. Extreme heat and lack of rain have left farms parched - with the National Union of Potato Producers (UNPT) saying production could fall by around 23 per cent year on year. This drop would make the season one of the worst ever recorded for the sector. "This season could mark one of the largest production slumps ever recorded for French potatoes", the organisation says.

 

The fall in yields could prevent some producers from meeting the volumes set out in their contracts with processors. The industry is therefore calling for "contracted volumes to be adjusted to reflect the reality of the harvest".

The average yield of table potatoes is expected to reach only 37.4 tonnes per hectare, compared with 43.5 tonnes in 2025. The UNPT is already talking about "the lowest yield seen in more than 30 years". The drop would be even sharper than that caused by the historic drought of 2022.

The situation is causing serious concern among growers. On some farms, the combined effects of heat and lack of water could lead to major losses and undermine their economic viability. For the UNPT, "the disastrous economic consequences of this exceptional situation" cannot be shouldered by farmers alone.

Faced with this situation, producers are demanding "exceptional" support and calling on the government to "engage in determined dialogue", particularly with its European partners. They want to avoid a "double whammy": substantial agricultural losses compounded by commercial difficulties.

As the harvest approaches, anxiety is growing across the sector. This season could leave a lasting mark on French potato production.

World.title: From iPods to wired headphones: Why more Gen Zers are picking retro tech
World.content:
Social media and the digital sphere has taken over much of our lives in the last few years. This has especially impacted younger generations such as Gen Z and Gen Alpha, who have practically grown up in the digital era.

 

Endless screen time, constant notifications and rising fear of missing out (FOMO) have led to more chronically online users and more mental health issues such as depression, anxiety and low self-worth.

A rising number of ads and tracking features, along with more data privacy and security concerns have also contributed to growing unease around popular social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok and Facebook now.

This has led to an increasing number of Gen Zers choosing to adopt more retro tech like flip phones, iPods and vintage cameras as a way to digitally detox and take a break from social media.

Why retro tech is becoming so popular with younger people

More Gen Zers are interested in early and mid-2000s tech, as a way of escaping the constant stream of notifications, pressure and anxiety that often accompanies most social media platforms.

Some also see tech like “dumb phones” as a way to reduce hours of daily smartphone scrolling and the resulting algorithmic noise, offering a slower, more peaceful experience.

These simpler, single-purpose gadgets also provide fewer distractions, as they lack ads, tracking and constant notifications, allowing people to focus fully on more important goals or just be present for friends and family. In some cases, it also means simply being less reachable.

In many cases, retro and physical tech provides tangible ownership, rather than endless streaming subscriptions, which could change rules or hike prices unexpectedly. This provides a tactile, intentional experience and real ownership of media, without the risk of losing albums due to sudden digital licensing dropouts.

For some Gen Zers, retro tech, such as vintage cameras and grainy photos can signify more authenticity than hyper-curated and filtered digital feeds. Similarly, some retro gadgets are increasingly sought after due to their unique designs and colours, in contrast to increasingly modern, minimalist tech.

In some cases, vintage tech is also a fun style or personal statement for Gen Zers interested in mid-2000s culture.

Which retro tech is Gen Z loving right now?

Although there are several retro gadgets making a comeback right now due to rising Gen Z interest, there are a few which have become particularly popular.

Early-2000s digital cameras and camcorders

These early digital cameras are once again seeing a rise, despite still being grainy, oversaturated and imperfectly designed. They represent a perfect escape from over-processed smartphone photography and capture raw aesthetics.

Gen Zers are loving the vintage colour grading and harsh flash glare offered by Y2K cameras, along with the element of surprise that comes from not seeing a flawless live preview. Handheld tape camcorders are also massive hits for filming nights out and festivals with a distinct nostalgic texture.

Some popular models include the Canon PowerShot series, with older models like the PowerShot ELPH and G-series seeing a marked boost due to viral social media trends and celebrity visibility.

The slim and colourful pocket friendly Sony Cyber-shot from the mid-2000s is also still valued for their distinct, retro built-in flash look, along with the Nikon Coolpix for its chromatic grain and early-era colour science.

Dumbphones and flip phones

Basic single-purpose phones are also making a huge comeback right now, mainly as a secondary device for weekends and social outings. Users often swap their SIM cards into vintage flip phones to intentionally disconnect.

These devices effectively limit access to notifications and apps that can distract from the social plans at hand, while still keeping essentials like calling and text messaging working.

This also helps cut down on screen time and doomscrolling, potentially boosting mental health.

While some believe that this is mainly a temporary trend-driven fad, others think that more people could choose to keep smartphones for their daily life and on the weekdays, while switching to dumb phones for fun plans.

Brands like Nokia/HMD are becoming particularly popular again, especially models like the Nokia 2660 Flip, prized for its outstanding battery, low cost and pocket-friendly size.

Handheld and classic consoles

Devices like the Nintendo Game Boy and PlayStation Portable (PSP) are other retro gadgets seeing a rise at the moment. These offer distraction-free gaming without the constant update loops and microtransactions often seen in modern gaming consoles now.

This provides an offline, low stress environment to people who still genuinely enjoy gaming with complete, functional games. It also removes the pressure of online leaderboards, daily quests and competitive multiplayer games.

Unlike modern digital libraries tied to expiring subscriptions, a dedicated handheld or physical cartridge also feels much more permanent and authentic, while costing far less.

In many cases, collecting older systems like the Game Boy, PS2 or SNES has become a trendy, culturally-driven hobby too, valued for long-lasting physical durability too.

Wired headphones and earphones

Wired headphones and earphones are seeing a boost too, mainly due to a mix of Y2K retro fashion trends, with the dangling wires being seen as a style statement. This has been driven by celebrity and pop star influence as well.

They are also considered to be more practical, as they don’t need to be charged and offer uninterrupted, lag-free audio for watching videos, gaming or listening to music. They are also much more affordable than high-end wireless alternatives, with the wire making them harder to drop and lose as well.

In some cases, it supports mindful tech habits, turning listening to music into a deliberate action rather than an invisible, all-day background noise.

Vinyl records and CDs

Vinyl records, CDs and retro-style cassette players also provide a fun, tactile ritual to music listening, which streaming platforms like Spotify lack. Touching album art, opening CD cases and sliding tapes into a deck can make music feel much more real and special.

Instead of skipping tracks every 10 seconds, putting on a whole album forces people to listen from start to finish, offering a deep listening experience.

Like dumb phones and handheld consoles, these offer real ownership forever too, something that is increasingly rare nowadays, while giving users a break from screen fatigue and digital noise.

Older, uniquely designed tech also provides a personal touch to spaces like bedrooms, allowing people to show off their distinct styles and taste.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: The Netherlands will not participate in the 'no longer neutral' 2027 Eurovision Song Contest
World.content:
The Netherlands will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria, the state broadcaster has said, citing divisions over the situation in Gaza. It's the second time the country is boycotting the event.

Dutch state broadcaster Avrotros said on Monday that the Netherlands will not be taking part in next year's Eurovision Song Contest (ESC).

The event can "no longer be considered neutral," given the war in Gaza, it said.

Eurovision boycotts

This year, the Netherlands was joined by Spain, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia in staging the biggest political boycott in Eurovision history in protest at Israel's participation. Hundreds of pro-Palestinian protesters also marched outside the event.

Avrotros Director-General Taco Zimmerman said international conflicts were increasingly affecting the contest and "undermining its neutral character," adding that it had "become a platform for division."



Four nations boycott Eurovision over Israel inclusion To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Earlier this month, ESC organizers announced new rules that bar any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

"However, the recently announced ‌changes ... do not provide sufficient confidence that ​the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest ⁠has ​been restored," Avrotros ​said.

The pop spectacle is watched by tens of millions of viewers around the world each year.

Israel came close to winning the competition in 2025 and 2026, placing second in both events.

The 2027 ESC will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, after singer Dara won this year's competition in Vienna, Austria.

Dara from Bulgaria won this year's Eurovision with the song 'Bangaranga' Image: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP

The Netherlands and Eurovision: 'Very close to our hearts'

The Netherlands took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest in 1956.

They have won it five times since then, most recently in 2019 with Duncan Laurence and his song "Arcade."

According to the Eurovision website, it was the first competition entry to reach 1 billion streams on Spotify.

The country's withdrawal from the next Eurovision is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," Zimmerman said.

"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.
