World.title: La larga escalada de la vivienda: las casas duplican el precio tras 12 años de subidas ininterrumpidas
World.content:
La curva que dibuja el encarecimiento de la vivienda en España durante la última década se parece más a una larga ascensión que a una montaña rusa. La estadística deja poco margen para la duda: según el Índice de Precios de Vivienda (IPV) del INE, desde comienzos de 2014 las casas se han revalorizado ininterrumpidamente durante 48 trimestres consecutivos, tomando como referencia la variación interanual. Desde entonces, el indicador ha permanecido siempre en terreno positivo, atravesando ciclos económicos, cambios en los tipos de interés y episodios de incertidumbre. El resultado es una racha de doce años de revalorizaciones ininterrumpidas que ha transformado el mercado residencial español. En ese periodo, el precio de la vivienda se ha disparado en buena parte del país, lo que ha provocado que el índice se haya multiplicado por más de dos. Dicho de otra forma: las casas ya valen más del doble que en el momento en que tocaron suelo durante la Gran Recesión.

Aunque en fechas recientes los precios han alcanzado máximos históricos en numerosas comunidades autónomas, la evolución no ha sido igual en todo el territorio. Desde el último recorte que experimentó el mercado inmobiliario en el primer trimestre de 2014, todos los territorios salvo Navarra han recuperado el valor perdido entre el pico de la burbuja de principios de siglo y su estallido.

Pero en algunas el rebote ha sido especialmente intenso. Madrid es el caso más extremo entre las grandes regiones: el índice de precios es ya 2,3 veces superior al de comienzos de 2014. También han doblado su valor Baleares (2,26 veces), Cataluña (2,13) y Andalucía (2,03). En el otro extremo se sitúan Extremadura (1,52 veces), Castilla-La Mancha (1,57) o Navarra (1,73), donde la revalorización ha sido más moderada, aunque eso no evita que las casas sean también más caras que nunca, según al serie estadística del INE. La Comunidad Foral, sin embargo, constituye una excepción, puesto los precios son hoy más altos que en 2014, pero sigue siendo la única comunidad que aún no ha recuperado completamente las pérdidas registradas tras el estallido de la burbuja.

La explicación hay que buscarla en una década larga de subidas prácticamente ininterrumpidas que se ha acelerado en los últimos años. Tras un arranque tímido entre 2014 y 2016, comunidades como Madrid, Cataluña o Baleares empezaron a registrar avances anuales sostenidos de entre el 6% y el 12%, impulsados por la recuperación económica y la vuelta de la demanda. A partir de 2024, el ritmo ganó todavía más velocidad, lo que derivó en que Andalucía cerrase ese año con un alza interanual del 13,4%; Madrid, del 10,3%; Comunidad Valenciana, del 12,2%; y Murcia, del 11,7%. En 2025 y comienzos de 2026, muchas regiones han encadenado incrementos de dos dígitos superiores al 10%, consolidando una subida que ha llevado a varias de ellas a duplicar con holgura el valor que tenían en la pasada década.

Para Ignacio Ezquiaga, economista y experto inmobiliario, la actual escalada de precios no puede entenderse como un fenómeno independiente del vivido durante la burbuja inmobiliaria. “Están muy relacionados”, señala. A su juicio, la corrección que siguió al estallido de la crisis financiera resultó insuficiente para devolver el mercado a una evolución más ligada a la capacidad económica de los hogares. “Fue una ocasión perdida para volver a una senda más normal de precios de la vivienda”, advierte.

Ezquiaga identifica además una creciente desconexión entre el mercado residencial y las rentas medias. “Puede que las rentas altas sigan teniendo recorrido en el mercado actual, pero por el camino se han quedado todas las demás”, explica. En su opinión, el mercado se ha ido orientando cada vez más hacia compradores con mayor capacidad adquisitiva, mientras el acceso a la vivienda se complica para una parte creciente de la población. “Nadie puede comprarse una casa ahora y ya casi tampoco alquilarla”, sostiene el experto, que considera difícil que una dinámica así pueda mantenerse indefinidamente sin provocar tensiones económicas y sociales.

Por su parte, Óscar Martínez, presidente de la Asociación Profesional de Expertos Inmobiliarios (Apei), añade que la intensa escalada de los precios está complicando incluso el trabajo de valorar los inmuebles, puesto que los propietarios tienen expectativas cada vez más altas. “Llegan con unos precios en la cabeza, les propones otro y te siguen pidiendo más, porque consideran que sus viviendas valen mucho más”, explica por teléfono. Martínez cree además que la tendencia seguirá al alza mientras persista el desequilibrio entre oferta y demanda. Y recuerda que se están construyendo unas 100.000 viviendas al año, cuando según algunas estimaciones serían necesarias el doble, una escasez que continuará presionando los precios al alza.

Pau A. Montserrat, profesor de Economía Financiera de la Universitat de les Illes Balears (UIB), reconoce el fuerte encarecimiento de la vivienda en la última década, aunque matiza que su relevancia depende del perfil del comprador. “Si tú compras tu casa para vivir, lo que son las estadísticas de precio no te tienen que preocupar demasiado”, sostiene, al considerar que la decisión debe analizarse, siempre que pueda pagarse, con horizontes de “40, 50 o 60 años”. A su juicio, la vivienda habitual tiene un “valor de uso” que trasciende su cotización y, por ello, su compra puede seguir siendo razonable incluso en momentos de precios elevados. Distinto es el caso de quienes adquieren una segunda residencia o una vivienda para alquilarla: en esos casos, advierte, el momento del ciclo inmobiliario adquiere una importancia decisiva.

Sin tregua

Para Montserrat, el origen del problema está en una “crisis de oferta de manual”. Por eso rechaza las recetas encaminadas a contener artificialmente los precios y defiende actuar sobre el desequilibrio estructural del mercado. “El precio es información, un termómetro que refleja la falta de viviendas disponibles”, señala. Desde su punto de vista, la solución pasa por aumentar la oferta residencial, impulsar la construcción de más viviendas, favorecer promociones adaptadas a nuevas necesidades habitacionales y dotar de mayor seguridad jurídica tanto a promotores como a propietarios.

Obreros en la construcción de un edificio de viviendas en Sevilla. PACO PUENTES

El profesor también reclama agilizar los trámites urbanísticos y reducir los retrasos en la concesión de licencias, al tiempo que aboga por unas reglas más estables para quienes invierten en vivienda. Solo así, sostiene, será posible reducir el déficit acumulado de inmuebles y aliviar progresivamente la presión sobre los precios. Una necesidad que cada vez comparten más expertos en un mercado donde la escasez de oferta se ha convertido para muchos en la principal explicación de las tensiones actuales.

De momento, los datos no apuntan en esa dirección. Según el último informe de Tinsa, la mayor tasadora del país, el precio medio de la vivienda volvió a acelerarse en julio, con un incremento interanual del 15,5%, situándose ya un 1,8% por encima de los máximos registrados durante la burbuja. El avance es aún más intenso en las áreas metropolitanas (17,9%), las capitales y grandes ciudades (17,3%) y la costa mediterránea (16,9%); mientras que Baleares y Canarias registran una subida del 11,2% y el resto de municipios, del 10,1%.

Tras doce años de revalorizaciones casi ininterrumpidas, el mercado residencial español sigue avanzando sin encontrar apenas resistencias. Con la oferta lejos de cubrir la demanda y los precios ya por encima de los máximos de la burbuja en buena parte del país, la gran incógnita ya no es cuánto han subido las viviendas, sino cuánto tiempo más podrán seguir haciéndolo.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Última hora de la entrada de inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | Elma Saiz considera una “irresponsabilidad mayúscula” las declaraciones de Feijóo sobre confinar Ceuta
World.content:
Murcia solicita al Gobierno reforzar los medios de la Guardia Civil para “proteger las costas” de la llegada de inmigrantes

El presidente de la Región de Murcia, Fernando López Miras, ha enviado una carta al jefe del Ejecutivo, Pedro Sánchez, en la que solicita reforzar los efectivos de la Guardia Civil en la Región, así como sus medios marítimos y tecnológicos utilizados para la vigilancia y el control de estos incidentes “con el fin de proteger las costas de la Región de Murcia y frenar la llegada de lanchas con inmigrantes”, según ha publicado en un mensaje en la red social X.

En su carta, López Miras muestra su “gran preocupación” por la situación que se está produciendo en las costas de Murcia donde “en el plazo de apenas cuatro días, se ha registrado la llegada de lanchas rápidas que, con total impunidad, han llegado hasta la orilla trasportando inmigrantes a plena luz del día, sin que hayan sido interceptadas por las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado”, algo que, según el jefe del Ejecutivo murciano, está produciendo “gran alarma social y sensación de inseguridad” entre la ciudadanía.

Fernando López Miras habla en su carta de la falta de medios de la Guardia Civil en la Región y hace hincapié en que “la única patrullera disponible para atajar esta incesante llegada de lanchas motoras ilegales, no está actualmente operativa por avería”, una situación que califica de “inadmisible”. “Urge también un incremento de los medios tecnológicos de vigilancia, como sensores, radares o drones, que permitan controlar y prevenir incidentes de esta naturaleza”, pide el presidente de Murcia en su carta, donde también solicita “información actualizada y en tiempo real acerca de cuántos medios marítimos dispone en estos momentos el Estado para la vigilancia del litoral de la Región de Murcia”.

“Hay que lanzar ya una señal clara y contundente a estas mafias que operan sin escrúpulos para que sean conscientes de que las costas de la Región de Murcia están protegidas con una estrecha y permanente vigilancia. Garantizar la seguridad debe ser una prioridad inmediata”, zanja el presidente murciano.

World.title: La sombra de Estados Unidos se alarga sobre el sur de Groenlandia: “Vamos a perder nuestras casas”
World.content:
El Museo de Narsarsuaq ya no tiene un horario fijo. Desde que el aeropuerto cerró en primavera, apenas llegan visitantes a esta remota localidad del sur de Groenlandia. No obstante, si alguien pregunta por la casa de Ole Guldager y se acerca a pedirle que lo abra, él accede encantado. El museo ocupa uno de los barracones de la antigua base militar, un edificio alargado de madera, pintado de rojo y con chimenea de ladrillo. Junto a la entrada se exhibe el motor radial de un avión de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, corroído por décadas de exposición a la intemperie. Detrás del edificio se extiende la pista de aterrizaje que soldados de Estados Unidos construyeron en tiempo récord. Hoy, sin embargo, ese mismo país emerge no como un aliado del pasado, sino como una creciente amenaza para la soberanía y los recursos naturales de la isla, especialmente en lugares como Narsarsuaq, una de las tres bases que Estados Unidos aspiraría a reabrir.

Cuando Guldager enciende las luces, de la penumbra emergen uniformes, fusiles y carabinas, teléfonos de campaña, una camilla metálica del antiguo hospital, máquinas tragaperras y cartas confiscadas por la censura que relataban el aislamiento extremo y que nunca llegaron a su destino. Las salas reconstruyen la vida cotidiana de los miles de militares, pilotos y enfermeras estadounidenses que pasaron por la antigua base. Entre los cientos de fotografías destacan varias de Marlene Dietrich, tomadas en 1944. Durante unas horas, la actriz llevó el espectáculo de Hollywood hasta aquel inhóspito rincón entre fiordos y montañas para levantar el ánimo de las tropas.

Ole Guldager, en la entrada del Museo de Narsarsuaq. Álvaro González

Guldager llegó a Narsarsuaq siendo un niño. Nació en Dinamarca, pero su padre trabajaba en el aeropuerto civil en el que se había convertido la antigua instalación militar tras la marcha de los estadounidenses a finales de los años cincuenta. Historiador y arqueólogo —además de uno de los escasos apicultores de la isla—, ha dedicado buena parte de sus 58 años a investigar sobre el lugar donde creció y decidió quedarse.

El último avión aterrizó en abril. El aeropuerto se cerró porque abrió otro en Qaqortoq, la capital regional, donde viven unas 3.000 personas, y no tiene sentido mantener dos para una población tan pequeña. Pero la realidad es que desde entonces, Narsarsuaq se ha ido vaciando. Guldager calcula que de los 150 habitantes que tenía quedan unos 40. Todo giraba alrededor del aeropuerto, que durante más de seis décadas fue la principal puerta de entrada al sur de la isla, absorbiendo cada verano el tránsito de miles de pasajeros. Ahora hay semanas en las que apenas llega una decena de visitantes. El hotel, uno de los más grandes de Groenlandia, bajó la persiana el mismo día que el aeródromo.

Entre quienes no se plantean marcharse está Storch Lund. Nieto de Henrik Lund —el poeta que compuso la letra del himno de Groenlandia—, creció en una granja al otro lado del fiordo y se mudó a esta orilla siendo adolescente para trabajar como aprendiz de mecánico. Llegó a dirigir el aeropuerto durante más de dos décadas, además de regentar una cafetería y una tienda de souvenirs que cerró hace unos meses. También creó una empresa para trasladar a turistas a otras localidades. Hoy solo uno de sus barcos sigue operando con escasa demanda; los otros dos permanecen amarrados. A sus 69 años, le cuesta asimilar que “en Narsarsuaq ya no ocurre nada”.

Es en ese vacío donde ahora reaparece Estados Unidos.

Mientras el pueblo agoniza, la sombra de Donald Trump se alarga sobre él. El presidente estadounidense, que ya trató de comprar Groenlandia a Dinamarca durante su primer mandato, amenazó a principios de año con hacerse con el control de la isla “por las buenas o por las malas”. La tensión se rebajó después de que varios aliados europeos enviaran tropas al territorio ártico en respaldo de la soberanía danesa y la crisis se encauzó hacia la vía diplomática. Desde hace siete meses, representantes de Dinamarca y Groenlandia negocian entre bambalinas en Washington con la Administración Trump los términos de una expansión militar de la primera potencia mundial en la isla más grande del planeta, de tan solo 56.000 habitantes.

En esas conversaciones, Estados Unidos reclama la soberanía del territorio que ocupen sus futuras instalaciones militares en la isla —un estatus similar al de las bases británicas en Chipre—, una exigencia que no están dispuestos a aceptar los representantes daneses y groenlandeses.

La estrategia de Washington se apoya en el acuerdo bilateral de defensa firmado con Copenhague en 1951, un tratado que permite ampliar, previa solicitud, la presencia militar estadounidense en este territorio del Reino de Dinamarca. El general Gregory Guillot, jefe del Comando Norte de Estados Unidos, informó en marzo al Senado sobre la intención de establecer tres nuevas “zonas de defensa” en Groenlandia, con el objetivo de reforzar la vigilancia sobre los submarinos nucleares rusos y contrarrestar la creciente influencia de China en el Ártico.

En mayo, cuatro semanas después de que el aeropuerto internacional de Narsarsuaq fuera degradado a helipuerto, personal de la Infantería de Marina y representantes de la Embajada de Estados Unidos en Dinamarca llegaron para inspeccionar la pista de aterrizaje, el puerto de aguas profundas y otras instalaciones de la antigua base.

El pueblo de Narsarsuaq, junto a la pista de aterrizaje. Álvaro González

Guldager teme que el retorno de las tropas estadounidenses termine por desahuciar a los vecinos que aún aguantan en Narsarsuaq. “Vamos a perder nuestras casas y a tener que irnos del lugar donde hemos vivido y trabajado toda la vida”, lamenta. Autor de un libro sobre las decenas de instalaciones militares que Estados Unidos construyó en Groenlandia durante la ocupación nazi de Dinamarca, Guldager recuerda que durante la ampliación, en 1953, de la base de Pituffik —la única que mantiene Washington en la isla, al noroeste—, decenas de familias inuit fueron reubicadas por la fuerza a 130 kilómetros de sus hogares.

“Los estadounidenses lo construyeron todo, pero este es mi hogar”, remarca Guldager. Con nostalgia, evoca cómo en apenas tres años aquella llanura deshabitada se transformó en una ciudad con carreteras, talleres, comedores, hospital, cine, cancha de baloncesto y gimnasio. En los estertores de la Segunda Guerra Mundial llegaron a vivir allí unas 4.000 personas, más que en cualquier otra localidad groenlandesa de la época.

Con el nombre en clave de Bluie West One, la base de Narsarsuaq formó parte de una red de escalas crucial para trasladar aviones militares desde América hasta los frentes de Europa y el norte de África. Más de 10.000 aeronaves repostaron o fueron reparadas allí durante el conflicto.

Estados Unidos abandonó la base en 1958 dejando una profunda huella ambiental; una herencia tóxica para una población cuya identidad depende del equilibrio con su entorno. El paisaje costero quedó sembrado de escombros, chatarra, tuberías, baterías y miles de bidones oxidados. A unos pocos kilómetros, el antiguo hospital militar, con capacidad para 250 camas, fue pasto de las llamas en los años setenta. Nadie retiró las placas de amianto, y pequeños fragmentos blancos de este material tóxico yacen dispersos por el valle. Los vecinos temen que los fuertes vientos sigan arrastrando partículas peligrosas hacia el pueblo, aunque hoy les preocupa más Donald Trump.

Un tanque de combustible oxidado, cerca de la antigua base militar estadounidense en Narsarsuaq. Álvaro González

Las consecuencias del cierre del aeropuerto y el fantasma del regreso estadounidense también se sienten al otro lado del fiordo. Pese a estar a solo tres kilómetros, Qassiarsuk y Narsarsuaq pertenecen a mundos distintos. Aunque cruzar esa franja de agua apenas lleva 15 minutos, la acumulación de hielo, los fuertes vientos o la densidad de la niebla pueden cortar durante días la comunicación entre ambas orillas. Qassiarsuk se alza sobre los vestigios de la granja donde Erik el Rojo se estableció a finales del siglo X, tras ser desterrado de Islandia. Allí bautizó al territorio como Groenland (tierra verde, en nórdico antiguo) y sentó las bases de la colonización vikinga.

Lejos de la clásica estampa helada, Qassiarsuk deslumbra en verano entre colinas de un verde intenso, salpicadas de casas de vivos tonos rojos, amarillos y azules. Aunque el pueblo tiene apenas 50 habitantes, es uno de los principales núcleos ganaderos de Groenlandia. Esta actividad, al igual que la agricultura, se concentra casi exclusivamente en la franja de la isla situada al sur del círculo polar ártico.

Una vista del fiordo desde Qassiarsuk, a finales de junio. Álvaro González

Un camino de ocho kilómetros lleva hasta Tasiusaq, donde una sola familia mantiene en funcionamiento la granja y el albergue. Allí, Aviaja Lennert y la novia de su hijo se afanan en la cocina para preparar la cena a unos huéspedes alemanes que están a punto de llegar con sus mochilas, tras más de dos horas de trayecto a pie desde Qassiarsuk. Moverse por la isla requiere paciencia: sin carreteras que conecten localidades, el transporte depende del barco y el helicóptero, y si no hay agua de por medio, los desplazamientos cortos se realizan en buggy, moto de nieve o caminando. Para reponer fuerzas tras la caminata, las anfitrionas han preparado un menú que incluye pan casero, sopa de pescado y cordero asado con patatas de la zona y hierbas silvestres recogidas por ellas. De postre, compota de ruibarbo.

Lennert divide su tiempo entre el cuidado de las 600 ovejas de la explotación, la atención a los viajeros y las clases que imparte a los pocos niños de la escuela de Qassiarsuk. Pese a sus esfuerzos por diversificar los ingresos, la familia afronta una etapa delicada tras el cierre del aeropuerto. Este verano han recibido muchos menos viajeros que en años anteriores. Ahora reaparece, además, una preocupación que Lennert creía desterrada: la minería, un peligro latente capaz de arruinar los recursos naturales de los que depende su subsistencia.

La granja y la vivienda de Aviaja Lennert, en junio en Tasiusaq. Álvaro González

Su granja está cerca de Kvanefjeld, un yacimiento que alberga uno de los mayores depósitos de tierras raras y uranio del mundo. Lennert creyó que aquella amenaza había quedado atrás hace cinco años, cuando celebró entre lágrimas la victoria electoral de Inuit Ataqatigiit, el partido ecologista que había prometido prohibir la extracción de uranio para frenar la explotación de Kvanefjeld. Ella fue una de las voces más activas del movimiento Urani Naamik (No al uranio), cuyo sol naranja y sonriente permanece pintado en un costado de su establo. “Es muy importante para nosotros tener una naturaleza sana de la que podamos obtener nuestros alimentos”, argumenta para explicar su férrea oposición a los proyectos extractivos que pueden contaminar la zona. Hoy le inquieta el interés de Trump —al que se refiere como “el innombrable”— tanto por el control de la isla como por la inmensa riqueza de sus recursos naturales.

Mientras Kvanefjeld permanece bloqueado, las miradas de Washington se posan sobre otro gigantesco yacimiento de tierras raras a escasos kilómetros. Tanbreez alberga reservas prácticamente libres de uranio, por lo que su explotación no está prohibida por ley. Consciente de su valor estratégico, la diplomacia estadounidense maniobró para evitar que el proyecto cayera en manos chinas y facilitó su traspaso a la firma neoyorquina Critical Metals. La operación cuenta con el firme respaldo de la Administración Trump, que ha movilizado a la agencia estatal de crédito a la exportación para inyectar hasta 120 millones de dólares, en medio de informaciones que apuntan al interés de inversores vinculados al entorno del magnate —incluido su propio hijo Donald Trump Jr.— en el desarrollo de la mina.

El presidente estadounidense insiste en mantener el pulso. Aunque a partir de febrero rebajó el tono de sus amenazas, en la cumbre de la OTAN que se celebró en julio en Ankara reiteró que la inmensa isla “debería estar controlada por Estados Unidos y no por Dinamarca”. A principios de agosto, Trump publicó una imagen en las redes sociales en la que una figura gigante del mandatario se cierne amenazante sobre un asentamiento del territorio ártico, acompañada de un escueto mensaje: “Hola, Groenlandia”.

Aviaja Lennert, delante de su establo con el símbolo de Urani Naamik, este verano en Tasiusaq. Álvaro González

Esta voracidad extractiva chocó la semana pasada contra el muro regulatorio de la isla. El Ejecutivo groenlandés ordenó el aplazamiento de un polémico proyecto de exploración petrolera en el este del territorio dirigido por Greenland Energy, una firma tejana vinculada al entorno de Trump. La compañía, que llegó a trasladar el material necesario, pretendía iniciar perforaciones sin los permisos pertinentes, lo que provocó una “seria advertencia” de las autoridades locales.

La UE busca afianzar su influencia

Ante el avance de las pretensiones de Washington, la Unión Europea intenta marcar terreno y afianzar su influencia en el territorio autónomo danés. Barry Andrews, eurodiputado irlandés y ponente del Parlamento Europeo para las relaciones con Groenlandia, reclama un frente común y advierte contra las ambiciones de la Casa Blanca. “Debemos dejarle claro a la Administración Trump, una y otra vez, que la soberanía de Groenlandia se debe respetar, no podemos confiar ya en Estados Unidos”, subraya por correo electrónico. Andrews apuesta por duplicar la inversión europea en la isla hasta los 500 millones de euros en el próximo marco presupuestario.

En esa misma línea, la danesa Christel Schaldemose, vicepresidenta de la Eurocámara, aboga por “invertir más y generar mejores oportunidades de desarrollo”. La socialdemócrata incide por teléfono en que la UE debe ser el socio preferente de la isla, pero siempre respetando que la decisión sobre la explotación de los recursos y el futuro de la minería corresponde de forma exclusiva a los groenlandeses.

Ese derecho a decidir es el que llevó a la comunidad del sur a movilizarse en masa contra el megaproyecto de Kvanefjeld cuando, hace un lustro, sintieron amenazada su forma de vida. En esa resistencia ciudadana participó activamente Inga Gísladóttir, una profesional de perfil inusual —trabajadora social, informática y controladora aérea— que además recorre el mundo como narradora de mitología nórdica. Nacida en Islandia, Inga acaba de cumplir 15 años en Groenlandia y viene de pasar tres meses en Qaqortoq, formando a los controladores del nuevo aeropuerto.

Su postura ante la puja geopolítica por los recursos de la isla es categórica: “Que esta sea una tierra enorme y muy poco poblada no significa que cualquiera pueda venir a adueñarse de ella; pertenece a quien quiere conservarla”. En cuestión de días dejará Narsarsuaq sin saber cuál será su próximo destino. Tras regresar de una caminata para contemplar por última vez el glaciar que asoma a pocos kilómetros del pueblo, Gísladóttir espanta los mosquitos mientras evoca la profunda conexión inuit con la tierra: “Aquí la relación con la naturaleza no es extractiva; no se percibe como algo de lo que sacar tajada, sino como un patrimonio que debemos disfrutar y preservar para las siguientes generaciones”.

World.title: Inheritance wave will increase housing inequality, experts warn
World.content:
A wave of inheritances over the next decade is set to drive up house prices in the Netherlands even further, a report by financial experts has said.

An estimated €300 billion will be passed on by the baby-boomer generation between 2024 and 2023, much of which will be reinvested in property, according to financial advice agency Van Bruggen.

Mortgage expert Oscar Noorlag warned that the transfer of wealth would increase inequality, as the benefits will be mainly felt by the richest households, many of whom are already homeowners.

The cash will allow them to move up the ladder or invest in a suitable retirement home. But at the other end of the scale people living in rental properties will see their costs rise without having a substantial inheritance to fall back on.

In 2024 the richest 10% of households owned 56% of all capital wealth, while the average householder had built up a fortune of €563,000 compared to €40,400 for the average tenant.

“It’s not just income that determines what people do in the housing market,” Noorlag said. “The wealth of people’s parents and grandparents is playing an increasing role.

“But not everyone has access to that family wealth, and that income inequality is threatening to transfer to the housing market.”

Senior housing

Van Bruggen’s advice goes against the common assumption that the housing market cools off as the population ages, because older people are less likely to move up the ladder.

Since the 1970s the proportion of owner-occupied houses in the Netherlands has risen from 35% to 59%, while the 2.3 million people (12.7%) living in social rental housing generally have the lowest incomes and savings.

House prices have risen by 240% since the end of the last crash in the summer of 2013, despite a brief dip at the end of the pandemic and are still rising, although the rate has cooled from more than 10% in early 2025 to 4% last month.

Noorlag said the government needed to prioritise building senior housing so that older people could move out of the homes where they raised their children.

“When older people can move into a suitable home, more houses become available for the next generations,” he said. “That allows for more house moves that the whole market benefits from.”

World.title: Police arrest 14-year-old for impersonating a policeman
World.content:
Police have arrested a 14-year-old boy in Zwolle for impersonating a police officer in order to rob the homes of elderly people around the city. The boy, from Hendrik-Ido-Ambacht in Zuid-Holland, was working with an older man from Rotterdam.

A series of reports were made to police in the area about fake policeman knocking on the doors of houses around Zwolle, according to regional broadcaster RTV Oost. At least two houses were burgled with money and jewellery being taken.

The police identified the suspects through CCTV and arrested both of them when they were spotted in a car. The victims have had their belongings returned to them.

Young people posing as police officers is a growing crime, according to local police. A community officer told NOS that youths are being recruited by older people and are simply carrying out orders.

Last month, a 13-year-old from Spijkenisse was arrested for the same crime. He had managed to steal €20,000 worth of jewellery.

The police reported around 500 fake police agent incidents last year, according to news site NU.nl. Almost all follow a similar pattern: they make phone calls or send letters to vulnerable older people telling them there have been neighbourhood robberies and their belongings are at risk.

They then go to their houses under the guise of safeguarding them, before stealing from them.

World.title: Warm week ahead, thunderstorms likely on Thursday
World.content:
The week starts warm and sunny across the Netherlands, but is set to break on Thursday with heavy thunderstorms.

Monday brings plenty of sun and highs of 21 to 24°. Tuesday is warmer at 23 to 25° in much of the country, though the southeast is cloudier.

Wednesday turns muggy, reaching 24 to 26° with a rising chance of showers later on. Thursday is the warmest day at 25 to 28°, and close to tropical in the southeast, before heavy showers and thunderstorms move in from the afternoon. Some could be severe, with hail and strong gusts, the national weather service KNMI said.

Friday will be cooler, around 19 to 22° with further showers, and the weekend – the last of the meteorological summer, which ends on August 31 – looks cooler still at about 21°.

KNMI had no weather warnings in force as of Sunday evening but says alerts for the Thursday and Friday storms are likely. It issues these up to 48 hours ahead.

World.title: Investigation after Feyenoord fans set off fireworks at Cambuur
World.content:
The Dutch football association KNVB will review its rules for dealing with disturbances at matches after five supporters were injured when fireworks were set off during Cambuur Leeuwarden’s home game against Feyenoord at the weekend.

Referee Danny Makkelie restarted the match in the De Kooi stadium after a 20-minute break, but questioned afterwards whether the guidelines should be changed.

At least one Cambuur fan suffered an eye injury while others had burns and hearing loss when Feyenoord fans let off a barrage of flares and fireworks in the 12th minute of the game. It is not known how the fireworks got into the stadium.

One firework landed at the feet of Feyenoord’s goalkeeper, Tjark Ernst, but he was unhurt. The current guidelines state that a match should be abandoned if a player is struck by fireworks, but say nothing about supporters.

“I asked the KNVB twice whether supporters being hit counted or not,” Makkelie told ESPN. Acting mayor Foort van Oosten instructed the referee to restart the game after consulting police.

“It’s an agreement made between the clubs, not us,” Makkelie explained. “I don’t know what the reason for it is, because it’s just as bad whether players or supporters are hit.”

Face coverings

Police were unable to arrest the culprits on the spot because the suspects were wearing balaclavas and their faces were obscured in the smoke. Efforts to identify them are continuing.

The KNVB will discuss the incident during its regular review meeting later this week.

When the game finally restarted, Feyenoord put their hosts to the sword, racing to a 4-0 lead by half-time, with Gjivai Zechiel opening the scoring in the 17th minute and Ayase Ueda bagging a penalty just before the break.

Cambuur pulled two goals back after the interval as Feyenoord eased off, before Zechiel’s second condemned the Frisian side to a third successive defeat.

PSV comeback

Groningen, who started the weekend as joint Eredivisie leaders, briefly threatened an upset in Eindhoven when Brynjolfur Willumsson gave them an early lead against PSV.

But the champions hit back, Ruben van Bommel causing mayhem down the left flank as PSV ran out 5-1 winners, with Croatian veteran Ivan Perisic scoring twice.

AZ Alkmaar are the only team with maximum points after three games after beating Fortuna Sittard 2-0 in Limburg.

The home side were reduced to 10 men after just four minutes when Ole Romney was sent off for stamping on Mateo Chávez. AZ struggled to make their advantage count, but Leeroy Echteld’s half-time substitutions proved decisive as Calvin Stengs twice set up Jizz Hornkamp for the goals.

PEC break duck

PEC Zwolle picked up their first points of the season by winning 2-0 at Heerenveen, but ADO Den Haag are still waiting after going down 3-1 at Go Ahead Eagles, who rose to second place in the table.

In Rotterdam, Sparta came back three times against Utrecht to claim a point and leave new manger Anthony Correia still looking for his first win. Defender Nick Verschuren scored the final equaliser in the 96th minute for Sparta.

Ajax, Twente and NEC Nijmegen were all allowed to reschedule their matches because of their European commitments in midweek.

Results

Saturday

Fortuna Sittard 0-2 AZ Alkmaar

Heerenveen 0-2 PEC Zwolle

Sparta Rotterdam 3-3 Utrecht

Sunday

Cambuur Leeuwarden 2-5 Feyenoord

Go Ahead Eagles 3-1 ADO Den Haag

PSV Eindhoven 5-1 Groningen

Postponed: Twente Enschede v Telstar (September 9), Ajax v Willem II Tilburg (September 15), NEC Nijmegen v Excelsior (September 16)

World.title: Coach carrying German school pupils crashes on A28
World.content:
A coach carrying German schoolchildren crashed off the A28 motorway near Wezep in Gelderland in the early hours of Monday, closing the road in both directions. At least eight people were taken to hospital, some seriously injured, according to reports.

The coach, with more than 50 people on board, came off the road after colliding with a van at around 4.15am, according to police and the regional safety authority. Most of those aboard were teenage pupils.

The van was torn in two by the impact, and its driver was among those taken to hospital. Others were treated for minor injuries at the scene. Three trauma helicopters were sent to the crash.

The Austrian-registered coach overturned on and landed on its side. The cause is not yet known, and police forensic investigators are examining the site.

The A28 is shut in both directions between ’t Harde and Wezep until the evening rush hour, Rijkswaterstaat said. Traffic heading towards Zwolle is being diverted via the A1 and A50 at Hoevelaken, and towards Amersfoort via the A50 and A1 at Hattemerbroek.

Drivers face delays throughout the day, expected to last past rush hour, according to broadcaster NOS.

World.title: High earners buy nearly half of Dutch electric cars
World.content:
The Netherlands’ shift to electric cars is being driven overwhelmingly by its wealthiest households, while lower earners buy up the country’s oldest and most polluting vehicles, new figures from national statistics office CBS show.

Of the roughly 259,000 fully electric cars and plug-in hybrids bought or changed hands in 2025, the highest-earning 10% of households took almost 75,000 – more than a quarter of the total. Add the next bracket down and the top fifth of earners account for close to half of every plug-in car sold.

At the other end, the lowest-earning 10% bought around 6,000, about 2% of the total. What they did buy skewed old and diesel: two-thirds of the cars bought by the poorest fifth were more than 10 years old, and diesel’s share was highest among the lowest earners.

The split reflects what people can afford. Most cars that change hands in the Netherlands are second-hand – of 1.7 million bought or transferred in 2025, only 148,000 were new – and the used market remains overwhelmingly petrol, with nearly 1.4 million of the total running on it.

The figures come as the government prepares to step in. From the last quarter of 2026, a scheme aimed at lower and middle incomes will let households scrap an old petrol or diesel car and claim a subsidy towards a second-hand fully electric one. The cabinet has set aside €52 million over three years for the measures.

The scheme is a direct answer to a long-standing criticism – that state support for electric driving has mostly reached the wealthy – that these figures now bear out.

World.title: Norris wins final Dutch Grand Prix as Verstappen crashes out
World.content:
Lando Norris won the final Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort on Sunday, while Max Verstappen crashed on the opening lap of his last home race.

Norris, the reigning world champion, started from pole and won ahead of the Mercedes pair Kimi Antonelli, who leads this year’s championship, and George Russell. It was his second win in a row.

Verstappen lost control at the final corner moments after the start and hit the wall, the fourth time he has failed to finish this season. He was uninjured by the crash.

It was the first time he didn’t make it to the podium at Zandvoort since the race returned in 2021. He won the first three editions and finished second in the last two.

“It was a hard hit, but I’ve had harder ones,” Verstappen told reporters. He said he had seen a dry line forming and thought he could get back on the throttle, “but that didn’t work out well.” He was more frustrated by his pace all weekend, and said he hoped for better at the next race, in Monza.

The race was halted to clear the debris. When it restarted Antonelli passed Norris and led for more than half the race before Norris retook the lead. On Saturday, Russell had won the first sprint race held in the Netherlands, with Verstappen sixth.

The final weekend

It was the sixth and last edition of the revived Dutch Grand Prix, which the organisers chose to end rather than renew, saying they wanted to stop while the event was still at its peak.

Around 105,000 fans attended on Saturday and Sunday, but Friday did not sell out for the first time, with some 5,000 tickets unsold, according to broadcaster NOS. The first editions had needed a ballot.

King Willem-Alexander presented the trophy. The weekend was also marred by long queues on Friday and crowding that left thousands of fans late for Saturday’s sprint race.

Sporting director Jan Lammers called the six years an economic success and a boost for the region. The circuit is not closing, and has said it will host the all-electric Formula E series from 2027.

World.title: Zandvoort gears up for its last Formula 1 Grand Prix
World.content:
Formula 1 is set to stage its final Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort on Sunday afternoon, ending a six-year run, as rising costs pushed the organisers to end it.

Reigning world champion Lando Norris will start first on the grid. Max Verstappen, racing at home for the final time and out of this year’s title fight, will start seventh.

George Russell won Saturday’s sprint race with Verstappen sixth, the Dutchman then qualified only seventh, blaming “fundamental problems” with his car. He has also been fighting a cold. It rained on Sunday morning but the tracks are expected to be dry for the race.

Verstappen won the first three races after Formula 1 returned to Zandvoort, in 2021, 2022, and 2023. Norris won in 2024 and Oscar Piastri last year.

Why it is ending

When the organisers announced it would be ending in December 2024, they said they wanted to finish while the event was still at its peak rather than gamble on rising costs.

“There were various options on the table to continue,” said Robert van Overdijk, the director of Circuit Zandvoort. “We could have rotated with other circuits, there were opportunities to carry on every year as well. In the end it is our decision.”

Zandvoort and the British Grand Prix at Silverstone are the only races on the calendar that run without government financial support, while circuits in Qatar and Saudi Arabia pay hundreds of millions to host a race.

The Dutch event is financed privately by a group of family firms, and the AD newspaper has put the cost of staging it at close to €80 million.

The drivers’ regret

Lando Norris said he was sorry to see the race go, telling broadcaster NOS he preferred compact circuits like Zandvoort and that dropping it had not been the drivers’ choice.

Sporting director Jan Lammers wrote an open letter to fans saying that a small country had brought one of the world’s biggest sporting events back “to a place where many thought it impossible”, and said almost two million spectators had passed through the gates since the return.

A six-year run

The race returned in 2021 after a 36-year absence, the previous Dutch Grand Prix having been won by Niki Lauda in 1985. Its revival was driven by Prince Bernhard, a cousin of the king, who bought the circuit a decade ago to bring Formula 1 back to the Netherlands.

Bernhard sold his stake in the track earlier this year. Since the return, the event has drawn around 100,000 fans a day, most of them dressed in orange for Verstappen, and turned the 4.3km dune circuit into one of the season’s set-piece weekends.

The circuit itself is not closing. It will keep hosting other racing and has said it will bring the all-electric Formula E series to Zandvoort from 2027.

World.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.title: Polish NGOs urge PM’s “right-hand man” to withdraw constitutional court candidacy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A group of Polish civil society organisations has urged a former government minister to withdraw his candidacy to become a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, saying his close ties to the prime minister could undermine confidence in the court’s independence. In a joint statement, the nine organisations say that restoring the legitimacy of the court, which has been in crisis since 2015 following illegitimate judicial appointments made by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, requires not only addressing legal irregularities but also rebuilding public trust. “The existence of the Constitutional Tribunal as an organ of judicial power only makes sense if it is an independent arbiter,” they say. 🔴Wspólnie z innymi organizacjami apelujemy do dr. M. Berka o rezygnację z kandydowania do TK, a do Sejmu o wybór osoby niezależnej politycznie. Droga do praworządności to nie „odbijanie” Trybunału, ale odbudowa jego autorytetu. Przeczytajcie nasz apel, link w komentarzu ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/LPlbk39lNr — Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) August 20, 2026 The appeal follows Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s announcement that Maciej Berek, who until recently served as a government minister and whom Tusk has described as his “right-hand man”, would be put forward as a candidate for the Constitutional Tribunal. The choice has drawn particular attention because Tusk came to power promising to “depoliticise” the court after the previous PiS government appointed former politicians as judges. “Regardless of the extent to which the tribunal has become politicised, the way to reform this institution cannot be for it to be ‘recaptured’ or ‘taken over’ by another ruling majority,” the NGOs write in the statement. The organisations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Institute of Public Affairs and the Stefan Batory Foundation, say Berek’s close ties to the current political leadership could cause his appointment to be perceived as political, regardless of his legal qualifications or personal integrity. “Not only must courts and tribunals operate independently and impartially, but citizens must also recognise and have confidence in that independence and impartiality. This is not possible when judges are appointed whose links to the government are immediately apparent,” the organisations add. “We therefore call on Dr Maciej Berek to withdraw his candidacy in the interests of the independence of the constitutional judiciary.” The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 The organisations also argue that Berek’s nomination goes against a principle that the current ruling coalition sought to introduce: that anyone who has held political office within the previous four years should be barred from appointment to the tribunal. Berek was a government minister until last week. The coalition’s proposal was included in a bill approved by parliament in 2024. However, the Constitutional Tribunal itself later ruled the provision unconstitutional after former President Andrzej Duda, an ally of PiS, referred the legislation for review. “Although this law has not come into force, it would be reasonable for the Sejm to adhere to the standard it has adopted,” they said, referring to the lower chamber of the parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 However, the selection of Berek, whose candidacy was put forward by MPs from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has exposed divisions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from centre-right to left. “We were supposed to be different from PiS; we were supposed to do things differently, not exactly the same way,” Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, told Polsat News. Paweł Śliz, leader of the centre-right Poland 2050’s (Polska 2050) caucus, said Berek would make an excellent Constitutional Tribunal judge were it not for his recent role as a government minister. “I consider him an excellent, outstanding professional; I value his experience and expertise. However, my position on this matter is unequivocal. I will not compromise my principles,” he told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition opposing Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. Last week, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz told PAP on Thursday that “there are serious doubts” about Berek’s formal qualifications to become a Constitutional Tribunal judge. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland summons Israeli ambassador over discontinued investigation into killing of Gaza aid workers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. “Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.” Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 20, 2026 The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból. The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation. On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”. The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF. However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful. The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action. ⚖️ IDF prosecution rules on five FFAM cases: The IDF says its General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism has completed reviews of approximately 150 exceptional wartime incidents since the beginning of the war and transferred them to the Military Prosecution. Decisions… pic.twitter.com/H5g4qOu5e2 — Israel Realtime (@IsraelRealtime) August 19, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying that it was “greatly disappointed to receive the information provided about the discontinuation of the proceedings by the Israeli military authorities”. It announced that it had summoned the Israeli ambassador in order to “communicate a critical assessment of the actions taken to date to clarify the causes and course of the tragedy”. It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”. “The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”. We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024. And we fundamentally disagree with their decision about criminal investigations into the IDF airstrikes that killed our team. Read our full statement here:… — World Central Kitchen (@WCKitchen) August 19, 2026 The IDF’s findings were also condemned by WCK itself, which called them “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. It added that, “at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody”. The NGO repeated its demand for an independent investigation into the incident, “because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”. On Friday, the UK, Canada and Australia, whose citizens were also killed in the strike, issued a joint statement calling the IDF’s decision to drop the investigation “shameful” and another example of the lack of accountability for incidents in Gaza. Joint statement from the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom on Israel closing the investigation into strikes on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza on 1 April 2024 ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/V3CZe286tN — Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (@FCDOGovUK) August 21, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Main image credit: World Central Kitchen

World.title: New official tasked with promoting Poland criticised over error-strewn, potentially AI-generated report
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing errors and which shows signs of being generated by artificial intelligence. The document mislocated major Polish cities and included bizarre language mixing Polish and English. It was marked as being part of a project financed by the sport and tourism ministry, though the ministry itself has denied that claim. The opposition has called on prosecutors to investigate potential misuse of public funds. ⁉️ Czy “Markę Polska” ma nam wygenerować sztuczna inteligencja? ⁉️ Czy Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki zapłaciło 200 000 złotych w ramach zadania publicznego za raport wygenerowany przez AI? ⁉️ Czy mogę prosić Panią Minister prof. @b_mroz_gorgon o odniesienie się do tych pytań… pic.twitter.com/lM2AY88oAh — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 The official in question, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, is a professor at Wrocław University of Economics who was appointed three weeks ago as the government’s plenipotentiary for the promotion of Poland’s brand, a newly created position. She was presented at a press conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. However, this week, journalists and commentators began highlighting cases of bizarre errors from a report, titled A Self-Portrait of the Poles (Polaków Portret Własny), published last year with Mróz-Gorgoń named as the author, in her position as president of a think tank called Marka Polska (Brand Poland). The report contained some glaring errors, such as describing the city of Katowice as being in “north central” Poland (whereas in fact it is in the south) and Wrocław as being in the “northwest” (when it is actually in the southwest). Geografia – czyli gdzie leżą Katowice A propos miast jest też ciekawy chochlik lub też, jakby to powiedział ktoś złośliwy, klasyczna halucynacja AI. Przy opisie badań FGI miasta opisane są w następujący sposób (zdjęcie poniżej): 👉 Olsztyn – północny wschód 👉 Szczecin -… pic.twitter.com/SF6XBRfhWS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 Other parts contain strange analysis, such as noting that “after World War Two, Germany did not build its brand on the Holocaust”. The text also features unusual language, including random use of words in English, some of which have been turned into Polish ones. It is also regularly features words written in capital letters. One sentence, for example, refers to “INSTABILNOŚĆ” and “REZILIENCE”, presumably meaning “instability” and “resilience”, but neither of which is a Polish word. Another section claims that 95% of Poles born after 1990 are “polilingwalni” (an invented Polonised version of “polylingual”) who speak “angielski fluent”, a strange linguistic mix that means they speak English fluently. As well as the unusual language, the very claim that 95% of young Poles speak fluent English, as well as that many additionally speak Mandarin, has been questioned by many commentators. The report also contains bizarre errors in footnotes, which are numbered randomly (on one page, three consecutive footnotes are numbered “41, 517, 6”) and some of which are completely empty. A number of expert commentators have suggested that the text contains clear indications that it was generated by AI, a claim supported by evidence from programmes that check texts for AI-generated content. AI czy nie AI, oto jest pytanie Czytając ten raport kilkukrotnie, trudno mi było pozbyć się wrażenia, że nikt poważny, a szczególnie naukowiec z tytułem doktora habilitowanego, nie wygenerowałby dużych części raportu, za który zapłacili podatnicy, w jakimś LLM. No bo przecież… pic.twitter.com/jyTexgmeXS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 As well as bearing Mróz-Gorgoń’s name as author, the report also features on its front cover the logo of the sport and tourism ministry. The first page then includes a note saying that the project was carried out under an initiative co-financed by the ministry. After the issue began to draw attention and criticism on Thursday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the report was not ordered by them, was not part of any agreement to which the ministry was a party, and that no request to use the ministry’s logo was submitted. However, a social media post last November by deputy sport and tourism minister Piotr Borys shows him attending an event to present the report. He thanked Mróz-Gorgoń for coordinating the project and inviting him to the presentation. 📚W Akademii Leona Koźmińskiego odbyła się prezentacja raportu „Polaków Portret Własny”, przygotowanego Think Tank Marka Polska. To wyjątkowe wydarzenie poświęcone premierze badań dotyczących DNA Marki Polska. 🧬To pierwsze tak kompleksowe badanie, które pokazuje, kim jesteśmy… pic.twitter.com/jb7KdCJTPM — Piotr Borys (@piotr_borys) November 26, 2025 On Thursday evening, Mróz-Gorgoń herself addressed the controversy in an interview with Polsat News. She said that the report was actually a “work in progress” that “should never have appeared in the public space”. However, she still defended the work, saying that “the research was conducted reliably” and “the conclusions stand up to scrutiny”. But she also admitted that the writing of the report had been “aided by artificial intelligence”. In separate remarks to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), she said that “we used AI tools solely for transcription, summarising and text editing; they did not design research content or draw conclusions…We worked according to social science methodology, diligently and without cutting corners”. Meanwhile, on the Marka Polska think tank’s website, where the report had been published, it was initially changed on Thursday to being marked as a “draft version” before later being deleted entirely. Od raportu i deklaracji, że “praca badawcza [została] przeprowadzona zgodnie z zasadami nauk społecznych, rzetelnie i merytorycznie, w oparciu o opisaną metodologię”, przez “work in progress”, aż do “Oops! That page can’t be found”. Myślę, że to słowo “Oops!” jest najlepszym… pic.twitter.com/OaSTxkwKwa — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 On Thursday evening, the main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), announced that it was submitting requests to both prosecutors and the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (ABW) to investigate the use of around 200,000 zloty (€46,380) in state funds for the project that the report was allegedly part of. PiS has also called on Mróz-Gorgoń to resign or to be fired. On Friday, a deputy digital affairs minister, Dariusz Standerski, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that “all the circumstances surrounding the creation of this report will be clarified”. The controversy around Mróz-Gorgoń comes just days after the sport and tourism ministry was involved in the launch of a new advertising campaign designed to encourage tourism to Poland, but which many commentators have argued was poorly conceived and executed. World.title: Poland tests 250 km/h train speeds for planned cuts to intercity journey times
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
