World.title: Parrots Rocky and Kiki: Tbilisi Zoo’s brightest residents – video
World.content:
Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

Tbilisi Zoo is home to two species of macaws: scarlet macaws (Ara macao) named Rocky and Kiki, and blue-and-yellow macaws (Ara ararauna) named Chico and Paco. Their bright plumage catches visitors’ attention at first sight.

The macaws at Tbilisi Zoo are currently in the middle of their breeding season. Chico and Paco are expecting chicks. They usually incubate their eggs for 24–28 days. During this period, both parents actively protect and care for their future offspring.

Rocky and Kiki have become particularly cautious during this period. They often hide from people and rarely leave their enclosure. If you are planning to visit them at the zoo, keep in mind that they may be difficult to spot at the moment.

Macaws are known for their strong bonds. Pairs almost always stay together: they preen each other’s feathers, look for food together and protect each other when danger threatens.

With proper care, macaws can live for 50–60 years, and sometimes even longer — more than 70 years. Rocky’s exact age is unknown, but he is the oldest parrot at Tbilisi Zoo. Despite his advanced age, Rocky still has the same short-tempered and grumpy nature he has always had.

Once, when a keeper was a little late with a treat — a nut — Rocky immediately made his “protest” known by biting him on the finger. Because of their powerful beaks, macaw bites can be very painful and may cause serious injuries.

Macaws are incredibly intelligent birds. They have excellent memories, and some can even imitate human voices and words.

Although macaws are often kept as pets, caring for them is no easy task. They need plenty of space, daily attention, mental stimulation and constant variety in their surroundings.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan move toward integration of payment systems
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 24. The central banks of Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are discussing the integration of payment systems, and payment companies from both countries are already in talks regarding practical cooperation.

This was stated by Timur Ishmetov, Governor of the Central Bank of Uzbekistan, in response to a question from Trend’s special correspondent during a press briefing held as part of the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum.

According to Ishmetov, the central banks of the two countries are already cooperating through various platforms and have several areas of interaction.

“We are already in practical talks with the Central Bank of Azerbaijan, for example, on integrating our payment systems. A couple of our payment companies are also already in talks with companies in Azerbaijan on integration,” Ishmetov said.

He noted that he expects practical results from this cooperation in the near future.

According to the Central Bank chairman, cooperation in financial technology can help create a larger regional market for businesses, particularly startups and fintech companies.

“There is an area, especially financial technology, where cooperation is a win-win strategy for everybody. Instead of each country focusing on its own market, we can cooperate and open up the markets for all our businesses, especially startups, fintechs and technology companies,” he said.

Ishmetov emphasized that cooperation between the two countries would allow them to exchange experience and create broader opportunities for the development of financial technologies across the region.

The official made the statement to reporters on the sidelines of Kurultai elections in Astana.

“The elections in Kazakhstan were conducted in accordance with the law and in an orderly manner. We also observed that the citizens of Kazakhstan, from the youngest, starting at age 18, to the elderly, actively participated in the elections despite yesterday’s weather conditions. This is a good example of how the state of Kazakhstan, together with its people, is moving forward on a common path.

Mesten noted that the delegation conducted its observation not only in Astana but also in Almaty. In addition, the delegation has been here for four days since its arrival. The authorities have emphasized cooperation with the private sector and attracting investment as key tools for developing infrastructure and creating modern, competitive facilities.

The reconstruction of the Ak-Keme hotel in Bishkek was presented as an example of this approach, combining state assets with private investment and management expertise.

He noted that the mission welcomes the efforts of electoral authorities and other stakeholders aimed at implementing the new electoral system within a relatively short timeframe following the constitutional reform.

Furthermore, Guliyev added that the OTS mission views this first electoral process as an opportunity to strengthen public participation, citizen trust, and the development of the country’s representative institutions.

World.title: “AzInTelecom” Cybersecurity Services Gain Global Recognition
World.content:
“AzInTelecom” LLC, a company within AZCON Holding, has become a member of FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), an international cybersecurity organization.

As a result, “AzInTelecom” has been recognized by FIRST as the sectoral Computer Incident Response Center for Azerbaijan’s transport sector and has been granted “Transport CERT” team status. As part of the membership process, the team’s activities were assessed in accordance with the “SIM3” model, and its compliance with international standards was confirmed based on an on-site assessment.

This status enables “AzInTelecom” to promptly neutralize cyberattacks originating from abroad in cooperation with international partners, exchange cyber threat intelligence via the MISP platform, take part in the organization’s voting process, and participate in its working groups.

The acceptance of “AzInTelecom” as a FIRST member confirms that the company operates in accordance with international standards in the field of cybersecurity and is recognized as a trusted partner by the global cybersecurity community. At the same time, it enables the company to be represented on the same global platform as such world-leading companies as “Google”, “Amazon”, “Microsoft”, “Apple”, “Cisco” and “CrowdStrike”, contributing to strengthening cyber resilience in the transport sector and developing institutional capabilities.

It should be noted that “AzInTelecom” develops its activities in line with the Information Security and Cybersecurity Strategy of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2023–2027, continuously strengthening its technological capabilities. The company will continue contributing to further strengthening the country’s digital security by expanding its cybersecurity capabilities and international partnerships.

World.title: Suspended sentence, $100 fine for man's naked attack on country ambulance
World.content:
A man who smashed his head through the windscreen of an ambulance while naked on a public street in Western Australia's Goldfields has been handed a suspended sentence and $100 fine.

Brian Charles Parfitt attacked the ambulance, and the paramedics inside, on December 7 last year after he had been spotted behaving erratically on the streets of Boulder, 600km east of Perth.

Parfitt, 26, attempted to climb the first ambulance on scene before mounting the second and repeatedly smashing his head into the windscreen.

The paramedics inside drove back and forth in an attempt to dislodge him, before he smashed his head through the windscreen and began crawling inside.

The St John Ambulance staff fled the vehicle and ran to the second ambulance, with Parfitt apprehended a short time later and placed into an induced coma.

Parfitt's lawyers had previously indicated he was having a "mental health episode" at the time of the incident, but further details have not been mentioned during court proceedings.

Video of the incident, which the ABC has chosen not to republish, was circulated widely on social media and sparked a campaign from St John's around the near-constant violence faced by the ambulance service's staff.

Prosecutors said Parfitt threatened bystanders with a pair of scissors taken from the ambulance. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Prosecutors urged prison term

As Parfitt faced the Kalgoorlie Magistrates Court on Monday for sentencing, prosecutors urged an immediate jail term.

Police prosecutor Carl Logan said the 26-year-old, who appeared via video link from Casuarina Prison, was naked in the vicinity of women and children, and had threatened to kill a bystander with scissors taken from the ambulance.

Sergeant Logan said Parfitt had a lengthy criminal record, with the attack coming four months after his release from prison on other charges and causing $4,000 damage to the ambulance.

The court heard he had failed to engage with rehabilitation programs and represented a high risk of future offending.

Defence points to family support

Defence lawyer Leneva Polmear submitted a letter from Parfitt's Perth-based father, describing his pride in his son's efforts to turn his life around.

Ms Polmear said the family had made arrangements with a metropolitan crisis support service to ensure Parfitt had access to appropriate help.

Parfitt's attack caused $4,000 damage to the ambulance. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Sentencing Parfitt, Magistrate Donna Webb said she had only been willing to consider a non-custodial sentence if the 26-year-old's father was willing to take him in.

She told the court she was also required to factor in Parfitt's significant mental health issues and the 261 days he had already spent in custody.

Describing the 13-month suspended prison term as a likely "last chance", she said Parfitt would need to do everything right to avoid further time in custody.

Magistrate Webb urged the 26-year-old to remain in Perth after his release from prison.

"Kalgoorlie seems to be a trap for you," she said.

Attacks on paramedics rising

Parfitt's offending came amid a significant rise in attacks on paramedics across Western Australia, with incidents rising 11.9 per cent in 2025.

Rebecca Thompson says she was traumatised by the attack. (ABC News: Nic Perpitch)

Kalgoorlie patient transport officer Rebecca Thomspon was on duty and in the ambulance during Parfitt's attack.

"I have three young children at home and I feared for my life whilst I was on that job," she said at the launch of a campaign to tackle violence against paramedics.

"It shouldn't be like that."

She described the incident as the most traumatic moment of her life.

World.title: International company's plan for multi-billion-dollar data centre in regional Qld
World.content:
With the energy demands of artificial intelligence prompting broader policy debates across Australia, regional Queensland is now facing the reality of hyper-scale expansion with a $31.9 billion data centre being proposed for the Western Downs.

The Western Downs Digital Park, set to be the largest facility of its kind in Australia, has been earmarked for a 725.5-hectare plot near Dalby, roughly 250 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

The company behind the project is Singapore-based developer Zerra DC, which operates hyper-scale data centres across the Asia Pacific.

A coal seam gas well near Wambo Feedlot, on the Western Downs. (ABC Southern Queensland: Nathan Morris)

The site, 37km north-west of Dalby, is currently home to a 24,000-head feedlot owned by Wambo Cattle Company.

Although this proposed data centre is strategically located near major regional power stations, there are ongoing concerns across the country about energy consumption and water security as the development and construction of data centres surges.

A map showing the proposed site of the Western Downs Digital Park and surrounding energy sources. (Supplied: Urbis)

The federal government is currently refining proposed new national rules for how data centres consume energy, including a requirement for them to purchase power from renewable energy sources.

In Southern Queensland, there has been a recent push from the Toowoomba Regional Council to ensure data centres do not encroach on drinking-water sources in the region.

Councillor Rebecca Vonhoff said the council took a national lead in passing a motion.

"We have this prime industrial land, we own our water infrastructure, we provide drinking water to our residents and, most importantly, we have a personal and very deeply felt connection to water, having lived through some devastating droughts," she said.

Water and energy consumption

While the Western Downs Digital Park plans to prioritise air-cooled technology and avoid reliance on town water infrastructure, the construction and operation will still be water intensive.

During construction, it would require about 522 kilolitres of water a day.

That would be followed by 26.9 megalitres per building for a one-time flush-and-fill process, equivalent to the average annual water use of 155 Australian households.

Under regular operation, the centre would use about 16.5kL of water each day.

It would source its water from coal seam gas water, rainwater harvesting, water delivery, recycled wastewater, and on-site surface water, according to the development application.

Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith says there are a lot of questions being raised about the data centre proposal. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Beyond water security, the centre could draw heavily on power networks, but Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith said, as the "energy capital of Queensland", the region was uniquely positioned to handle the load.

"We've built a lot of energy infrastructure in our region that has benefited our region," he said.

"So, if there needs to be more built, well, bring it on."

He said there would be a rollout of community consultation about the proposal.

"Questions around water, questions around power, around geography — they're the main questions that we're hearing out of our community," Cr Smith said.

"But certainly, those questions around water are very real and the applicant will need to deal with those."

Queensland Minister for Water Ann Leahy said the community should have a voice in this proposal, just like any other major project.

World.title: Matildas star receives rousing welcome in return after mother's death
World.content:
Matildas midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross has played her first match in more than five months after taking time away from football to spend time with her mother before her death.

Cooney-Cross was sent on in the 63rd minute as Arsenal recorded a 1-0 pre-season win over Paris FC in Borehamwood.

The 67-time international recorded her first minutes since the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup final in March, when she started in the Matildas' 1-0 loss to Japan in Sydney.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother Jessica Cooney was diagnosed with terminal Stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

"You're my biggest inspiration and the person I aspire to be," Cooney-Cross wrote on social media after her mother's death.

"Mum, my favourite part is knowing that I'm a little piece of you."

The 24-year-old returned to Arsenal's pre-season training on August 17, with the Gunners' Women's Super League campaign set to begin on Sunday evening against former Socceroo Dario Vidosic's Brighton & Hove Albion.

Cooney-Cross received a rousing ovation at Meadow Park as she was substituted on alongside compatriot Steph Catley.

Loading Instagram content

The former A-League Women's star with Melbourne Victory and Western Sydney Wanderers was involved in the build up to Canadian attacker Olivia Smith's 91st minute winner.

Arsenal's final pre-season match is against Charlton Athletic on August 26.

The Addicks signed Australian trio Emily van Egmond, who marked a national record 170 international appearances during the AFC Women's Asian Cup, alongside fellow Matildas midfielder Leah Davidson and youth international Grace Johnston, following the club's promotion from the Women's Super League 2 in May.

Meanwhile, goalkeeper Jada Whyman is returning to A-League club Sydney FC after a stint in Sweden.

Whyman is yet to play for the Matildas but has been selected in multiple national squads.

World.title: Exclusive CCTV captures the violence facing Coles workers
World.content:
For teenagers looking for their first job, an opportunity in retail is one of the most sought after gigs.

But in Victoria, retail workers are facing growing safety concerns.

In exclusive video obtained by 7.30 and captured during the past four months, CCTV shows shocking incidents of aggressive behaviour towards Coles staff and, at times, other customers.

In one instance, a customer was armed with a hammer and threatens a staff member as they were leaving the store, and in a second attack, a security guard was physically thrown into a check-out machine by a customer.

Loading...

Ruth Sumner, 70, has worked at Coles for 30 years. She said it was time the abuse against workers stopped.

"I enjoy my job. I'd just like to be able to do it without getting abused basically or worrying about whether somebody's going to come flying around the plaza with weapons," she said.

Ruth Sumner says she experiences verbal or physical abuse on a regular basis. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Last year, in a union survey of about 3,000 workers across Australia, 88 per cent of people said they had been verbally abused.

One in four said they had been physically attacked.

Ms Sumner says she feels anxious about her safety when she clocks on for a shift.

"The physical violence, irrespective of what anybody thinks, once is too much. Because once could end somebody's life," Ms Sumner said.

" I've seen aggression progress, especially since COVID. I thought people would come out kinder and they've actually, I don't understand, but their mentality is worse. "

Incidents have almost doubled in two years

Coles's chief operations and supply chain officer Matt Swindells said there had been a dramatic increase in abuse towards staff in Victoria.

"We've had rising instances of what we would call threatening situations, particularly towards our team members and particularly in Victoria over the last two years," he said.

"To give you some idea, they've grown 85 per cent in Victoria over that period.

"Whilst we call them threatening situations, what we really mean are either verbal assaults or physical altercations, or in some instances using product as a weapon, like a bottle of wine or a tin of tomatoes."

Matt Swindells says staff look after each other and protect customers before worrying about stock. (ABC News)

In comparison, Coles said threatening situations across the nation have increased by 65 per cent over the same period. South Australia is the only jurisdiction where it has declined by 16 per cent.

"We would have an internal system that can provide a text alert when incidents occurred, and my phone would go off repeatedly every day, which in itself is pretty sad," Mr Swindells said.

In Coles stores across Victoria, there are more security measures needed than in any other state, like body-worn cameras on staff and motion detection cameras in aisles.

There are also security guards who patrol the stores to keep the peace but only intervene in violence if it is safe to do so.

Coles staff in Victoria wear body-worn cameras to deter violence and most stores have motion security cameras in aisles to track customers. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"There are clear standards that we have, and we work with our security team on what we expect," Mr Swindells said.

"At every moment, the intent of the team, whether it's security or Coles, is to look after each other, protect their customers and protect themselves before we start worrying about protecting stock and putting anyone at risk."

The main challenge for retailers in Victoria is the repeat offenders.

"They will come back, and at some point there has to be an intervention that's more than us over-servicing a customer or the police making an arrest and to come back out on bail within hours," Mr Swindells said.

"We're not here to uphold the law or to be the judge, jury or government, but we clearly would ask for faster support with the workplace protection orders so we can support the police."

Victoria Police has increased the number of police officers patrolling Melbourne's CBD to combat retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Since March, Victoria Police have flooded the city with double the number of officers patrolling high-risk areas to tackle retail crime and anti-social behaviour. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Assistant Commissioner Jo Stafford told 7.30 arrests were up since March, with 260 arrests made for a range of offences from theft to assaults and public disorder.

But repeat offenders remain a challenge for police and Assistant Commissioner Stafford said the force would support measures that would target them.

"That is an issue for government, but in terms of any initiatives that help protect our workers, Victoria Police would be supportive of," she said.

Workplace protection orders in Victoria

Workplace protection orders are court-ordered bans on violent repeat offenders that restrict them from entering a retail store for a period of time.

Last month Victorian Premier Ben Carroll promised workplace protection orders would be in place across the state by July 2027.

Ben Carroll says the Workplace Protection Order scheme will be introduced to protect workers. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Victorian state secretary of the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association Michael Donovan said the laws need to come into effect much sooner.

"Ideally, we would like to see it before Christmas. It's a very busy period, and there does tend to be a spike in customer abuse and violence," he said.

" This is a crisis and the government needs to address it. "

Michael Donovan says there tends to be a spike in abuse and violence during the Christmas period. (ABC News: Rachel Clayton)

Workplace protection orders are already in effect in the ACT and South Australia.

Mr Swindells said Coles welcomed the Victorian premier's announcement.

"South Australia implemented the same policy from start to finish in six months. So again, we know it can be done. We know it works," he said.

"We welcome the change from the government in Victoria. We would just ask for it to be accelerated."

For Ms Sumner, she is nearing the end of her professional life, but she is speaking out to protect the next generation of retail workers.

"If I drop dead tomorrow, I want to know that I've done something to make life better or help make life better for the people to come after us."

World.title: England bowler Brydon Carse under investigation over nightclub video
World.content:

The ECB would not confirm whether Carse was still ⁠in the squad for the second test against Pakistan. Reuters has contacted Carse's county side Durham ‌to request comment ‌from the player.

World.title: 'Vector for antisemitism' platformed on media network that got government grant
World.content:
A Sydney-based podcast network that received federal grant funding to support social cohesion platformed a known conspiracy theorist who was deported and received a lifetime ban from Australia, an inquiry has heard.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion was told on Monday that American livestreamer Sneako, whose real name is Nicolas Kenn De Balinthazy, was deported from Australia in May after initially being granted a visa.

During his visit, Sneako was interviewed by OnePath Network, an Australian Islamic-themed podcast based in Sydney that was established in 2014.

The Anti-Defamation League, an organisation that combats antisemitism, describes Sneako as "one of the most prominent vectors for antisemitism, white supremacy, and misogyny in the manosphere" with an audience of millions.

Sneako was deported from Australia in May. (Supplied: OnePath Network)

It said his following was predominantly made up of men and boys, and that his extremist and antisemitic content had been amplified across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

The commission heard Sneako had previously been banned from YouTube, Twitch (an interactive livestreaming service) and TikTok.

$308,000 grant for podcast network

Public documents show OnePath Network's parent organisation, OPN Media Limited, received a $308,000 grant from the Department of Home Affairs under the independent multicultural media transformation and sustainability program.

The funding is designed to support social cohesion and the sustainability of independent multicultural media outlets.

Department of Home Affairs secretary Stephanie Foster was shown a screenshot of the grant issued to OnePath Network during Monday's hearing.

"Would you agree that it's an entirely inappropriate use of grant money to platform Sneako, who is a person who received a lifetime ban from entering this country because of views he's expressed publicly?," counsel representing various Jewish bodies, Nicholas Bender SC, put to Ms Foster.

Ms Foster said she was unaware of the screenshot.

"We will always, when information is provided to us, investigate its validity and it's appropriateness," she said.

In response to the funding allocation, a spokesperson for OnePath Network said in a statement that OPN Media was among 60 recipients of the grants scheme.

"OPN Media takes the work of the Royal Commission and its editorial responsibilities seriously," it said.

"Questions put to a witness during a hearing are not findings made by the Commission."

The OnePath interview with Sneako was titled, 'Who really is Sneako? The Manosphere, Islam and Israel' and was published in June.

The interview covered Sneako's rise to fame, his conversion to Islam, his time with Kanye West and his departure from the manosphere.

"Just based on that information, that raises a very substantial concern that this grantee is acting inappropriately, doesn't it?," Mr Bender SC asked. "As I said, we will always when we receive information that would suggest that the grantee was acting inappropriately investigate that," Ms Foster answered. "I'm reluctant to say anymore at this stage so I don't prejudice that process."

Sneako's visa cancelled

Sneako's visa was cancelled, and he was deported from Australia in May after media reporting about his visit.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said at the time that Sneako would never be allowed to return to Australia.

"Our government has made it very clear we will use every power available to us to protect our community from people coming to this country to spread hatred," Mr Burke told News 24, formerly Sky.

Mr Burke has said that Sneako would never be allowed back into Australia. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The inquiry heard that, three weeks before Sneako's arrival in Australia, he led a crowd in a chant invoking violence against Jews and had published material online presenting Chabad as a criminal conspiracy.

The Anti-Defamation League has documented a history of antisemitic conspiracy theories and Holocaust denial by Sneako, including his participation in an antisemitic chant in New York in April 2026.

Mr Bender SC asked Ms Foster whether Sneako should have been granted a visa in the first place.

"The decision-maker would have assessed the facts in front of them, and if the facts were identical to those that led to the cancellation of the visa, then it's not unreasonable to suggest that decision-maker would've made that decision in the first instance," she said.

"But without the facts I can't assume any of that."

Mr Bender pressed Ms Foster further.

"Do you agree that somebody who had done those things, according to the department's policies, should not be granted a visa?," Mr Bender put to Ms Foster.

Ms Foster would not be drawn on the matter.

"I'm just not able to make those assumptions," she said.

"If we have information which would preclude someone from being issued a visa based on our act then we would not have issued the visa."

Addressing antisemitism claims

During the OnePath interview, Sneako was asked about previous antisemitic comments he had made.

"According to Zionists, they'll say anyone who is critical of Israeli is antisemite," he said.

The statement from OPN Media also stressed that a disclaimer posted on its YouTube channel, and read out by the presenter prior to the interview, stated that it does not invite guests onto its platform because it agrees with everything they have "ever said or done".

"Having someone on should never be read as a blanket endorsement of all their views," it said.

"As a Muslim organisation, we reject all forms of hate speech based on race, ethnicity, or religion, including anti-Semitism and any language that mocks or trivialises the suffering of any community from past tragedies.

"At the same time, we firmly reject any attempt to conflate anti-Semitism with legitimate criticism of Israeli state policy, and we reject the weaponisation of that term to silence those speaking out against genocide."

A Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory by the UN Human Rights Council found that genocide was occurring in Gaza, but Israel has denied the allegations against it.

World.title: Specialist ship arrives to cart SpaceX rocket from Christmas Island
World.content:
Like a certain extraterrestrial, SpaceX's Starship 40 is set to depart its adopted safe harbour of Christmas Island and head for home.

But, far from Hollywood special effects, a highly specialised watercraft is helping it make the 17,000 kilometre journey back to Starbase, Texas.

The Forte docked within sight of Starship 40 on Sunday. (Supplied: Svyatoslav Shanygin)

The Forte is a heavy-lift, semi submersible cargo carrier sailing beneath a Maltese flag.

The ABC tracked the vessel using publicly available marine traffic data from Indonesia to Christmas Island's Flying Fish Cove, where it docked late on Sunday evening.

The Forte has anchored within a few hundred metres of Starship 40, where it will sink its stern to load the floating 52-metre-long rocket directly from the water.

Islander Lisa Preston described the spectacle as awe-inspiring.

"It's quite surreal going past it on a boat and having a look at this rocket," she said.

"Then we've, as humans beings, designed this other piece of machinery that can pull that out of the ocean and semi-submerge and float itself again and sail off with the rocket.

" I've been living here nearly 30 years and this will make one of the top 10 experiences. "

It is believed the Forte is making final preparations to load the wayward space shuttle. (Supplied: Lisa Preston)

Christmas Island Tourism Association chair David Watchorn headed out before sunrise to watch the Forte up close, calling it the biggest vessel he had ever seen at Christmas Island.

"It's huge, it pales [other ships] in significance," Mr Watchorn said.

Sad farewell

The rocket's presence on the remote Australian territory has caused lots of excitement in the tight-knit island community, especially among its youngest residents.

George says he had "so many books about planets", then a rocket landed in his backyard. (Supplied)

Space enthusiast George Pride, age 9, said it was something he and his schoolmates would never forget.

"I went like one metre away from it," he said.

" It's massive, it's very interesting and you can see all the heat shields. "

Ellyse, 10, called the past week a "once in a life" opportunity. (Supplied)

Ellyse Ingwersen, age 10, said she would be sad to see it go.

"It was a really cool spaceship, I think it's like a once in a life opportunity."

Retrieved for analysis

The recovery mission comes almost a week after Starship 40 was towed to Christmas Island, more than 1,500 kilometres off Western Australia's coast.

The ship, described by SpaceX as the upper-stage attached to the world's most powerful booster, made a controlled touchdown in the Indian Ocean on July 24.

SpaceX rocket splashes down off Christmas Island A SpaceX rocket is being towed off Christmas Island after landing in the Indian Ocean in an unusual spectacle for locals.

It then spent 24 days at sea as crews from the mainland battled rough weather and delays.

At the time, a spokesperson for the Australian Space Agency confirmed the federal government was assisting SpaceX with its efforts.

During an earnings call earlier this month, SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said the flight of Starship 40 demonstrated the "core capabilities" of an orbital mission and return to Starbase for "catch".

It is expected to return to Texas for analysis by engineers.

The company hopes to launch, catch, and reuse its rockets going forward, with last month's soft splashdown a key test of its performance.

David Gozzard, a senior research fellow at the University of Western Australia, said the retrieval would yield crucial data.

"It's going to help design future starships, so that when they make them reusable and are flying each one again and again … they will be a much more reliable and robust product," he said.

Loading...

Yet in a post to his X account last week, Mr Musk admitted a catch attempt on dry land was still some way off.

"If there had been a tower out to sea where we practised landing the ship, it would have been caught," he wrote.

"First reflight (sic) of the ship will be either [the] end of this year or early next.

" That will be a fork in the road of history for consciousness reaching the stars. "

World.title: Police charge man over attempted $1 million prison drone drug delivery
World.content:
A 47-year-old man has been charged over allegedly using a drone to deliver more than $1 million worth of drugs into a Townsville prison.

Corrective services officers brought down the drone in May when it was spotted over the Townsville Correctional Centre.

Officers found a package attached to the drone containing methylamphetamine and GBL, a large quantity of prescription drugs, syringes, a glass pipe, a mobile phone and a SIM card.

A 47-year-old man has been charged with five counts of supplying dangerous drugs into a correctional facility.

The drone was carrying contraband estimated to be worth $1 million. (Supplied: Queensland Corrective Services)

He has also been charged with trafficking dangerous drugs, dealing with a prohibited item in a corrective services facility, supplying a medication and drone-related offences.

The man will face the Townsville Magistrates Court on Tuesday.

Detective Acting Inspector Erica Gray of the Corrective Services Investigation Unit said the charges are a "disruption" to the supply of drugs into Queensland prisons.

"Preventing drugs from entering correctional facilities is critical to the safety of staff, prisoners and the broader community," she said.

A similar incident was reported at the prison in 2022 when officers found a drone that had crashed while carrying illicit drugs and tobacco.

A man faced charges in 2023 over the incident.

World.title: Pressing need for private boys schools to change entrenched hierarchy
World.content:
LifestyleGenderPrivate schools Editorial Pressing need for private boys schools to change entrenched hierarchy The Herald's View Editorial August 24, 2026 — 8:00pm

August 24, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The continuing failure by Sydney’s high-fee private boys schools to boost gender equality on their boards is under scrutiny amid renewed concerns about how a mix of privilege and concentrated masculinity affects schools’ culture. There have long been calls for all-male schools to show greater leadership on gender issues. These intensified in 2021, when 22-year-old former Kambala student Chanel Contos delivered a disturbing list of allegations from young women who said they had been sexually harassed or assaulted during high school or shortly after by young men who attended nearby Sydney private boys schools. Sydney woman Chanel Contos organised a petition in 2021 that prompted hundreds of women to share graphic stories about being violated by their male peers at private schools. Illustration by Michael Howard Contos’ focus was consent education, which is now a feature of the curriculum from kindergarten to year 10. Schools can work on boys’ perception of women in other ways, too, and one of them is embracing female leadership.



Yet a new Herald analysis shows men still outnumber women on the governing boards of most Sydney’s high-fee private boys schools. Only two have attained gender equity. The culture of private boys schools has been put under the spotlight again after allegations that three Scots College students, all in their early teens, raped a girl in Bondi Junction. In a separate incident, three older teens – including two boys from St Gregory’s in Campbelltown – have been accused of raping a teenage girl. Related Article Opinion

Gender equality This Christian church has banned women elders. It’s a dangerous move Kylie Maddox Pidgeon Psychologist Gender diversity at the top filters down to the culture of the school. Female board representatives can help schools develop strong approaches to sexual consent education, to preparing boys for working alongside women as adults, and to navigating the horrendous social media algorithms to which many are exposed. Yet Sydney’s high-fee private boys schools have still struggled to achieve stronger female representation.



Some are hampered by tradition, others by rules. Their boards and councils are replete with old boys and male church members. That said, some schools cast off the old church governance and have switched to corporate-style boards to take control of assets and ensure they met governance standards. Kate Harper, an experienced consultant focusing on board search and leadership succession initiatives, said independent schools could look to the Australian Institute of Company Directors principles for not-for-profit boards. These recommend an appropriate mix of people with a diverse set of skills, experience and backgrounds that align with the organisation’s purpose, vision and strategy. “It is hard to see how a council dominated by one gender can effectively guide the school’s executive on preparing their students to deal with the many challenges and risks associated with social media, sexual consent, as well as preparation to join an increasingly gender-equal workforce,” she said. Many of Sydney’s high-fee private girls schools have reflected societal change and introduced equal gender or near-equal gender splits for board appointments. Boys’ schools must do the same.



The old-fashioned ideas that shaped these boys’ schools need a reboot. For the good of their students, the sector must embrace female leadership and relegate male bastion councils to the past. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: The bayside council, a missing recording, and closed-door vote notes
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The bayside council, a missing recording, and closed-door vote notes Matt Dennien August 24, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Right to Information answers (and questions) from the Redlands, how to move 584 boxes of sensitive docs, plum jobs from City Hall to 1WS, and more. A still-unresolved question hangs over the most senior appointed job on Brisbane’s bayside: what happened in the closed-doors meeting of Redland councillors on February 3 last year? After that meeting, then acting (now actual) chief executive Louise Rusan was parachuted in from outside the selection panel shortlist for council’s second crack at filling the $500,000 gig. Minutes from a contentious closed-door meeting of Redland City Council have been released to Brisbane Times under Right to Information laws. Good luck reading them. Michael Howard Thanks to the magic of Right to Information, we have some heavily redacted answers.



Council policy dictates that all so-called workshops and briefings are recorded – with that footage and an associated transcript held by the office of the chief executive. Circus used the information-release scheme to seek access to recordings and transcripts from that fateful meeting, and the follow-up a week later where Rusan fronted councillors. We were initially knocked back entirely by legal services manager Peter Cardiff because the 46 pages and one video found were deemed “not in the public interest” and would reveal personal information about candidates. (We explicitly said we weren’t fussed if those obviously sensitive details were withheld.) But wait – only one video for two meetings? We filed an internal review of the decision.



When that landed some time later, council’s principal audit and integrity services adviser Kailesh Naidu decided to release what were said to be “minutes taken by a council officer following the interviews of the unsuccessful CEO candidates”. This is despite the guidelines also dictating formal minutes are not to be taken. And while these were bizarrely redacted to withhold even councillor’s names, our news reporting on the issue helps fill in the black bars a touch. The minutes don’t seem to negate any of the concerns raised about how the closed-door vote departs from the public recruitment process, or if there was political interference.



(The council has repeatedly rejected such allegations, insisting proper processes were followed. We don’t suggest otherwise, only that questions have been raised internally and by external figures.) But we digress. Contained in the internal review decision was another detail: no recording is said to have been taken of the February 3 meeting “because all councillors and the mayor were present”. The guidelines certainly don’t place any such qualifications around the recording of the confidential meetings – though council backgrounding since has sought to suggest the guidelines didn’t apply to that type of meeting, and the notes weren’t formal minutes. So, what does the council formally have to say for itself? A spokesperson reiterated the process was consistent with local government laws.



“The appointment of the current CEO was a decision of Council in a General Meeting held on Wednesday 19 February 2025,” the spinner said in a written response to questions. Helpful. The recruitment matter is far from the only one being wrangled by the council at present, with leaks galore and mayor Jos Mitchell’s extended leave driving heated online debate among other councillors and political figures. A pointed submission by Cardiff on behalf of the council to the ongoing parliamentary inquiry into councillor conduct said the council had seen elected figures “avoid accountability” by being absent and suggested those on extended leave be subject to a misconduct probe. Police union and corruption watchdog discipline blue (again) goes public The regular appearances of state corruption watchdog figures before their parliamentary oversight committee are almost always worth a watch.



If not for some actual new information, then for the sport of MPs trying to goad Crime and Corruption Commission chair Bruce Barbour into revealing something about any of the agency’s tightly held probes into their political opponents. Queensland police union president Shane Prior and Crime and Corruption Commission chair Bruce Barbour have had at it in the paper. Catherine Strohfeldt / Dominic Lorrimer Last week, Barbour politely palmed questions around a handful of matters – think “Operation Cranberry” into the torpedoed recruitment of Krispin Hajkowicz as chief health officer, or former parole board president Michael Byrne’s alleged misuse of travel funds – into the private session of the hearing. Another element emerging from the committee session was a days-long subsequent public tit-for-tat between Barbour and police union president Shane Prior in the paper. Prior had taken umbrage with Barbour’s apparent “misleading” remarks about ongoing legal matters involving the watchdog’s disagreement with police about how it handles disciplinary matters where officers have unrecorded convictions.



Barbour has issued a rare public statement standing by his words. More detail emerged on Monday, when a watchdog spokesperson said three of the matters it had initiated in the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal involved officers guilty of domestic violence offences who had not faced disciplinary action by police. How do you move 584 boxes of sensitive docs? Not in a ute – this time Another detail from the session also caught Circus’ eye: what was being done with 584 boxes of papers from the mothballed Connolly-Ryan inquiry into the CCC’s predecessor? Launched in 1996 by the fledgling Borbidge government, the inquiry was shut down by the Supreme Court a year later over a strong case of “ostensible bias” against its chair Peter Connolly.



Connolly had been accused of interfering with an independent probe being conducted for the then-Criminal Justice Commission into a memorandum of understanding between the police union and Coalition. So it is that the parliament – via the watchdog’s watchdog, Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner Dr Daniel Morgan – ended up lumped with the load of docs. Speaker of Queensland Parliament Pat Weir (centre) with Mitchell Kunde and Dr Daniel Morgan, in an image posted to announce the appointment of Morgan as the state’s Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner in June last year. Facebook / Pat Weir “Previously I think Mr [Mitchell] Kunde and somebody from the parliament used a ute to do it [move them],” Morgan said of the efforts from the commissioner’s longstanding principal legal officer to get the trove to a strongroom at the front of Old Parliament House. A document detailing a request to move them again (back in 2022) noted the records take up “six compactus bays and three locked storage cupboards” and would free up “many additional years’ worth of storage” if relocated.



And relocated they were due to be last Thursday morning. How? Circus feels Morgan’s description of last week’s plans is worth repeating in full. “Obviously, we were concerned to maintain the integrity of the documents. We literally cannot have them falling off the back of a truck. I made inquiries about an appropriate firm that had the necessary security experience and equipment. This firm has previously acted for the parliament and for the police. They are sensitive. They are not particularly highly secured documents, but we just need to know that the integrity is there that what has been packed is what has been delivered. We will be supervising that. I think we can ensure there will be locks on lots packed.” Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner Dr Daniel Morgan Quizzed by parliament’s crime and corruption committee chair, Ferny Grove Labor MP Mark Furner, about whether the papers were digitised, or whether the shift to the archives at Daisy Hill meant they would be, Morgan said there was “no further step intended”. Mermaid Beach LNP MP Ray Stevens then also jumped in, curious if this was out of cost concerns and seemingly confused as to why the boxes “which are not important apparently” are being retained but not digitised. In Morgan’s assessment, he didn’t see any benefit in this “apart from history”, with no one having sought access to them for some time. Kunde put this period at 15 years.



Morgan also noted the “special circumstances” around the inquiry and the subsequent custody of the related documents given to his office. Special circumstances indeed. And the kind that would probably make for some good (digitised) reading! Jobs, jobs and more jobs, from City Hall to the Tower of Power Readers looking for a change of scenery at work, look no further. This week has been a particularly lucrative one for job ads finding their way to the Circus tent. And what jobs they are. For the administratively minded, there’s an assistant ombudsman gig going over at the Queensland Ombudsman office, responsible for managing the team probing local government matters.



While reporting to the deputy ombudsman, who knows whether still-outgoing big boss Anthony Reilly’s boots will have been filled before applications close next Friday. Down at City Hall, the Olympic City council is apparently seeking to echo their Los Angeles counterparts by hiring an “international sports diplomacy project manager”. The headcount-happy Department of Premier and Cabinet are busy filling vacant roles – but what about the hiring squeeze? Matt Dennien That role will apparently be responsible for leading a related strategy, luring national Olympic and Paralympic committees, international federations and other groups to town and landing pre-Games training camps, global sporting partnerships and other related events. No pressure. The headcount-happy Department of Premier and Cabinet are also chasing an executive director of economic policy and director of communication, digital and design.



These last two raised our eyebrows given Crisafulli and Co’s keenness to put roadblocks in the way of new and even existing non-frontline roles. These ones? Vacancies for existing roles, a government flack tells us. Circus wonders what “vacancy management plan” hoops might exist at the top of the Tower of Power. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Swans staff give police statements as Heeney loses kids’ footy camp role
World.content:
Four Swans officials have given statements to police investigating an alleged sexual assault, as AFL boss Andrew Dillon banished the five suspended Sydney players from the Brownlow Medal count and confirmed the league would later conduct its own probe. The development came as one of the five players, Isaac Heeney, was dumped by a business he helped design that runs football camps for kids - 5th Quarter Camps. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney at last year’s Brownlow. He won’t be invited this year. AFL Photos “5th Quarter Camps is aware of a police investigation involving one of its shareholders, Isaac Heeney,” the business said in a statement to this masthead. “Although the investigation remains ongoing and no charges have been laid, given the circumstances and the seriousness of the matter, we can confirm Isaac Heeney will no longer have any involvement in 5th Quarter Camps.



“5th Quarter Camps takes seriously its responsibility to families, communities and commercial partners. We are committed to providing an environment founded on safety and respect, and doing everything in our power to ensure the wellbeing and experience of every child and family attending our camps remains at the centre of what we do.” The five Swans players suspended by Sydney for breaching the club’s behavioural standards are Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon. They were stood down for the remainder of the season after drinking, staying out late and inviting women back to the team hotel following their win over Essendon in round 23. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine The players’ club-imposed suspensions are separate from a Victoria Police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of last Monday morning at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. No charges have been laid and a source with knowledge of the players’ position has said they deny criminal wrongdoing.



This masthead has previously reported that Heeney is a focus of the investigation. A source with knowledge of the police investigation, speaking anonymously, confirmed Sydney’s senior coach Dean Cox, football boss Leon Cameron, head of player wellbeing and development Brett Kirk and head of media and communications Tom Chadwick had given accounts to police. Callum Mills of the Swans embraces head coach Dean Cox after their game on Sunday. Getty Images The Swans declined to comment, citing the investigation. The four Sydney staff were not in the hotel room at Pullman East Melbourne when a woman alleges she was sexually assaulted.



Cameron, Kirk and Chadwick accompanied the five Swans players, who have since been handed club-imposed bans for the remainder of the season, in two cars as they drove home to Sydney from Melbourne last Monday afternoon. No Swans officials are accused of inappropriate behaviour and the club has previously said it had no issue with the conduct of Cox, who returned to the hotel not long after midnight. Andrew Dillon faces the media. AFL Photos via Getty Images At least two men aside from the five suspended players were in the hotel room on the night of the alleged sexual assault. This masthead revealed on Sunday that at least one fresh allegation of sexual assault and multiple claims of sexual conduct without consent had been made by the three women at the centre of the investigation.



It is not known which men the allegations are about, and to date police have only referenced “a report of a sexual assault”. This masthead is not suggesting any of the men in the room engaged in conduct of a sexual nature without consent, only that it has been alleged. Dillon said the AFL would not open its own investigation until the police probe was completed. “Those matters at the moment are under police investigation, so the AFL won’t be conducting any of its own inquiries until after the police investigation is finished,” he said. Loading “We don’t know where that will go and, at that stage, when that’s completed, the AFL will [undertake] some inquiries. I think what is clear is the Swans are taking action with the support of the AFL based on the information that is at hand now, and there’s been accountability for those players that were involved last week.”



The five players are still eligible to win the award for the AFL’s best and fairest player. “The invitations to the Brownlow will be going out this week. Those players won’t be invited,” Dillon said. “They are still eligible for the Brownlow but they’re under a club suspension, which goes until the end of the season.” Dillon said it was a matter for the Swans whether the players should still be allowed to win the club best and fairest. Dillon did not rule out the players being deregistered. Related Article Sydney Swans ‘Don’t abandon the club’: Swans fans ready to show support after week of turmoil



“Again, I’m not going to go into hypotheticals. We’ve got a police investigation that is underway. Once that’s completed, the AFL will make its own,” he said. Dillon said he was unaware if there was a recording of the alleged incident. “Look, I am not aware of that but, again, if there is a tape that’s relevant to the police investigation, it should be forwarded on to the police.” He denied the league had a wider cultural problem. “I think the actions of a few don’t take away from the thousands of people involved in football at all different levels who do great things all the time,” he said. “But what we do know is that we can do things better, and we’ll continue to do that, and we’ll continue to learn a bit better.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: CFMEU headquarters raided in secret-commissions probe
World.content:
Two senior CFMEU officials temporarily detained by Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk after detectives swooped on the union’s Victorian headquarters on Monday have dismissed allegations of union corruption or kickbacks involving the former boss of a bikie gang. The arrest and release of five serving CFMEU officials by Taskforce Hawk on Monday, with two facing minor charges, marks the most dramatic intervention yet by the elite police unit launched to tackle suspected crime and corruption in Victoria’s construction sector and which is now also gathering information for the upcoming royal commission. A Taskforce Hawk officer enters the CFMEU headquarters in Elizabeth Street in the CBD on Monday. Justin McManus The police action is a blow for the Albanese government-backed CFMEU administration two years into its attempt to reform the union, but it is not surprising given newly appointed administrator Michael Crosby’s recent concession that the scandal-tainted union had cleaned up in every jurisdiction except Victoria. In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Crosby confirmed that Hawk had “executed search warrants at six addresses, including CFMEU Victoria’s office, as part of an investigation into alleged secret commissions in the construction industry”.



“Criminals and bad actors in construction remain a major threat to the workers, which is why we need greater regulation and scrutiny across the sector,” Crosby said, warning that “anyone associated with criminal elements will have absolutely no place in this union’s future”. Police revealed homes in Chirnside Park, Westbury, Gisborne, Powelltown and Somerville were also searched on Monday. Investigators seized four CFMEU vehicles, 10 mobile phones, several laptops, documents, iPads, USBs, a .22 rifle and a prescription drug. The five men arrested were a 36-year-old from Chirnside Park, a 46-year-old from Westbury (near Moe), a 27-year-old from Gisborne, a 56-year-old from Powelltown and a 37-year-old from Somerville. A Chirnside Park man was charged with possessing a schedule 4 drug and bailed to appear at Ringwood Magistrates’ Court on November 10. A man from Westbury was charged with failing to store a long-arm firearm and ammunition as required. He was bailed to appear at Latrobe Valley Magistrates’ Court on January 11.



Three other men were released pending further inquiries. “The investigation relates to allegations of drug trafficking as well as secret commissions,” a police statement said. Crosby revealed that he had ordered an internal investigation into the allegations, while also cautioning against rushing to judgment in respect of any of the officials arrested on Monday. “Taskforce Hawk has confirmed that to date no charges have been laid against any CFMEU official as part of this investigation. There is a presumption of innocence and the branch will continue to offer support whilst the investigation is ongoing,” he said. Also concerning for Crosby is the police decision to arrest one of his administration’s key reformers, Jason “Spike” Deans, a CFMEU official who multiple union and industry sources told The Age is respected as honest and hardworking.



Deans, the most senior of the union figures detained and released by Hawk, has stridently denied that the CFMEU has ever assisted the industrial relations business run by former Mongols bikie chief Tyrone “Little Ty” Bell. Deans, who was promoted to a key Victorian union leadership post just weeks ago by the CFMEU administration, told The Age he wanted to “make it very clear” that he and his fellow union official Matt Montebello had engaged in no impropriety in connection to Bell’s work as a union mediator. Montebello was also arrested and released without charge on Monday. “There has never been any untoward or any illegal activity from myself or Matt with … that little fella [Bell],” Deans said when contacted about the police inquiry when it was revealed by The Age last week.



“I’ve taken on this role because I care about good union members and their families. If anyone thinks that I’m here for the position or status they are very wrong. Matt Montebello was arrested as part of the raid on CFMEU headquarters on Monday. “I’m going to do what I need to do to get this union back into a functional position and I will make decisions that some people are not going to like. I will be ruthless to protect this union if I need to.” There is no suggestion by this masthead that Deans, Montebello or any of the other three officials arrested and released are engaged in any unlawful behaviour, only that police suspect they hold information relevant to their ongoing inquiry. When The Age contacted Montebello last week to ask him why he was a person of interest in Taskforce Hawk’s ongoing investigation into Bell and allegations the ex-bikie chief tried to influence the CFMEU, he also denied having any improper dealings with Bell.



“I’ve never taken a cent off him, mate,” Montebello said. Asked if he had ever discussed with Bell the CFMEU’s disruption of a Melbourne building project last September – the industrial dispute at the centre of the Hawk probe into Bell– Montebello denied any knowledge of the union action. “Don’t know what you’re talking about, mate,” he said, before hanging up. Last Thursday, The Age revealed that Bell, a former national vice-president of the Mongols outlaw bikie gang, was being probed by police over allegations he offered inducements to officials still serving in the CFMEU in return for their support of his business, Dynamis HSR. The Age also revealed that the Taskforce Hawk operation that led to Monday’s arrests and a raid of the CFMEU’s Swanston Street headquarters was examining whether CFMEU organisers leaked Bell information or co-ordinated union activity with him in order to advance the interests of Bell’s industrial relations consultancy.



Bell’s connections to the CFMEU were cultivated via two channels: his relatively brief stint as a CFMEU delegate working for building company Markscon, and his long-standing social and schooling ties to serving and ex-CFMEU organisers and delegates, including Montebello and his brother Kane Montebello, a high-ranking Hells Angels member who also served as a union delegate. Three CFMEU sources said the administration had sought and received reassurance from Matt Montebello that he had cut ties or was carefully managing his familial relationships with people linked to outlaw motorcycle gangs. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Ex-bikie boss under investigation over alleged inducements to CFMEU officials In addition to his brother, Montebello’s cousin has also held a role with the Hells Angels and was briefly recruited into the union. An undated photo circulating in the construction industry, but which appears to be several years old, shows Montebello wearing a Hells Angels support singlet. There is no suggestion he has ever held a role in the club or been involved in bikie activity.



Montebello’s brother, cousin and Bell were among the highest-profile serving and ex-bikie gang members recruited into the CFMEU between 2021 and 2024, only to be forced out in July 2024 when this masthead’s Building Bad series first broke. Last week, Bell described the police allegations as “just ridiculous” and defended Matt Montebello. “I’ve been friends with him since primary school, and his brother and I feel very sorry for the guy, because he loves his job,” Bell said. “I hope you don’t write anything bad about that guy, because he’s a very good dad, a very good person,” he said. CFMEU assistant administrator Matt McGowan said: “CFMEU has been made aware of a police operation this morning as part of Taskforce Hawk. As this is a live police matter, CFMEU cannot comment further at this time.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Deaths of 10 young people put eastern suburbs mental health services on alert
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMental health Deaths of 10 young people put eastern suburbs mental health services on alert Grant McArthur August 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two youth suicide clusters in Melbourne’s east involving the deaths of 10 people, the youngest aged 13, have raised new concerns about Victoria’s troubled mental health system. Youth mental health services in the east were put on alert in response to rising teenage tragedies over nine months, but Victoria’s health watchdogs have failed to launch a review to determine if there are any systemic issues or access issues at the heart of the cases. Concerns about Victoria’s youth mental health services have increased following two suicide clusters in Melbourne’s east. Aresna Villanueva A total of 10 young people, including at least six children under 16, died in September-October last year and May this year. The mass tragedies are the latest revelations regarding Victoria’s youth mental health system to emerge during an investigation by The Age, and follow the closure of a children’s mental health service at a major Melbourne hospital this month pending a bullying investigation into its staff. In parliament on Friday, opposition health spokesperson Georgie Crozier named the service as Austin Health’s child inpatient unit.



Separately, the boss of Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service resigned this month, a day after it was revealed she was leading the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service as a fly-in, fly-out CEO, as reports mount of violence, drug use and patient deaths in its first year of operation. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force The state coroner is awaiting briefs of evidence before deciding whether to group the teen death cases together for investigation, or examine each individually. Victoria’s Department of Health confirmed its youth mental health services provided post-suicide support to the area after being alerted to the rising deaths. But because it does not have records of the children receiving help at public hospitals before they died, neither the Chief Psychiatrist, Safer Care Victoria nor the Suicide Prevention and Response Office are reviewing the suitability or capacity of services in the area. A mental health specialist working in Melbourne’s east, who is not authorised to speak publicly, said most children and families seeking help via emergency department and phone triage lines did not receive admission to specialised public child and youth mental health services, and they feared lives were being lost as a result.



“There are definitely systemic issues,” the senior clinician said. “How terrible that we weren’t helping them, and they were in this trouble. Obviously, something isn’t working. “In triage and ED, they reject the majority of kids that present. They reject them because they haven’t got the capacity to see them. They are the kids we should be seeing, but a lot of them get turned away because there’s no capacity for them to be seen.” Major public hospital networks Eastern Health and Austin Health both operate child and youth mental health services in the city’s east, where the clusters occurred. A Coroners Court spokesperson confirmed the Eastern Melbourne Primary Health Network advised it on October 31, 2025, of a potential cluster of deaths, involving people aged 13 to 22, in its service catchment area. “The investigations into these deaths are in the early stages and once the coronial briefs are received the coroner will review the evidence to determine the next steps of the investigations and if the circumstances of the cases make it appropriate to conduct a cluster investigation,” the spokesperson said.



The coroner was later notified of the suspected suicides of a further four young people, aged 13 to 18, in Melbourne’s east in May this year. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence “Coroners are investigating these cases individually and are awaiting coronial briefs of evidence for the investigations.” A Department of Health spokesperson said the Coroners Court alerted it to suspected suicides in September 2025 and again in May 2026, prompting the Chief Psychiatrist to engage with Eastern Health to undertake post-suicide support activities with local services, including headspace and Victoria Police. “Every suicide is one too many, and the loss of life to suicide has long-lasting and far-reaching impacts on loved ones and community members,” the spokesperson said.



“While these young people were not receiving care through a public mental health service at the time of their death, the Department of Health, the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist and local services have worked together to support the local communities.” Youth mental health pioneer Professor Pat McGorry said the scale of the deaths and extreme young age of those involved was unusual and demanded investigation, particularly as they have coincided with a 50 per cent rise in the prevalence of mental ill health in young people in the same age group. “I’m extremely concerned at the lack of transparency about the situation and the apparent lack of co-ordinated action to respond,” McGorry said. “In the eastern region, as elsewhere across Victoria, the public mental health system has not been reformed or properly resourced to respond to this public health crisis, and it has been a low priority since the [mental health] royal commission, despite the level of unmet need. “The result is that young people at great risk who present to emergency departments or triage lines are typically rejected in very large numbers. If this were occurring with any other potentially life-threatening condition, it would be regarded as a scandal.”



Phillipa Thomas, chief executive of peak body Mental Health Victoria, said suicide clusters were complex and unusual occurrences and needed to be examined to determine if the events relate to each other and whether they could have been prevented. “At this stage it is unclear what, when, and if any contact was in place for each of these young people with mental health services prior to their deaths. Where it was, the coroner will consider the role of safety and quality for each individual. But its August – that’s nearly a full year that’s gone by,” Thomas said. “I’m troubled by the possibility that these young people may have sought help and not received it. I’m equally troubled by the possibility that they didn’t seek help at all.” While she could not comment directly on the cases, Royal Australian & New Zealand College of Psychiatrists’ Victorian spokesperson Dr Nardine Elzahaby said the state’s youth mental health system was plagued by gaps.



She said acute public health services had become “adult models retrofitted for young people” which did not meet their needs, while services such as headspace did not cater for those with more severe illness who did not yet need, or could not get into, a specialist mental health service. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress “There is a gap. There is a missing middle of patients who require care that are not too unwell to meet youth area mental health criteria, but they are too unwell to be looked after by headspace,” Elzahaby said. “Do young people have to rely on emergency departments to get child and youth suicide programs? ED is hardly ever the right place for young people, and it really impacts them.” An Eastern Health spokesperson said the families, friends and communities affected by the recent suicides were in their thoughts, and the service has an active role in co-ordinating post-suicide responses with local services, schools and other agencies to assist vulnerable young people who may be at increased risk.



“In addition to providing specialist inpatient and community-based mental health services, Eastern Health works closely with local primary care providers, schools, community organisations and other partners to support the mental health and wellbeing of young people across the region,” the spokesperson said. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy.
