World.title: The Sydney private school boards that have the gender mix right – and all the ones that don’t
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation The Sydney private school boards that have the gender mix right – and all the ones that don’t Christopher Harris August 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Only two of Sydney’s high-fee private boys’ schools have attained gender equity on their governing boards, prompting concerns that councils dominated by men are ill-equipped to grapple with issues of sexual consent, misogynistic social media content and preparing students for the modern workforce. A Herald analysis of the leadership of 42 high-fee schools shows men outnumber women on the boards of most Sydney private boys’ schools, according to 2025 figures published by the government’s Workplace Gender Equality Agency. The culture of private boys’ schools has been in the spotlight amid allegations that three students from Scots College allegedly raped a girl in a Bondi Junction alleyway last month. In a separate incident, three teens – including two boys from St Gregory’s in Campbelltown – have also been accused of raping a teenage girl this month. The school is co-ed in primary and single-sex for high school.



At Scots College, 88 per cent of the board are men, according to the 2025 figures. Its website lists one woman on its board, but it has recently appointed a second woman not publicly listed. The Gender Equality Agency data used in this analysis pertains to the 2024-25 financial year and is reported as percentages. It is the second year the data has been published. At Scots, 88 per cent of the board are men, according to the Gender Equality Agency data in 2024-25. Steven Woodburn When the Herald last reported on the issue of school boards five years ago, King’s had only one woman on its 18-member board. It now has 15 council members, three of whom are women. Shore had four women five years ago on its 18-member board, and now it has three. Under the school’s governing act, its council must be half clergy and half laymen.



Kate Harper, an experienced consultant focusing on board search and leadership succession initiatives, said many independent schools required their council to often include representatives from relevant stakeholder groups such as alumni and parent associations, and religious bodies. Related Article Opinion

Private schools Stop blaming the school for sexual assaults: the buck stops closer to home Louise Clegg Former lawyer “As not-for-profit entities, independent schools can look to the Australian Institute of Company Directors principles for not-for-profit boards which recommend an appropriate mix of people with a diverse set of skills, experience, and backgrounds that align with the organisation’s purpose, vision and strategy,” she said. “Many Sydney independent schools have seen their enrolments diversify substantially over recent decades, with some becoming co-educational schools, and more international families enrolling. “Current Council composition may therefore no longer be sufficient and should evolve to reflect this diversity.”



Harper said gender diversity at the top filters down to the culture of the school and the student experience. “It is hard to see how a council dominated by one gender can effectively guide the school’s executive on preparing their students to deal with the many challenges and risks associated with social media, sexual consent, as well as preparation to join an increasingly gender-equal workforce.” Sydney Grammar’s board of trustees is 70 per cent men, according to the gender equality agency data. Its composition is governed by an act of parliament, stipulating six official trustees be drawn from the state attorney-general, speakers of the Legislative Assembly and Council, and senior maths and classics professors from Sydney University. It has five elected trustees, including two women now. In practice, only two of those listed office holders are active trustees: NSW Legislative Council President Ben Franklin, and University of Sydney associate professor of maths and statistics Milena Radnovic.



At Trinity Grammar, about 80 per cent of board positions were occupied by men. The school’s constituting document stipulates that three seats are reserved for former students (who are boys), and six seats are reserved for Sydney Anglican clergymen, and another for the archbishop. “Therefore, there are only eight seats available to be filled by women; at present, three of these eight seats are taken by women,” a school spokesperson said. Saint Ignatius’ College Riverview has an equal gender split on its governing council. Dion Georgopoulos The spokeswoman said the “day-to-day leadership of the school tells a very different story”. “On campus, women occupy a significant number of senior, student-facing, leadership roles. From heading academic curriculum, middle school pastoral care, to leading our preparatory school, our boys see, learn from, and respect female authority figures every day.”



St Aloysius and Riverview were the only two boys’ schools with an equal gender split. Knox Grammar has a near-equal gender split. Headmaster Scott James said the school consciously sought to achieve a broad mix of skills, experience and perspectives, including gender balance. “We believe this strengthens governance and better supports the school’s long-term interests,” he said. By comparison, six girls’ schools with an equal gender split: MLC, St Catherine’s, Meriden, SCEGGS, Loreto Kirribilli and Stella Maris College. Several others, including Tara and Santa Sabina, have boards dominated by men. Ravenswood’s council is 60 per cent men.



Ravenswood principal Sue Floro said membership may fluctuate due to tenure and appointment timing. “We do aspire to achieve gender equity on our school council, and this remains our focus as members reach the end of their nine-year maximum tenure on the council, and we seek to recruit council members with complementary skill sets,” she said. Stephen Codrington, an experienced former school principal and consultant to school boards in Australia and overseas, said a high-functioning board required a diversity of perspectives. “I think gender is part of that, but I also think age and culture are an important part of that as well. I think if you only look at gender, I think you’re oversimplifying,” he said. He noted some schools had worked to include younger adults who were more in touch with the reality of young people they were teaching, but said it was vital that leaders were intentional about the school culture they were creating.



“You don’t just allow it to develop and evolve … A good school will try to direct the culture of the school, and that actually is a joint operation of both the head and the board … and frankly … every other teacher and adult in the school – they’re all part of setting the culture.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Shein was fast fashion’s next big thing. Now it’s fighting for a second act
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRetail Shein was fast fashion’s next big thing. Now it’s fighting for a second act Sui-Lee Wee August 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Shein was once one of the most talked-about companies in retail. It could spot what Generation Z wanted and, within days, turn those trends into $US10 ($13.95) mesh dresses and $US5 crop tops. Its clothes were so cheap and its churn of new styles was so relentless that #Sheinhaul became a phenomenon on TikTok. Shein overtook bigger rivals such as Zara and H&M, started planning an initial public offering and, at one point, was valued at nearly $US100 billion. Shein is gearing up to list, but at a fraction of its peak valuation. AFP Now the buzz has faded. After years of delay, Shein is close to going public — this time at a fraction of its peak valuation. It is searching for new ways to grow after the United States and Europe dismantled tariff exemptions on cheap goods that had helped underpin its low-cost model. Sales have fallen sharply in the United States, its largest market. And the company has offered investors few specifics about where meaningful new growth will come from.



Related Article Exclusive

Fast fashion Made by Shein: The ultra-fast fashion giant is pitching itself to Aussie clothing labels “For a company as hyped as it was for such a long time, the music has seemingly run out,” said Juozas Kaziukenas, an independent e-commerce analyst. No Chinese fashion brand has been as successful as Shein at going global. And yet the company remains unusually reclusive. Its founder and CEO, Sky Xu Yangtian, is so private that until he appeared publicly in February, most photographs circulating online purporting to show him were false. Even a senior overseas Shein executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak with the media, said he had never met or interacted with Xu. Shein declined requests for an interview. The timing and pricing details of its market debut have not been announced, but the company filed a prospectus with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange last month.



Shein has taken pains to distance itself from its Chinese origins. In 2019, it established its headquarters in Singapore and deregistered its original Chinese corporate entity a few years later. The aim was, in part, to navigate Chinese rules governing companies seeking offshore listings and clear a path toward an IPO in New York. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump tightens screws on Chinese giants by shutting 87-year-old loophole Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The strategy failed. In the United States, Shein encountered intense, bipartisan scrutiny from lawmakers over its supply chain and labour practices. After abandoning its New York listing effort in 2024, it turned to London, where it faced similar resistance from non-government organisations and other protesters. That left Hong Kong as the last major viable venue. But after years of delay, analysts say Shein may have missed its moment. The turn toward Hong Kong has also put Shein in the awkward position of having to re-embrace the Chinese identity it once tried to play down. In China, the company has faced criticism for “blooming in China but bearing fruit abroad” — a phrase suggesting that Shein built its success in the country while redirecting profits overseas.



Then, in February, the famously elusive Xu suddenly appeared before officials in Guangdong province. “Guangdong is Shein’s root,” he declared, announcing that Shein would invest about $US1.4 billion over the next three years to build a supply chain hub there. Shein packages in a factory in the garment district in Guangzhou, China. NYT Chinese media initially covered the speech. Then some articles began disappearing from the internet. Lu Minghe, a veteran journalist, posted a notice showing that Shein had demanded that his public WeChat account remove an article about Xu’s appearance, citing “infringement”. Even as Shein recalibrates its relationship with China, a more fundamental problem hangs over any potential listing.



Jianggan Li, founder of Momentum Works, a consultancy that has followed Shein closely, said prospective investors had told him that they sensed little enthusiasm from its founders. Related Article Fashion retail Kmart, Shein sued by Aussie fashion label Sabo Skirt for allegedly ripping off designs “There hasn’t been any effort to drum up interest,” Li said. “I don’t feel there’s a strong desire for the management to make the company public, aside from the fact that the investors want to exit.” Investors are asking how Shein can keep growing. President Donald Trump’s decision last year to end a policy that had allowed billions of dollars of low-cost imports to enter the United States duty-free dealt a major blow in its single biggest market. In May 2025, Shein began raising prices in the United States. In the first quarter of 2026, US net revenue fell 14.3 per cent to $US2 billion, the company said.



Europe could pose an even greater challenge. Last month, European authorities announced a €3 ($4.89) flat fee on e-commerce parcels that had previously entered duty-free. Europe accounts for more than a third of Shein’s revenue. In its prospectus, Shein warned that although it was too early to assess the impact of the situation in Europe fully, it “could be generally in line with or exceed the impact observed in the US. President Donald Trump last year ended an exemption that allowed duty-free imports for certain goods. AP Shein is now trying to convince investors that its future goes beyond ultra-cheap clothes by selling access to the system it built to design, produce, market and deliver products quickly. So far, there is little evidence that the supply chain strategy is paying off. Since offering the service as a pilot in 2023, Shein has signed up only about 20 brands. The program generated less than 1 per cent of its total net revenue in 2025, according to the company. Shen Meng, a director at Chanson & Co., an investment banking firm in Beijing, said Shein succeeded in part because it was willing to squeeze its own costs and margins — trade-offs that other brands using its platform may be unwilling to accept.



“It’s hard to see any outstanding advantages in Shein’s transition,” Shen said. Shein is also branching out into furniture, cosmetics, pet products and electronics. Non-apparel goods accounted for more than a third of its revenue in the first quarter. Other analysts are similarly sceptical that Shein has found a second act. “It’s not clear, other than really cheap, ultrafast fashion, what they’re going to be able to generate,” said Sucharita Kodali, an e-commerce expert at Forrester, a research agency. Shein’s first act was remarkable.



It was founded in 2012 by Xu and three colleagues at a marketing firm that helped Chinese exporters sell products online. In 2015, it shortened its name from Sheinside to Shein. Related Article Copyright Dazy v Dazie: The Iconic sues Shein for ripping off exclusive label During the COVID-19 pandemic, as online shopping exploded, Shein’s popularity surged. The company saturated the internet with s aimed at young consumers, enticing them with extremely low prices and constantly changing designs. By 2022, Shein became the world’s biggest online fashion retailer. That year, it was valued at $US98.2 billion and backed by a roster of big-name venture capital investors. The secret was a system built to compress the traditional fashion cycle. Shein used algorithms to track emerging trends, then placed initial orders of a few hundred units to test demand. The model allowed it to introduce approximately 4,700 new apparel styles a day. Zara, by comparison, produces 20,000 a year, according to analysts.



Shein paired that technology with an industrial ecosystem concentrated in Guangdong, where spinners, weavers, seamstresses and small factories could rapidly manufacture orders as small as 100 pieces. But Shein has struggled to duplicate its Chinese supply chain model in countries such as Turkey and Vietnam, according to Li of Momentum Works. At the same time, competitors like Temu arrived with even broader product assortments and even lower prices. Kaziukenas said he had scoured Shein’s prospectus to find the answer to a question that he’d had for years: “What is the future of Shein?” He added: “I don’t think we got that answer.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: Angus Taylor organised taxpayer grants for Brethren charity backing Pollie Pedal
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalExtremism Angus Taylor organised taxpayer grants for Brethren charity backing Pollie Pedal Michael Bachelard and James Massola August 24, 2026 — 7:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor arranged $33,000 in federal government grants for the religious charity providing food for his Pollie Pedal bike ride, with the money coming from the heavily criticised Morrison-era “stronger communities” program. Taylor has defended the Rapid Relief Team charity, which is part of the controversial Plymouth Brethren Christian Church. The church ran an undisclosed multimillion-dollar pro-Peter Dutton campaign at the last election, which included paying neo-Nazis and other far-right figures to disrupt campaign events. Pollie Pedal 2026 riders. The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church’s charity, the Rapid Relief Team, is a sponsor of the ride, which this year is raising funds for SAS veterans charity Wandering Warriors and their families. Instagram The Brethren charity is a major sponsor of the charity bike ride and is supplying breakfast each morning. Taylor, who is on the ride with Liberal Party federal president Tony Abbott, brushed aside questions on Monday about the church, instead praising the charity’s work.



“We’re being supported by the Rapid Relief Team, and they are an extraordinary group of people,” Taylor said. “Rapid Relief supports state emergency services, state rural fire service organisations across this country, and they do an extraordinary job. And I’m very proud to have been served by them, and I saw them starting up in my own electorate after the Yass fires back in 2013. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations Exclusive Brethren secretly paid far-right activists to perform stunts disrupting the federal election “They have been there every time when there has been a flood, when there has been a fire. We saw Lily Hooper, the very tragic death of a girl in my electorate in the Nattai National Park [south-west of Sydney] just last week, they were out there. “RRT was out there, supporting our emergency service organisations. That is an extraordinary organisation, and I am very sure many Labor members have been supported by that same organisation because of the great work they [the RRT] do.” Records kept by the federal government show the Rapid Relief Team won dozens of government grants across the country, worth $680,000 between 2020 and 2023 under a program in which the local MP selected the recipients and invited them to apply.



In Taylor’s seat of Hume, the Brethren charity won its first grant, for $22,000 – the maximum available – to buy a coolroom trailer in 2021 to “facilitate the safe distribution of food to the community”. Two years later, the charity in Hume received another $11,000 for a coffee trailer to “support emergency services and the community”. Related Article Exclusive

Australia votes ‘Private intel’: Inside the far-right group disrupting the election In its latest financial statement, the Rapid Relief Team reported a surplus of $263,105, and a retained surplus of $4.6 million. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese demanded Taylor explain Liberal links to the far-right activists who campaigned against and heckled Labor and Greens candidates during the 2025 election.



Speaking in Perth, Albanese said he had been calling for some time for people to turn down the temperature in politics, and recounted how those activists had disrupted press conferences, appeared at his hotel unannounced, acted aggressively at polling booths and appeared at events in the seats of Dickson in Brisbane and Bennelong in Sydney. “The Liberal Party needs to explain why it is that these people were connected with the campaign in favour of Liberal candidates, wearing Liberal Party T-shirts, being paid to disrupt our democratic traditions. Democracy is a precious thing and election campaigns are important,” he said. “It’s time the Liberal Party fronted up and answered how all this occurred, because it didn’t just appear. People don’t know where candidates are, just turning up, and the involvement in these outside forces, many of whom have been involved in activity that is anathema to most Australians.” There is no suggestion that Taylor knew of or supported the Brethren payments to far-right figures. But after this masthead revealed these details of the Brethren campaign, Byron Fay, executive director of political funding group Climate 200, referred the church to the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission for investigation. During a parliamentary hearing on Friday into electoral matters, Liberal MPs and Nationals leader Matt Canavan sympathised with the Brethren’s view that the questions they were being asked about the group’s role in the election were examples of religious discrimination.

World.title: Nothing improves when city growth is unfettered
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Nothing improves when city growth is unfettered August 24, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. MEGACITY The same old bureaucratic words are trotted out in an attempt to reassure us about the plan to make Melbourne a megacity: environmental sustainability, equity, access and so on (“Labor pledges to halt Melbourne’s urban sprawl, but planners ask if we’re heading to a megacity mess”, 24/8).

Yet, we can’t even manage a small area such as Footscray to ensure safety for all (“The pain ripping my home apart”, 24/8). Let’s face it, modern life is very complex, profit-based

vested interests are entrenched and immovable, public resources can’t meet needs, and nothing is going to improve through unfettered growth.

Fiona White, Alfredton Jess Wilson’s report card on environment

As a local who cares about our environment, as most Victorians do, I was pleased to see state Opposition Leader Jess Wilson commit to turning the privately owned Box Hill Brickworks site into a public park and promise $20 million to ensure that outcome.

Well done, Jess Wilson and the Liberals, for supporting a campaign for public green space which has significant

community support.

Such opportunities to add to green space are rare and often opposed by developers. People need green space to thrive, and

our unique insects, birds and animals species also need space in urban environments.

With our environment facing increasing challenges from invasive species, land clearing and climate change, it would be beneficial for our community if Wilson also acknowledged the biodiversity crisis we are facing and backed a comprehensive climate policy to help preserve our unique natural history for the future. Everything is connected, and our economy ultimately relies on our environment.

We know those unique species and ecological systems will struggle to adapt to the speed of climate change. More and more species are already being added to the threatened species list.

Threats like the South Australian algal bloom which devastated marine ecosystems are becoming more likely.

David Hudspeth, Burwood



State opposition on a losing gamble

Jess Wilson’s Coalition wants to scrap clean energy transmission projects and rely on expensive, polluting gas instead (“Bill fears in power line pledge″⁣, 23/8). Where will the Victorian Coalition source that gas, how will they build the infrastructure needed to deliver it to households, and how will they cover the cost? We have just two years before the ageing Yallourn coal-fired power station closes.

Abandoning transmission projects like VNI West puts Victoria’s energy security at risk. In 2026, doubling down on gas is a gamble our state doesn’t need.

Karen Lamb, North Geelong No to more dirty, expensive gas

It’s 2026 and we’re still talking about dirty, expensive gas as if it were some kind of cure-all (“Domestic gas policy sparks industrial revival hopes”, 24/8).

A gas-led industrial revival? A Victorian Coalition plan to replace coal with gas (“Bill fears in power line pledge”, 23/8)? No, thank you.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Streets of our town

I’ve enjoyed reading the series of personal stories of the places people live in our wonderful city for many years. It reminds me of the special, lovely and colourful nature of our life here in Melbourne.

However, I was particularly struck and appreciative of the honest and moving story of my neighbouring suburb of Footscray by Ceridwen Spark (″⁣My suburb gentrified decades ago. Now its residents are afraid to walk the streets″⁣, 23/8).

Thank you, Ceridwen, for sharing the joys and struggles your community faces every day. I hope the government and others may invest and do whatever is necessary to ensure that your place thrives and grows into the future. Tim Hoffmann, Brunswick THE FORUM Moving right ahead

Imagine 10 years ago – even five – that the federal president and leader of one of Australia’s two major political parties had accepted hospitality at a public event from an organisation whose elders ″⁣paid neo-Nazi affiliates and far-right figures to bully and intimidate politicians″⁣ (24/8).

Ask yourself what would have happened then if this president and leader had uttered words to the effect of ″⁣nothing to see here″⁣; and if their own members had described any inquiry into these neo-Nazi supporters as ″⁣persecution″⁣, ″⁣madness″⁣ and a “hyperpartisan witch hunt”.

Ask yourself how far to the right Australian political discourse has moved in the past few years. Then ask yourself what has changed, and what darkness lies ahead.

Nick Eckstein, Kangaroo Ground



Charity status review

News of the ongoing political connections of the Plymouth (Exclusive) Brethren fosters thoughts that the community is actually paying for their practices via the Australian Charities Non-for-Profit Commission whereby they buy their lifestyle tax-free.

There needs to be a clean out of the Australian Charities Non-for-Profit Commission register which has more than 60,000 listed charities. This will be a monumental challenge.

But rather than penny-pinching from pensioners, reach out to

the big money.

Margaret Raffle, Keilor East Politicians not listening

Prime Minister Albanese had every reason to respond to the majority who want strong laws to control gambling advertising, but for his own reasons, he hedged. After much wrangling, laws were passed in parliament that were a long way short of what was needed. The PM’s comment was that ″⁣we listened, and I think we got the right balance”.

To me, that response is far from accurate. Maybe he has silenced dissent, but the public’s reaction will probably cost Labor the next election.

David Lamb, Kew East Losing faith in leaders

Is it any wonder the public is losing faith in our politicians?

From Anthony Albanese receiving questionable advice about appearing on the appalling Bush Talk podcast, to the government failing to act on gambling advertising despite widespread public support for reform, and now Angus Taylor and Tony Abbott accepting hospitality from the Exclusive Brethren during a bicycle ride, questions about political judgment and accountability continue to arise.

The allegations surrounding links between some Brethren figures and far-right or neo-Nazi affiliates make the decision to accept such hospitality all the more concerning.

Australians deserve better political leadership, greater accountability and a stronger commitment to the public interest. But one thing is certain: the answer cannot be One Nation.

Nathan Feld, Glen Iris Start your own church

It was perhaps a suitable metaphor when Angus Taylor fell off his bike at the Pollie Pedal bike ride under the sponsorship of the Plymouth Brethren (24/8).

The brethren’s selective principle of reportedly providing financial support on the one hand to nobble Labor, while eschewing members from being involved in the political process, is an interesting contradistinction.

I think I might start my own church.

Peter Russo, West Brunswick Winner takes all era

The Plymouth Brethren may not vote, but are ready to hand out material at election time spruiking for the Liberals.

Politics is becoming so underhanded and corrupted with a win-at-all-costs approach. No wonder a lot of us have lost confidence in politics.

It would be good to see an election without those who provide support for parties and waiting for favours in return.

Nola Cormick, Albert Park



Not happy, Jeff

Re your correspondents on “former premiers” (Letters, 24/8): Economic rationalism brought about the destruction of so much that gave real and sustained meaning to “community” with

the devastation of highly functioning rural communities a tragic result.

I am reminded of this every time my rural-based grandchildren are transported anything from one to 2 hours for weekend sport participation.

The size of the leagues demands extreme dedication from parents who have often already travelled distances to their workplaces daily during the week.

One can argue that we all make choices but the erosion of “home time” and the current cost of fuel plus the state of the roads make the accessing of sporting competitions arduous and probably prohibitive for some.

With the centralising of educational facilities and local governments, many highly functioning rural communities have been diminished in a way that was immediately devastating.

Those small communities no longer have a general store, a post office, a pub or school; therefore people relocated or bore the brunt of travelling significant distances to access services.

The cost to the small communities of rural Victorian people – social, financial and historical – has been destructive in a way that is immeasurable.

Still not happy, Jeff.

Mary-Louise Tehan, Queenscliff When is fair, fair?

It seems unlikely Australia will increase unemployment benefits in the ways Sean Kelly suggests (“Harm done now can be harm forever; how government delay can derail lives”, 24/8).

For example, the idea that unemployment payments should be tied to previous income so that a newly unemployed person is not “effectively removed, instantly, from the life you lived before” would be quickly dismissed as being unfair.

People would ask why some unemployed people should receive a higher benefit than others.

Principles of fairness underpin Australia’s system of social welfare payments.

In 1975, the Whitlam government removed means testing for the age pension for everyone aged 70 or older.

Of course, subsequent governments rolled back that universal eligibility so that payments are better targeted at those who reaĺly need them. That’s the Australian way.

In the event that mass unemployment caused by

artificial intelligence generates calls for a universal basic income in Australia, get ready for howls of protest: “That’s not fair! They don’t need it!“

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills Business AI absence

When will big business step up and show some leadership in the great AI debate?

What do they see as the impact on entry-level jobs?

What do they envisage the longer-term impact will be on overall employee numbers?

How will the widespread usage of AI change employee roles,

and what will this mean for educating, training and job security for workers?

The announcement of a parliamentary bipartisan committee to examine these issues is welcome (“Labor, Coalition unite to ring-fence AI”, 22/8) but based on the gambling advertising legislation passed by the government and opposition, it will probably produce only pusillanimous recommendations.

The onus lies with business to propose how AI can be used to enhance societal, employment

and profitability, and then work with government to achieve

these objectives.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick Stop gas expansion

It seems incredible that the gas industry is looking for opportunities to scale up production (“Domestic gas policy sparks industrial revival hopes” 24/8) when we have witnessed a devastating summer in Europe and North America, and 2026 is set to be the hottest year on record.

Yes, we need to protect Australia from economic shocks such as the spike in fuel prices, but we also need to phase out fossil fuel use as soon as possible to have any chance of arresting the climb in global temperatures and incidents of extreme weather.

Wind and solar are not finite resources and, once infrastructure is in place, not subject to wildly fluctuating world prices.

In addition, they do not contribute to an increase in carbon in the atmosphere.

By all means, reduce exports of gas to ensure local supply, but we shouldn’t use this as a chance to expand and profit from an

industry that will exacerbate our climate crisis.

Graeme Lechte, Pascoe Vale Keep gas supply local

Good to see our gas may gradually seep through to local users (24/8). Australia should not be selling to overseas nations who make a fortune reselling the gas.

The focus should be on making gas usage more climate-friendly instead of selling it off.

Doris LeRoy, Altona



Nature trumps market

Debates about carbon accounting systems distract from the fact that iconic native animals, plants and ecosystems are endangered and need urgent protection (“New forest proposal to dwarf Koala Park”, 23/8).

NSW Premier Chris Minns promised to create the Great Koala National Park, but after election added the condition that its forests generate carbon offsets.

His ″⁣solution″⁣ to threats from “logging, climate change, species decline and huge bushfires” is to make it cheaper for companies

to keep polluting rather than reduce emissions.

The ″⁣market″⁣ doesn’t always produce the best outcomes. What have we lost when we can recognise the value of something only after putting a price on it?

Protecting nature is a responsibility of governments, not a legitimate function of ″⁣the market″⁣.

Julia Croatto, Kew AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Plymouth Brethren

The LNP is in bed with the Plymouth Brethren, who have a record of supporting the LNP during elections. The Brethren should be stripped of their charity status and sent packing from Australia.

Paul Chivers, Box Hill North I’m comforted that the Brethren Christian Church maintains its tax-free status by providing breakfast to the participants in the annual pollie pedal bike ride.

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South



Give the lobbyists a permit and a set of rules. If you break the rules, your permit is cancelled. It’s not too hard, is it?

John Marks, Werribee AFL

If the Swans’ problem is bird flu, as your correspondent suggests (Letters, 24/8), then there’s surely a message in that for the Hawks, Pies, Eagles and any other teams on the wing.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor Well done, Sydney Swans! In the big picture, and as a unit, you have responded well to the slurs and vilification.

Paul Murchison, Kingsbury Wildcard Weekend: the excitement of seeing if your team is eliminated this week or next.

Matthew Gilbert, Mont Albert Essendone! If it wasn’t for hope, I’d be drowning in my tears.

Graham Cadd, Dromana



Furthermore

Trump is at war with Iran, now he is at war with Canada. Has he still got his eyes on a Nobel Peace Prize?

John Walsh, Watsonia Barely a day passes without the television news not reporting a catastrophe involving a stolen car.

Is it not possible to encourage the motor vehicle industry to make car theft a near impossibility?

Bruce Love, East Melbourne Thank you, Richard Glover (″⁣The worst part of ageing? Nobody knows what I’m talking about any more″⁣, 22/8).

At the risk of sounding like a broken record, my carbon copy conversational experiences mean that I can sometimes feel like a shag on a rock!

Jennifer Ferneyhough, Melbourne The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The bayside council, a missing recording, and closed-door vote notes
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The bayside council, a missing recording, and closed-door vote notes Matt Dennien August 24, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Right to Information answers (and questions) from the Redlands, how to move 584 boxes of sensitive docs, plum jobs from City Hall to 1WS, and more. A still-unresolved question hangs over the most senior appointed job on Brisbane’s bayside: what happened in the closed-doors meeting of Redland councillors on February 3 last year? After that meeting, then acting (now actual) chief executive Louise Rusan was parachuted in from outside the selection panel shortlist for council’s second crack at filling the $500,000 gig. Minutes from a contentious closed-door meeting of Redland City Council have been released to Brisbane Times under Right to Information laws. Good luck reading them. Michael Howard Thanks to the magic of Right to Information, we have some heavily redacted answers.



Council policy dictates that all so-called workshops and briefings are recorded – with that footage and an associated transcript held by the office of the chief executive. Circus used the information-release scheme to seek access to recordings and transcripts from that fateful meeting, and the follow-up a week later where Rusan fronted councillors. We were initially knocked back entirely by legal services manager Peter Cardiff because the 46 pages and one video found were deemed “not in the public interest” and would reveal personal information about candidates. (We explicitly said we weren’t fussed if those obviously sensitive details were withheld.) But wait – only one video for two meetings? We filed an internal review of the decision.



When that landed some time later, council’s principal audit and integrity services adviser Kailesh Naidu decided to release what were said to be “minutes taken by a council officer following the interviews of the unsuccessful CEO candidates”. This is despite the guidelines also dictating formal minutes are not to be taken. And while these were bizarrely redacted to withhold even councillor’s names, our news reporting on the issue helps fill in the black bars a touch. The minutes don’t seem to negate any of the concerns raised about how the closed-door vote departs from the public recruitment process, or if there was political interference.



(The council has repeatedly rejected such allegations, insisting proper processes were followed. We don’t suggest otherwise, only that questions have been raised internally and by external figures.) But we digress. Contained in the internal review decision was another detail: no recording is said to have been taken of the February 3 meeting “because all councillors and the mayor were present”. The guidelines certainly don’t place any such qualifications around the recording of the confidential meetings – though council backgrounding since has sought to suggest the guidelines didn’t apply to that type of meeting, and the notes weren’t formal minutes. So, what does the council formally have to say for itself? A spokesperson reiterated the process was consistent with local government laws.



“The appointment of the current CEO was a decision of Council in a General Meeting held on Wednesday 19 February 2025,” the spinner said in a written response to questions. Helpful. The recruitment matter is far from the only one being wrangled by the council at present, with leaks galore and mayor Jos Mitchell’s extended leave driving heated online debate among other councillors and political figures. A pointed submission by Cardiff on behalf of the council to the ongoing parliamentary inquiry into councillor conduct said the council had seen elected figures “avoid accountability” by being absent and suggested those on extended leave be subject to a misconduct probe. Police union and corruption watchdog discipline blue (again) goes public The regular appearances of state corruption watchdog figures before their parliamentary oversight committee are almost always worth a watch.



If not for some actual new information, then for the sport of MPs trying to goad Crime and Corruption Commission chair Bruce Barbour into revealing something about any of the agency’s tightly held probes into their political opponents. Queensland police union president Shane Prior and Crime and Corruption Commission chair Bruce Barbour have had at it in the paper. Catherine Strohfeldt / Dominic Lorrimer Last week, Barbour politely palmed questions around a handful of matters – think “Operation Cranberry” into the torpedoed recruitment of Krispin Hajkowicz as chief health officer, or former parole board president Michael Byrne’s alleged misuse of travel funds – into the private session of the hearing. Another element emerging from the committee session was a days-long subsequent public tit-for-tat between Barbour and police union president Shane Prior in the paper. Prior had taken umbrage with Barbour’s apparent “misleading” remarks about ongoing legal matters involving the watchdog’s disagreement with police about how it handles disciplinary matters where officers have unrecorded convictions.



Barbour has issued a rare public statement standing by his words. More detail emerged on Monday, when a watchdog spokesperson said three of the matters it had initiated in the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal involved officers guilty of domestic violence offences who had not faced disciplinary action by police. How do you move 584 boxes of sensitive docs? Not in a ute – this time Another detail from the session also caught Circus’ eye: what was being done with 584 boxes of papers from the mothballed Connolly-Ryan inquiry into the CCC’s predecessor? Launched in 1996 by the fledgling Borbidge government, the inquiry was shut down by the Supreme Court a year later over a strong case of “ostensible bias” against its chair Peter Connolly.



Connolly had been accused of interfering with an independent probe being conducted for the then-Criminal Justice Commission into a memorandum of understanding between the police union and Coalition. So it is that the parliament – via the watchdog’s watchdog, Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner Dr Daniel Morgan – ended up lumped with the load of docs. Speaker of Queensland Parliament Pat Weir (centre) with Mitchell Kunde and Dr Daniel Morgan, in an image posted to announce the appointment of Morgan as the state’s Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner in June last year. Facebook / Pat Weir “Previously I think Mr [Mitchell] Kunde and somebody from the parliament used a ute to do it [move them],” Morgan said of the efforts from the commissioner’s longstanding principal legal officer to get the trove to a strongroom at the front of Old Parliament House. A document detailing a request to move them again (back in 2022) noted the records take up “six compactus bays and three locked storage cupboards” and would free up “many additional years’ worth of storage” if relocated.



And relocated they were due to be last Thursday morning. How? Circus feels Morgan’s description of last week’s plans is worth repeating in full. “Obviously, we were concerned to maintain the integrity of the documents. We literally cannot have them falling off the back of a truck. I made inquiries about an appropriate firm that had the necessary security experience and equipment. This firm has previously acted for the parliament and for the police. They are sensitive. They are not particularly highly secured documents, but we just need to know that the integrity is there that what has been packed is what has been delivered. We will be supervising that. I think we can ensure there will be locks on lots packed.” Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner Dr Daniel Morgan Quizzed by parliament’s crime and corruption committee chair, Ferny Grove Labor MP Mark Furner, about whether the papers were digitised, or whether the shift to the archives at Daisy Hill meant they would be, Morgan said there was “no further step intended”. Mermaid Beach LNP MP Ray Stevens then also jumped in, curious if this was out of cost concerns and seemingly confused as to why the boxes “which are not important apparently” are being retained but not digitised. In Morgan’s assessment, he didn’t see any benefit in this “apart from history”, with no one having sought access to them for some time. Kunde put this period at 15 years.



Morgan also noted the “special circumstances” around the inquiry and the subsequent custody of the related documents given to his office. Special circumstances indeed. And the kind that would probably make for some good (digitised) reading! Jobs, jobs and more jobs, from City Hall to the Tower of Power Readers looking for a change of scenery at work, look no further. This week has been a particularly lucrative one for job ads finding their way to the Circus tent. And what jobs they are. For the administratively minded, there’s an assistant ombudsman gig going over at the Queensland Ombudsman office, responsible for managing the team probing local government matters.



While reporting to the deputy ombudsman, who knows whether still-outgoing big boss Anthony Reilly’s boots will have been filled before applications close next Friday. Down at City Hall, the Olympic City council is apparently seeking to echo their Los Angeles counterparts by hiring an “international sports diplomacy project manager”. The headcount-happy Department of Premier and Cabinet are busy filling vacant roles – but what about the hiring squeeze? Matt Dennien That role will apparently be responsible for leading a related strategy, luring national Olympic and Paralympic committees, international federations and other groups to town and landing pre-Games training camps, global sporting partnerships and other related events. No pressure. The headcount-happy Department of Premier and Cabinet are also chasing an executive director of economic policy and director of communication, digital and design.



These last two raised our eyebrows given Crisafulli and Co’s keenness to put roadblocks in the way of new and even existing non-frontline roles. These ones? Vacancies for existing roles, a government flack tells us. Circus wonders what “vacancy management plan” hoops might exist at the top of the Tower of Power. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Swans staff give police statements as Heeney loses kids’ footy camp role
World.content:
Four Swans officials have given statements to police investigating an alleged sexual assault, as AFL boss Andrew Dillon banished the five suspended Sydney players from the Brownlow Medal count and confirmed the league would later conduct its own probe. The development came as one of the five players, Isaac Heeney, was dumped by a business he helped design that runs football camps for kids - 5th Quarter Camps. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney at last year’s Brownlow. He won’t be invited this year. AFL Photos “5th Quarter Camps is aware of a police investigation involving one of its shareholders, Isaac Heeney,” the business said in a statement to this masthead. “Although the investigation remains ongoing and no charges have been laid, given the circumstances and the seriousness of the matter, we can confirm Isaac Heeney will no longer have any involvement in 5th Quarter Camps.



“5th Quarter Camps takes seriously its responsibility to families, communities and commercial partners. We are committed to providing an environment founded on safety and respect, and doing everything in our power to ensure the wellbeing and experience of every child and family attending our camps remains at the centre of what we do.” The five Swans players suspended by Sydney for breaching the club’s behavioural standards are Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon. They were stood down for the remainder of the season after drinking, staying out late and inviting women back to the team hotel following their win over Essendon in round 23. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine The players’ club-imposed suspensions are separate from a Victoria Police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of last Monday morning at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. No charges have been laid and a source with knowledge of the players’ position has said they deny criminal wrongdoing.



This masthead has previously reported that Heeney is a focus of the investigation. A source with knowledge of the police investigation, speaking anonymously, confirmed Sydney’s senior coach Dean Cox, football boss Leon Cameron, head of player wellbeing and development Brett Kirk and head of media and communications Tom Chadwick had given accounts to police. Callum Mills of the Swans embraces head coach Dean Cox after their game on Sunday. Getty Images The Swans declined to comment, citing the investigation. The four Sydney staff were not in the hotel room at Pullman East Melbourne when a woman alleges she was sexually assaulted.



Cameron, Kirk and Chadwick accompanied the five Swans players, who have since been handed club-imposed bans for the remainder of the season, in two cars as they drove home to Sydney from Melbourne last Monday afternoon. No Swans officials are accused of inappropriate behaviour and the club has previously said it had no issue with the conduct of Cox, who returned to the hotel not long after midnight. Andrew Dillon faces the media. AFL Photos via Getty Images At least two men aside from the five suspended players were in the hotel room on the night of the alleged sexual assault. This masthead revealed on Sunday that at least one fresh allegation of sexual assault and multiple claims of sexual conduct without consent had been made by the three women at the centre of the investigation.



It is not known which men the allegations are about, and to date police have only referenced “a report of a sexual assault”. This masthead is not suggesting any of the men in the room engaged in conduct of a sexual nature without consent, only that it has been alleged. Dillon said the AFL would not open its own investigation until the police probe was completed. “Those matters at the moment are under police investigation, so the AFL won’t be conducting any of its own inquiries until after the police investigation is finished,” he said. Loading “We don’t know where that will go and, at that stage, when that’s completed, the AFL will [undertake] some inquiries. I think what is clear is the Swans are taking action with the support of the AFL based on the information that is at hand now, and there’s been accountability for those players that were involved last week.”



The five players are still eligible to win the award for the AFL’s best and fairest player. “The invitations to the Brownlow will be going out this week. Those players won’t be invited,” Dillon said. “They are still eligible for the Brownlow but they’re under a club suspension, which goes until the end of the season.” Dillon said it was a matter for the Swans whether the players should still be allowed to win the club best and fairest. Dillon did not rule out the players being deregistered. Related Article Sydney Swans ‘Don’t abandon the club’: Swans fans ready to show support after week of turmoil



“Again, I’m not going to go into hypotheticals. We’ve got a police investigation that is underway. Once that’s completed, the AFL will make its own,” he said. Dillon said he was unaware if there was a recording of the alleged incident. “Look, I am not aware of that but, again, if there is a tape that’s relevant to the police investigation, it should be forwarded on to the police.” He denied the league had a wider cultural problem. “I think the actions of a few don’t take away from the thousands of people involved in football at all different levels who do great things all the time,” he said. “But what we do know is that we can do things better, and we’ll continue to do that, and we’ll continue to learn a bit better.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: CFMEU headquarters raided in secret-commissions probe
World.content:
Two senior CFMEU officials temporarily detained by Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk after detectives swooped on the union’s Victorian headquarters on Monday have dismissed allegations of union corruption or kickbacks involving the former boss of a bikie gang. The arrest and release of five serving CFMEU officials by Taskforce Hawk on Monday, with two facing minor charges, marks the most dramatic intervention yet by the elite police unit launched to tackle suspected crime and corruption in Victoria’s construction sector and which is now also gathering information for the upcoming royal commission. A Taskforce Hawk officer enters the CFMEU headquarters in Elizabeth Street in the CBD on Monday. Justin McManus The police action is a blow for the Albanese government-backed CFMEU administration two years into its attempt to reform the union, but it is not surprising given newly appointed administrator Michael Crosby’s recent concession that the scandal-tainted union had cleaned up in every jurisdiction except Victoria. In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Crosby confirmed that Hawk had “executed search warrants at six addresses, including CFMEU Victoria’s office, as part of an investigation into alleged secret commissions in the construction industry”.



“Criminals and bad actors in construction remain a major threat to the workers, which is why we need greater regulation and scrutiny across the sector,” Crosby said, warning that “anyone associated with criminal elements will have absolutely no place in this union’s future”. Police revealed homes in Chirnside Park, Westbury, Gisborne, Powelltown and Somerville were also searched on Monday. Investigators seized four CFMEU vehicles, 10 mobile phones, several laptops, documents, iPads, USBs, a .22 rifle and a prescription drug. The five men arrested were a 36-year-old from Chirnside Park, a 46-year-old from Westbury (near Moe), a 27-year-old from Gisborne, a 56-year-old from Powelltown and a 37-year-old from Somerville. A Chirnside Park man was charged with possessing a schedule 4 drug and bailed to appear at Ringwood Magistrates’ Court on November 10. A man from Westbury was charged with failing to store a long-arm firearm and ammunition as required. He was bailed to appear at Latrobe Valley Magistrates’ Court on January 11.



Three other men were released pending further inquiries. “The investigation relates to allegations of drug trafficking as well as secret commissions,” a police statement said. Crosby revealed that he had ordered an internal investigation into the allegations, while also cautioning against rushing to judgment in respect of any of the officials arrested on Monday. “Taskforce Hawk has confirmed that to date no charges have been laid against any CFMEU official as part of this investigation. There is a presumption of innocence and the branch will continue to offer support whilst the investigation is ongoing,” he said. Also concerning for Crosby is the police decision to arrest one of his administration’s key reformers, Jason “Spike” Deans, a CFMEU official who multiple union and industry sources told The Age is respected as honest and hardworking.



Deans, the most senior of the union figures detained and released by Hawk, has stridently denied that the CFMEU has ever assisted the industrial relations business run by former Mongols bikie chief Tyrone “Little Ty” Bell. Deans, who was promoted to a key Victorian union leadership post just weeks ago by the CFMEU administration, told The Age he wanted to “make it very clear” that he and his fellow union official Matt Montebello had engaged in no impropriety in connection to Bell’s work as a union mediator. Montebello was also arrested and released without charge on Monday. “There has never been any untoward or any illegal activity from myself or Matt with … that little fella [Bell],” Deans said when contacted about the police inquiry when it was revealed by The Age last week.



“I’ve taken on this role because I care about good union members and their families. If anyone thinks that I’m here for the position or status they are very wrong. Matt Montebello was arrested as part of the raid on CFMEU headquarters on Monday. “I’m going to do what I need to do to get this union back into a functional position and I will make decisions that some people are not going to like. I will be ruthless to protect this union if I need to.” There is no suggestion by this masthead that Deans, Montebello or any of the other three officials arrested and released are engaged in any unlawful behaviour, only that police suspect they hold information relevant to their ongoing inquiry. When The Age contacted Montebello last week to ask him why he was a person of interest in Taskforce Hawk’s ongoing investigation into Bell and allegations the ex-bikie chief tried to influence the CFMEU, he also denied having any improper dealings with Bell.



“I’ve never taken a cent off him, mate,” Montebello said. Asked if he had ever discussed with Bell the CFMEU’s disruption of a Melbourne building project last September – the industrial dispute at the centre of the Hawk probe into Bell– Montebello denied any knowledge of the union action. “Don’t know what you’re talking about, mate,” he said, before hanging up. Last Thursday, The Age revealed that Bell, a former national vice-president of the Mongols outlaw bikie gang, was being probed by police over allegations he offered inducements to officials still serving in the CFMEU in return for their support of his business, Dynamis HSR. The Age also revealed that the Taskforce Hawk operation that led to Monday’s arrests and a raid of the CFMEU’s Swanston Street headquarters was examining whether CFMEU organisers leaked Bell information or co-ordinated union activity with him in order to advance the interests of Bell’s industrial relations consultancy.



Bell’s connections to the CFMEU were cultivated via two channels: his relatively brief stint as a CFMEU delegate working for building company Markscon, and his long-standing social and schooling ties to serving and ex-CFMEU organisers and delegates, including Montebello and his brother Kane Montebello, a high-ranking Hells Angels member who also served as a union delegate. Three CFMEU sources said the administration had sought and received reassurance from Matt Montebello that he had cut ties or was carefully managing his familial relationships with people linked to outlaw motorcycle gangs. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Ex-bikie boss under investigation over alleged inducements to CFMEU officials In addition to his brother, Montebello’s cousin has also held a role with the Hells Angels and was briefly recruited into the union. An undated photo circulating in the construction industry, but which appears to be several years old, shows Montebello wearing a Hells Angels support singlet. There is no suggestion he has ever held a role in the club or been involved in bikie activity.



Montebello’s brother, cousin and Bell were among the highest-profile serving and ex-bikie gang members recruited into the CFMEU between 2021 and 2024, only to be forced out in July 2024 when this masthead’s Building Bad series first broke. Last week, Bell described the police allegations as “just ridiculous” and defended Matt Montebello. “I’ve been friends with him since primary school, and his brother and I feel very sorry for the guy, because he loves his job,” Bell said. “I hope you don’t write anything bad about that guy, because he’s a very good dad, a very good person,” he said. CFMEU assistant administrator Matt McGowan said: “CFMEU has been made aware of a police operation this morning as part of Taskforce Hawk. As this is a live police matter, CFMEU cannot comment further at this time.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Deaths of 10 young people put eastern suburbs mental health services on alert
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMental health Deaths of 10 young people put eastern suburbs mental health services on alert Grant McArthur August 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two youth suicide clusters in Melbourne’s east involving the deaths of 10 people, the youngest aged 13, have raised new concerns about Victoria’s troubled mental health system. Youth mental health services in the east were put on alert in response to rising teenage tragedies over nine months, but Victoria’s health watchdogs have failed to launch a review to determine if there are any systemic issues or access issues at the heart of the cases. Concerns about Victoria’s youth mental health services have increased following two suicide clusters in Melbourne’s east. Aresna Villanueva A total of 10 young people, including at least six children under 16, died in September-October last year and May this year. The mass tragedies are the latest revelations regarding Victoria’s youth mental health system to emerge during an investigation by The Age, and follow the closure of a children’s mental health service at a major Melbourne hospital this month pending a bullying investigation into its staff. In parliament on Friday, opposition health spokesperson Georgie Crozier named the service as Austin Health’s child inpatient unit.



Separately, the boss of Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service resigned this month, a day after it was revealed she was leading the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service as a fly-in, fly-out CEO, as reports mount of violence, drug use and patient deaths in its first year of operation. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force The state coroner is awaiting briefs of evidence before deciding whether to group the teen death cases together for investigation, or examine each individually. Victoria’s Department of Health confirmed its youth mental health services provided post-suicide support to the area after being alerted to the rising deaths. But because it does not have records of the children receiving help at public hospitals before they died, neither the Chief Psychiatrist, Safer Care Victoria nor the Suicide Prevention and Response Office are reviewing the suitability or capacity of services in the area. A mental health specialist working in Melbourne’s east, who is not authorised to speak publicly, said most children and families seeking help via emergency department and phone triage lines did not receive admission to specialised public child and youth mental health services, and they feared lives were being lost as a result.



“There are definitely systemic issues,” the senior clinician said. “How terrible that we weren’t helping them, and they were in this trouble. Obviously, something isn’t working. “In triage and ED, they reject the majority of kids that present. They reject them because they haven’t got the capacity to see them. They are the kids we should be seeing, but a lot of them get turned away because there’s no capacity for them to be seen.” Major public hospital networks Eastern Health and Austin Health both operate child and youth mental health services in the city’s east, where the clusters occurred. A Coroners Court spokesperson confirmed the Eastern Melbourne Primary Health Network advised it on October 31, 2025, of a potential cluster of deaths, involving people aged 13 to 22, in its service catchment area. “The investigations into these deaths are in the early stages and once the coronial briefs are received the coroner will review the evidence to determine the next steps of the investigations and if the circumstances of the cases make it appropriate to conduct a cluster investigation,” the spokesperson said.



The coroner was later notified of the suspected suicides of a further four young people, aged 13 to 18, in Melbourne’s east in May this year. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence “Coroners are investigating these cases individually and are awaiting coronial briefs of evidence for the investigations.” A Department of Health spokesperson said the Coroners Court alerted it to suspected suicides in September 2025 and again in May 2026, prompting the Chief Psychiatrist to engage with Eastern Health to undertake post-suicide support activities with local services, including headspace and Victoria Police. “Every suicide is one too many, and the loss of life to suicide has long-lasting and far-reaching impacts on loved ones and community members,” the spokesperson said.



“While these young people were not receiving care through a public mental health service at the time of their death, the Department of Health, the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist and local services have worked together to support the local communities.” Youth mental health pioneer Professor Pat McGorry said the scale of the deaths and extreme young age of those involved was unusual and demanded investigation, particularly as they have coincided with a 50 per cent rise in the prevalence of mental ill health in young people in the same age group. “I’m extremely concerned at the lack of transparency about the situation and the apparent lack of co-ordinated action to respond,” McGorry said. “In the eastern region, as elsewhere across Victoria, the public mental health system has not been reformed or properly resourced to respond to this public health crisis, and it has been a low priority since the [mental health] royal commission, despite the level of unmet need. “The result is that young people at great risk who present to emergency departments or triage lines are typically rejected in very large numbers. If this were occurring with any other potentially life-threatening condition, it would be regarded as a scandal.”



Phillipa Thomas, chief executive of peak body Mental Health Victoria, said suicide clusters were complex and unusual occurrences and needed to be examined to determine if the events relate to each other and whether they could have been prevented. “At this stage it is unclear what, when, and if any contact was in place for each of these young people with mental health services prior to their deaths. Where it was, the coroner will consider the role of safety and quality for each individual. But its August – that’s nearly a full year that’s gone by,” Thomas said. “I’m troubled by the possibility that these young people may have sought help and not received it. I’m equally troubled by the possibility that they didn’t seek help at all.” While she could not comment directly on the cases, Royal Australian & New Zealand College of Psychiatrists’ Victorian spokesperson Dr Nardine Elzahaby said the state’s youth mental health system was plagued by gaps.



She said acute public health services had become “adult models retrofitted for young people” which did not meet their needs, while services such as headspace did not cater for those with more severe illness who did not yet need, or could not get into, a specialist mental health service. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress “There is a gap. There is a missing middle of patients who require care that are not too unwell to meet youth area mental health criteria, but they are too unwell to be looked after by headspace,” Elzahaby said. “Do young people have to rely on emergency departments to get child and youth suicide programs? ED is hardly ever the right place for young people, and it really impacts them.” An Eastern Health spokesperson said the families, friends and communities affected by the recent suicides were in their thoughts, and the service has an active role in co-ordinating post-suicide responses with local services, schools and other agencies to assist vulnerable young people who may be at increased risk.



“In addition to providing specialist inpatient and community-based mental health services, Eastern Health works closely with local primary care providers, schools, community organisations and other partners to support the mental health and wellbeing of young people across the region,” the spokesperson said. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy.
